en: A kalabaw is a living animal, so it is not an earth material, even though it walks on soil and drinks water that are earth materials.
A living tree is not called an earth material; the soil it stands in and the water it drinks are earth materials around it.
Abaca is a relative of the banana that is native to the Philippines; instead of fruit, the fiber from its stalk is made into strong rope and cloth.
Abaca fiber is used to make strong papers such as tea bags and some kinds of banknote paper.
Abaca is a relative of the banana because both belong to the Musa family, but abaca is grown for fiber, not fruit.
To get clean abaca fiber, the leaf stalks are stripped or scraped to remove the soft pulp.
PHIVOLCS lists about two dozen volcanoes as active, which means they have erupted in recent times or still show unrest.
When waves rub rocks against each other, they grind and slowly turn into sand.
In dry places, wind carrying sand repeatedly strikes rock and slowly grinds and carves it—this is called abrasion.
In absolute dating, scientists measure the amount of radioactive isotopes remaining in a rock to determine its actual age in years.
Absolute zero (−273.15°C or 0 Kelvin) is the coldest possible temperature, where particles have minimum thermal energy and barely move; it has never been fully reached in practice.
Absolute zero is 0 K, equal to −273.15°C — the lowest possible temperature.
Absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, is about -273 degrees Celsius.
Absolute zero — the lowest possible temperature — is −273.15 °C, or 0 Kelvin.
A shallow 'beach' of foam or slope at the far end soaks up waves so they do not bounce back and mess up the pattern you are measuring.
The electricity reaching the outlets in our homes is alternating current, meaning its flow keeps reversing direction.
Nikola Tesla invented the AC (alternating current) motor.
Nikola Tesla patented his AC motor in 1888.
Tesla's AC motor works using a rotating magnetic field that spins the motor.
Some thorny trees are home to ants that attack any animal trying to eat the tree.
Planets formed by accretion: tiny grains of dust and ice stuck together into bigger rocks called planetesimals, which kept colliding and growing until they became planets.

When a plate subducts, sediment on its surface is often scraped off and piles up as an accretionary prism; this is a chaotic mixed pile of rocks found in front of many subduction zones, including those around the Philippines.
Accurate measuring means using the marks on the tool carefully and not guessing the last digit from far away.
Acetobacter bacteria use oxygen to convert alcohol into acetic acid, which is how vinegar including coconut vinegar (sukang tuba) is made.
Vinegar is made in two steps: first yeast turns sugar into alcohol, then Acetobacter bacteria use oxygen to turn that alcohol into acetic acid, which gives vinegar its sourness.
Acid and base solutions can carry electricity because they contain moving ions; this is also why salt water can conduct electricity.
When an acid reacts with many metals, hydrogen gas comes out as bubbles and a dissolved salt is left behind.
When an egg is soaked in vinegar, the acid reacts with the calcium carbonate of the shell and releases carbon dioxide bubbles, until the hard shell dissolves away.

Acid rain dissolves limestone and marble by reacting with calcium carbonate; this erodes marble buildings and also creates karst caves through centuries of dissolution — seen in Palawan's limestone landscapes.
Acids usually taste sour, while bases taste bitter and feel slippery.
When an acid and a base react, they neutralize each other and usually form a salt and water.
Not all acids and bases are safe — strong ones like muriatic acid and strong drain cleaner (lye) are dangerous and can burn skin and eyes, so they must be handled carefully and with protection.
Acids usually taste sour, like calamansi and vinegar.
Activation energy is the smallest amount of energy needed to start a reaction, like the heat or spark that gets burning going.
Active Filipino games like patintero and tumbang preso are exercise that strengthens the muscles and heart.

In hospitals, activated charcoal is sometimes used for a person who swallowed poison. Because it has many holes and a huge surface area, it can soak up some poison in the stomach before the body absorbs it. But it is not a casual home remedy—only a doctor should give it, and it does not work on every poison.

An enzyme is a protein with a correct shape that speeds up reactions in the body. When it is 'active', its 'active site' is in the right shape so it works. But if it gets too much heat, its shape changes—this is called 'denatured'—and it no longer works, like egg white that hardens and never goes back once cooked.
In passive transport, substances drift in or out of a cell from high to low concentration without using energy, while active transport must spend energy to pump them the opposite way.

After heavy exercise, there is 'active recovery' and 'complete rest'. In active recovery, you still do light movement like slow walking to help blood flow and keep your muscles from stiffening. In complete rest, you fully relax and do nothing. Both matter depending on how tired your body is.

A seed can be 'dormant' or sleeping—still alive but not growing yet and waiting for the right time. Once it gets enough water, warmth, and air, it becomes 'active' and starts to sprout, pushing out a root and shoot. That is why some seeds can be stored a long time and still sprout when planted in the right conditions.
Pouring the liquids in slowly and gently helps the layers stay separate in a density column.
In additive colour mixing, combining red, green, and blue light produces white light — this principle is used in TV and phone screens.
Humans are not the only ones with adrenaline—animals have it too. When a bigger animal attacks, adrenaline helps a deer or cat suddenly run very fast to escape.
After the danger passes, the body stops releasing adrenaline, and your heartbeat and breathing slowly return to normal. This is why you calm down after a few minutes.
When you are nervous, adrenaline moves blood away from your skin toward the big muscles. That is why your hands feel cold, and sometimes sweaty too—it is your body preparing to move.
When adrenaline kicks in, it slows down digestion because energy is sent to the muscles and heart first. That is why your stomach can feel uneasy or you lose your appetite when nervous.
Adrenaline does not use nerves to send its orders. Instead, it flows through the blood as a chemical messenger, so it can reach the heart, lungs, and muscles all at the same time.
Adrenaline tells the liver to release stored sugar (glucose) into the blood. This extra sugar becomes the instant energy you need to run or fight.
Adrenaline helps in short bursts, but if you are constantly stressed and your body always has adrenaline, it becomes tiring and not good for the heart. That is why rest and calming down matter.
Sometimes you shake when you are very scared. This happens because adrenaline has filled your muscles with so much ready energy that, even before you use it, they want to move.
Adrenaline prepares the body to act quickly by speeding up breathing and giving extra energy.
Fireworks mix very loud sound and very bright light, so the protection is to watch from far away with an adult, never in the hand.
Young children need an adult to help put on sunscreen and a hat, because those safety measures only work if they actually cover the skin.
Birds like swallows and swifts are called aerial insectivores because they catch their insect food while flying.
Swallows and swifts are often busiest catching insects at dawn and dusk, when many insects are in the air.
An African elephant can stand about 3 meters tall at the shoulder.
When afritada is cooked, the heat changes the taste, color, and firmness of the meat and vegetables, and this is a chemical change that cannot be turned back into raw food.
After ashfall, officials may test drinking water and warn about ash on grass, so returning home includes checking food and water, not only the roof.
After ashfall, wet ash on a roof is heavy, so clear it carefully from a safe stance and never let children play on a loaded roof.
After the cyclone, typical outdoor conditions include fallen branches, mud, and downed lines, so the 'weather' people meet is messy even in lighter wind.
After the sky looks calmer, floodwater may still stand in streets and fields, so the after-weather includes leftover water, not only sunshine.
After ashfall, people with breathing trouble should keep using protection and follow health advice, because fine ash can bother lungs even when the sky looks clearer.
After the clouds thin, air can feel very humid and then hot, because the ground is soaked and the Sun may shine on standing water.
After does not mean the event is over for rivers and slopes; typical after-weather includes extra caution until water and soil settle.
After many hours of cyclone rain, hillsides can still fail in landslides, a ground condition that belongs to the after stage.
After a big ash-producing eruption, some valleys use rain and river warnings because lahars can come at night days later, long after the crater grows quieter.
After people go home, recovering farms and cleaning ash can take a long time, so 'after' is a stage, not a single afternoon.
Sometimes bright sun returns soon after the cyclone, but that heat on wet ground does not mean rivers have already dropped to safe levels.
After the loudest blast, do not rush home until PHIVOLCS lowers the alert and local officials say the roads and slopes are safe enough.
After an eruption, heavy rain can still send lahars down rivers, so a falling alert level does not cancel watching the weather on ash-covered slopes.
After the cyclone moves away, the strongest winds usually drop first, but rain and thick clouds can linger for hours or longer.
Ingredients from seaweed are used to thicken foods like ice cream and chocolate milk.
A PAGASA or NASA education page is a trustworthy secondary source you can use to confirm class ideas about sunlight and weather.
Movement, sound, and light only send information if both people agreed on the code first; a random blink does not yet mean a word.
The Agusan Marsh in Mindanao is one of the largest wetlands in the Philippines and home to many birds and fish.
The third most abundant gas in air is argon, about 0.93% of the air.
The third most abundant gas in air is argon, at about 0.93% of the air.
Earth's atmosphere has five main layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, and exosphere.
Car airbags use a rapidly released gas (usually nitrogen) to fill the airbag within milliseconds of a crash. The fast inflation of the airbag protects the passenger from impact.
When we breathe in, we take in oxygen from the air.
The gas we breathe in is oxygen.
When we breathe out, we release carbon dioxide (CO2).
The gas we breathe out is carbon dioxide (CO2).
Carbon dioxide (CO2) is only a very small part of the air — about 0.04%.
An air conditioner passes air over cold coils that soak up heat and moisture, so the air comes out cooler.
Air resistance grows as an object moves faster, so a light wide thing may slow its speeding up while a compact rock keeps gaining speed longer.
The air gap between a roof sheet and ceiling acts as insulation — reducing the amount of heat that passes from the hot roof into the room below.
Gases like air have very low viscosity, so they flow much more easily than liquids.
Air is a good heat insulator, so the trapped air in our clothes helps keep us warm.
Trapped air is a good insulator because heat moves through it very slowly.
Trapped air is a good insulator, which is why a thick sweater, animal fur, and fluffy materials full of tiny air pockets keep heat in.
Even air has mass, so a balloon filled with air weighs more than an empty one.
Air has weight even though we cannot see it, so it is matter.
Air resistance is a real force you can feel on a fast bike; it is the extra reason some light objects lose the falling 'race'.
The air around you is an earth material too: it is a non-living mixture of gases that fills the space of the environment.

Fresh air is clean and safe to breathe, but when smoke from vehicles or fires mixes in, it becomes dirty — this is called air pollution. In crowded cities like Manila the air is dirtier, so trees that help clean it are important.

What is the difference between air and a vacuum? Air is full of gas particles, while a vacuum is space with no air or gas at all. Outer space is nearly a vacuum — so there is no sound there, because sound needs air or some material to travel through.
Air is an insulator, so electricity does not normally jump through it except when it is very strong, like lightning.
As you climb a very high mountain, the air gets thinner — there is less oxygen in each breath. That is why climbers on tall mountains like Mount Apo or Mount Pulag feel out of breath and tire easily.
Air has no color and no smell, so we cannot see it.
Joseph Priestley is credited with discovering oxygen in 1774.
The oxygen in the air is the gas that fire needs in order to burn.
All over the world the main proportions of air stay about the same — roughly 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen — so we breathe safe air almost anywhere.
Plants release oxygen into the air while making their food.
Air pollution from factories and vehicles causes acid rain, which damages plant leaves and alters the chemistry of soil and water.
A balloon expands as it rises because the outside air pressure is lower, letting the air inside push the rubber outward.
Air pressure is measured using an instrument called a barometer.
On a high mountain, water boils at a lower temperature because the air pressure there is lower.
Very high on a mountain like Mount Apo the air is thin and pressure is low, so climbers can find it harder to breathe.
Pressure is measured in pascals, where one pascal equals one newton of force on each square meter.
Air does not push only downward—it presses in all directions: up, down, and sideways.
At sea level, the average air pressure is about 101 kilopascals (1 atmosphere).
When you suck on a straw, you remove the air inside it, so air pressure pushes the drink up into your mouth.
When you suck on a straw, you lower the air inside it, so air pressure pushes the drink up.
When you pull a syringe's plunger, you lower the pressure inside, so outside air pressure pushes liquid in.
In a vacuum or in outer space, there is almost no air, so there is almost no air pressure.
Air has weight, so the mass of air above us presses down and creates air pressure.

Gas pressure comes from millions of its particles constantly hitting the walls of a container from the inside. This pressure pushes equally in all directions — which is why a balloon or tire becomes firm when filled with air.
In air, a feather falls slower than a rock because air resistance pushes back harder on the lightweight feather.
Air is real stuff that takes up space, which is why a balloon grows bigger when you fill it with air.
As you go higher in the atmosphere, the air gets thinner, so it is harder to breathe at high places.
Air is an earth material you cannot hold in your hand the way you hold a pebble, but it still fills the environment around every living thing.
In muddy or warm water that is low in oxygen, breathing air helps fish like the catfish and climbing perch survive.
An air conditioner works like a refrigerator: it takes heat from inside the room and moves it out to the air outside, keeping the room cool.
Like a fridge, an air conditioner does not make cold; it removes heat from inside the room.
A fan inside the air conditioner blows the cooled air out into the whole room.
Insulated walls and ceilings slow the entry of heat from outside — this reduces how hard an air conditioner must work and saves electricity.
An air conditioner and a refrigerator work on the same principle: both use a refrigerant that absorbs and releases heat.

The lowest setting isn't always better. A comfortable temperature like 24-25°C is kinder to your body: you won't get too chilly, and it avoids illnesses like colds from being too cold. The thermostat helps keep it there.

If the aircon's filter is dirty, it struggles to cool the room, so the compressor runs longer before the thermostat reaches the set temperature. The result: it uses more electricity. That's why cleaning the filter regularly matters.

A thermostat is like the aircon's little sense of feel. It has a sensor that detects how warm the air in the room is. When the room is hotter than the temperature you set, it tells the aircon to keep cooling; when it's cool enough, it stops.

In an ordinary aircon, the thermostat just turns the compressor fully on or off. In an inverter aircon, instead of shutting off completely, it slows the compressor down to hold the temperature. Because of this, it saves more electricity and keeps the cooling steadier.

Many think setting the aircon straight to the lowest (like 16°C) cools the room faster. That's not true. It blows cold at the same rate; the only difference is the aircon runs longer before it stops, so it uses more electricity.
Setting the air conditioner to a less cold temperature makes it use less electricity.

There are newer 'smart' thermostats you can control with a phone app even when you're away from home. You can even schedule the room to cool before you arrive, or have the temperature rise automatically when nobody's there to save energy.
An air conditioner has a thermostat that measures temperature and automatically stops cooling when the room is cool enough.

Sometimes you notice the aircon is still blowing air but it doesn't feel cold anymore. Often that's because the set temperature was reached, so the thermostat turned off the cooling while the fan keeps running. When the room warms up, the cold comes back.
Airlines reroute around ash clouds after eruptions, because even a modest Philippine blast can send ash high enough to hurt engines.
The airplane changed travel because a trip that once took months by ship can now be done in just hours, making it much easier to reach faraway countries.
An airplane's engine or propeller pushes air strongly backward, which thrusts the plane forward. The plane needs enough of this forward speed before its wings can make lift.
Four forces act on an airplane: lift pushing it up, weight pulling it down, thrust from the engines pushing it forward, and drag from the air holding it back.
Some planes use a spinning propeller that pushes air to move forward, while jets blast out hot gas; jets are usually faster and used for long trips.
A pilot turns and climbs an airplane by moving small parts on the wings and tail (flaps and rudder), which change how the air flows around it.
In 1903, brothers Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first flight in a powered airplane, which lasted only about 12 seconds on its first flight.
The Wright brothers (Orville and Wilbur Wright) of America built the first airplane that flew.
Harmful substances like alcohol and illegal drugs affect how the nervous system sends signals. They can slow thinking and damage the brain, which is why they are dangerous, especially for children.
Rubbing alcohol is less dense than water, so it can form the very top layer in a column.
Alcohol and vinegar mix completely with water and do not separate, unlike oil.
When there is no soap and water, alcohol or hand sanitizer can kill many germs on your hands.
In a mix of alcohol and water, the alcohol boils first because its boiling point is lower (78 vs 100 degrees Celsius).
Buzz Aldrin was the second person to walk on the Moon, right after Neil Armstrong in 1969.
Alert Level 1 means low unrest, such as extra steam or small quakes, a time to review family plans even if there is no eruption yet.
Alert Level 2 means unrest is increasing, so communities near the slopes should stay informed and be ready to leave if the next level is raised.
Alert Level 3 means magma is close enough that a hazardous eruption is possible in the coming weeks, so people in danger zones should prepare to evacuate.
Alert Level 5 means a hazardous eruption is underway, so the job is to stay out of the danger zone and follow official rescue and shelter instructions.
A volcano can look calm at Alert Level 3 if magma is still rising inside; the instruments, not the pretty cone, set the number you should follow.
PHIVOLCS volcano alert levels are a numbered scale that tells communities how serious the unrest is and what they should prepare to do.
PHIVOLCS uses alert levels from 0 to 5 to show how dangerous a volcano is at a given time.
PHIVOLCS alert levels rise and fall as unrest changes, a pattern communities use to decide when to prepare or when to go home.
Some microalgae can store large amounts of oil in their cells; scientists study using algae as a renewable biofuel that could replace fossil fuels.
Carrageenan, extracted from red algae such as Kappaphycus farmed in the Philippines, is used in the food industry to thicken and stabilize ice cream, dairy products, and more.
In the rocky shores of the Philippines, tide pools are home to various algae; green and red algae grow on rocks and provide food and shelter for small animals.
Algae and seaweed are used as organic fertilizers in farming; they are rich in nitrogen, phosphorus, and other minerals that boost plant growth and improve soil health.
One example of an alkali metal is sodium (Na), which is part of the table salt we eat.
When burned, sodium gives a bright yellow flame in a flame test.
The alkali metals are in Group 1 of the periodic table and are very reactive metals.
The alkali metals such as sodium and potassium are in the first column of the periodic table; they are soft and very reactive, reacting violently when dropped in water.
An alkaline battery contains zinc (anode), manganese dioxide (cathode), and potassium hydroxide solution as electrolyte; the chemical reaction between these produces electrical energy.
One example of an alkaline earth metal is calcium (Ca), which makes our bones strong.
Almost every cell in your body holds the exact same genes, but a different set is active in each type, which is why they do different jobs.
All warm objects, including our own bodies, give off heat by radiation, even though we cannot see it. The hotter the object, the more it radiates.
The Sun's gravity pulls on the planets and keeps them in their orbits.
Crickets, grasshoppers, and katydids belong to one group of related jumping insects.
Allelopathy is the process where some plants release chemicals into the soil that inhibit the growth of neighboring plants—a form of natural competition for nutrients and water.
An allergy happens when the immune system overreacts to something that is actually harmless, like dust or pollen.
A doctor can find out what a person is allergic to using a skin test that checks how the skin reacts to allergens.
Allergies usually come without a fever, while a viral cold often brings a mild fever.
The alligator also has a very strong bite, among the strongest of all reptiles.
By alloying, people can change a metal's properties—such as its hardness, weight, or color—to suit what they need.
An alloy is a material made by mixing two or more metals, or a metal with another element.
Most of the metals we see every day, like coins and tools, are alloys rather than pure metals.
Alloys are usually made by melting the metals, mixing them while liquid, and letting them cool together.
An alloy is a mixture of two or more metals, like bronze made from copper and tin, to make it stronger.
Alloys have different properties from their component metals — for example, steel is stronger than pure iron or pure carbon separately.
The amount of each metal added changes the alloy's properties, so there are many different kinds of steel for different uses.
Alloys are often stronger and tougher than the pure metals that were mixed to make them.
An alloy is a mixture, not a new chemical substance, so the original metals are still present inside it.
Atoms of different sizes block the layers of metal atoms from sliding, making an alloy harder to bend or break.
An alloy is a mix of metals (or a metal plus another element) made stronger or more useful. For example, steel is iron mixed with carbon, and bronze is copper mixed with tin.
Aloe vera (sabila) is a plant with thick leaves full of a clear gel, and that gel is used to soothe skin that has been burned or sunburned.
Alpha radiation is the least penetrating and can be stopped by a sheet of paper or by skin.
Alugbati (Malabar spinach) is a climbing leafy vegetable with thick succulent leaves, cooked as a vegetable because it is rich in vitamins and iron.
Recycling aluminum cans saves a huge amount of energy — it takes far less power to melt an old can than to make brand-new aluminum from rock.
Aluminum melts at about 660 degrees Celsius (660°C).
Aluminum is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust.
Dental amalgam is an alloy of mercury, silver, tin, and copper used for tooth fillings; it is durable and inexpensive, but there is ongoing debate about the small amount of mercury it contains.
Amedeo Avogadro, the man behind Avogadro's law, was an Italian scientist.
Like other quartz, amethyst grows into a shape with six sides that ends in a pointed tip. This shape is natural and not carved by people; it simply grows that way.
Inside geodes, amethyst often grows together with other minerals like clear quartz or calcite. They grow side by side because they come from the same mineral-rich water.
When amethyst is heated strongly, it loses its purple color and turns yellow or orange. This yellow stone is called citrine. So amethyst and citrine are actually like siblings.
Some people believe amethyst has healing powers, but there is no scientific proof of this. Amethyst is simply a beautiful mineral made of quartz and a little iron, not magic.
Amethyst is a purple kind of quartz that gets its color from tiny amounts of iron mixed into the crystal.
Amethyst is often imitated using purple-colored glass. But real amethyst feels cooler to the touch and has natural color variation inside, while glass has even color and warms up easily.

Lots of amethyst is mined in countries like Brazil and Uruguay, where the geodes are very large. The Philippines is better known for quartz and other minerals, but quartz is the very family amethyst belongs to.
Why does purple appear and not another color? The special form of iron inside amethyst absorbs some colors of light and lets purple pass through. That is why our eyes see purple.
The ammonia used to clean glass is a strong base with a sharp smell.
The chemical formula of ammonia is NH3 — one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms.
Animal waste and urine are broken down by bacteria into ammonia, a process called ammonification.
An amoeba moves by extending pseudopods (false feet) — cytoplasm flows into these extensions, pulling the amoeba forward.
More solute can dissolve when there is more water, and a small amount of water gets saturated sooner.
The ampere measures electric current — how much electricity is flowing.
The ampere (A) is the only electrical unit among the seven SI base units.
The unit of electric current is the ampere (amp), named after Andre-Marie Ampere.
The word amphibian means two lives, because they live in water (as young) and on land (as adults); an example is the frog.
Some frogs and toads make poison from glands in their skin; they are often brightly colored as a warning to other animals not to eat them.
Amplitude is how high a crest rises above the still-water level; a bigger dipper splash makes taller waves in the same tank.
Amplitude means a bigger disturbance in both, but the picture is height on a transverse rope and extra squeeze in a longitudinal sound.
The height or size of a sound wave is called its amplitude; the bigger the amplitude, the louder the sound.
The green anaconda is one of the strongest snakes, able to squeeze its prey with crushing force.
Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine and is called the 'father of the computer'.
Andesite is a common volcanic rock in Ring of Fire volcanoes, including those in the Philippines; it is thicker (more viscous) than basalt and can produce more explosive eruptions.
In billions of years, the Milky Way and Andromeda are expected to collide and merge.
The nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way is Andromeda.
Andromeda is the nearest large galaxy to us, a neighbor of the Milky Way.
Unlike most galaxies, Andromeda is moving toward the Milky Way, and in billions of years the two galaxies are expected to collide and slowly merge.
Anemia is a condition where the blood has too few healthy red blood cells or too little hemoglobin.
Anemia can usually be treated by eating iron-rich foods or taking iron supplements prescribed by a doctor.
An anemometer measures wind speed, often in kilometers per hour (km/h), which PAGASA uses to tell how strong the wind is in a storm.
The clownfish (like Nemo) lives among a sea anemone's tentacles without being stung, thanks to a special mucus on its skin. The anemone protects the fish, and the fish keeps the anemone clean.
Even though it looks like a flower, a sea anemone is an ANIMAL, not a plant. It does not make its own food like a plant does—it eats small animals with its tentacles.
Dr. Angel Alcala is a marine biologist known for building artificial coral reefs to help fish populations grow in the sea.
Angel Falls in Venezuela is the tallest waterfall in the world, so high that the water turns into fine mist before it reaches the ground.
When light hits a mirror, the angle it comes in at equals the angle it bounces off at.
A wave that hits a wall at a slant bounces off at a matching slant, a pattern you can mark with two arrows on the tank diagram.
The glowing lure is an adaptation that helps the anglerfish catch food in its dark surroundings.
The anglerfish can control its light. By sending more or less blood (which carries oxygen) to the esca, it can make the light brighter or dimmer, or even blink it to better attract prey.

How does the anglerfish catch prey? It attracts small fish with the glowing esca, which looks like tasty bait. When the prey comes close to inspect the light, the anglerfish suddenly gulps it down with its huge mouth.
The glowing bait attracts small fish to come close, and then the anglerfish eats them.
Female anglerfish have a modified dorsal spine on their head tipped with a glowing lure — the light comes from bacteria living inside the lure and attracts curious fish in the deep sea darkness.
The anglerfish's fishing lure is actually a changed spine from a fin on its back.
It is called an anglerfish because it is like a fisher that uses bait to catch its food.
Some animals travel far to have their young in a safe place for the babies.
Migration is dangerous because animals can run out of energy, be caught by predators, or be hit by storms.
Days getting shorter is a signal that tells animals it is time to migrate.
Many animals find their way over long journeys using different cues: smell, the position of the sun and stars, Earth's magnetic field, and memory of landmarks. This is called navigation.
Many animals in cold places have larger bodies and smaller ears and tails than their relatives in warm places — a big body with small ears and tails loses its heat more slowly.
Animals cannot eat sunlight, but they eat plants or eat animals that ate plants, so their food energy still started in the Sun.
Animals get the nitrogen they need by eating plants or other animals.
Many animals stay together in a group so they are safer from predators.
Humans are not the only ones with a nervous system — animals like dogs, fish, and birds have one too. It is what lets them sense, move, and respond to their surroundings.
Many animals hear sounds we cannot: a dog can hear a special whistle that seems silent to us, and bats and mice can hear even higher pitches.
Some animals like dogs and bats can hear very high-pitched sounds that people cannot hear.
Annatto (atsuete) seeds give Filipino dishes like kare-kare and tinola their orange-red color; it is a natural food coloring used for thousands of years.
In an annular eclipse, the Moon is farther away and does not fully cover the Sun, leaving a bright ring called the ring of fire.
You should not take medicine meant for another person because each body needs something different.
Male ants (drones) have wings and live only to fly and mate with a new queen—after mating, they die.
Ants help the environment because their digging loosens and mixes the soil, and they spread seeds that can grow into new plants.
When she is new, the queen digs a small chamber and raises her very first young all alone. Once they grow into worker ants, the workers take over finding food so the queen can just keep laying eggs.
Queens of some ant species can live for 20 to 30 years—while workers typically live only weeks to several months.
A nest does not always have just one queen. Some kinds of ants, like certain fire ants, can have many queens in a single colony, which lets them grow in number very quickly.

After just one nuptial flight, a queen never needs to mate again for the rest of her life. She stores the sperm in a special part of her body and uses it to fertilize millions of eggs over many years.
A young female ant that still has wings but has not yet mated is called an 'alate' or a virgin queen. She only becomes a true queen once she has flown, mated, and begun laying eggs.

If ants invade your house and you only kill the workers, they keep coming back because the hidden queen keeps laying eggs. So experts use bait that the ants carry back to the nest, in order to reach and remove the queen too.
An ant can lift objects up to about 50 times its own body weight.
The ant is a social insect: no single ant can survive alone, instead the whole colony works as one big team with a division of labor.
Worker ants have different jobs: some search for food, some care for the eggs and young, and others clean or repair the nest.
Worker ants are sterile females; they forage for food, defend the nest, and care for eggs and larvae.
Ophiocordyceps fungus infects carpenter ants and controls their behavior—compelling the ant to climb to a specific height on a plant before it dies, releasing spores from the ant's head.
Antacid medicine for an upset stomach is a base — it cancels the excess acid in the stomach by neutralization to relieve the burning feeling.
When a fizzing antacid tablet is dropped into water, it bubbles because the reaction releases carbon-dioxide gas. This kind of medicine also helps reduce acid in the stomach.
The anthurium is an ornamental plant with a shiny, heart-shaped red part we often think is the flower, but its true tiny flowers sit on the pointed center spike.

If you move at a perfectly constant speed from start to end, your average speed equals that constant speed exactly. But if you sometimes speed up and slow down, the average speed falls between your fastest and slowest.
Average speed is the total distance traveled divided by the total time, even if the speed changed during the trip.
When you stop to rest or get caught in traffic, that time still counts in your average speed. That is why average speed is often lower than your fastest running pace.

A common mistake is thinking that if you go 40 km/h then 60 km/h, your average is 50 km/h. That is not always right when the times differ. The correct way is always total distance divided by total time.
When you run one full 400-meter oval in 80 seconds, your average speed is 400 divided by 80, which is 5 meters per second, even if you sped up and slowed down while running.
Coaches use average speed to track whether an athlete is improving. If a player's time drops over the same distance, their average speed is higher, which is a sign of progress.
Average speed is used to estimate when you will arrive. If a trip is 240 kilometers and the bus averages 60 km/h, it will take you about 4 hours to get there.
Average speed always has a unit of distance per time, like meters per second (m/s) or kilometers per hour (km/h). We use km/h for vehicles and m/s for classroom experiments.

Average speed is different from acceleration. Average speed is how fast overall, while acceleration is how quickly the speed changes. You can have a high average speed but zero acceleration if you move steadily.
Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time of a whole trip, while instantaneous speed is the speed at one particular moment, like what a speedometer shows.
If you walk 1 kilometer to school and arrive in 15 minutes, your average speed is about 4 kilometers per hour, which is a typical human walking speed.
After three or more trials, many investigations use the average so one odd measurement does not pull the answer too far.

Because a single bacterium is so tiny, they are hard to count one by one. Instead, scientists let them multiply on a dish until they form a visible blob called a colony. Each blob came from just one bacterium that multiplied into millions.

Inside a ball-and-socket joint, smooth cartilage covers the ends of the bones. It acts as a cushion and makes things slippery so the bones don't rub or grind against each other when you move.

There is a special liquid inside a ball-and-socket joint called synovial fluid. It works like oil in a machine, making movement smooth so your joint stays loose and doesn't stiffen.
A hinge joint like the knee and elbow bends and straightens in only one direction, while a ball-and-socket joint like the shoulder can rotate in all directions.

A ball-and-socket joint is different from a pivot joint. A pivot joint, like the one at the top of your neck, only rotates in one direction—letting you shake your head 'no.' A ball-and-socket, though, moves in all directions, not just rotating.

Barnacles use their cirri — long feathery modified legs — to filter small food particles from water; when covered by water, a barnacle extends its cirri and beats them through the water to capture food.
A barnacle is a small sea animal with a hard shell that cements itself tightly to rocks, ships, and shells, and filters food from the water.
Because barnacles strain tiny bits out of the water, they help in a small way to keep the seawater clean and balanced. They are part of a healthy ocean ecosystem.
The gaps between a barnacle's cirri act like the holes of a sieve: they catch small bits of food, but the very tiniest still slip through with the water.
A barnacle's cirri legs are not just for catching food. They also use them to feel the water and sense danger, which is why they snap shut quickly when a shadow or movement comes near.
Unlike a fish, a barnacle cannot chase food because it is cemented to a rock by its own natural glue, head-down. So it must wait for the food to come to it.
On many Philippine shores you can see barnacles clustered on rocks, posts, and the sides of boats. They are often sharp, so be careful walking on the rocks!
A barnacle's favorite food is plankton: super tiny plants and animals that float in seawater and are almost too small to see.
A barnacle can only feed when the high tide covers it with water. When the tide goes out and they are left in the air, they shut up and wait for the water to come back.
After a young barnacle glues itself down, it then builds the hard shell around itself that serves as its home and armor.
A barnacle's glue is made of special proteins that link tightly together to form a tough, waterproof bond.
A barnacle does not stick only to rock; its glue also works on wood, metal, plastic, and glass underwater.
Water usually ruins glue, but a barnacle pushes the water off the surface first before sticking, so its glue still works underwater.
The barnacle's hard shell is made of calcium carbonate, the same hard material found in seashells and chalk.
When safe inside its hard shell, the barnacle opens its lid and sweeps out feathery legs to catch tiny food drifting in the water.
Barnacles often crowd tightly together on one rock. Being packed together keeps them safer and makes it easier to find a partner to make babies.
On many rocky shores in the Philippines, you can find barnacles stuck to rocks, on pier posts, and even under boats.
A barnacle's hard home is made of plates standing like a wall, with smaller plates on top that open and close like a little door.
A barnacle has a hard shell made of small plates that protects its soft body from harm.
A mussel has two big shells that open like a book; a barnacle instead has several hard plates joined together to form a round wall.
A young barnacle swims freely in the sea first, then picks a spot and glues down for life.
Barnacles and limpets are often found together on rocky seashores where the tide covers and uncovers them each day.
Barnacles often live crowded close together on rocks, which makes it easier to reproduce.
Because a barnacle can't move once it's stuck, it needs to settle close to other barnacles so it can have babies. That's why you often see them crowded together on the same rock or boat.

Did you know some kinds of barnacle are eaten by people? The goose barnacle, for example, is treated as a tasty seafood in some countries and can even be expensive. Not every barnacle is just a boat-clinger—some are food too!
On many rocky seashores in the Philippines, you can see barnacles stuck to the rocks at low tide. They're sharp, so be careful and don't step on them barefoot—they can cut you!
Barnacle glue is super strong and sticks even when wet or underwater—something hard for humans to copy. Scientists study it to make new glues, even glues that could seal wounds inside the body!
There's a special kind of barnacle made for life on whales—called the whale barnacle. Its base grows down into the whale's thick skin so it won't fall off no matter how fast the whale swims.
Barnacles often live crowded close together on one rock, so thousands of them can cover a single spot.
The baro't saya is a dress made of cloth woven from fibers such as cotton or piña, threads interlaced together before being sewn.
When a barometer reading falls, it often signals rain or a storm is coming; when it rises, the weather is usually about to improve.
Air pressure is often measured in hectopascals (hPa) or millibars (mb).
The traditional Barong Tagalog is often woven from piña, fibers taken from pineapple leaves, a natural plant fiber that is thin yet strong.
Meteor Crater in Arizona is a huge hole almost a kilometer wide, made by a metal meteorite about 50,000 years ago.
When thick basalt lava cools slowly, it contracts and forms hexagonal columns of rock called columnar joints — similar formations can be seen along some Philippine sea cliffs.
Basalt is an igneous rock formed from lava that cooled quickly at the Earth's surface.
Basalt is the main rock of the ocean floor; when lava erupts underwater, it cools quickly and forms pillow-shaped mounds called pillow basalt.
Basi is a traditional Ilocos wine made from sugarcane juice, where yeast eats the sugar through fermentation and turns it into alcohol.
Ilocos basi is a wine made from sugarcane juice fermented by yeast, tiny microbes that eat the sugar and produce alcohol.
When a basketball player jumps, they push hard on the floor downward (action), and the floor pushes them upward (reaction) — which is what lifts them into the air.
Bats can hear ultrasound up to about 100,000 Hz, which they use for echolocation.
A bat is a mammal, not a bird, even though it flies — it feeds its young with milk.
Some bats migrate to other places to follow the fruits and flowers they eat.
Many bats send out sound from their mouth or nose and catch the returning echoes with their large ears.
In Batesian mimicry, a harmless animal copies the appearance of a dangerous one so predators avoid it.
Bathing regularly with soap removes dirt and germs that can cause illness in our body.

A young bat is not good at echolocation right away, it has to practice as it grows. At first its calls are weak and clumsy, but they slowly improve as it experiments night after night. Like a child learning to talk, a bat's skill is sharpened with practice.

How does a bat drink without stopping its flight? A flat, smooth water surface bounces its sound straight down, so the bat hears it as clear and knows it can be a drinking spot. The bat swoops low and sips water while still in the air.

When a bat closes in on an insect, it sends out sounds much faster, almost a blur of clicks. This is called a feeding buzz. More clicks mean more information about exactly where the prey is in the final moment before the catch.

The sonar that ships and submarines use to find things underwater works much like what a bat does! They send out a sound, wait for the echo, and learn if something is there. Many human inventions copy clever tricks that animals already use.
Unlike birds, a bat cannot easily take off from the ground because its legs are too weak to run. So it hangs upside down — to fly, it simply lets go and drops into the air.
While hanging, a bat uses its two free wings to groom itself — it cleans its fur and wings with its tongue and claws. This is important to keep its wings healthy and ready to fly when night comes.
Many animals such as bats live inside caves because they are dark and sheltered.
It is not true that bats are blind; they can all see, even though most move around in the dark.
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly using their wings.
Most of the sounds bats use are so high-pitched (ultrasound) that human ears cannot hear them.
Strong acids like battery acid are dangerous because they can burn and damage things.

Scientifically, a 'cell' is a single unit (like one AA battery giving 1.5 volts), while a 'battery' properly refers to two or more cells connected together — though in everyday use the words are interchangeable.
A battery's energy comes from a chemical reaction between the electrodes and the electrolyte.
When a battery is used, its chemical energy changes into electrical energy, or electricity.
Every battery has a positive and a negative end — it must be inserted in the correct direction inside a device for current to flow properly.
Old batteries contain chemicals that can harm the environment, so they should be thrown away properly and not just in the trash.
A dry cell battery has a carbon rod in the center (positive terminal), a zinc outer casing (negative terminal), and a paste electrolyte between them that allows the chemical reaction.
The electrolyte inside a battery is a liquid or paste that allows ions to move between electrodes — this sustains the chemical reaction that produces electrical current.
The electricity a battery supplies can become light, heat, sound, or motion, depending on the device connected to it.

A battery's energy density measures how much energy it stores per kilogram — lithium-ion batteries have much higher energy density than lead-acid batteries, which is why they are used in smartphones and electric vehicles.
A fuel cell is a type of battery that uses hydrogen and oxygen to generate electricity — its only by-product is water, making it a clean energy source.
When batteries are connected in parallel (positive to positive, negative to negative), the voltage stays the same but the supply lasts longer because each battery contributes part of the current.
In remote Philippine villages not yet connected to the power grid, solar panel and battery combinations provide electricity for lights, radios, and small appliances.
A battery goes dead when nearly all the chemicals inside it have been used up by the reaction.
Old batteries should not be thrown in ordinary trash because they contain heavy metals like lead and mercury that can leach into soil and water and cause pollution.
Connecting a battery's positive and negative terminals directly with a wire and no resistance causes a huge current that heats the battery and wire dangerously — do not short-circuit a battery.
When two 1.5-volt batteries are connected in series (positive to negative), the total voltage is 3 volts — this is why many flashlights use two or three batteries connected end to end.
A battery stores energy and provides electric current to a circuit.
A battery does not actually store electricity itself; it stores chemicals that are ready to react and make electricity.
The first true battery was made by Alessandro Volta in the year 1800, which is why the unit of voltage is called the 'volt'.
The first battery was invented by Alessandro Volta.
Volta's battery was made of disks of zinc and copper.
A car battery is a lead-acid wet cell that uses liquid sulfuric acid as electrolyte and provides 12 volts to start the engine and power the car's electrical components.
Garlic grows underground as a bulb made of many small pieces called cloves. Each clove can be planted to grow a new garlic plant.
A whole garlic clove has little smell, but when it is crushed or chopped, the chemicals inside it mix and make the strong smell that flavors our food.
The monitor lizard uses its forked tongue to detect scents in its environment, helping it find food and sense predators.
Philippine monitor lizards are much smaller than the Komodo dragon of Indonesia, which is the world's largest monitor lizard.
The monitor lizard, called bayawak, is one of the largest lizards in the Philippines and can grow longer than a child.
The monitor lizard is a cold-blooded reptile, so it basks in the sun to warm its body and gain energy.
Many beach plants grow low and flat against the ground, so strong winds and storms cannot easily knock them over or pull them out.
The sandy soil at the beach has few nutrients and dries out fast, but beach plants can still grow there because they are suited to live in tough conditions.
By looking at the shape of a bird's beak, we can guess what kind of food it eats.
A beaker is a glass container with markings on its side used in the laboratory to measure the volume of a liquid.
Beaufort Force 12, the highest level, is hurricane force, with winds of 118 km/h (73 mph) or more.
Force 12 on the Beaufort scale is hurricane strength, about 73 mph (118 km/h) and up.
The Beaufort wind force scale was created in 1805 by Francis Beaufort, a British Royal Navy officer.
The Beaufort scale measures the strength or speed of the wind.
The Beaufort scale runs from Force 0 (calm) to Force 12 (hurricane).
The Beaufort scale describes wind strength from 0 (calm) up to 12 (hurricane force).
A beaver stores branches underwater near its home so it can eat them when the river surface freezes over.
The beaver, a large rodent, uses its strong ever-growing teeth to cut down trees.
In 1903, three people — Henri Becquerel, Marie Curie, and Pierre Curie — shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for radioactivity.
Bed bugs are tiny insects that hide in cracks and mattress seams during the day and emerge at night to feed on sleeping people—their flat bodies let them squeeze into very narrow spaces.
Colony Collapse Disorder is the mysterious disappearance of large numbers of worker bees from hives, threatening crops that depend on bee pollination.
A single honeybee colony can have up to about 50,000 to 60,000 bees.
In the waggle dance, a bee uses the sun as a compass — the angle of its dance from straight up tells the others the direction of the food relative to the sun.
Bees and flowers help each other: the bee gets nectar, and in return it carries pollen so the plant can make seeds.
Honeybees make honey from flower nectar and store it in their hive as food.
Besides the waggle dance and sun compass, bees also memorize landmarks around their hive to help them return home after long foraging trips.
Bees are important pollinators—they carry pollen from one flower to another, which helps many of the crops we eat to produce fruit and seeds.
There is only one queen bee in each hive, and she is the only one that lays eggs — she can lay thousands of eggs every day.
A honeybee's stinger has tiny barbs that catch in the skin, so when it stings and flies away, its belly tears and the bee dies.
Even though bees can sting, they are very important to nature. They help plants make fruit through pollination, and they also make honey. So bees should not be killed without good reason.
After a sting, it is normal for the spot to swell, turn red, and itch for some hours or days. This is the body's way of fighting the venom, and it usually goes away on its own.
Even though it hurts, scientists study bee venom because it has chemicals that might be useful in medicine. For example, they are testing it as a possible treatment for pain and swelling.
Apis cerana (the Asian honey bee) is native to Asia including the Philippines—it differs from the European honey bee (Apis mellifera) and is better adapted to local diseases and predators.
Bees can see ultraviolet (UV) light invisible to humans; many flowers have UV patterns that guide bees directly to the nectar.
Bees have special spots on their back legs where they pack and carry pollen back to the hive.
Bees are important to farming because they help many of the fruits and vegetables we eat to grow.
There are thousands of kinds of bees in the world, and not all of them make honey.
Bees do not just see color, they also remember it. When they find a flower with lots of nectar, they remember its color so they can return and find similar ones. This is a form of learning.
A bee's eyes read fast movement more quickly than ours. So even when flying past flowers swaying in the wind, they can still see clearly, and it is hard to catch them by surprise.
A bee actually has five eyes: two large compound eyes on the sides of its head, and three tiny simple eyes called ocelli on top. The three small ones help it sense how bright the surroundings are.
Colorful flowers are not bright just to look pretty; over time they developed these colors and UV patterns to attract bees. Bees help flowers reproduce, and flowers give bees food in return.
Most bees come out from morning to afternoon because they need light to see flowers. At night it becomes hard for them to see, so they return to their hive and rest.
Bees can see ultraviolet light that we cannot, but they have trouble seeing the color red.
Because we know bees have favorite colors and patterns, we can plant flowers they are truly drawn to, like blue and yellow ones. In this way we help keep bee populations many and healthy.
Worker bees are female bees that gather nectar, clean the hive, and care for the baby bees.
Beeswax candles burn cleaner than paraffin (petroleum-derived) candles, producing less smoke and soot; beeswax is a natural wax secreted by honeybees.
Many beetles are colored like leaves, wood, or soil so they can hide and avoid being seen by predators.
Beetles are the insect group with the most species — over 400,000 known kinds.
Most beetles have hard, chewing jaws, so they can eat leaves, wood, or other insects.
Beetles (order Coleoptera) have more known species than any other animal group—over 400,000 species have been discovered.
Beetles have more kinds (species) than any other group of animals on Earth.
The before stage is when people board windows and bring animals in, matching weather that is turning but has not yet peaked.
A falling air-pressure reading is a typical before-the-storm clue, because a cyclone is a strong low-pressure weather system.
Early before-the-storm hours can still look deceptively fine in one town while the cyclone is already wet and windy in another.
Before an eruption, walk or list the evacuation route to higher ground away from rivers, so during a night alert you are not choosing a path in panic.
Before any eruption, families should know whether their house sits inside a permanent danger zone or a lahar path on a PHIVOLCS map.
Before and during unrest, get the alert level from PHIVOLCS or local officials, not from a rumor that the volcano 'looks angry' today.
Before unrest grows, pick a family meeting place outside the danger zone, so during an evacuation no one waits on a close slope for the others.
Before alerts rise, pack water, food, medicine, and a mask in a go-bag, because leaving is faster when the bag is already by the door.
Communities near Mayon or Taal practice eruption drills before a crisis, so during a real alert people already know the meeting place and the route.
Rain before the cyclone can start as scattered showers, then grow more frequent as rainbands move closer to the place.
Before land winds peak, the sea near the path often grows rougher, with bigger swells that already make small-boat weather unsafe.
Before is mostly warning weather: rising wind and building clouds. During is the peak of rain and destructive wind in that place.
A school bell is a sound that sends the same information to many people at once: it is time to gather or time to change activity.
When part of a wave front enters shallower water, that part slows and the front can bend, a change of direction you can see in the tank.
In Benguet in northern Luzon, people have mined gold for a long time, even before the Spanish arrived.
Bernoulli's principle: the faster a fluid or air flows, the lower its pressure.
Silver is the best electrical conductor of all the metals.
Archaeologists have found that betel chewing is very old, going back thousands of years, based on ancient remains showing signs of chewing.
Betel chewing is not done only in the Philippines; millions of people also do it in India and other parts of South and Southeast Asia.
Some think betel nut is tobacco, but they are different. Betel nut is the seed of the areca palm, while tobacco comes from a different plant. They are sometimes combined, but they are not the same.
The betel leaf is used to wrap the sliced nut and lime before chewing.
The betel nut is very hard, so it is sliced thin before being added to the quid.
Betel chewing spread across Southeast Asia and the Pacific thousands of years ago.
The Philippines' Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) manages fisheries, issues red tide warnings, and enforces fishing regulations to protect marine resources.
Bibingka rises while cooking because its leavening releases carbon dioxide gas, and heat from the coals above and below cooks it through.
Bibingkang malagkit is sticky because glutinous rice is rich in a kind of starch that turns gummy when cooked with heat.
A bicycle has two wheels, which is why it is named 'bi' (two) and 'cycle' (wheel).
Based on scientific evidence, the universe is estimated to be over ten billion years old, about 13.8 billion years since it began in the Big Bang.

According to Big Bang theory, the universe began as an extremely hot and dense state about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since; the cosmic microwave background radiation is the leftover heat from this early state.
The Big Bang was not an explosion inside space, but the stretching of space itself everywhere at once.
The Big Bang was not an explosion within space but the sudden expansion of space itself, so galaxies move apart because the space between them is stretching.
The Big Bang is a scientific theory supported by a lot of evidence, not just a guess.
The Big Dipper is a group of seven bright stars shaped like a ladle, and its two end stars point to the North Star that shows which way is north.
Using the two outer stars of the Big Dipper, you can find Polaris (the North Star).
The Big Dipper is made of seven (7) bright stars.
Very massive stars end in a powerful explosion called a supernova, which can briefly shine brighter than an entire galaxy.
In general, bigger instruments make lower notes, which is why a cello sounds lower than a violin.
Objects with more mass have stronger gravity, which is why the Sun's gravity is so strong.
The biggest dam and power station in the world is the Three Gorges Dam in China.
Flying reptiles like Pteranodon were not true dinosaurs but pterosaurs.
Mauna Loa in Hawaii is the largest active volcano on Earth.
Bile helps break large fats into tiny droplets so they are easier to digest.
In the Binasuan dance, water stays in the glasses because the dancer keeps each glass level and moves smoothly to stay balanced.
Using both eyes together to see depth is called binocular vision.
Carl Linnaeus created the two-word scientific naming system for animals and plants.
A scientific name has two parts: the first is the genus (a larger group of closely related kinds) and the second is the species name, like Homo (genus) and sapiens (species) for humans.
In the Philippines, the binturong is found on the island of Palawan and nearby islands.
The binturong has a long, grasping tail that can grip tree branches like an extra hand.
The binturong can rotate its hind ankles backward so it can climb down a tree head-first.
Even if trash is biodegradable, that does not mean it can be littered anywhere — biodegradable waste can smell, attract flies and rats, and spread sickness if not disposed of properly.
Soap is more biodegradable than many synthetic detergents — soap breaks down in nature more readily, while some detergents can harm river ecosystems.
Different wastes take different times to break down: fruit peels take only a few weeks, paper a few months, but plastic takes hundreds of years and glass almost never breaks down.
Genetic diversity gives a species the ability to adapt to changes and resist diseases — when a small population undergoes a genetic bottleneck, the species becomes more fragile.
The Philippines is a biodiversity hotspot—a place with very many native animals and plants found nowhere else, which must be protected.
The mangroves along Philippine coasts act as homes and nurseries for many young fish and shrimp.
Endemism is so high in the Philippines that almost all of its native frogs are found nowhere else in the world.
Cutting down forests destroys the homes of endemic animals, so many of them are now in danger of disappearing.
In biogas, bacteria feed on animal waste inside a sealed container with no air, and as it rots it gives off a gas that can be used as cooking fuel.
Scientists use coral bleaching as a bioindicator of ocean health — when corals begin to turn white, it signals severe thermal stress in the ocean.
Trees have an inner biological clock that helps them know when to fold and open their leaves.
Fat-soluble toxins like DDT are stored in animals' body fat and become more concentrated at each level of the food chain — this is why apex predators accumulate the most toxins.
Spiders in rice fields are natural pest controllers—they feed on leafhoppers, flies, and other insects that damage rice; preserving spider populations is an important part of IPM.
Plant roots growing in a rock crack get bigger and slowly pry the rock apart—a kind of biological weathering.
This light comes from a chemical reaction between a substance called luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase.
Some sea creatures use their light as a signal to find a mate.
Some sea animals use their light as a signal to find a mate in the darkness.
Some sea animals make their own light from their bodies, which is called bioluminescence.
Most light from sea creatures is blue or green because blue light travels the farthest through water.
Poisons such as mercury can build up little by little going up a food chain, so the predators at the top may end up with the highest amount of toxin in their bodies.
Biomass energy is energy from plants and organic waste — plants store the sun's energy and release it when burned or when they decompose.
Biomass is energy from things that were once alive, like wood or crop leftovers; it is renewable if new plants keep being grown to replace them.
Biomass energy comes from materials that come from living plants and animals, like wood and waste.
The four main biomolecules in living things are carbohydrates, lipids or fats, proteins, and nucleic acids such as DNA.
Biomolecules such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids (fats), and nucleic acids are the molecules that make up all living things.
A bird's beak is covered in keratin, the same material as our fingernails, and it keeps growing.
Instead of a heavy jaw and teeth, a bird has a lightweight beak, so it is not weighed down in flight.
Birds lay eggs with hard shells and often care for them in a nest.
Many migratory birds can sense Earth's magnetic field, like having a natural compass that helps them know direction while flying long distances.
Migration is dangerous because birds can grow exhausted, go hungry, or get caught in strong storms.
Shorter days are a signal that tells birds it is time to prepare for migration.
Some egrets seen in Philippine ricefields are migratory birds that come from faraway places.
Before migrating, birds eat a lot to store fat that they use as fuel for the long flight.
Birds are also guided by land features like coastlines, rivers, and mountains during migration.
Some birds fly thousands of kilometers each migration, from the far north to the far south.
Some birds can sense Earth's magnetic field, which acts like a built-in compass that guides their migration.
Many small birds migrate at night because the air is cooler and the stars help guide them.
When the north turns cold, many migratory birds visit the wetlands of the Philippines to rest and feed.
Protecting wetlands and coastlines is important because they are the resting and feeding places of migratory birds.
Geese fly in a V shape to save energy, because flying behind another bird is easier.
Birds-of-paradise have unusual dances and feathers that the male displays to impress the female.
Some birds use the sun's position as a compass; because the sun moves across the sky during the day, they combine it with an internal clock to keep their direction correct.
Birds have a large breastbone called a keel where the strong flight muscles attach.
Today's birds are considered the descendants of small feathered dinosaurs — so in a way, dinosaurs never fully disappeared.
Birds have no teeth; they use their beaks to grab and swallow food whole.
In many birds, bright color is a sign that the male is healthy, so the female chooses him.
All birds lay eggs, and most sit on them to keep them warm until they hatch.
Birds have a special breathing system that takes in lots of oxygen, giving them the energy to fly for a long time.
Each feather has a stiff central shaft with many tiny barbs that hook together like a zipper.
Parent birds feed their chicks until the young are strong enough to fly out of the nest.
A bird flaps its wings to make both lift and forward push at the same time. An airplane instead has fixed wings for lift and engines or propellers for the forward push, so it does not need to flap.
A hummingbird moves its wings in a figure-eight pattern, which lets it stay floating in one spot in the air (hovering). This way it can drink nectar while staying in place.
Not everything that flaps actually flies! A penguin flaps its wings to swim underwater, almost like it is flying through the sea. It uses the same kind of motion but in water instead of air.
The long, stiff flight feathers on the wings catch the air so the bird can fly.
Not all birds can fly; some, like the ostrich, run on the ground instead of flying.
Even though they are hollow, a bird's bones have tiny crisscross struts inside that keep them strong without adding weight.
Birds descended from certain dinosaurs, and even some of those dinosaurs had hollow bones. So light bones aren't new to birds—they've existed for a very long time.
Many ask: do birds float because their bones are hollow? Light bones help a bit, but the bigger reason they float on water is their feathers and trapped air.
Like an eggshell that's thin yet strong because of its curved shape, a bird's bone is light yet strong because of its design—being strong doesn't always mean being heavy.
Why does a bird need light bones? A lighter body is easier for the wings to lift into the air. If the bones were heavy, flying would be much harder.
A bird's body is very light, so the air does not struggle to hold it up while it flies.
Migrating birds find their way using the sun, the stars, and Earth's magnetic field as guides.
Many birds build nests out of twigs, leaves, and grass to hold their eggs safely.
A bird sitting on a single wire is not shocked because there is no complete path for electricity to flow to the ground.
An owl cannot move its eyes, so it turns its head far around to look to the sides and behind it.
The Philippine Eagle is one of the largest and strongest eagles in the world, and it is the national bird of the Philippines.
Water birds like ducks have webbed feet that help them paddle through water.

Not all of a bird's feathers are the same. The stiff, long flight feathers on the wing grip the air so the bird can fly, while the soft down feathers underneath keep its body warm. The two kinds work together so the bird can both fly and stay warm.

When a bird pushes its wing down, the feathers close and overlap to catch the air and make a push. When it lifts the wing back up, the feathers part slightly to let air slip through without dragging it back. This way it pushes well without wasting effort.

Wings do more than lift — when a bird flaps downward, it pushes air backward and down. By the law of force, the air pushes back, so the bird is driven forward and up. This is how it moves forward through the air.
Some birds like eagles fly for a long time with hardly any flapping — this is called gliding or soaring. They ride rising warm air (thermals) that lifts them up, so they save energy on long flights.

The wings are moved by large muscles in the bird's chest. These muscles pull the wing down powerfully to flap. That is why strong-flying birds have big, strong chests — that is where their wing power comes from.

It is a mistake to think a bird's wing is just an extra arm with feathers. In truth, the wing is a changed form of the front limb — it still has bones similar to the bones in a human arm. So it is not a separate part but comes from the same body region.

Wing shapes differ depending on how a bird lives. Fast-flying birds have pointed, narrow wings, while birds that soar for a long time, like eagles, have broad wings. The shape matches the way each bird flies.

The size of the wings must match the weight of the bird's body. Heavier birds need bigger wings to make enough lift. That is why large birds like eagles have very large wings, while small birds get by with small wings.

The hardest part of flying is taking off from the ground. Here the bird must flap very fast and hard to make enough lift from a standing start. Once it is up and moving fast, it is much easier to stay flying.
The birthstone for April is the diamond, which is clear and colorless.
The birthstone for December is the turquoise, which is a blue-green color.
The birthstone for March is the aquamarine, which is a light sea-blue color.
The birthstone for May is the emerald, which is green in color.
Many poisonous plants are bitter, so a bitter taste can act as a warning to the body.

The Philippines is a leading producer of South Sea pearls — pearl oysters (Pinctada maxima and other species) are farmed in Palawan and Davao provinces where the warm, clean water provides ideal conditions for pearl growth.
Black carbon soot in the air absorbs the sun's heat, so it adds to the warming of the atmosphere and the melting of ice.
Gas and dust swirling into a black hole get extremely hot and glow brightly, and this is one of the ways scientists can find a black hole they cannot see directly.

When matter falls toward a black hole, it spirals into an accretion disk — a hot, glowing whirlpool of gas; some of the most energetic black holes shoot relativistic jets of matter perpendicular to the disk at close to the speed of light.
We cannot see a black hole directly because it gives off no light; instead, scientists know it is there by watching its effect on nearby stars and gas.
Scientists use black holes as natural laboratories to test ideas about gravity; for example, they detected ripples called gravitational waves when two black holes merged far out in space.
In 2019, scientists captured the first-ever photo of a black hole using telescopes around the world working together, showing a dark center ringed by glowing gas.
The biggest stars can collapse into a black hole, a place with gravity so strong that not even light can escape.
Although nothing can escape from inside a black hole, some black holes shoot out powerful jets of gas and energy from the swirling gas just outside, reaching far across space.
A black hole's strong gravity can bend the path of light that passes nearby, so sometimes we can even see the light of stars that are right behind it.

A stroke is more effective when you fully submerge the blade in the water. If the blade is too shallow and its top breaks the surface, bubbles and splashing form and your effort is wasted. But it should not be too deep either; it is enough that water covers the whole blade as you pull.

Why do you have to paddle again and again? Because water has drag, a resistance that pulls back on the boat and slows it. When you stop paddling, the boat gradually slows until it stops because of this drag. So a steady push is needed to keep it moving.

The right paddle length depends on the size of the person and how high the boat sits in the water. It should be long enough to reach and sink the blade properly without bending over too much. Too short and you struggle to reach; too long and it is awkward to swing and more tiring.

Have you noticed the boat keeps gliding even when you pause between strokes? That is because of momentum: a moving object tends to keep moving. So each time you stroke, you build up motion, and the boat coasts forward before slowing again from drag.
When you paddle a boat, the paddle pushes the water backward, and the water pushes the boat forward.

You can use the paddle not only to go forward but also to turn. If you paddle only on the right side, the boat turns left; if only on the left, it turns right. You can also hold the blade in the water on one side to use it like a rudder.

A paddle is held by both hands and is not attached to the boat. An oar, on the other hand, is fixed to the side of the boat by an oarlock, so it works like a lever with a pivot. That is why a paddler faces forward, while a rower faces backward.

You cannot paddle on dry land no matter how hard you try. The paddle needs water to push backward, and that water is what pushes you forward. With no water to press against, there is no reaction to push the boat. Water is thicker and heavier than air, so it is much better to push against.

The wider the paddle blade, the more water it can catch and push in one stroke. More water pushed backward means a stronger push forward. That is why paddles are wide at the end and not thin like a stick.

A similarity is that both can be absorbed: curtains soak up sound, and a dark cloth soaks up light, turning wave energy into a little heat.
Both can be graphed against time at one place, so a microphone trace of sound and a float bouncing on a ripple can look like similar wiggles.
Both kinds can be a one-time pulse or a repeating train of cycles, so 'wave' does not always mean a long ongoing tone or wiggle.
Both kinds can bend around openings: sound can go around a doorway, and water waves can spread after passing a gap in a barrier.
Both kinds can meet and add or cancel: two sounds can make beats, and two water ripples can make a pattern of still and moving spots.
Sound can change if the source moves, if you move, or if both move, because what matters is how you close the gap.
A similarity is that both kinds can bounce: sound can echo from a wall, and a rope wave can reflect from a held end.
Both kinds can form standing patterns in a bounded space, such as a guitar string for transverse motion and an organ pipe for sound.
A similarity is that both longitudinal and transverse waves carry energy from one place to another without the particles making the whole trip.
A similarity is that particles oscillate about a rest place in both kinds; the difference is only the line along which they oscillate.
Both kinds have a period, the time for one full cycle, whether that cycle is a rope bump or one squeeze-and-spread of air.
A similarity: both tend to spread and weaken with distance from the source, which is why a far shout and a far lamp both seem weaker.
A similarity is that each wave has a travel direction you can point to, even when particles in a transverse wave are moving across that arrow.
Both kinds have amplitude: how far particles move from rest, as height on a rope or as how tightly air is squeezed in a sound.
Both kinds have frequency, meaning how many cycles pass a point each second, whether the cycle is a wiggle or a squeeze.
Both kinds have a wavelength: crest-to-crest for a transverse wave, or compression-to-compression for a longitudinal wave.
When two waves of either kind overlap, they add their disturbances for a moment, then can pass through and keep going.
Sound is slower in air than in water, and rope waves are slower on a heavier rope; in both kinds the medium sets the speed.
In a rope wave and in a sound wave, energy moves forward while the rope bits and the air bits stay in their neighborhood.
A similarity: Earth scientists use both types of earthquake waves to learn what is inside the planet, because they travel differently.
A similarity is that people use both kinds to send information: sound for talking, and transverse radio or light waves for broadcasts.

Calcium is what makes your bones hard. It works like cement that fills in the bone so it becomes firm and does not break easily.
Some think bones are dead objects, but they are alive and constantly changing. The body removes old parts and replaces them using fresh calcium.
As people get older, calcium slowly leaves the bones so they become weaker. That is why grandmothers and grandfathers can break a bone more easily if they fall.
Calcium is good, but that does not mean you should overdo it. The body takes only what it needs and removes the excess, so eat just the right amount each day.
Filipino children need enough calcium for growing strong bones; good sources include milk, cheese, sardines with bones, and leafy vegetables like malunggay.
Calcium helps best when you also exercise. When you run, jump, or play, it signals your bones to become stronger. So eating calcium and playing actively make a great pair.

Some kids think that the more calcium you eat, the faster your bones get strong. But that's not true. Your body only needs the right amount; extra calcium isn't used and can even cause problems. A balanced diet is best.
It's better to drink milk than soda. Drinking too much sugary soda can affect how strong your bones get, while milk brings the calcium you need. Choose milk or water instead of soda.
Calcium needs a helper so your body can absorb it: vitamin D. We get vitamin D when sunlight touches our skin. So playing outside actually helps your bones use the calcium better.
