Right after you blow out a candle, a thin white smoke rises that is actually still wax vapor. If you bring a lit match to that smoke without touching the wick, the flame can race down the smoke and relight the candle. This proves it is the wax vapor, not the wick itself, that burns.

In the Philippines, where brownouts often happen during typhoons, candles often become emergency lights when there is no electricity. They are easy to carry and need no battery or socket. So it is good to keep candles and matches ready at home before a strong typhoon arrives.

The hottest part of a candle flame is the blue area near the bottom, close to the wick. There is more oxygen there, so the wax burns more completely and cleanly. The yellow part higher up is actually cooler than this blue base, even though it looks brighter.

A candle flame always points upward because hot air is light and rises, while cooler, heavier air sinks to take its place. This constant rising of heat shapes the flame upward. Without gravity, like in space, a flame is not pointed but more like a round ball.

It is not the liquid wax itself that burns in a candle. The flame's heat warms the liquid wax that climbs the wick until it turns into a gas (vapor), and that wax vapor is what actually burns to make the flame. That is why there is a tiny pool of melted wax below the flame before it becomes vapor.

The yellow light of a candle flame comes from extremely tiny bits of carbon (like little specks of soot) that get so hot they glow and give off light. As they rise through the flame, most of them burn up completely. The few that do not burn escape as black smoke or collect as soot.
If you hold a cold spoon over a candle flame, black soot sticks to it — proof that the smoke carries carbon that did not fully burn.
The long canine teeth of dogs and lions are used to grab and hold onto prey.
The pointed teeth at the corners, called canines, are spear-shaped for tearing tough food like meat — which is why they are shaped differently from the flat teeth in front and back.
An adult has 4 canine teeth.
The pointed teeth, called canines, are used to tear food such as meat.
A difference: your ear detects longitudinal sound, not the transverse electromagnetic waves of radio or light, which need other sensors.
In thin capillaries, oxygen and nutrients pass from the blood into the body's cells.
Capillaries are so thin that oxygen, nutrients, and waste products can pass through their walls directly into and out of cells.

Rising damp in buildings is caused by capillary action — water rises through the bricks and mortar of the wall from wet ground. To prevent this, builders install a waterproof layer (damp-proof course) near the base of the wall.
In a candle, the wick acts as a capillary tube. Melted wax is drawn up through the thin fibres of the wick by capillary action and reaches the flame where it vaporises and burns.
Water can climb up very thin tubes or a plant's stem even against gravity — this is called capillary action.
Capillary action can lift water upward even though gravity pulls water down. It needs no pump or machine to do this.
Water or oil climbs up cloth and wicks through capillary action. This is how oil rises up a lamp wick to keep the flame burning.
Capillaries are the smallest, thinnest blood vessels, where oxygen and nutrients pass into cells and wastes are picked up.
Cut flowers stay fresh in a vase because water climbs up their stems through capillary action.
Not all liquids climb — mercury, for example, actually sinks lower in a narrow tube because its cohesion is stronger than its adhesion to glass.
Water climbs higher in a narrower tube. The thinner the space, the stronger the pull lifting the water up.
Capillary action alone is not enough to reach the top of very tall trees. Transpiration — water evaporating from the leaves and pulling water up — also helps.
Paper towels soak up water through capillary action. The tiny gaps between the paper fibers act like little tubes that water climbs into.
A sponge soaks up water because it is full of tiny holes that act like little tubes. Water climbs into these holes by capillary action.
If you bridge a paper strip from a cup of water to an empty cup, water travels across the paper by capillary action until the two cups are even.
Capiz shells used in traditional Philippine windows and parols are translucent — they let in soft light but do not form a clear image.
Scientists help endangered animals by breeding them in safe centers before releasing them back into the wild.
A car on a highway typically travels at about 100 kilometers per hour.
Karl Benz patented his first car, the Benz Patent-Motorwagen, in 1886.
The carabao has wide hooves, so it does not easily sink in muddy ground.
The carabao is a ruminant that chews its previously swallowed food again to digest it fully.
The carabao eats only plants such as grass, so it is called a herbivore.
A carabao uses thick lips and a strong tongue to wrap around and pull blades of grass before cutting them with its teeth.
A carabao never eats meat or other animals; it eats only plants because it is a herbivore.
In the Philippines, besides grass, farmers also feed the carabao rice straw left over after the rice harvest.
Sometimes a carabao licks salty soil or rocks to get minerals that the grass alone does not give it enough of.
In the Philippines, you often see a carabao soaking in the muddy edges of rice paddies, streams, or ponds, especially at noon. That is where it cools off after working in the heat while plowing.
As a carabao ages, it may show some paler patches on its body, a little like a person's hair turning gray.
A carabao's wide horns are often dark gray or black too, matching the color of its skin.
It is a mistake to think a carabao is gray only because it is dirty. Gray is its real skin color even when it is clean.
A carabao's thick hide can be made into tough leather for shoes, belts, and other things.
The carabao is a kind of water buffalo. Some water buffalo are almost black, but our carabao is usually gray.
The carabao loves water and often bathes in rivers or streams.
Like all mammals including humans, the carabao has a beating heart that pumps blood throughout its body.
The carabao, a large mammal, can live for about 20 to 25 years when well cared for.
Kids often ask: 'Doesn't the calf need the milk?' A mother carabao makes more milk than her calf can drink, so there is extra that can be taken without the calf going hungry.
The carabao eats grass and drinks water; its body uses the nutrients from the grass to make milk. So it is important that the carabao is healthy and well fed.
The carabao is a mammal, so a female carabao makes milk in her body to feed her calf. Farmers collect the extra milk for our food.
It is a mistake to think milk is blood turned white. Milk is made in special parts of the mother's body (mammary glands) from nutrients carried by the blood — but the milk itself is not blood.
Note: the 'carabao mango' is a sweet Philippine mango simply named after the carabao — it is not made from carabao milk.
Carabao milk looks white because many tiny droplets of fat and protein float in it; these scatter light, so we see it as white.
Because it is part of life in the countryside, the carabao is often mentioned in Filipino songs, poems, and folk stories.
The carabao became the national animal because of how many ways it helps: it plows, pulls carts, gives milk, and symbolizes the hardworking Filipino.
Kids often get confused: the national animal is the carabao, not the tamaraw. The tamaraw is a smaller, wild animal found only on Mindoro island.
Just like the carabao for the Philippines, other countries also have their own national animals, such as the tiger in India and the kangaroo in Australia.
The carabao is treated as the national animal because it stands for being hardworking and patient, qualities that Filipinos are proud of.
The carabao has appeared on old Philippine coins because it is important to farmers.
The carabao also pulls carts and heavy loads for farmers.
The scientific name of the carabao (water buffalo) is Bubalus bubalis.
The carabao is very strong, so it can pull carts and heavy loads.
The carabao wallows in mud or water to cool its body — evaporation of water from its skin removes heat, and the mud acts as a shield against direct solar radiation.
The carabao wallows in mud or water to cool its body when it is hot.
The carabao wallows in mud or water to cool its body, because it has few sweat glands and overheats easily.
When mud dries on a carabao's skin, it works like a shield against the hot sun and biting bugs such as mosquitoes and flies.
Carabaos are good swimmers and can cross rivers or lakes. They are naturally comfortable in water, so they are not afraid to swim.
A carabao loves water and mud more than a cow does. That is why you will more often see a carabao soaking in water than a cow.
A baby carabao is called a calf and it drinks milk from its mother.
Carbohydrates alone are not enough. In a balanced meal, rice (carbohydrates) is paired with a viand that has protein and a little fat. Carbohydrates give energy while protein builds the body.
When you wake up, your body's energy is low because you slept for many hours. A breakfast with carbohydrates like champorado or rice gives you the energy to stay alert in class.
Carbohydrates from rice, sweet potato, and corn are the body's main source of energy for playing and studying.
Many people think carbohydrates are bad and make you fat. That is not true. Our bodies need carbohydrates for energy. The only problem is when we eat far too much of them.
To turn glucose into energy, your body needs oxygen, which you get by breathing. Your cells combine glucose and oxygen to make energy, much like fuel burning needs air.
There are three kinds of carbohydrates: sugar found in fruit and sweets, starch found in rice and potatoes, and fiber found in vegetables. They are all carbohydrates but they do different jobs.
Where do the carbohydrates in rice come from? Plants make them using sunlight in a process called photosynthesis. So when you eat rice, you are getting energy that the sun stored in the plant!
Carbon-14 dating is used on things that were once alive, such as wood and bone, but it reaches back only about 50,000 years, so it cannot date very old fossils.
The chemical symbol for carbon is C; it is the basis of all living things.
Carbon is not created or destroyed — it is just used over and over. The carbon in your breath today may once have been part of a dinosaur long ago.
Carbon dioxide in the air is usually balanced because trees and oceans absorb it, but human activity is now adding too much.
In the natural cycle, the carbon released and absorbed is nearly equal, keeping nature in balance.
Many think diamonds last forever, but if you heat one enough it will actually burn and turn into a gas (carbon dioxide), because it is just carbon.
Scientists can now grow real diamonds in a lab using heat and pressure, and they are true carbon just like the ones from the ground.
It is a myth that diamonds come from coal. Most diamonds formed very deep in the Earth, even older than the plants that became coal.
In nature, diamonds grow into neat shapes with pointed corners, often like two pyramids joined together, because their atoms line up so evenly.
Diamonds sparkle because they bend and bounce light around inside, making the light flash and split into colors before it comes out.
Most diamonds are incredibly old, formed billions of years ago, making them older than almost all living things on Earth.
Diamonds are carried up to the Earth's surface by fast, deep volcanic eruptions that bring them from far underground.

Carbon dioxide is heavier (denser) than ordinary air, so it can settle in low places. Because of this and because it does not support burning, CO₂ is used in some fire extinguishers to smother flames.
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and sinks to the floor. That is why CO2 fire extinguishers are effective — the CO2 sinks and covers the burning area, displacing oxygen and smothering the fire.
Carbon dioxide is a gas that is part of the air. Even though it is only a small part of the atmosphere, it is very important because plants use it and it traps heat.
Carbon dioxide is only a small part of the air mixture, but plants use it to make food, and we add some every time we breathe out.
Jan Baptist van Helmont first identified carbon dioxide as a gas and coined the word 'gas'.
One molecule of carbon dioxide (CO2) has two (2) oxygen atoms.
As the amount of carbon dioxide in the air rises, Earth's average temperature rises too.
Carbon is the main element that makes up the bodies of all living things on Earth.
Carbon is an element that is a main building block of all living things. It is inside your body, in plants, and in every animal.
Carbon (such as diamond) is one of the most heat-resistant materials, melting at about 3,550 degrees Celsius.
Why does bread turn dark when over-toasted? Because of the heat, its sugar and other parts get partly burned, leaving black carbon behind. That is why it looks like charcoal when it is really burnt.
The charcoal used for grilling barbecue is almost pure carbon left over from wood. When wood is burned slowly with little air, the water and gases leave, and the black carbon stays behind.

In the Philippines, coconut shells are turned into charcoal and 'activated carbon.' Because it is almost pure carbon full of tiny holes, it is used to filter water and air — an important export product of the country.
The oil and coal we burn today are carbon that came from plants and animals that lived millions of years ago. They were buried before fully decaying, and over time their carbon became fossil fuel.
The 'lead' in a pencil is not lead metal but graphite — another form of carbon. It is soft and flakes off easily, so it leaves a black mark on paper when you write.
By weight, carbon is the second most common element in the human body (after oxygen) — roughly a fifth of your weight is carbon. It is in your muscles, fat, bones, and skin.
Carbon is an element found in all living things — in plants, animals, and your own body. Carbon is also what charcoal and pencil lead are made of.
Carbon is an element found in all living things, including our bodies and our food.

Where does the carbon in a body go when a living thing dies? Decomposers like bacteria and fungi break it down, and the carbon returns to the soil and air as carbon dioxide, ready for new plants to use again.

The carbon atoms in your body are not new — they were used by other living things before. The carbon in your breath right now may once have been inside a plant or even a dinosaur. The same carbon just cycles around again and again.
Why does food give energy? Because its carbon molecules (like sugar and fat) hold energy in the carbon connections. When your body uses oxygen to break them apart, that energy is released.

Why is carbon the center of life and not some other element? Because one carbon atom can connect to four other atoms and form long, varied chains and shapes. This flexibility allows the complex molecules of life.
When fuel does not burn completely, it gives off carbon monoxide — a poisonous gas with no smell or color that is dangerous to breathe in.
The chemical formula of carbon monoxide is CO — one carbon atom and one oxygen atom.
Plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis in the day, but they also release some when they respire, especially at night. Overall, they usually absorb more than they release.
A carbon sink is anything, like a forest or ocean, that absorbs and stores a lot of carbon.
When an animal eats a plant, carbon moves from the plant into the animal's body. This is how carbon travels along the whole food chain.
In CO2, the C stands for carbon and the O2 stands for two oxygen atoms.
Carbon forms a huge number of different compounds because it bonds easily with other atoms, making it the main building block of all living things.
Volcanoes also release carbon dioxide from inside the Earth into the air. This is a natural part of the slow carbon cycle, like the volcanoes in the Philippines monitored by PHIVOLCS.
An apex predator is a carnivore at the very top of the food chain — an animal that almost no other animal hunts, like a lion or a shark.
Carnivores have shorter intestines than herbivores because meat is easier to digest than plants, so they do not need a long path for food.
A carnivore is an animal that eats other animals, like a snake that eats rats.
There is a kind of carnivore called an insectivore — animals like bats, frogs, and lizards that mainly eat insects.
The shark is a carnivore of the sea — using its many sharp teeth, it eats fish and other animals in the water.
Carnivore and herbivore teeth are different: carnivores have sharp teeth for tearing meat, while herbivores have flat, wide teeth for grinding plants.
Carnivores have sharp, pointed teeth (fangs) used to grab and tear meat. You can see this in cats, dogs, and lions.
Even though they eat insects, carnivorous plants still make their own food from sunlight through photosynthesis like other plants — the insects are just extra nutrients.
Even though they eat insects, these plants still make their own food from sunlight through photosynthesis.
These plants eat insects because they grow in poor soil that lacks nutrients like nitrogen.
Carp is another freshwater fish that is raised in fishponds.
A carrier has one hidden recessive allele but can still pass it on to its offspring.
Carrying capacity changes: it is higher in the rainy season when food is plenty and lower during a drought.
Carrying capacity is the largest number of a kind of organism that an environment can support without running out of food, water, and space.
When animals are too crowded, disease spreads faster and their numbers go down.
A larger habitat with plenty of food has a higher carrying capacity than a small place.
When too many grass-eating animals crowd a place, the plants get used up and the land is damaged.
When forests in Mindoro are lost, the carrying capacity for the tamaraw drops, so very few remain.
In nature, the number of animals usually settles close to the carrying capacity of their place.
If the number of animals stays at the carrying capacity, the place can keep replacing its food.
When you carry a load while walking on flat ground, almost no work is done against gravity because the load does not rise.
Cartilage is smooth, flexible tissue that covers the ends of bones at joints, preventing bones from rubbing together.
Cassava is made into flour and used in snacks such as cassava cake.
Eating raw or undercooked cassava can cause vomiting, dizziness, and other illness.
Cassava is a starchy root crop that is cooked as food in many parts of the Philippines.
Cassava is different from sweet potato; they are different plants even though both are edible roots.

The Cassini spacecraft orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017; during its mission it deployed the Huygens probe onto Titan and studied Saturn's rings in detail. In 2017, it was deliberately plunged into Saturn's atmosphere (the 'Grand Finale') to protect Saturn's moons from contamination.
A cat scratches objects to keep its claws sharp and to leave a scent that marks its territory.
A cat cleans itself by licking its own fur.
Cats and dogs have sharp teeth that are suited for eating meat.
A cat cannot see in complete darkness; it still needs at least a little light, such as moonlight or starlight.
A cat's two eyes face forward side by side, helping it judge distance well before pouncing on prey.
A cat's eyes can see well even in dim light, so cats move around well at night.
A cat's eyes, whiskers, and claws all work together so it can see, feel, and catch prey at night.
The position of a cat's whiskers shows its mood; they push forward when it is curious and pull back when it is scared.
A cat's long whiskers act like sensitive feelers that sense touch from objects around it.
A cat usually has 24 whiskers, 12 on each cheek.
A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up, because it lowers the energy needed to start the reaction.
Before becoming a chrysalis, the caterpillar keeps eating leaves and sheds its skin several times to grow.
A larva such as a caterpillar eats a lot, especially leaves, so it can grow quickly before becoming a pupa.
Fish have a lateral line system — a row of pressure-sensitive cells along the body — that allows them to detect pressure waves and vibrations in water, similar to how we hear sound in air.
The catfish eats almost anything, such as small animals, worms, and bits of plants.
The catfish's skin is slippery because of a thin slimy coat that protects it from germs and injury.
The white cattle egret often follows a carabao to eat the insects it stirs up, so both animals benefit from this relationship.
Cattle are herbivores, so they eat grass and leafy plants.
No plants grow in a cave's darkness, so where does food come from? A big source is guano, the droppings of bats. Many tiny insects and animals eat the guano, and they in turn become food for others.
Many cave animals have tiny eyes or are fully blind. Since there is no light in the dark, eyes are useless, so over many generations they shrank away to save the body the energy of building them.

Cave life is easily harmed. Used to silence, darkness, and cool air, cave animals can die when people disturb them, shine lights, or pollute the cave. That is why it matters to protect caves and not carelessly disturb them.
Not every cave stays totally dark — in some caves tiny creatures like glowworms make their own light (bioluminescence). They use this glow to lure and trap small insects that fly toward it.
Many cave animals have thin, moist skin, so they must stay in the damp, cool parts of the cave. If their surroundings dry out, they die easily — which is why they are rarely found in dry spots.

Cave animals are different from night-roaming (nocturnal) animals like owls. A nocturnal animal still has large, healthy eyes for the dim moonlight, while a true cave animal has no working eyes because a cave has no light at all.

Many Philippine caves, such as those in Bohol, Samar, and Palawan, are home to unusual little animals like cave crickets and pale eyeless shrimp. They are part of our country's living richness (biodiversity).

Not every animal in a cave is a true 'cave animal.' Bats sleep in caves by day but fly out at night to eat fruit or insects. They still have eyes and color — they are only cave visitors, unlike true troglobites that never leave.
An echo in a cave happens when the sound of your shout bounces off the hard rock walls and comes back to your ears.

Why should we protect caves that have cave fish? They are used to very clean, still water inside the cave. If dirt or pollution gets in from outside, they are easily harmed because there are so few of them and nowhere else to go.
Blind cave fish have a special body sense that can feel even tiny movements in the water.

Why do scientists study cave fish? Because they naturally lost their eyes and can survive on little food, doctors learn how eyes form and how the body handles sugar. This helps them understand some human health problems.
Some cave fish are blind or have no eyes because sight is useless in total darkness.
In a cave there is no day or night, it is always dark. So some cave fish lost the natural body clock that tells when to sleep. Unlike us, who get sleepy at night, they cannot tell what time it is.

Are there cave fish in the Philippines? The Philippines has many caves, like in Sagada and Palawan, and inside them live animals suited to the dark, such as bats, shrimp, and cave invertebrates. Many of these also lost color or live in darkness, just like cave fish elsewhere.
The mineral formations inside a cave, such as stalactites and stalagmites, are called speleothems.
No green plants grow inside a dark cave because plants need sunlight to make their food.
When mineral water flows down a cave wall, it builds a smooth sheet of rock called flowstone.
The cave swiftlet is a bird that lives in dark caves and uses sound (echolocation) to find its way in the dark.
Caves form when underground water dissolves rock and hollows out a large space.
Giving a home shade and good airflow reduces the need for air conditioning and electricity.

The cell cycle has checkpoints that check if everything is correct before proceeding to division — if DNA is damaged, the checkpoint halts division to prevent errors from being passed to daughter cells.
Before a cell divides, it first grows and copies all of its DNA so that each new cell will be complete.
Robert Hooke was the first to see and name the 'cell' using a microscope in 1665.
Normal cells divide only when signaled to divide and stop when signaled to stop — cancer cells do not respond to these signals and continue dividing without stopping.
Plants grow at the tips of roots and shoots because that is where the meristem is — a region of cells that continuously divide to lengthen the plant.
The cell membrane acts as a gatekeeper, controlling what enters and exits the cell.
Peroxisomes are organelles that store enzymes to break down harmful molecules like hydrogen peroxide — liver cells are rich in peroxisomes that help detoxify the blood.
Ribosomes make proteins that the body needs for growth and repair.
Plant cells have three structures absent from animal cells: a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole — in contrast, animal cells have centrioles that help with cell division.
Cells stay small because as a cell grows its surface area to volume ratio decreases — this means it becomes harder for larger cells to import nutrients and export waste efficiently.
Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann proposed the cell theory, that all living things are made of cells.
Animal cells have no cell wall, so they are softer and often more rounded in shape.
Some living things like bacteria are made of just a single cell for the whole body.

Bacteria are true cells with DNA, cytoplasm, and a cell membrane so they have characteristics of living things — viruses are not true cells and lack many characteristics of living things so they are not clearly alive or dead.
Bones are not dead structures — bones contain living cells called osteocytes that maintain the bone and osteoblasts that build new bone tissue.
All living things are made of tiny units called cells.
In the Philippines, the most common cancers in women are breast and cervical cancer, while lung cancer is common in men — early detection and a healthy lifestyle help prevent them.
Robert Hooke first used the word "cell" in 1665 when he looked at cork under a microscope.
Cells divide to make more cells, which is how we grow and how our wounds heal.
Cells divide to make more cells, which is how we grow and how wounds heal.
Every cell has a thin covering called the cell membrane that controls what goes in and out.
Similar cells group together to form tissues, which build up into organs and body systems.
Similar cells group together to form tissues, and tissues build up organs.
The mitochondria make energy from food, which is why they are called the cell's powerhouse.
During mitosis, plant cells form a cell plate in the middle to separate the two new cells, while animal cells form a cleavage furrow that pinches in the middle to divide.
Muscle contraction works through the sliding filament theory — myosin heads grab and pull actin filaments causing the sarcomere to shorten and the muscle to contract.
Nerve cells do not directly touch each other — between two nerve cells is a gap called a synapse where chemicals called neurotransmitters carry the message from one nerve to the next.
The thin skin of an onion is easy to look at under a microscope to see plant cells.
All organelles of a cell work together — the nucleus gives instructions, ribosomes make proteins, the Golgi ships them, and mitochondria provide energy for all these processes.
The cell is the smallest unit of life that can live and work on its own.
Volvox is a colonial alga that shows an early stage of cell specialization — most of its cells work for movement while a few are specialized for reproduction — a simple division of labor.
Stem cells have different levels of potential: totipotent cells like the zygote can become any cell type, pluripotent can become most types, and multipotent can become only a limited range.
The human body is made of trillions of cells that work together to keep us alive.
The vacuole is like a storage bag inside the cell that holds water and food.
Aerobic respiration makes much more ATP than anaerobic respiration because glucose is fully broken down.
Respiration returns carbon dioxide to the air, which plants use again in photosynthesis.
Energy is stored in the chemical bonds of glucose, and respiration releases it.
When you exercise, cellular respiration speeds up to make more energy.
The energy from respiration is stored in a molecule called ATP, the cell's energy "currency."
Cellular respiration is the process by which cells release energy from food.
The Celsius scale is named after Anders Celsius, a Swedish astronomer.
There are two common temperature scales: Celsius and Fahrenheit.
The Celsius scale is named after Anders Celsius, a Swedish astronomer.

Water freezes (turns to ice) at 0 degrees Celsius (0°C).

Cement is a fine powder made from limestone and clay that are burned together in a very hot kiln.
Modern Portland cement was invented by Joseph Aspdin in 1824.
Too much water in a concrete mix weakens the hardened concrete by creating pores that reduce structural strength; the water-to-cement ratio must be carefully controlled.
To find the center of gravity of an irregular shape, hang it from different points and mark the plumb line each time — the point where all lines cross is the center of gravity.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa tilts but does not fall because its center of gravity still falls within the footprint of its base.
When stacking blocks, the tower topples when its center of gravity moves beyond the edge of the bottom block's support area.
Sumo wrestlers adopt a low, wide stance to lower their center of gravity, making it much harder for opponents to push them over or lift them.
The center of gravity of an object is the point where all of its weight seems to be concentrated. The object can be balanced at this point without toppling.
When you carry something heavy in one hand, you naturally lean your body the other way so your center of gravity stays over your feet. That is how we keep our balance.
An object is more stable when its center of gravity is low and its base is wide. That is why something wide and heavy at the bottom is hard to tip over.
The abbreviation for centimeter is "cm".
One centimeter equals 10 millimeters.
The bite of a large centipede is painful and can cause swelling in a person, but it is usually not deadly to a healthy human.
Centipedes and millipedes are cold-blooded, so they depend on the warmth around them to stay active.
In many Filipino homes, we see a house centipede with long, numerous legs that runs fast across walls or bathrooms. Its many legs help it quickly chase the insects it eats, like cockroaches.
When a centipede or millipede moves, its many legs push in orderly waves, so they do not get tangled.
A centipede's many legs are made for running fast on land, not for swimming. It prefers to live in damp places like under rocks or dry leaves, where it can scurry using all its legs.
Millipedes help the soil by breaking down rotting leaves into nutrients.
Even at constant speed, an object in circular motion has an acceleration pointing toward the center, because the direction of its velocity keeps changing.
Centripetal force changes only the direction of the motion, not the speed, which is why the speed stays the same in uniform circular motion even as it keeps turning.
When you swing a bucket of water in a circle, a force pulls it toward the center (centripetal force) and keeps the water from spilling — even when the bucket is upside down at the top.
Taal's 1911 eruption is one of the deadly events still talked about, showing a lake volcano can be dangerous more than once in a century.
Scientists have much clearer eruption records for the last hundred years than for older times, because instruments and agencies now watch daily.
Octopuses and cuttlefish change color to blend into their surroundings and hide from enemies.

Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish have thousands of chromatophores in their skin — each is a sac of pigment controlled by a tiny muscle that stretches or shrinks it, enabling color changes in milliseconds.
Their skin has thousands of tiny color cells called chromatophores that muscles open or close to change color.
Cephalopods like squid and cuttlefish are considered smart and have larger brains than most other invertebrates.
Ceramics like plates and pots are made of clay hardened by fire — they are very hard and can take the heat of a stove, but they are also brittle and shatter when dropped.
Bricks and tiles are also ceramics because they are made from clay fired in heat.
Ceramic does not let electricity flow through it, so it is used as an insulator on power poles.
At the lower back of the brain is a part called the cerebellum that helps with balance and smooth movement, like walking or dancing.
The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and it handles thinking and planning.
Ceres was discovered in 1801, the first object found in the asteroid belt.
Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and is also considered a dwarf planet.
Chalk is made of calcium carbonate.
A chameleon does not change color by moving paint — it has tiny crystals in its skin that it spaces closer or farther apart to change which color of light bounces back.
When it spots an insect, the chameleon points both eyes at the prey together to judge how far away it is.

Scientists use chromatography to find out what substances are in ink, food, or medicine.
A single black ink is often a mixture of many colored pigments, not just one color.
The dot of color should sit above the water line, not underwater, so it doesn't just wash away.
In paper chromatography, water rises up the paper and carries the colors upward with it.
After chromatography, you can see streaks of different colors lined up along the paper.
Have you seen chromatography without knowing it? When water drips on writing and the ink spreads outward with a streak of color at its edge, that's chromatography happening in real life.

Real-world use: investigators use chromatography to find out what ink was used in a letter. If two inks split into different color patterns, they know different pens were used the document might be forged.
In chromatography, a liquid like water travels up a paper. As it moves, it carries the parts of a mixture along. Some parts get carried fast and others slow, so they spread apart and separate.
Misconception: that chromatography adds or paints new colors. Not true. It puts nothing new in the colors that appear were already inside the mixture. It only separates the ones already hidden there.

Worth remembering: chromatography only separates mixtures made of different substances. It cannot break apart a single pure substance like clean water, because there's only one thing in it nothing to separate.
Why use paper? Paper has tiny gaps that soak up water, so the liquid climbs up on its own. On plastic or glass the liquid won't soak in, so chromatography wouldn't work.
How are results read? Scientists look at how far each color climbed compared to the water. A given substance always travels the same relative distance, so this can be used to identify what it is.
Why do some colors climb higher? A substance that doesn't stick much to the paper and prefers to travel with the water rises higher. One that clings tightly to the paper stays lower down.
Colors that dissolve more easily in the water travel farther up, which is why they separate.

Why are wires made of metal? Current flows easily through metals like copper — these are called conductors. Rubber or plastic are insulators that block current, so they are used to coat wires so they are safe to hold.
In a simple circuit, current travels around the whole loop — leaving one end of the battery, passing through the bulb, and returning to the other end. It is not used up in the bulb but keeps flowing.

When a battery is reversed in a DC circuit, the current direction also reverses — an LED will stop glowing (since it is a diode that only allows one direction), and a DC motor will spin the other way.

In a parallel circuit, the path branches so the current splits across separate routes. This is how home wiring is set up — so even if you turn off one light, the others keep working, because each has its own path.
When you charge a phone, current flows from the wall outlet into the charger, and it fills the phone's battery with energy. Later, current from that battery is what powers your screen and apps.

In a series circuit where bulbs are connected one after another in a single loop, the current is the same in every part. None is lost or added — however much passes through the first bulb, the same passes through the next.
A fuse contains a thin wire that melts when current is too large — it breaks the circuit to prevent fire, but the fuse must be replaced after it melts (unlike a circuit breaker which resets).
When part of a circuit is broken or open, electricity cannot flow through it, so the bulb will not light.
Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the sum of all voltages around a closed loop equals zero — this means all energy supplied by the battery is used up by the circuit components.
Philippine homes have several branch circuits in the panel — heavy appliances like air conditioners and ovens need their own dedicated circuit to avoid overloading a single breaker.
Any device connected to a circuit — called the 'load' — has its own resistance — light bulbs, electric fans, and motors all provide resistance that controls the current flowing through them.
For a circuit to work, every connection must be clean and tight. If a connection is loose, the bulb may flicker or stop lighting altogether.
Household wiring in the Philippines uses parallel circuits — so turning off the living room light does not affect the kitchen light, and every outlet receives 220 volts.
Electrical resistance is a material's opposition to current flow — thick, short wires have low resistance while thin, long wires have higher resistance.
In a series circuit, total resistance equals the sum of all individual resistances — so adding more resistors in series reduces the current throughout the whole circuit.
A bulb's filament is thin and has high resistance, so it opposes the flow of current. That resistance is what makes the filament heat up until it glows.
In a series circuit, the current is the same at every point — because there is only one path for electrons to flow, the same amount of current passes through every component.
A short circuit happens when the two ends of the battery connect directly without passing through the bulb. Too much current flows, so the wire heats up quickly and can cause a fire.
When a short circuit occurs, current becomes enormous — the fuse or circuit breaker trips to protect the wires from overheating and potentially causing a fire.
In science, circuits are drawn using symbols: a line for a wire, a short-and-long line pair for a battery, and a circle with a cross for a bulb. This is called a circuit diagram.

The carbon dioxide released when oil, coal, and gas burn is a greenhouse gas that traps heat and warms the Earth.

Carbon naturally moves in a cycle: animals release it and plants and the sea soak it up. It used to be balanced. But because people burn so much fuel, more is released than absorbed, so carbon dioxide builds up.

It is called the greenhouse effect because it works like a greenhouse, a glass room for plants. The glass lets in the sun's heat but keeps it from leaving, so it stays warm inside. The gases in the atmosphere do the same thing.

Even as a kid, you can do something to cut carbon dioxide: turn off lights and gadgets when not in use, walk or bike for short trips, and plant trees. They seem small, but when many people do them, it is a big help for the world.

Many people think the warming world is caused by the ozone hole, but these are different things. The ozone hole is about UV rays that burn skin. The greenhouse effect is about heat trapped by gases. The two have different causes.

Not all of the greenhouse effect is bad. Without some carbon dioxide in the air, Earth would be far too cold and freeze over. The natural greenhouse effect is why the temperature is comfortable enough for life.

Some think carbon dioxide is what we breathe in to live, but that is wrong. Oxygen is what we need to breathe in; carbon dioxide is what we breathe out. A little CO2 is not poison, but in the atmosphere, too much of it warms the world.

To cut down carbon dioxide, people use energy from the sun (solar) and wind, which give off no smoke. The Philippines gets a lot of sunshine, so it is a good source of electricity that does not add to greenhouse gases.

Besides carbon dioxide, rice farms and animals like cattle and water buffalo release methane, another strong greenhouse gas. Since the Philippines has many rice fields, this is also part of the story of a warming world.
Trees soak up carbon dioxide from the air when they make food through photosynthesis. So when forests are cut down, more carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere and the world warms faster.
Carbon dioxide is not the only greenhouse gas. Others include methane (from garbage and animals), water vapor, and nitrous oxide. All of them trap heat in the atmosphere.

Fish, amphibians, and reptiles are cold-blooded — their body temperature changes with their surroundings.
Cold-blooded animals, such as snakes and lizards, get their heat from their surroundings.
Cold-blooded animals, like snakes and lizards, depend on the warmth of their surroundings, so they bask in the sun to warm up.
The body temperature of cold-blooded animals goes up when it is warm outside and down when it is cold.
Heat is not the only danger; some vaccines are also damaged by freezing, so the storage must not be too cold either.
If a vaccine gets too warm, it can spoil and stop giving protection even if it is still injected into a child.
The cold chain is an unbroken system of cooling that keeps vaccines cold all the way from the factory to a child's arm.
In places without steady electricity, solar-powered refrigerators driven by sunlight are used to keep vaccines cold.
Some vaccine bottles have a small label that changes color when they have been too hot, warning health workers not to use them.
Not all deserts are hot; there are also cold deserts like Antarctica that get almost no rain.
People often catch colds and flu more during the rainy and cooler months in the Philippines.
Washing your hands often with soap helps stop you from catching a cold or flu.
Antibiotics do not cure a cold or flu because they only fight bacteria, not viruses.
When you have a cold or flu, getting plenty of rest and drinking lots of water helps you recover.
When something cools down, it contracts or gets smaller.
The drops on the outside of a cold glass come from water vapor in the air, not from water leaking out.
Gather every listed material on a tray first, then start the steps, so a missing spoon does not pause the test halfway.
In any collision, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after — called conservation of momentum, seen when billiard balls collide.
In a colloid the particles are medium-sized, so they stay suspended and do not settle out.
Milk is an example of a colloid because tiny droplets of fat are suspended in its water.
The Tyndall effect occurs when a beam of light becomes visible passing through a colloid like milk, because the tiny particles scatter the light.
There are different kinds of colloids such as foam, gel (like gelatin), and emulsion like mayonnaise.
Dark objects absorb more radiant heat, while white objects reflect more of it away.
Inside the eye are tiny cells called cones that detect color when there is enough light.
Colour blindness occurs when some cones in the retina are missing or do not work correctly — the most common type is difficulty distinguishing red from green.
Color blindness is usually passed from parents to their child through genes.
Color blindness is more common in boys than girls because it is inherited through the X chromosome, and boys have only one X.
Besides cones, the eye has rod cells that help us see in dim light but cannot see color.
There are different types of color blindness; the most common mixes up red and green, but a few people struggle with blue and yellow.
Of the three, octopuses and cuttlefish are fastest because they use muscles, while chameleons rely on crystals and are slower.
Changing color is not magic; it happens because of special skin cells that hold color inside them.
A star's color shows how hot it is: blue-white stars are the hottest, while reddish stars are cooler.
Holding up a red card or a green card is a movement-and-color message, a cousin of a traffic light that two people can copy in a classroom game.
Many colorful birds use their bright feathers to attract a mate.
The Colosseum could hold about 50,000 to 80,000 spectators.
Octopuses and cuttlefish can change colour within one second using special skin cells called chromatophores — they use this to hide from predators or communicate with other cephalopods.
Scientists say the colugo is one of the closest relatives of primates such as monkeys and humans.

While gliding, the colugo can change the shape of its skin a little to turn or head where it wants to go. By tightening or loosening the membrane on each side, it lines itself up to land on the right branch.

Both the colugo and the flying squirrel glide through the air, but the colugo's skin is wider. In the colugo, the membrane reaches even between the fingers and to the tail, so it can cross farther than a flying squirrel.
The colugo feeds on leaves, young shoots, flowers, and fruits of plants.
Most of the water the flying lemur needs comes from the fresh leaves it eats.
Even though it is called a flying lemur, the colugo is not a true lemur but belongs to its own group called Dermoptera.

The patagium is not only for gliding. The mother colugo folds it to make a kind of hammock or pouch where she can hold her baby. While the mother glides through the air, the baby stays safe inside the folded membrane. So the patagium is also like a home for the little colugo.

Both the colugo and the bat have a skin membrane, but they are used differently. A bat can flap its wing to rise and truly fly. The colugo's patagium, however, is only for gliding downward; it cannot be flapped. So the two travel through the air in different ways.

When an enemy comes near, like a snake or an eagle, the colugo quickly leaps and glides away using its patagium. Because it can move fast to a faraway tree, it is hard to catch. So the gliding membrane is also a way for the colugo to stay safe.
The colugo has a wide flap of skin called a patagium that stretches from its neck to its tail tip and between its legs.
The Philippines has its own colugo called the kagwang, found in the forests of Mindanao.
The colugo is threatened when forests are cut down because it needs trees close together to glide between.
In wind instruments like the flute, the air inside vibrates by resonance, and the length of the tube sets the pitch.
The combined gas law merges the laws of Boyle, Charles, and Gay-Lussac into the single relationship PV/T = constant.
Combustion is a chemical reaction in which a substance reacts rapidly with oxygen, releasing heat and light, and usually forming carbon dioxide and water.
The solid central part of a comet is called the nucleus, and when it nears the Sun, its ice vaporizes and forms a fuzzy cloud of gas and dust around it called the coma.
A comet's nucleus is like a dirty snowball — a mix of ice, dust, and rock.
A comet is a space object made of ice, dust, and rock, sometimes called a 'dirty snowball'.

A short-period comet is one that returns to the inner solar system in less than 200 years; most of these originate from the Kuiper Belt and their orbits can be calculated and predicted by astronomers.

Most comets come from very cold regions at the outer edge of our solar system, such as the Kuiper Belt and the more distant Oort Cloud. From there, some comets are occasionally sent on paths toward the Sun.

When a comet nears the Sun, the heat melts its ice and releases gas and dust that form a long tail. The tail always points away from the Sun, not behind the comet, because the Sun's wind and light push it outward.
Many comets have two tails: one tail made of gas and another made of dust.
A comet is made of a lot of ice, so it grows a tail, while an asteroid is mostly rock or metal and has no tail.
Most comets come from the cold, distant outer parts of the solar system, far from the Sun, where their ice stays frozen.

Comets originate from two regions: short-period comets (that return quickly) come from the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune, while long-period comets come from the distant Oort Cloud at the outer edge of the solar system.
Barnacles attach to a whale's skin to ride along into food-rich waters, while the whale is barely affected—a classic example of commensalism.
In commensalism, one partner benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed.
When a bird builds its nest on a tree branch, it gains a safe home, while the tree is neither helped nor harmed—this is commensalism.
Commensalism is not always permanent—depending on conditions, it can shift into mutualism (if both start to benefit) or parasitism (if one starts to be harmed).
In Philippine fields, the cattle egret follows carabaos and cattle to eat the insects stirred up by their walking—the bird benefits while the animal is unaffected.
In commensalism, one organism usually benefits by getting a free ride, shelter, or food scraps from a larger organism that does not notice or get bothered by it.
In phoresy, tiny creatures hitch a ride on a larger animal to move to a new place—like some insects that cling to a bird or fly, getting transport without bothering the carrier.
The remora has a suction-like pad on its head to attach to a shark; it gets a free ride and eats leftover scraps, while the shark hardly notices it.
Commensalism and parasitism differ: in parasitism one is harmed (like lice on a person), but in commensalism the other is not harmed at all.
The host is not harmed because the commensal does not take its food or energy—it only takes the host's extras, leftovers, or unneeded space.
The remora fish attaches to a shark's body and eats its leftover food scraps, but the shark is not affected.
The common cold is caused by rhinoviruses and other viruses; antibiotics do not work against it because it is viral, not bacterial. Rest and fluids help recovery.
Hazard maps from past eruptions show which rivers and slopes were hit before, helping families talk about where danger tends to return.
Towns near active volcanoes practice listening for PHIVOLCS alerts, because the last hundred years show unrest can grow over hours or days.
After you hear a star-pattern name, compare it with a printed star chart so you can see which lights in tonight's sky the story is about.
Comparing Mayon's many eruptions with Pinatubo's rare giant blast helps families see that nearby volcanoes can follow very different clocks.
A compass needle can spin freely so it can turn to line up with north.
A compass needle points north because it is a tiny magnet pulled by Earth's magnetic field.
The star-shaped figure that shows the directions on a map is called a compass rose.
The competitive exclusion principle states that two species using exactly the same resources in the same place cannot coexist indefinitely.

Beetles also go through complete metamorphosis. Their larva is often a plump grub that lives in soil or wood, eating and growing, before becoming a pupa and then coming out as a beetle with hard wing covers.

Inside the pupa or cocoon, the caterpillar's body mostly breaks down into a thick nourishing mush. From special cells that were hidden all along, a new butterfly body is rebuilt — wings, legs, and eyes. So from outside it looks like nothing is happening, but a huge change is going on inside.
The four-stage change with a chrysalis is called complete metamorphosis, which bees and beetles also undergo.

Knowing the stages of metamorphosis is important for farmers. Usually it is the larva (the worm) that damages crops, because that is when they eat the most, not the adult insect. So if farmers know when the pest is in the larva stage, it is easier to protect the plants.
In a complete fracture the bone splits all the way into two, while in a partial fracture it only cracks without fully separating.
It is better to keep meat and oil out of compost because they smell and attract pests.

For compost to work well, it needs two kinds of material: 'greens' (wet things like vegetable peels) that give the microbes nitrogen, and 'browns' (dry things like dead leaves) that give energy. When the two are balanced, rotting is faster and doesn't smell bad.
Who works inside compost? Different teams: bacteria quickly eat soft things like fruit scraps, while fungi slowly break down tough things like leaves and twigs.
Healthy compost needs a mix of wet green scraps and dry brown leaves.
Compost is a natural fertilizer, so plants do not need chemical fertilizers as much.
A compost pile is a collection of kitchen scraps and leaves broken down by bacteria and fungi; the process generates heat and eventually creates rich fertilizer for plants.
Worm castings are packed with nutrients like nitrogen that plants need to grow. So when mixed into soil, plants grow healthier and faster — it works like a natural fertilizer.

An adult worm has a thick band (the clitellum) on its body. From it, the worm makes a tiny cocoon that holds eggs. From each cocoon, several baby worms hatch — which is how they multiply in a worm bin.
A worm bin should be kept in a shady, cool place because worms die in too much heat.
Worms have no eyes, but they have special cells in their skin that sense light and dark. So they know to move away from light and stay in the safe, dark soil even though they cannot see like we do.

Compost worms reduce household garbage. Instead of throwing vegetable scraps and fruit peels into the trash that ends up in a landfill, the worms eat it and turn it into fertilizer — a help to the environment.

In regular compost, leaves and waste rot in a hot pile with the help of bacteria and fungi alone. In vermicompost, worms help eat and break it down, so the result is faster and finer, and the pile does not need to get very hot.
When atoms bond, the compound that forms has different properties from its elements—like table salt being safe to eat even though it is made from dangerous sodium and chlorine.
A crane is a compound machine that uses pulleys to reduce force, a boom arm as a lever to extend reach, and a winch as a wheel and axle to wind the cable.
An escalator is a compound machine: a motor drives gears that move a continuous chain, which carries the steps up or down in a loop.
Gutenberg's original printing press was a compound machine using a large screw driven by a lever to press the platen onto paper, combined with rollers for inking.
A manual sugarcane press uses a long lever arm to turn two rollers (wheel and axle) that squeeze the cane to extract juice.
A wheelbarrow is a compound machine combining a second-class lever, where the wheel is the fulcrum and the handles apply effort, with a wheel and axle.
The compound microscope is widely credited to Zacharias Janssen of the Netherlands, around 1590.
Once a compound forms, it has new properties unlike its elements, like salt being safe to eat even though sodium alone is dangerous.
When atoms of two or more elements combine, they form a compound with new properties; for example, water is different from hydrogen and oxygen, which are both gases.
The elements in a compound cannot be separated easily; a chemical change is needed to break it apart.
CNG (compressed natural gas) is used as fuel in some buses and vehicles. It is mainly methane compressed at high pressure. It burns more cleanly than diesel or petrol and produces less pollution.
Longitudinal waves are also called compressional waves, so sound, ultrasound, and P-waves all belong on that same example list.
A difference to keep straight: compressions are crowded particles along the path, not taller bumps; taller bumps belong to transverse crests.
A computer or phone stores everything — pictures, words, and music — as millions of tiny switches that are simply on or off, written as 1s and 0s.
The brain of a computer is a tiny chip packed with billions of extremely small switches called transistors, which turn on and off incredibly fast to do calculations.
In modern cameras and telescopes, concave and convex lenses are combined to make sharper images. The concave lens helps fix certain light errors.
A concave mirror, which curves inward, gathers light together at a point called the focus.
A solution with a lot of solute in a little water is concentrated (strong-tasting); adding more water makes it dilute (weaker-tasting).
Adding little water to calamansi juice keeps it very sour; adding much water makes it mild. Concentration controls how sour the drink tastes.
Pollutant concentrations in water and air are often measured in parts per million (ppm); one ppm is equivalent to one drop of substance in one million drops of water.
The standard musical note A4 has a frequency of 440 Hz, used for tuning instruments.
The Concorde was a passenger jet that flew at Mach 2, about 2,180 km/h — twice the speed of sound.
Concrete hardens by a chemical reaction between cement and water called hydration — not simply by drying out; hydration produces new crystalline compounds that bind the mixture hard.
As concrete hardens and shrinks a little, it can crack, so builders add joints or gaps to control where cracks form.
As concrete sets, it gives off heat because the reaction with water releases energy.
Concrete hardens not by drying out but through a chemical reaction between cement and water, so it must be kept damp while it gains strength.
Concrete is a mix of cement, sand, gravel, and water that hardens into a stone-like material.
Even after concrete is hard, water remains locked inside its crystals through the chemical reaction.
The ancient Romans were the first to use concrete widely.
Concrete is very strong when squeezed or pushed, but weak when stretched or bent — so steel bars are placed inside it to keep it from cracking.
Clouds form when water vapor rises into cooler air and condenses into tiny droplets.
The dew point is the temperature at which water vapour in the air begins to condense into dew or water drops. When the air temperature falls below the dew point, dew forms.
Condensation is gas (vapor) changing back into liquid water, like dew on a cold glass.
In conduction, heat moves when two objects touch directly. That is why when you hold a metal spoon in hot soup, your hand feels the heat.
Metals are good heat conductors because they have free electrons that move quickly and carry energy — this is why metal pots heat up quickly.
Inside a capacitor, two metal plates are separated by a non-conducting material called a dielectric — the dielectric increases how much charge the capacitor can store.
Conductors like copper and other metals let electricity pass through easily, which is why wires are made from them.
Some sea snails called cone snails, found in Philippine seas, have a venom they shoot like a harpoon to catch prey.
After a class discussion, confirm a Sun idea in a trustworthy book or science site, so a guess about sunshine is checked, not just voted on.
The law of conservation of energy says that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.
The Law of Conservation of Mass, credited to Antoine Lavoisier, states that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
In a collision with no outside force, the total momentum of the objects before they hit equals the total momentum afterward — it is not lost, only shared around.

Long before modern calendars, ancient Filipinos and other native peoples used the changing constellations as a sign of the seasons — for example, when certain stars appeared, they knew it was time to plant or harvest.

It is a misconception that a constellation 'disappears' or dies when we can no longer see it. In truth it is still there — it has just moved to the same side as the Sun, so it rises in the daytime with the Sun and is washed out by its glare, hidden from our night view.

How can you notice the change? Look at the sky at the same time (say, eight in the evening) every few nights over several weeks or months. You'll see the constellations slowly shift westward, with new ones rising in the east — that's the proof that Earth orbits the Sun.
Near the Earth's poles, some constellations never set and can be seen all year, but they cannot be seen from the Philippines.
There are 88 official constellations (star patterns) in the whole sky.
Different cultures see different pictures in the same stars: what one calls a bear another might call a ladle or an animal. Many Filipino legends are tied to stars like Balatik.
The two end stars of the Big Dipper can be used as pointers to find Polaris, the North Star.
Constellations are hard to see in bright cities because the city lights hide the dimmer stars.
You do not need a telescope to see most constellations; your own eyes are enough on a clear night. Let your eyes get used to the dark and you will see many more stars.
The stars in a constellation can differ in color and brightness, from reddish to white or bluish.
To read the sky, people use a star map or star chart that shows where each constellation appears. Today there are also apps and planetariums that help point out the stars overhead.
Which constellations you can see depends on where you live on the Earth. Because the Philippines is near the equator, we can see stars from both the northern and southern parts of the sky.
There are twelve constellations called the zodiac, found along the path the Sun appears to travel across the sky during the year.
Constellations are groups of stars that form patterns in the sky, like the three lined-up stars Filipinos call Tatlong Maria (in Orion).
Most forces need to touch an object to act on it, but gravity, magnetism, and static electricity can pull or push without touching at all.
Continental crust, which forms the land, is thicker and lighter (made of granite), while oceanic crust beneath the seas is thinner and denser (made of basalt).
Because the plates move, the continents slowly drifted apart to where they are today.
The coastlines of South America and Africa look like they fit together like puzzle pieces, a clue that they were once joined.
Millions of years ago, all the continents were joined together in one huge landmass called Pangaea.
Keep one sample unchanged as a comparison, so you can see what happens when you do nothing as well as when you change one thing.
Write a short list of what you will keep the same, like water volume and stirring, so helpers do not quietly change the fair test.
In convection, hot water or air rises because it is lighter, and cold, heavier fluid sinks. This repeated rising and sinking is called a convection current.
If you hold your hand above a candle (not beside it), it feels much hotter — because the hot air from the flame rises straight up. That is convection you can feel with your hand.
Birds like eagles soar high with almost no flapping by riding on columns of warm rising air called thermals. These are air convection currents that birds use to stay aloft.
A hot air balloon floats because a burner heats the air inside it. The hot air is lighter than the cooler air outside, so the whole balloon rises up.
At night, land cools faster than the sea, so now the warmer air rises over the sea and cool air flows in from the land. This is the land breeze that blows from the land out to the sea.
Convection also happens deep inside the Earth: the very hot mantle slowly circulates as hotter rock rises and cooler rock sinks. This motion pushes the plates that PHIVOLCS studies.
Inside the Earth, the very hot, nearly molten rock of the mantle slowly rises and sinks by convection. This slow movement pushes the tectonic plates that cause earthquakes and volcanoes.
The habagat and amihan in the Philippines are large seasonal convection winds, caused by the uneven heating of huge land masses (continents) and oceans at different times of the year.
Convection happens only in fluids — liquids and gases like water and air — because their particles are free to move and flow. Solids do not convect because their particles are fixed in place.
A sea breeze is an example of convection: land heats up faster than the sea, so warm air over the land rises and cooler air from the sea moves in to take its place.
The air above the sea is cooler and heavier, so it sinks. After sinking, it moves toward the land to replace the warm air that rose. This circular movement is the convection loop.

Warm air rises for the same reason a hot-air balloon rises: when air heats up, its particles spread out so it becomes lighter than the cooler air around it. Lighter things float up. The same thing happens at the coast during the day.

Water heats up slowly and cools down slowly because it can soak up a lot of heat before its temperature rises. Land heats up quickly. Because of this difference, there is always a warmer side and a cooler side, which makes air move.
Hot air rises because it is lighter (less dense) — when heated, the particles move faster and the air expands, so there are fewer particles in the same space.
At a convergent boundary, two plates push together and collide; this is where tall mountain ranges, deep trenches, and frequent earthquakes and volcanoes form.

How can a microscope magnify so much? It uses two convex lenses in a row: the lens near the object (objective) magnifies the image first, then the lens you look through (eyepiece) magnifies it again — so you can see very tiny cells.
A convex mirror, which curves outward, spreads light apart and makes images look smaller.
A convex mirror gives a wide-angle view with a smaller image — used in vehicle side mirrors and road safety mirrors at blind corners.

What's the difference between convex and concave lenses? A convex lens bulges outward and is thick in the middle (it gathers light), while a concave lens curves inward and is thinner in the middle (it spreads light). Remember: 'concave' is like a 'cave' that hollows inward.
Eating well-cooked food and using clean water help prevent worms.
When grilling over charcoal, food is cooked by infrared radiation from the glowing embers — this radiation is absorbed by the food and heats it from outside.
When an egg is cooked it changes permanently and can never go back to being raw.
Cooking food with high heat kills many microbes, which makes cooked food safer to eat.
Cooking a pancake or egg is a chemical reaction driven by heat: the color, smell, and taste change because new substances form. It cannot be turned back into its raw state.
Cooking rice needs heat absorbed from the stove, so it is endothermic.
In 1543, Copernicus's book 'On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres', which laid out the heliocentric model, was published.
Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish astronomer, proposed the heliocentric model — that the Sun, not the Earth, is at the center of the solar system.
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Polish astronomer, from Poland.
Copper can kill many germs that land on it, so it is sometimes used on door handles that people touch often.
Copper surfaces kill many bacteria and viruses within hours through the oligodynamic effect; this is why copper doorknobs and surfaces are used in some hospitals to reduce infection spread.

Even though copper conducts better, the long power lines along roads are often made of aluminum. Why? Aluminum is much lighter, so it doesn't weigh down the tall towers, even though it's a bit worse than copper.
Copper doesn't rust easily the way iron does. Even over time it keeps conducting electricity well, so copper wires can last for many years.
Some kids think copper gets used up when electricity passes through it. No! The copper is just a path—it stays whole. Electricity flows in a loop around the circuit and doesn't eat the wire.
Copper is used for most electrical wires because it carries electricity very well, bends easily, and is much cheaper than gold, which is almost as good.
Copper carries not just electricity but heat too! That's why some pans and pots have copper on the bottom, so heat reaches the food quickly and evenly.
Inside the walls of your house, hidden copper wires carry electricity from the meter to the lights, outlets, and switches. That's why the bulb lights up when you flip the switch.
Copper has low 'resistance,' meaning it doesn't block the flow of electricity much. Because of this, very little energy is wasted as heat as electricity passes through the wire.

Some kids think that because copper conducts electricity well, it must also be magnetic. That's wrong! A magnet won't stick to copper. Conducting electricity and being magnetic are two different things.
Old copper wires can be melted down and made into new wire or other things. Because of this, copper isn't wasted and there's less trash, so recycling it is important.
Actually, silver conducts electricity a tiny bit better than copper. But silver is very expensive, so copper is chosen because it's almost as good while being much cheaper and plentiful.
Copper conducts electricity even better when it's cold than when it's hot. When hot, the atoms jiggle faster and get in the way of the electrons, so it conducts a little worse.
Why are some copper wires thicker? A thick wire gives electricity a wider path, so it can carry a stronger current without overheating. That's why air conditioners and big appliances use thick wire.
Copper forms a green coating called verdigris when exposed to moist air over a long time; this is the green color seen on old copper roofs and statues.
Copper was one of the first metals people used to make tools and weapons thousands of years ago.
Copper is the second-best conductor and is the metal most commonly used in electrical wires.
Copper develops a green coating over time because it oxidizes in the air.
Copra is dried coconut meat; when pressed, it yields coconut oil used in cooking and other products; the Philippines is one of the world's largest copra producers.
Like the kingfisher, the bee-eater and roller are both colorful, a trait this bird family shares.
An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef that grew around a sinking volcanic island, leaving a calm lagoon in the middle.
When seawater becomes too warm, corals expel their zooxanthellae and turn white — this is called coral bleaching.
The bright colors of living coral come from the tiny algae living inside it.
Stony coral tissue loss disease (SCTLD) and other coral diseases can spread rapidly through reefs — SCTLD is driven by bacterial pathogens and can destroy coral tissue within days to weeks.
Complex coral reefs with many coral types and many crevices and holes are home to more fish species because different corners offer different habitats and food sources.
Coral grows very slowly, so once a blast destroys it, it can take many years to recover.
Coral reefs grow very slowly, often only a few centimeters a year, so large reefs took thousands of years to form.
A coral is a living animal, not a rock, even though it looks hard.

Atolls form when a volcanic island slowly sinks and erodes — as the island subsides, the coral reef continues growing upward, eventually leaving a ring of reef surrounding a lagoon where the island once was.
Corals produce a thin layer of mucus that protects them from microbes, helps collect food particles, and provides nutrients to other reef organisms.
A coral polyp is like a tiny sac: it has a mouth in the middle ringed by little tentacles, and inside is a hollow space that works as its stomach where food is digested.
The thousands of polyps in one coral do not live alone — they are joined together by a thin layer of tissue, so when one polyp catches food, it can share it with the others.
Many coral polyps come out and feed at night to catch plankton with their tentacles.
Even though they cannot move, different corals still fight for space; some polyps stretch out special sweeper tentacles to sting and kill the polyps of a neighboring coral that grows too close.
A reef grows very slowly because the polyps add only a little to their stone each year; so a large reef can be hundreds of years old — which is also why it is so important to protect it.
Corals usually grow in warm, shallow, clear seawater where sunlight can reach them.
The reef built by countless polyps acts as a natural underwater wall: it breaks the force of big waves before they reach the shore, so it helps protect coastal towns during storms.
Polyps in a colony are connected to each other, so they can share food among themselves.
A coral polyp's tentacles carry tiny stinging cells, like little harpoons, that it uses to catch and stun the tiny prey floating in the water — which is why coral and jellyfish are relatives.
At night, coral polyps stretch out their tiny tentacles to catch plankton as extra food.
Each coral polyp has tiny tentacles it uses to catch small food drifting in the water.
Tubbataha Reef in Palawan is one of the most beautiful reefs in the world, built slowly by countless coral polyps over thousands of years; it is a protected World Heritage Site of the Philippines.

A coral polyp and a sea anemone look almost the same — both have a mouth ringed by tentacles — but the big difference is that coral builds a hard stony skeleton, while an anemone (Nemo's home) stays soft and builds no stone.
On reefs, small cleaner fish remove pests from bigger fish, and both animals benefit.
Coral polyps live together as one connected colony, not alone.
Coral reefs are called the 'rainforest of the sea' because they are among the most species-rich ecosystems on Earth.
The Philippines is home to nearly 2,500 species of reef fish — among the highest of any country in the world — because it lies at the heart of the Coral Triangle.
Warming and rising seas damage coral reefs, which fish and fishing communities depend on.
A coral reef is home to a huge variety of fish and other sea animals.
In protected ocean areas called marine sanctuaries, reefs and fish are allowed to recover and grow in number.

Many medicines come from animals that live on coral reefs. Some sponges and sea snails make special chemicals to defend themselves, and scientists use these to make medicines against cancer and other illnesses. So protecting the reef also protects possible cures.
Coral reefs protect the coast by weakening big waves before they reach the shore.
Tubbataha Reef in Palawan is a famous protected reef in the Philippines, full of sea life.
There are different kinds of reefs, such as fringing reefs along the shore and ring-shaped atolls.
A coral reef has distinct zones: the shallow reef flat near shore, the wave-breaking reef crest, and the deeper fore reef facing the open ocean.
Many reef builders live with tiny algae that need sunlit water, so some underwater life still depends on sunlight reaching the shallows.
Old coral rock in a wall is a non-living earth material now, even if living coral animals once built the reef it came from.
Parrotfish nibble on coral and release it as fine white sand.

A coral polyp builds a hard skeleton of limestone (calcium carbonate) around its body. When a polyp dies, its skeleton stays behind, and new polyps grow on top of it. Layer upon layer of skeletons over thousands of years builds the whole reef.

Many corals release their eggs and sperm into the water together on just a few nights each year, often around a full moon. These join to form baby corals, or larvae, that swim until they find a hard spot to settle and grow into a new polyp.

Marine biologists use 'coral gardening' — growing coral fragments in underwater nurseries before transplanting them to degraded reef areas; this technique has been successfully used to accelerate reef recovery in the Philippines.
Inside the coral live tiny algae called zooxanthellae that give it color and food.

A crab's claw has strong muscle inside, so it can crush the hard shells of snails or clams. The crab also uses its claws to defend itself, fight other crabs, and hold food.
A crab is cold-blooded, meaning its body temperature follows its surroundings. In cold water or weather it slows down and rests; when it is warmer, it becomes more active and moves easily.
A crab's eyes sit on top of two short stalks it can raise and swivel, like little periscopes. This lets it see all around even when its body is buried in sand or mud.

Crabs are important on the shore: by eating dead and rotting matter they help clean the beach, and by digging burrows they let air and nutrients into the sand or mud. In these ways they help keep the habitat healthy.

Crabs and spiders are both arthropods — both have no inner bones, a hard outer shell, and legs with joints. But they differ: a crab has ten legs and claws and lives in water, while a spider has eight legs and lives on land.
A crab uses its claws to hold food and to defend itself.
Most crabs have compound eyes at the ends of rigid eye stalks — this allows them to see nearly 360 degrees around themselves simultaneously, enabling rapid detection of predators.
A female crab carries thousands of eggs tucked under the flap on her belly until the eggs hatch into tiny young that swim in the sea.
Baby crabs, called larvae, are very tiny and swim in the water. At first their eyes are attached right to the head. As they grow and molt, the stalks that hold the eyes slowly develop.
Scientists study crab eyes to make special cameras and robots that can see a wide area all at once, just like a crab. These could help robots that keep watch or take pictures underwater.

Many people think crabs are blurry-eyed or nearly blind because their eyes are small. That is not true. Although they do not see fine details clearly, they are excellent at sensing movement and light all around them, which matters most for staying safe.
A crab's eyes sit at the tips of small stalks, so it can raise them to see all around or tuck them away when there is danger.
Crabs eat almost anything—fish, small animals, plants, and even dead things.
When a crab loses a claw or leg, it can regrow it as it molts and grows bigger.
Crabs usually walk sideways because of the way their leg joints bend.
