A crocodile can live in salty seawater because it has special glands on its tongue that get rid of extra salt from its body — something an alligator cannot do.
In crocodiles, it is not chromosomes but the temperature of the nest that decides whether an egg becomes male or female — certain warmth makes more males and other warmth makes more females.
Crocodiles are cold-blooded, so they lie in the sun to warm up their bodies.
Some people think crocodiles cannot see well on land, but that is wrong. A crocodile has strong eyesight even out of the water, so it can escape or catch prey even on the shore.
There is a hard ridge like an eyebrow above a crocodile's eye made of bone. It gives a little shade against the sun's glare and protects the eye while the crocodile waits in the water.
Humans have only two eyelids per eye, but a crocodile has three: an upper, a lower, and a clear third one for underwater. It also has a vertical pupil, not a round one like ours.
A crocodile's eyes sit on the sides of its head, so it can see almost all around it without turning its head. This helps it spot prey or danger from many directions.

Different plants take different nutrients from the soil. Corn, for example, is hungry for nitrogen, while other vegetables need more of other minerals. When you rotate crops, no single nutrient gets used up, so the soil stays rich.

Crop rotation can be used even in a small backyard vegetable garden, not just on a big farm. For example, if you plant tomatoes in one spot now, next plant mung beans or string beans there, then leafy greens after that. This way, the soil in your home garden stays healthy.

Good question: why is it not enough to just switch to any plant? Because plants that are relatives (in the same family) like tomato, eggplant, and potato share the same pests and diseases. So if you only switch to a relative, you do not really break the cycle. It is better to choose a crop from a different family.
Planting mung bean or other legumes after rice helps restore soil nitrogen because legumes have root bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air.
Legume plants enrich the soil because they leave behind nitrogen from the bacteria in their roots.

Some people think that just switching crops instantly makes the soil rich again. It is not that fast. Crop rotation helps slowly over many seasons, and it usually still goes together with good care like adding organic fertilizer. It is not magic but a patient method.

The largest known natural crystals in the world are selenite (gypsum) pillars in a cave in Mexico. Some crystals are over 10 metres long. They grew so large because they formed very slowly over millions of years.
Precious stones like rubies, sapphires, and emeralds are mineral crystals. Their colour and sparkle come from particular atoms incorporated into the crystal structure.
A geode is a rock that looks ordinary from the outside but is filled with beautiful crystals inside. The crystals grew from mineral-rich water that seeped inside the rock over many years.

The Mohs scale measures mineral hardness from 1 (talc, softest) to 10 (diamond, hardest). A mineral can scratch anything softer than itself but cannot scratch a harder mineral. Your fingernail is about 2.5 on the Mohs scale.
Ice is a crystal. Water molecules in ice are arranged in a hexagonal pattern because of how the molecules bond together. That is why snowflakes always have six arms.
The colour of crystal stones is usually caused by tiny amounts of impurities (other elements) inside the crystal. Amethyst is purple quartz coloured by iron and natural radiation.
Obsidian is a volcanic rock that is not a crystal — it is amorphous (no crystal structure) because the molten rock cooled too quickly for crystals to form. It is found near volcanoes such as Taal.
Pyrite, also called fool's gold, forms shiny gold-coloured cubic crystals. It is made of iron sulfide and is not real gold, but it fooled many early miners.
Crystals have flat faces and sharp edges because their tiny building blocks are arranged in a neat, repeating pattern.
A crystal's shape depends on how its atoms join into a repeating framework called a lattice.

Crystals that form slowly (for example, deep underground) grow larger. Crystals that form quickly (for example, in rapidly cooling lava) are smaller. That is why granite has large crystals and basalt has small ones.

When you heat sugar until it melts and becomes caramel, the crystal structure of the sugar is destroyed. When it cools, it does not return to crystals — caramel is an amorphous solid, not crystalline.
Crystallization is only a physical change—the salt is still salt even after it dissolved and reformed into crystals.
Crystallization is a separation method where a dissolved solid forms crystals when a saturated solution is cooled or the liquid evaporates.
Crystals start growing more easily on a rough surface like a string or rock than on smooth glass.
Crystals form when minerals slowly cool or dry, arranging their atoms into a neat, repeating shape.

By day a cuttlefish may sink deep to hide, and at night rise up to hunt. It does this by slowly changing the gas and water inside its cuttlebone.

Cuttlefish can make moving stripes of color flow across their skin to startle or mesmerize prey while hunting.

Scavengers like crows eat large dead animals, while decomposers are tiny fungi and bacteria that break down what is left.
Decomposers are living things that break down dead plants and animals, returning their materials to the soil.
As decomposers break down dead matter, they release carbon dioxide back into the air, much like breathing. This returns carbon to the atmosphere so plants can use it again in photosynthesis.
In composting, fruit peels, leaves, and vegetable scraps are gathered so decomposers can break them down. After a few weeks they become rich compost that feeds the soil for plants.
Decomposers like fungi and bacteria take the leftover energy from dead plants and animals at every level.
Most decomposers feed only on things that are already dead, unlike predators that hunt living prey. They wait for a plant or animal to die or fall before breaking it down.
The mold that appears on old bread or fruit is a fungus that acts as a decomposer. It spreads from tiny seed-like spores in the air and feeds on the food as it breaks it down.
Plant and animal bodies contain nitrogen needed for growth. When decomposers break down dead matter, they return nitrogen to the soil so new plants can use it again.
Fungi are not plants because they have no chlorophyll, so they cannot make their own food and take it from dead matter.

In the hot, rainy climate of the Philippines, dead leaves and animals in the forest break down very fast. So the layer of rotting leaves on a tropical forest floor stays thin even though there are many plants.

As decomposers eat dead matter, they also breathe like us — taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide into the air. So the release goes two ways: some nutrients go into the soil, and carbon goes into the air.

It's a misconception that decomposers attack living things. Most of them wait for a plant or animal to die first before breaking it down. So they are not 'harmful' — they wait for dead matter to use it and release its nutrients.

It's a misconception that only mushrooms are decomposers. True, many decomposers are visible, but most of the breaking down is done by bacteria we cannot see. Tiny as they are, they are the main ones releasing nutrients back to the soil.

Water treatment plants use decomposers to clean waste. They feed organic waste in dirty water to bacteria; the bacteria break it down and release simpler, safer substances — so the water becomes cleaner before going back to the river.

Scavengers and decomposers differ even though both eat dead things. A scavenger (like a crow or vulture) bites off big chunks of a dead animal. A decomposer breaks things down at the molecular level and then RELEASES nutrients into the soil — so they are the true recyclers.

Why aren't we buried under dead leaves and animals in the forest? Because decomposers keep breaking them down. Without them, dead matter would pile up meters high — but instead it is quickly returned to the soil as nutrients.
The dark, soft part of rich soil is called humus — it is made by decomposers from rotted plants and animals. Soil with plenty of humus is more fertile and better for growing crops.

Decomposition happens faster when it is warm and moist, because fungi and bacteria multiply quickly. In cold or dry places, breakdown slows down — which is why food keeps longer in a fridge or when dried.
In a decomposition reaction, a single substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances, often caused by heat or electricity.
In a decomposition reaction, one compound breaks apart into two or more simpler substances, such as water being split into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity.

In the deep parts of the ocean it is always dark and very cold because sunlight cannot reach down that far.
The anglerfish has a glowing lure on its head that it uses to attract and catch other fish in the dark deep sea.
Some deep-sea animals have very large eyes to catch even the faintest light in the darkness.

Bioluminescence in deep-sea animals is produced by a chemical reaction between luciferin (a type of pigment) and the enzyme luciferase — this reaction makes light with almost no heat, unlike human-made lights.
Scientists use strong vehicles called submersibles to explore the deep ocean.
Many deep-sea animals eat 'marine snow,' the tiny bits of dead animals and plants that drift down from above.
Many deep-sea animals have no large air spaces in their bodies and are mostly filled with liquid, so the high pressure does not crush them.
In the deepest parts of the ocean the water pressure is strong enough to crush an ordinary animal — so the fish there have soft bodies with no air bladder so they are not crushed.
Deep-sea animals are adapted to enormous pressure — their bodies lack air-filled cavities that would collapse under pressure, and their cells produce special chemicals to keep functioning.
Many deep-sea animals are colored red, which makes them nearly invisible because red sunlight does not reach those depths.
Many deep-sea animals move slowly and have a slow metabolism to save energy where food is scarce.
In a deep well, pumping the handle removes air inside the pipe, so outside air pressure pushes the water up.
The deepest-diving animal is Cuvier's beaked whale, which reached about 2,992 meters deep.

Your body is made of billions of tiny cells that are mostly water. When you get dehydrated, the cells lose water and shrink a little, so they cannot work as well as they should.

Some people think that as long as you drink something, you are hydrated, but sugary sodas and coffee are not as good as plain water. Some of them make you urinate more, so plain water is still the best choice against dehydration.
When it is hot or you are playing, your body sweats to cool down. But sweat is water from inside your body, so if you sweat a lot and do not drink, your body water drops and you become dehydrated.
The human body is about two-thirds water; it is in your blood, in your cells, and even in your brain. Because so much of us is water, even a small loss of it is felt by the body as dehydration.

A delta is a landform built at a river's mouth where the river reaches the sea and slows down, depositing the sediment it carries; the Pampanga River builds a small delta in Manila Bay that is gradually extending the coastline.
Scientists study the rings of old trees to learn about the weather and climate of past years.
Drums and pails of water should be covered tightly so mosquitoes cannot get in and lay eggs.

If you pour syrup, then water, then oil into a glass, they form three layers. The densest (syrup) sinks to the bottom, water in the middle, and oil (least dense) floats on top.
In a density column, different liquids stack in separate layers according to their density.
Differences in density are the reason liquids separate into distinct layers.

Ice is less dense than liquid water because of hydrogen bonds — when water freezes, its molecules arrange into a hexagonal lattice that is more open than liquid water, increasing volume by about 9 percent.
About nine-tenths of an iceberg is underwater. This is because ice density (0.92 g/cm3) is only slightly less than seawater, so only a small fraction sticks above the surface.

Aluminium has a density of about 2.7 g/cm3 — lower than iron (7.9 g/cm3) but still higher than water. That is why aluminium is used in aircraft: it is light but strong, so the plane is not too heavy to fly.

Earth's layers are arranged by density — the densest materials (iron and nickel) are in the centre (core), while lighter rocks are on the outside (crust). This happened early in Earth's history when it was molten.
The density of mercury is about 13.6 grams per cubic centimeter (13.6 g/cm³).

Mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature with a very high density of 13.6 g/cm3 — denser than iron. A piece of iron actually floats in mercury. It was used in old thermometers and barometers but it is toxic.
Whether something floats depends not on weight alone but on its density compared to the liquid.
Common substances and their densities: gold (19.3 g/cm3), iron (7.9 g/cm3), water (1.0 g/cm3), wood (~0.6 g/cm3), ice (0.92 g/cm3). Objects with density below 1.0 g/cm3 float in water.
The density of water is 1 gram per milliliter (1 g/mL).

Storing water is an adaptation that helps a plant survive in hot, dry places.

Detritivores like cockroaches and millipedes eat dead matter and shred it into small pieces so bacteria can decompose it faster.
More dew forms on clear, calm nights because the ground cools down faster without clouds or wind.
Morning dew is water droplets that form when the night air cools and vapor condenses on grass and leaves.
The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes too cold to hold all its water vapor, so it starts turning into dew or clouds; the higher the dew point, the more humid it feels.

Diabetes is one of the common diseases in the Philippines, so healthy eating and exercise are important to help prevent it.
Diabetes is not contagious—you cannot catch it by touching or being near someone who has it, because it is a problem with insulin inside the body, not a germ that spreads like a cold.
Before insulin was discovered as a medicine, severe diabetes had almost no cure; once scientists discovered it, it became one of the most important life-saving medicines, still used today.
Cells need sugar as fuel to make energy, so when insulin helps sugar get inside, the body can move, think, and grow.
In diabetes, there is not enough insulin or it does not work well, so blood sugar stays too high. That is why some people with diabetes need insulin injections.
To find out how high their blood sugar is, people with diabetes use a glucometer—a small device that measures sugar from a single drop of blood from the finger.
Insulin is a hormone—a chemical messenger carried by the blood from the pancreas to all the cells of the body to tell them to take in sugar.
Not the whole pancreas makes insulin—there are tiny clusters of cells in it called islets, and the beta cells inside them are the ones that make insulin.
Insulin cannot be swallowed because it is a protein that the acid and enzymes in the stomach would destroy; so it is injected to go straight into the blood.
In type 2 diabetes, insulin is still present but the cells no longer respond to it well, so sugar builds up in the blood; this is the most common type and is often linked to lifestyle.
Insulin and glucagon are like a bank: when sugar is plenty, insulin "saves" it in the liver, and when sugar is low, glucagon "withdraws" the saved sugar.
Diabetes cannot be fully cured yet, but it can be managed with healthy eating, exercise, and medicine.
In Type 1 diabetes, the pancreas makes almost no insulin, so the person needs insulin injections.
In type 1 diabetes, the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so the person needs insulin from outside the body.

To get the average speed of a whole trip, draw a straight line from the first point to the last point on the graph, and the slope of that line is the average speed — even if the real speed changed in between.

When you measure distance every few seconds and write it in a table, you can turn it into a distance-time graph: plot each pair (time, distance) as a dot, then connect the dots to see the whole motion.

When a line slopes downward on a distance-time graph, it does not mean time is going backward — it means the object is moving back toward where it started, so its distance from the starting point is shrinking.
On a distance-time graph, a straight line shows constant speed, but a curved line that keeps getting steeper means the object is speeding up or accelerating.
On a distance-time graph, a flat line means the object is at rest and not moving.
On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means the object is moving faster.

Picture a jeepney on its route: it moves (line rises), stops to pick up a passenger (line goes flat), then moves again — so its distance-time graph looks like a staircase of rise-flat-rise, a familiar picture of a trip in the Philippines.

Many kids think the highest point on a distance-time graph means fastest — but speed comes from the STEEPNESS of the line, not its height; you can be high up yet have a flat line, which means you have actually stopped.
A perfectly vertical line cannot exist on a distance-time graph, because it would mean the object jumped a distance in zero time — that would be infinite speed, which is impossible in real life.
A distance-time graph usually starts at the origin (zero time, zero distance) because at the very start of measuring, the object has not traveled anywhere yet and the clock has just begun.

If two lines on a distance-time graph have the same steepness (they are parallel), the two objects move at the same speed even though they never meet — maybe one just left earlier, but they are both traveling at one equal speed.
To get the speed from a distance-time graph, you divide how far the line rises (distance) by how far it runs sideways (time) — that ratio is the slope, and the slope is exactly the object's speed.

An eagle has sharp talons (claws) and a hooked, sharp beak. It uses the talons to grab and hold prey, and the beak to tear meat.
Deep inside the ear is a snail-shaped part called the cochlea, which is filled with fluid.
The ear makes a yellowish wax that traps dust and dirt to protect the inside of the ear canal.
We hear a sound when the vibrating air reaches and shakes the inside of our ear.
When there is illness or infection inside the ear, a person's balance can be affected and they may feel dizzy easily.
The ear can get an infection when germs grow inside it, which is why it may hurt during a cold.
Very loud sounds can damage the tiny parts inside the ear and weaken our hearing.
The ear is not just for hearing; it also helps with balance so you do not fall over.
The pinna — the outer flap of the ear — funnels sound into the ear canal and helps you locate which direction a sound is coming from.
After hearing a very loud noise like firecrackers, the ears sometimes seem to ring for a while.
Because we have two ears, we can tell which direction a sound is coming from.
The shape of the earlobe, whether attached or hanging free, is another example of an inherited trait.
Most of Earth's earliest rock has been destroyed by plate tectonics and erosion, so the record of the very first part of our planet's history is incomplete.
Early steam trains were powered by steam made from water boiled using burning coal.
People who work near loud machines may wear earmuffs, a sound protection kids can name even if they do not use them at school.
The ear has three main parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.
The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
Planet Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.
Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees.
The distance around the Earth (its circumference) at the equator is about 40,000 kilometers.
Earth's circumference around the equator is about 40,075 kilometers.
Earth's circumference around the equator is about 40,075 kilometers.
The circumference of Earth is about 40,000 kilometers.
The core is the hottest layer of the Earth. The temperature at its center reaches almost 5,000–6,000 °C — about as hot as the surface of the sun.
Earth's magnetic field comes from the swirling molten iron in its core.
The crust is not equally thick everywhere: the oceanic crust under the seas is thinner, while the continental crust that makes up the land is thicker.
One day on Earth lasts 24 hours, the time it takes to complete one full spin.
One day on Earth (one rotation) lasts 24 hours.
The layers become heavier and denser toward the center of the Earth, so the lighter rock is in the crust and the heavy metals iron and nickel are in the core.
Earth's diameter is about 12,742 kilometers.
The diameter of Earth is about 12,742 kilometers.
Earth is about 150 million kilometers away from the Sun.

An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up. In a solar eclipse, the Moon blocks the Sun, darkening the daytime. In a lunar eclipse, the Earth is in the middle, so its shadow falls on the Moon.
It is hotter near the equator and colder near the poles because the Earth is round. At the equator, sunlight strikes more directly; at the poles, it strikes at a slant, so the warmth is weaker.

Equinoxes occur twice a year (around March 21 and September 23) when day and night are nearly equal in length worldwide; solstices also occur twice a year (June 21 and December 21) when one of Earth's poles is most tilted toward or away from the Sun.
Earth acts like a giant magnet because the swirling molten iron deep in its core creates a magnetic field.
The Earth has four main layers: the crust, the mantle, the outer core, and the inner core.
The Earth acts like a giant magnet with a magnetic field around it.
The tallest mountain on Earth is Mount Everest, about 8,849 meters high.
Inge Lehmann, a Danish scientist, discovered in 1936 that the Earth's inner core is solid.
Earth's inner core is a hot, solid ball made mostly of iron and nickel.
The inner core is the deepest and hottest layer, yet it stays solid iron because of the enormous pressure squeezing it.
The Earth's inner core reaches about 5,400°C — as hot as the surface of the Sun.
The outward flow of heat from inside the Earth drives the slow movement of the plates, which in turn causes earthquakes, volcanoes, and the building of mountains.
Only about 29% of Earth's surface is land, and the rest is water.
The largest ocean on Earth is the Pacific Ocean.
One trip of the Earth around the Sun is not exactly 365 days — it is about 365 and a quarter days. So every four years we add an extra day (February 29) to the calendar — this is a 'leap year.'
The lithosphere is the Earth's rigid outer shell made of the crust and the very top of the mantle, and it is what is broken into the tectonic plates.
The difference between the lithosphere and asthenosphere is in how the rock behaves: the lithosphere is rigid and brittle, while the asthenosphere is hotter and able to flow.
The Earth has its own magnetic field that comes from electric currents inside its swirling, liquid outer core.
The Earth's magnetic field guides particles from the Sun toward the poles, where they create the colorful glowing lights in the sky called auroras.
The Earth's magnetic field acts like a shield that catches harmful particles from the Sun's solar wind, protecting life on the planet's surface.
Oddly, the place we call Earth's magnetic north is actually a south magnetic pole, which is why the north end of a compass needle is pulled toward it.
The Earth's magnetic poles slowly move over time, and over very long ages the whole magnetic field can even reverse direction.
People cannot yet dig all the way to the mantle because it is so deep, so hot, and under such high pressure that drills melt or bend long before reaching it.

Earth's plate tectonics is driven by convection in the mantle — hot rock slowly rises, spreads beneath the crust, and sinks back down; this process pulls and pushes tectonic plates, causing earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain building.
In the mantle, hot rock rises, cools, and sinks again — this is called convection. This slow churning is what pushes the Earth's tectonic plates to move.
People cannot travel to the mantle, so we learn what it is like from earthquake (seismic) waves that change speed and direction as they pass through the Earth.
The mantle is the Earth's thickest layer, made of very hot rock that, although solid, slowly flows over very long times.
The mantle is made of hot silicate rock rich in iron and magnesium, not molten lava but solid rock such as peridotite, which is usually dark in color.
Even though the mantle is deep, in places like Zambales in the Philippines ancient ocean floor with mantle rock has been pushed up, so we can actually see it.
The Philippines has many volcanoes like Mayon and Taal because here a plate sinks downward, where the mantle's heat helps melt rock into the magma that erupts from the volcanoes.
The mantle acts like a giant recycling system: old crust that sinks during subduction returns into the mantle, while new crust is made elsewhere from the mantle.
The mantle flows incredibly slowly — only a few centimeters per year, about as slow as your fingernails grow — so we never feel it even though it is moving.
The mantle is extremely hot, ranging from a few hundred degrees Celsius near the crust to over three thousand degrees Celsius near the core.
The mantle has an upper mantle nearer the crust and a lower mantle deeper down; with depth the pressure rises, so the rock becomes denser and stiffer.
The mantle is made of silicate rock, while the core beneath it is made mostly of the metals iron and nickel and is even hotter than the mantle.
Earth materials are the non-living things that make up the environment, such as rocks, soil, water, and air around a schoolyard.
Earth materials can move without being alive: wind blows sand, rivers carry pebbles, and gravity pulls rocks down a slope.

In space, an asteroid is a large rock orbiting the Sun; a comet is a ball of ice and dust with a tail when it nears the Sun; and a meteor ('shooting star') is a small rock that burns up entering Earth's atmosphere.
A mineral is a natural solid with one kind of composition (like quartz, gold, and rock salt). A rock is made of one or more minerals together. So minerals are the building blocks of rocks.
Monsoons (habagat and amihan) are strong winds that change direction each season. This happens because land and sea heat up and cool down at different rates through the year.
The distance from the Earth to the Moon is about 384,000 kilometers.
The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans, making the water rise and fall. This is called the tides. The water bulges out most on the side of Earth facing the Moon.
Gravity on the Moon is weaker than on Earth, so you weigh much less there. If you jumped on the Moon, you would rise much higher than on Earth.
The Moon orbits the Earth because Earth's gravity keeps pulling it in. But because the Moon is moving sideways so fast, it never falls down—it just keeps going around.
It takes the Moon about a month to travel all the way around the Earth. In fact, the word 'month' comes from the Moon's motion!
Many Filipino fishermen watch the tides caused by the Moon. They know when the water is highest or lowest so they can catch more fish.

The seasons in the northern and southern halves of the world are opposite. When it is summer in the north (like Japan), it is winter in the south (like Australia) — because they tilt differently toward the Sun.
Earth has five (5) oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern.

Earth's gravity pulls the air downward so it does not fly off into space. Because of this, the atmosphere with the oxygen we breathe stays in place. The Moon is small with weak gravity, so it could not hold onto any air.
Earth is the only planet known to have life, because it has water, air, and the right temperature.
Because of gravity, the Earth makes one full trip around the Sun every year.
Earth's outer core is liquid (molten metal) and it creates Earth's magnetic field.
There are two main kinds of seismic waves: the faster P-waves, which arrive first, and the slower S-waves, which follow.

A tsunami is a very large wave that forms when there is a strong earthquake under the sea. The movement of the ground pushes a huge amount of water, creating waves that can reach the shore. If the sea suddenly pulls back after an earthquake, that is a sign to run to higher ground or away from the coast. Not every earthquake makes a tsunami, but it is good to be ready.

The Earth's outer layer is broken into large pieces called plates that move slowly. When plates rub or collide, earthquakes and volcanoes occur. The Philippines sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, so it has frequent earthquakes and many volcanoes.
Earth is the third (3rd) planet from the Sun, after Mercury and Venus.

There are three kinds of rock: igneous (from cooled lava or magma), sedimentary (from layers of sand and mud that hardened), and metamorphic (rock changed by heat and pressure). In the rock cycle, one kind can change into another over very long times.
When lava cools and hardens, it locks in the direction of the magnetic field at that time, so scientists can read the Earth's past magnetism in old rocks.

The Coriolis effect is the deflection of moving objects like wind and ocean currents due to Earth's rotation; in the northern hemisphere wind systems spin counterclockwise (such as typhoons), while in the southern hemisphere they spin clockwise.
Earth rotates from west to east, which is why the Sun rises in the east.
Earth rotates on its axis at about 1,670 kilometers per hour at the equator.
Because Earth rotates once in 24 hours, it is divided into 24 time zones; the Philippines uses Philippine Standard Time (PST), which is 8 hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC+8).
The liquid outer core blocks and bends seismic waves, so there are regions on the far side of the Earth where no waves arrive, called the shadow zone.
The Sun is not really moving around us — it is the Earth that spins, which makes the Sun look like it rises and sets.

Not all stars are white — some are red, yellow, white, or blue. A star's color tells how hot it is: red stars are the coolest, while blue stars are the hottest. Our Sun is yellow-white, so its temperature is in the middle.

A 'falling star' or shooting star is not really a star at all! It is a small rock or dust from space that enters Earth's air very fast, so it heats up and glows as it burns. A real star is far away and does not fall to Earth.

The Sun, being a star, is the main source of energy for almost all life on Earth. Plants use the Sun's light to make food (photosynthesis), and animals eat plants or other animals. So even your food comes from the energy of a star!

To us, the Sun is special because it gives life to Earth — but across the whole universe, it is just an ordinary star. It is not the biggest, smallest, hottest, or coolest. There are many other stars about the same size and heat as it in space.
As you go deeper into the Earth, the temperature keeps rising, which is why deep mines are already hot and the mantle and core are far hotter still.
Tides are the rising and falling of the sea. They are caused by the pull of the Moon's gravity (and partly the Sun's) on Earth's water as the planet turns.
Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt is what causes the different seasons as it orbits the Sun.

Different countries have different times because the Earth spins — the Sun does not reach every place at the same moment. That is why there are 'time zones' so clocks match the Sun's position in each place.
Earth's spin makes the whole sky appear to turn, so watchers could tell passing hours from how far a constellation had moved.
About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, which is why it is called the Blue Planet.
One year on Earth lasts about 365 days, the time it takes to orbit the Sun once.
Earth goes around the Sun once in about 365 days — that is one year.
When an earthquake's shaking matches a building's natural frequency, the building vibrates harder and is more likely to break.
During an earthquake you should drop, take cover under a sturdy table, and follow the evacuation route out to a safe open space.
When an earthquake is very strong, the fault break can reach the surface and create a visible crack or step in the ground called a fault scarp.
Felt intensity is higher when the magnitude is larger, the focus is shallower, and the place is closer to the epicenter; it is also stronger on soft ground.

The PHIVOLCS Earthquake Intensity Scale (PEIS) uses Roman numerals from I to X to describe how an earthquake is felt: Intensity I is scarcely felt, Intensity VI is very strong (people are frightened and go outside), and Intensity X causes widespread building destruction.
Magnitude measures the total energy released by an earthquake, while intensity measures how strongly the shaking is felt at a particular place.
P-waves and S-waves from one earthquake make a natural contrast: same event, same rock, two particle motions, two speeds.
The strength (magnitude) of an earthquake is measured using the Richter scale.
The energy of an earthquake spreads outward from the focus as seismic waves, which shake the ground as they pass through it.
A machine called a seismograph is used to detect and record the shaking of the ground during an earthquake, even very weak ones.
Many Philippine earthquakes come from active faults, such as the Philippine Fault that runs through the islands.
The same movement of plates that builds mountains also causes earthquakes in the Philippines.
Earthworms are decomposers that eat dead leaves and organic matter; their castings are rich in nutrients and their burrowing aerates the soil.
The earthworm eats rotting leaves and soil. Its droppings make the soil richer, so it helps plants grow.
By crawling up and down, earthworms mix the soil, spreading nutrients through its different layers.
The earthworm has no eyes, but it has light-sensitive spots on its skin that feel light.
If the tail end of an earthworm is cut off, it can regrow that lost part.
Earthworms move by alternately stretching and contracting muscles and use tiny bristles called setae to grip the soil as they push forward.
Earthworms dig tunnels in the soil as they move, letting air and water into the ground and improving plant growth.
Earthworms improve soil by creating tunnels that aerate and drain the soil; they eat organic matter and their castings are a valuable fertilizer that enriches the soil.

How does garbage become fertilizer? The worm eats tiny bits of rotting leaves and vegetable peels, grinds them up inside its body, and passes them out as clean fertilizer. They work like tiny compost factories.
Many think a worm bin smells bad, but a healthy one has almost no smell or just an earthy smell. A bad smell means too much food was added and the worms have not eaten it yet.
Earwax is not just dirt but a natural protection — it traps dust and germs and slowly moves out on its own, so it should not be dug out deeply.
Earwax protects the inside of the ear and traps dust and germs.
The echidna lays a single egg and tucks it into a pouch on its belly until it hatches.
The echidna has sharp spines on its back that protect it from predators.
Brittle stars are relatives of starfish with thin, long arms that they use to move quickly across the seafloor.
Many echinoderms like starfish have a body divided into five parts, which makes them look star-shaped.
Young echinoderms, called larvae, have two matching sides at first and only become star-shaped as they grow.
The word 'echinoderm' comes from Greek and means 'spiny skin'.
The starfish and the sea urchin are relatives—both belong to a group of sea animals with spiny or rough skin called echinoderms.
Echinoderms have a special water vascular system inside the body that moves their tube feet using water pressure.
Reverberation is many rapid echoes from different surfaces blending together — large churches and caves often have strong reverberation.
Because we know how fast sound travels, an echo can be used to measure distance — ships use sonar, sending sound down and timing how long the echo takes to return.
To hear an echo as a separate sound, the gap between the original sound and the reflected sound must be at least 0.1 second.
An echo happens when sound bounces back to us after hitting a distant surface like a wall or mountain.
Modern fishing boats use an echo sounder or fish finder — it sends sound pulses downward and echoes from schools of fish appear on a screen.
The distance to a reflecting object can be calculated from echo timing: divide the total travel time by two (there and back), then multiply by the speed of sound.
Echolocation is a way of finding things by making sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back.
Bats are not blind, but they rely on echoes instead of sight to get around in dark caves and at night.
By listening to echoes, bats and dolphins can tell how close, how big, and what shape an object is.
Vapes or e-cigarettes also contain nicotine and are not safe, because they still harm the lungs.

Baily's beads are rays of sunlight passing through valleys at the Moon's edge just before totality in a solar eclipse; the last remaining ray creates the 'diamond ring' effect before the Sun is fully covered.
Modern astronomy explains eclipses as the Earth, Moon, and Sun lining up; indigenous watchers still could notice the repeating darkening without that diagram.
An eclipse is a natural event in the sky and is not a sign of bad luck or superstition.
Some communities used eclipse stories as a warning to stay calm and watch, which is one way they communicated that the darkening would pass.
To watch a solar eclipse safely, use special eclipse glasses or a pinhole projector, not ordinary sunglasses.
Scientists can predict the exact date and time of eclipses because the Sun, Moon, and Earth move in a regular way.
Some keystone species are called ecosystem engineers because they physically reshape the environment for other species.
Thomas Edison is famous for developing the first practical lightbulb for everyday use.
Eduardo Quisumbing was a Filipino scientist who studied and recorded thousands of medicinal plants in the Philippines.
It is often said that Eduardo San Juan made the moon buggy, but in truth the lunar rover was built by many NASA engineers and he is not proven to have made it alone.
Some eels can take in a little air through their moist skin, so they can survive a short time out of water.
Eels eat small fish, shrimp, and other small animals.
An eel has one long fin that runs along most of its back to its tail.
During the day an eel hides in holes or rocks, and at night it hunts for food.
An eel is a fish with a long, snake-like body.
Egg cells are made in the ovaries, not in the uterus and not in the vagina.
A chicken egg usually hatches after about 21 days, or three weeks.
Most mammals give birth to live young, but the platypus is a mammal that lays eggs.
Eggs from different animals come in different sizes, shapes, and colors.
After an ovary releases an egg cell, that egg cell can travel toward the uterus along a connecting tube.
In science, the eggplant is a fruit because it grows from a flower and holds seeds inside.
Eggplants come in different shapes; some are long while others are round.
The white egret is a long-legged, long-necked bird often seen in rice fields and ponds hunting for fish and insects.
The Eiffel Tower is named after Gustave Eiffel, the engineer whose company built it.
The Eiffel Tower is about 330 meters (330 m) tall, including its antennas.
Albert Einstein's famous formula is E=mc², which shows the link between energy and mass.
Albert Einstein won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921.
The modern e-jeepney is driven by an electric motor powered by a battery, so it does not release the black exhaust smoke that old diesel jeepneys do.
The ocean warming during El Nino causes coral bleaching; corals expel the algae that provide their food and colour when water becomes too warm.
Because El Niño brings drier weather, farmers' harvests often shrink — rice and corn dry out when there is not enough water for irrigation.
During El Nino, upwelling weakens and ocean nutrients decrease; fish populations fall and Philippine fishermen find it harder to make a good catch.
El Nino causes weather changes worldwide: it brings drought to Australia and India, heavy rain to Peru, and shifts typhoon and hurricane patterns in many regions.
During El Niño, the usual winds that blow westward along the equator weaken or reverse, so warm surface water piles up in the central and eastern Pacific instead of in the west near the Philippines.
El Nino is officially declared when sea surface temperature in the central Pacific (Nino 3.4 region) is more than 0.5°C above average for three consecutive months.
Because rain is scarce during El Niño, the water in dams and reservoirs drops, so there can sometimes be shortages of drinking water and of hydropower electricity.
Rubber is not the only elastic thing — metal springs and waistband elastics also return to shape after stretching.
Alessandro Volta invented the first electric battery that gave steady current in 1800.
An electric car has no engine that burns gasoline — instead it uses a big battery to run an electric motor that turns the wheels, so it is quiet and gives off no smoke.
The electric catfish is a type of catfish in African rivers that can release a shock to defend itself.
The electric eel often rises to the surface to gulp air because it cannot get enough oxygen from the muddy water.
The electric eel is not a true eel but a fish that can produce a powerful electric shock to stun prey and defend itself from predators.
When the eel suspects a hidden fish, it sends out two quick shocks. These make the hidden fish's muscles twitch, revealing where it is so the eel can strike.
Scientists used to think electric eels always hunt alone. But it was discovered that sometimes a group of them gathers and shocks together to herd many small fish into one spot.
To catch food, the electric eel releases its strong shock to numb or paralyze small fish. While the prey cannot move, the eel quickly swallows it.
When an electric eel feels threatened, it can leap upward and press its head against an attacker to deliver a stronger shock.
When an electric eel cannot flee, it sometimes leaps up out of the water and presses its head against the threat so the shock hits harder. It does this to scare off large animals that come close.
Even though it is called an electric eel, it is not a true eel but a different kind of fish.
An electric eel cannot keep firing strong shocks one after another forever. After several big shocks, it needs to rest a moment to build up enough charge again—like a battery that must recharge.
An electric eel's shock is painful and dangerous to people, so it should not be touched even when it is in the water.
Even though it is long and looks like a snake, the electric eel is a fish—not a snake and not a reptile. It has gills and lives in water like other fish, and does not crawl on land.
Many electric fish have poor eyesight, so they rely on electricity to know what is around them.
The electric ray (Torpediniformes) can deliver powerful electric shocks (up to 200 volts in some species) that it uses to stun and incapacitate prey before eating it.

Many people think an electric eel gets shocked by its own electricity. An eel is mostly not bothered by its own shock because little of it passes through its body and its important body parts are protected, so it stays safe even though it makes the shock itself.
One of the strongest electric animals is the electric eel that lives in the rivers of South America. It can release a shock strong enough to knock down a large animal or protect itself.
If an animal fires its shock again and again, it slowly gets weaker, like a battery running low. It needs to rest a little while so its shock can build back to full strength.
Electrical energy is the energy from moving electric charges, like electricity.
The energy used by electricity is power multiplied by time, so it is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), the unit you see on an electric bill.
Electrical energy powers household devices such as lights, televisions, and electric fans.
Do not pour water on an electrical fire; instead, switch off the main power first.

A circuit breaker is like an automatic switch in your house. When too much electricity flows through a wire and it starts to overheat, the breaker snaps off by itself to cut the power and prevent a fire.

Many plugs have a third prong. This is the ground wire that carries any stray electricity safely down into the earth, so we don't get shocked if an appliance like a fridge or washing machine has a fault.
In appliances, electrical energy changes into other forms — light in a bulb, heat in a flat iron, and sound in a speaker.
An electric current flowing in a metal wire is really electrons moving along together.
Electric bills are measured in kilowatt-hours, which tell how much energy a home has used.
In electrolysis, an electric current is passed through water to split it into two gases: hydrogen at one electrode and oxygen at the other.
Like an ordinary magnet, an electromagnet only attracts objects made of iron or steel, not copper or aluminum.
When you wind wire around an iron nail and run current through it, it becomes an electromagnet, a magnet you can switch on and off.
The electromagnet shows that electricity and magnetism are connected, which is called electromagnetism.
An electromagnet is a magnet made by electricity, so it is magnetic only while electric current flows.
An electromagnet has a north pole and a south pole, just like an ordinary magnet.
The wire of an electromagnet heats up when current flows through it for a long time.
Placing a piece of iron inside the coil of wire makes the electromagnet much stronger.
When you wrap a nail with wire and connect it to a battery, it becomes an electromagnet that can pull iron objects while current flows.
In 1820, the scientist Hans Christian Oersted noticed a compass needle move near a wire carrying electric current.
If you reverse the direction of the current, the north and south poles of the electromagnet switch places.
Soft iron is used as the core because it becomes a magnet quickly and quickly loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.
Speakers use an electromagnet to create vibrations that become the sound we hear.
When you turn off the current, the electromagnet loses its magnetism, so it can be switched on and off.
When a magnet is moved in and out of a coil of wire, it generates a flow of electric current; this is the principle behind generators.
The electron has a negative charge.
Electrons move so fast around the nucleus that they form a cloud-like region.
J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897.
The electron is the lightest of the three subatomic particles.
Electrons move around the outside of the atom's nucleus.
The electron is the lightest of the three particles; it is about 1,800 times lighter than a proton.
Electron shells fill from the innermost outward, and each shell has a limit — the first shell can hold up to 2 electrons and the second up to 8.
An atom's electrons are arranged in shells, or energy levels, around the nucleus, and the farther a shell is from the nucleus, the higher its energy level.
J.J. Thomson discovered the electron, the tiny particle with a negative charge.
Electronegativity is an atom's ability to attract electrons in a bond; a large electronegativity difference between two atoms creates a polar bond, while a small difference creates a nonpolar bond.
Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons, and a big difference in it leads to a polar or ionic bond.
A diode is a semiconductor device that allows current to flow in only one direction — it is used to convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) in power supplies.
LED bulbs stay cool to the touch — because LEDs convert a larger fraction of electrical energy into light, wasting very little as heat compared to incandescent bulbs.
To protect an LED, Ohm's law is used to find the correct resistor value — if the battery is 9 V and the LED needs 2 V at 20 mA, the resistance needed is (9-2)/0.02 = 350 ohms.
Soldering is the process of joining electronic components to a PCB using molten solder (usually a tin-silver alloy) — when cooled, it forms a strong electrical and mechanical connection.
A QR code is a type of barcode that uses a pattern of black and white squares to store information — a cellphone camera reads the pattern and links to a website, message, or other data.
A solar cell is a photovoltaic device using silicon semiconductor — photons from sunlight knock electrons loose in the silicon p-n junction, producing electricity directly from light.

Switches come in many types for different purposes — toggle switches for lights, push buttons for doorbells and calculators, and dimmer switches to raise or lower bulb brightness without turning it off.

A transistor is a semiconductor device with three parts (base, collector, emitter) — a small current at the base controls a much larger current between collector and emitter, making it useful as a switch or amplifier.
Atoms bond to one another by transferring or sharing their outer electrons.
Oganesson (Og), element number 118, is the last element on the periodic table.
Helium (He) is element number 2 on the periodic table.
Carbon is element number 6 on the periodic table.
Each element has a short chemical symbol of one or two letters, such as O for oxygen, H for hydrogen, and C for carbon.
Hydrogen (H) is the lightest element.
Mercury (Hg) is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature.
Mendeleev left gaps in his table and correctly predicted elements that had not yet been discovered.
Carbon is the element with the most known compounds, in the millions, making it the basis of life.
An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom, such as oxygen, carbon, or gold.
Oxygen is element number 8 on the periodic table.
The symbol for oxygen is O, and it is element number 8.
Some element symbols come from old Latin names: Fe for iron (ferrum), Au for gold (aurum), and Na for sodium (natrium).
The chemical symbol for gold is Au, from the Latin word 'aurum'.
Each element has a chemical symbol, such as O for oxygen and H for hydrogen.
Each element has a short symbol of one or two letters — for example, O for oxygen, C for carbon, Fe for iron, and Au for gold. Scientists use these to write elements quickly.
An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions — it is the simplest kind of matter.
Diamond and the black core of a pencil (graphite) are both made of one element—carbon. They look different, but carbon cannot be broken into anything simpler.
Gold is an element—it cannot be broken down into other substances. That is why gold jewelry stays gold even after hundreds of years.
It is a misconception that cutting a copper wire into pieces makes it a different substance. No matter how small, every piece is still copper, not something simpler.
By ordinary chemical means, an element truly cannot be broken down. Only nuclear change (like in the Sun) can turn one element into another, but that is not a chemical process.
We breathe oxygen, an element. We cannot make it from simpler substances—we only collect it from air, like in hospital oxygen tanks.
Each element has its own symbol like O for oxygen or Fe for iron. One symbol means one kind of atom that cannot be broken down.
A mixture like sand and salt can be easily separated, but that is not breaking down an element. An element itself cannot be separated into any parts.
Two or more elements can combine to form a compound, such as hydrogen and oxygen forming water.
Each element gives off or absorbs its own distinctive colors of light, so scientists can tell what elements are in a star even if it is on the far side of the universe.
The heavier elements in our bodies, like carbon and oxygen, were made inside stars long after the Big Bang.
Each element is made of only one kind of atom; gold is made only of gold atoms.
An elephant's body is so big that it eats a large amount of plants every day.
Elephants eat only plants such as grass, leaves, and fruit.
The elephant has the heaviest brain of any land animal, weighing about 5 kilograms.

Water rolls off a bird's smooth feathers, so it stays dry even in the rain.
When wet, a bird shakes its body to fling water off its feathers and dry quickly.
The tank is for seeing three features: shape as crests and troughs, size as width and height, and movement as travel, bending, and bounce.
February has 28 days, and 29 days in a leap year.

The body uses feedback so hormones do not become too much or too little, keeping them in balance.
The body controls hormone levels through feedback, like a thermostat that stops production when there is enough. In this way it keeps the inside of the body balanced (homeostasis).
The body uses feedback: when temperature rises or falls, the body responds to bring it back to the right level.
If you feel the middle of your back, you can feel the bumps of bone — that is your backbone, which proves you are a vertebrate.
A metal floor feels colder than a wooden floor even at the same temperature — because metal is a better conductor and draws heat from your feet more quickly.
No feeling is bad — even anger or sadness is normal; what matters is how we show or handle them.
Feldspar is the most common mineral group in the Earth's crust.
Feldspar is the most common mineral in Earth's crust and is found in almost all igneous rocks like granite; it has a hardness of 6 and shows clear cleavage planes.
Feldspar is the most common mineral group in the Earth's crust.
The femur, or thigh bone, is the largest bone in the human body. It supports our weight when we walk, run, or jump.
Without oxygen, yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide through alcoholic fermentation — the basis of making beer, wine, and other alcoholic beverages.
A bioreactor is a large tank used in industry to grow microorganisms at large scale; it is used to produce antibiotics, insulin, and other products.
The bubbles in rising bread dough or fermented drinks are carbon dioxide gas produced by microorganisms during fermentation.
Some helpful microbes are used in fermenting foods like pickles, making them sour and longer-lasting.
Kimchi is a Korean fermented vegetable made by lactic acid bacteria; fermentation preserves the vegetables and adds probiotics beneficial for digestive health.
Through fermentation, gut bacteria turn the tough fiber into small substances the animal can absorb as energy.
Fermentation is when helpful microbes change food — like fermented fish, pickled vegetables, and yogurt — and the sourness and flavor come from substances those microbes make.
Fermentation is a controlled change made by helpful microbes, so it is different from spoilage caused by harmful microbes.
In fermentation, yeast gets energy from sugar even with little or no oxygen, producing alcohol and carbon-dioxide gas.
Many fermenting microbes can work even without air, which is why containers for yogurt and bagoong are often sealed or covered.
Fermentation helps food last longer because it keeps spoilage microbes from growing.
The helpful microbes used in fermentation eat and multiply fast, so they use up the sugar and space that spoilage bacteria would need — they basically out-compete the harmful microbes for food.
Fermentation does not just make food last longer — it also preserves nutrients and can even add vitamins and helpful gut bacteria.
The salt used in salting and fermenting pulls water out of the food and out of microbes, and without enough water harmful bacteria cannot grow.
Adding a starter — like a little old ferment or vinegar — gives lots of helpful bacteria right away, so the food turns sour quickly before harmful microbes can move in.
Tapai is a fermented food made from rice or cassava across Southeast Asia; yeast and other microorganisms give it a sweet-sour taste and a soft texture.
A young fern leaf is tightly coiled like a curl, and it slowly unrolls as it grows.
A young fern leaf starts curled up like the coiled end of a violin, and it slowly unrolls as it grows.
Some ferns grow on the branches or trunks of trees, not in the soil, but they are not parasites — they only use the tree as a place to perch.
A whole fern leaf is called a frond. It has a stalk and many small leaflets lined up on both sides.
Not all ferns are small. Some kinds called tree ferns grow as tall as trees and can be found in cool, wet forests in the Philippines.
A fern has two forms in its life cycle: the large plant we see that makes spores, and a tiny separate form that grows from a spore before a new fern appears.
Even without flowers, ferns and mosses are green and make their own food from sunlight, just like other plants.
Ferns and mosses need a thin film of water to reproduce, because their sperm cells must swim to reach the egg cells.
Instead of seeds, ferns and mosses reproduce using spores — tiny, dust-like grains that can grow into new plants.
A fern is a plant with no flowers and no seeds — instead it reproduces using tiny spores.
Ferns reproduce through spores found in brown dots called sori on the underside of their leaves.
A ferry horn can sound higher as the boat comes into port and lower as it leaves, a waterfront example of a moving sound source.
In fertilization, a sex cell from the female (the egg) joins with a sex cell from the male (the sperm) to form a single new cell.

In the Philippines, a sudden high fever can be a warning sign of dengue, a disease spread by mosquitoes. If a high fever lasts three days or comes with bruising, it's important to see a doctor right away.
When you have a fever, you often feel tired and achy. That's because your body uses a lot of energy to fight the illness, so it signals you to rest.
Many common Philippine illnesses like the flu and dengue come with a fever because the body is fighting the germs.

Warmth slightly speeds up the chemical reactions inside the body. So during a fever, the immune system's cells move and make defenses a little faster — as if the body's fight has been turned up a notch.
Many germs that make us sick are adapted to grow at the body's normal 37°C. When a fever raises the heat a little, the conditions are no longer ideal for them, so they multiply more slowly.

There is a difference between a low fever and a high fever. A low fever (around 38°C) is often helpful and the body can handle it, while a very high one is exhausting and may be dangerous. That is why it is important to measure it with a thermometer to know how serious it is.
When body temperature rises above 37 degrees Celsius, a person has a fever.
A fever often makes us feel tired and weak because the body uses a lot of energy to fight the germs.
When germs invade, the body releases chemicals called pyrogens that signal the brain to raise the temperature.
You feel sleepy with a fever because the body repairs fastest during sleep. While you sleep, your body makes new cells and strengthens its defenses. Sleepiness is like a signal saying 'rest now.'
Fever itself is a defense, not just an illness. Your body heats itself up because many germs struggle to survive in the heat. So when you rest, you help your body carry out this plan.
When a fever is ready to break, the body sweats because evaporating sweat cools the skin.
During an infection, the hypothalamus raises its set temperature, so the body works to become hotter than usual.
A very high fever, especially one reaching around 40 degrees Celsius, should be checked by a doctor.
Because less and less energy reaches each higher level, only a small number of large predators can be supported at the top of a food chain.
Fiber found in vegetables, fruits, and whole grains helps with good digestion and regular bowel movement.
Pulses of light in a fiber-optic cable are transverse electromagnetic waves used to send information, not longitudinal sound pulses.
Fibonacci was an Italian mathematician famous for a series of numbers called the Fibonacci numbers.
A male fiddler crab has one claw that is very large and one that is small, and it waves the big claw around on the mudflats.
Bagoong, patis, and buro are Filipino foods made through fermentation by microbes.
Many Filipino foods are made by fermentation, such as tuba, basi, vinegar, bagoong, and atchara, where yeast or bacteria change the flavor and preserve the food.
As more dirt is trapped, a filter clogs up and the liquid flows through more slowly.
Filter feeders like mussels and oysters help keep ocean water clean and clear.

Filtering works because the tiny holes of a filter hold back the larger solid pieces while the liquid passes through — so sand is separated from water. It relies on particle size, not any chemical change.
To find the number of neutrons, you subtract the atomic number (proton count) from the mass number — for example, 12 minus 6 gives 6 neutrons in carbon.

You can estimate hardness using your fingernail (about 2.5), a coin, and glass as testing tools.
Fingernails grow faster than toenails, partly because the hands are used more and have a stronger flow of blood to them.
A phone's fingerprint sensor reads the unique lines and curves on the tip of your finger, and because no two people have the same fingerprint, only you can unlock it.
While a baby is still in the womb, the inner layer of skin (the basal layer) grows faster than the outside, so it buckles and folds like a curtain. These folds become the lines of the fingerprint.
The ridges of your fingerprints help your fingers grip things tightly, like a tire with tread. They also help you feel the texture of the things you touch.
To match two fingerprints, experts look at tiny details called minutiae, like where a ridge ends or where it splits into two. Matching these points is what proves the prints are the same.
Police and investigators use fingerprints to find out who was somewhere, because no two people have the same fingerprint. The slight oil from your skin gets left behind whenever you touch something.

There is a very rare condition called adermatoglyphia in which some people are born with no fingerprints at all. Because of this, they have trouble unlocking phones or getting IDs, but they are otherwise healthy people.

Even though identical twins look the same and share the same DNA, their fingerprints are still different. This is because the exact shape of the lines forms from how the baby moves and touches things in the womb, not just from DNA.
Each finger except the thumb has three hinge joints, which lets us curl it into a fist.
Fingertips have a very high density of touch receptors, making them among the most sensitive parts of the body to touch and pressure.
End the report by saying what one interview or one book could not tell you, because honest gathering includes the gaps, not only the neat stories.
Ants such as fire ants live together in a colony where one queen lays the eggs while thousands of worker ants gather food and care for the nest.
A fire extinguisher puts out fire by coating it with a chemical or gas that blocks the oxygen.
A fire extinguisher puts out a fire by smothering the flames so they lose the oxygen the fire needs to keep burning.
A fireball is an unusually bright meteor, usually caused by a rock larger than an ordinary shooting star.
In big wildfires, people clear a firebreak — a strip with no plants — so the fire runs out of fuel and stops.
Larvae of some firefly species live in water and feed on snails and other soft-bodied animals—these larvae also glow even though they are aquatic.
Fireflies blink their lights to find a mate at night.
A firefly has a chemical called luciferin that glows when a helper substance called luciferase acts on it.

How does a firefly's light work? Inside its body, a special chemical mixes with the oxygen it takes in. When they react together, the energy comes out as light — not as heat. That's why we call it a 'chemical reaction,' like a tiny laboratory inside its belly.
Just how cold is a firefly's light? It's only barely warmer than the firefly's own body. If it were hotter, it would burn its own body! So the light has to be cold to keep the firefly safe.

In some places in the Philippines like Palawan, there are rivers lined with mangrove trees where thousands of fireflies gather on one tree. The tree looks full of twinkling stars from their cold light. Tourists ride boats to watch this.
A firefly's light is usually yellow or greenish. This color is easy to see in the dark of night, so their mates can notice it quickly.
Firefly populations in the Philippines are declining due to light pollution and destruction of their habitats such as mangroves where they gather to mate.
A firefly is a kind of beetle that can make its own light in its tail to find a mate at night—this light is cold and gives off almost no heat.
Too much bright light in cities makes it hard for fireflies to see each other's blinks.
The firefly squid is a small squid that can make its own blue light from its body.
Some kinds of fireflies flash all at the same time, like a group of lights blinking together.
In some places, like the mangroves of the Philippines, thousands of fireflies in one tree flash all together, like dancing lights in the night.

The YELLOW color in fireworks comes from SODIUM salts.

A first aid kit holds bandages, gauze, and other supplies for first aid.
When a nose bleeds, you should lean the head slightly forward and gently pinch the soft part of the nose until the bleeding stops.

A fish underwater appears closer to the surface than it really is because light refracts as it exits the water into air.
Most fish cannot breathe in air because their gills dry out when they are out of water.
A fish is cold-blooded, so its body temperature matches the temperature of the water around it.
Before some Taal unrest, fish in the lake have died when the water changed, a local sign people have noticed in more than one year.
When there are too many fish in a pond, oxygen runs low and they get sick easily.
The fish sold at the market is a protein-rich food caught from the sea or fishponds.

In the Philippines, many fish sanctuaries are managed by the community or barangay itself. The fishers themselves make the rules and stand guard (sea wardens) so no one breaks them. Because they benefit, they also protect it — this is why many sanctuaries succeed.

It is a mistake to think a fish sanctuary is 'wasted' space because fishing is banned there. In truth the sanctuary becomes a fish 'factory' — it restocks the surrounding waters. So overall, fishers catch MORE than when there was no sanctuary.
Inside a fish sanctuary, fishing is not allowed so the fish can multiply first before they move out into the nearby sea.

There is a 'spillover effect'. When the sanctuary fills with fish, the extra fish swim out past its boundary. So even though fishing is banned INSIDE, fishers catch MORE just OUTSIDE, near the sanctuary.
Most fish have bodies covered in scales that protect them and help them slide through water.
When a school of fish swims together, it confuses a predator about which one to chase.
Fish tinola is a nourishing dish because the fish gives protein while the ginger and malunggay leaves add vitamins.
The Philippines has a law, the Fisheries Code, that bans blast and cyanide fishing and punishes those who break it.
A fisherman throws a net into the water to catch all at once a school of fish that swim together in a group.
Fishermen sew and mend the tears or holes in their nets so fish cannot escape and the net lasts a long time.

Even though some algae make food from sunlight like plants, most are placed in the kingdom Protista because their bodies are simple, often single-celled or without the true roots, stems, and leaves that real plants have.
The animal kingdom is for creatures that cannot make their own food, so they eat other living things, and most can move. This includes fish, birds, insects, and even humans.
Living things are commonly grouped into 5 kingdoms: Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista, and Monera.
Textbooks often divide living things into five large groups called kingdoms.

Even though we can think and speak, humans still belong to the animal kingdom. This is because we don't make our own food from sunlight, we eat other living things, and we can move, like other animals.

The five-kingdom system is not frozen or permanent; as scientists learn more, it changes. Some books now teach six kingdoms because bacteria were split into two groups. It is normal for the way we classify life to keep improving.

One of the biggest differences between kingdoms is whether their cells have a nucleus. Only bacteria (Monera) lack a true nucleus, while animals, plants, fungi, and protists have cells with a nucleus that holds their DNA.

The kingdom Protista is the 'odds-and-ends group'; it holds living things that don't fit as animals, plants, or fungi, like amoeba, paramecium, and some algae. Most are single-celled and are often found in water.
From the fossil record, scientists have identified five major mass extinctions in Earth's history, in each of which a large fraction of the world's species disappeared.

Some animals have much sharper senses than humans. For example, dogs smell far better, eagles see sharper, and bats "see" in the dark using sound. Nature matched these senses to how each animal lives.
Beyond the five senses, we also have a sense of balance located deep inside the ear. It helps us stand without falling over. That is why when we spin fast, we feel dizzy for a while.
Humans have five senses: sight (eyes), hearing (ears), smell (nose), taste (tongue), and touch (skin). Each one has its own body part that helps us experience the world.
Our senses get used to constant smells or touches. That is why if you stay long in a kitchen, the smell of cooking seems to fade. The smell is still there — the brain just learns to stop noticing it.
Our senses warn us about danger. When we smell smoke, we know there is a fire; when something is hot, we pull away quickly. The senses do this to keep us safe.
A fixed pulley changes the direction of the force, so you can pull down to lift a load up.
A single fixed pulley has a mechanical advantage of 1 — it does not multiply force, it only changes the direction of the force.
Bubbling or fizzing when things are mixed is a sign that a new gas is being made — it is one clue that a chemical reaction is happening.
Mixing vinegar and baking soda is a chemical change because it fizzes and gives off carbon dioxide gas.
A flag flapping is moving cloth, not a clean textbook wave; better transverse examples are a shaken rope or a light beam.
Raising or lowering a colored flag is a movement-and-color signal people have used so a far partner can see a yes or a no.
The pulley at the top of a flagpole is a simple machine that makes raising the flag easier—you pull the rope down and the flag goes up.
A blue flame is hotter and cleaner-burning than a yellow or orange flame.
Flame-test colors appear because the metal's ELECTRONS jump to higher energy and release light as they fall back.
