Inside a flamingo's beak are tiny comb-like plates that block the mud and let only the food through.
Flamingo parents feed their chick a special red milk made by their own bodies.
The flamingo's leg looks like its knee bends backward, but that joint is actually like its ankle. Its real knee is higher up, hidden under its feathers.
When feeding, a flamingo turns its head upside down in the water and filters tiny food from the mud. Its beak works like a strainer that catches food while pushing the water out.
You can often see a whole flock of flamingos all standing on one leg at the same time. They are each staying warm and resting together while in the shallow water.
A flamingo can hold its one-legged stance easily because it does not use much effort or muscle to do it.
Flamingos have long legs so they can stand in shallow water while looking for food. Because their body stays high above the water, their feathers stay dry while they feed.
There are no wild native flamingos in the Philippines, but you can see some in zoos like the Manila Zoo. There, Filipino kids can watch flamingos standing on one leg up close.
A flamingo doesn't always use the same leg; it switches which leg it lifts. This way each leg gets a chance to rest and one leg doesn't get too tired.
A flamingo has webbing between its toes that helps keep it from sinking into the mud. This spreads out its foot so it can stand more steadily on soft mud or sand.
Many flamingos live in salty or harsh lakes where few other animals can survive.
A flamingo stamps the mud with its feet to stir food up from the bottom into the water.

Flammable materials like gasoline can ignite easily at room temperature, while combustible materials like wood need a higher temperature to ignite; both are fire hazards but flammable materials are more dangerous.
A flash flood is a sudden flood that rushes in quickly when very heavy rain falls in a short time and the ground cannot soak it up fast enough.
A flashlight converts the chemical energy of a battery into electrical energy and then into light — a simple example of energy conversion.
Two people can send information with a flashlight by agreeing that one blink means yes and two blinks mean no, even when they are too far to talk.

Scientists have a word for how tightly packed an object is: density. If an object is denser (heavier for its size) than water, it sinks; if it is less dense than water, it floats. This is the real measure of floating.
A submarine is a boat that can sink or float on purpose. It has tanks that fill with water to make it sink, and fill with air to make it float back up to the surface.
Kiapo (water lettuce) is a floating plant found in ponds and streams in the Philippines. It looks like a small lettuce floating on the water, with soft, velvety leaves.
Some people think the green stuff floating on a pond is just trash or dirt. But it is a living plant with leaves and roots that makes its own food from sunlight, just like other plants.
Floating plants are often mistaken for algae. But a true floating plant like duckweed has real leaves and roots, while algae has no such parts and is just like green slime in the water.
Many floating plants like water lettuce have leaves arranged in a circle (a rosette), like an open flower. This spreads the weight over a wide area so the plant floats steadily without tipping over.

In most land plants, the tiny breathing pores (stomata) are on the underside of the leaf. But in floating plants these pores are on the top of the leaf, because that is the side facing the air, not the water.
When the dry season nears and water gets low, some floating plants make tough little buds that sink into the mud. There they wait until the water returns, then grow and float again.

Flood basalt eruptions are enormous eruptions that lay down sheets of basalt across hundreds of thousands of square kilometres; they happen over a few million years and release enough CO2 to warm the climate and trigger mass extinctions.
A debris flow is a fast-moving mixture of water, mud, sand, and large rocks; it is faster and more dangerous than an ordinary landslide and often happens during heavy rain in mountains.
During severe floods, people sometimes have to evacuate by boat to higher, safer ground, because deep and fast-moving floodwater is dangerous.
During flooding, children should not go outside or carry non-essential things; safety and listening to parents and authorities is most important.
IRRI developed flood-tolerant rice varieties with the SUB1 gene; these can survive up to 2 weeks of complete submersion, which is critical for farmers in flood-prone areas of the Philippines.
In cities like Metro Manila, flat concrete and asphalt surfaces do not absorb rainwater, so all rainfall becomes runoff and causes street flooding.
Green infrastructure such as parks, street trees, and permeable pavement reduces urban flooding by absorbing rainwater before it becomes runoff.
It is not true that Agapito Flores invented the fluorescent lamp; this is just a myth.
Floss is a special thread used to remove food and dirt that get stuck between the teeth.
Flour is passed through a fine sieve to remove lumps and make it light and smooth.
A flower with all four parts is called a complete flower, while one missing a part is an incomplete flower.
The filament is the thin stalk of the stamen that holds up and supports the anther.
Many kids ask: which part becomes the fruit? The ovary inside the pistil grows and becomes the fruit! So before a mango was a mango, it was once the ovary of a mango flower.
A flower usually has four main parts: the petals, sepals, stamens, and pistil.
The pistil is the female part of the flower. It has a sticky tip (stigma) that catches pollen, and at the bottom is the ovary that later becomes a fruit with seeds inside.

Have you noticed the bananas we buy have almost no seeds? That is because people chose and grew seedless bananas so they are nicer to eat. Instead of seeds, they are planted from shoots or pieces of the plant.
In the Philippines, mango farmers help more flowers turn into fruit. They care for bees and protect the flowers, because more pollinated flowers means more mangoes to harvest.
Did you know every fruit starts as a flower? After pollen reaches the flower, the bottom part of the flower (called the ovary) grows bigger and becomes the fruit that holds the seeds.
The pistil is the female part of the flower that receives pollen and where seeds are formed.
Each seed can grow into a new plant when it is planted in the soil.
In self-pollination pollen goes to the same flower, but in cross-pollination it goes to a different flower.
The style is the stalk of the pistil that connects the stigma to the ovary, and pollen travels down it to the ovule.
Plants can be divided into flowering ones like gumamela and non-flowering ones like ferns.
The flowerpecker's gut processes mistletoe berries very quickly, so it passes the whole seed onto another branch where it can grow.
COVID-19 is not the only virus that spreads this way; the flu and colds are also respiratory viruses that spread through droplets.
The flu spreads quickly in crowded places like schools because people are close together.
There is a flu vaccine that helps protect the body against the influenza virus.
A difference: fluids such as air and water readily carry longitudinal sound, but they do not carry a simple side-to-side S-wave the way rock can.
Agapito Flores was a Filipino electrician, but there is no evidence that he invented the fluorescent lamp.
The word "fluorescent" comes from the mineral fluorspar, not from the name Flores.
Fluoride in toothpaste strengthens enamel and helps prevent tooth decay.
Fluoride in toothpaste reacts with tooth enamel to form fluorapatite, a harder mineral that is more resistant to acid attack from mouth bacteria, helping prevent cavities.
A fly has only two (2) wings, which is why its group is called Diptera (meaning 'two wings').
The flying fish escapes by gliding into the air so that tuna and dolphins cannot eat it.
The flying fish leaps from the water and glides through the air using its wide fins, but it does not truly fly.
The flying fish is a sea fish with wide, wing-like fins that let it leap from the water and glide through the air to escape predators.
At night, flying fish are attracted to lights, so they sometimes leap onto boats.
A flying fish does not really fly like a bird; it glides through the air without flapping wings.
Flying fish live in warm ocean waters, including the seas around the Philippines.

The flying fish has enormously enlarged pectoral fins that act like wings — the fish builds speed underwater using its powerful asymmetric caudal fin before launching and gliding up to 200 meters above the water.
Large fruit bats or flying foxes are important to forests as pollinators and seed dispersers, but they are threatened by hunting and habitat loss.
Flying foxes are large fruit bats that roost together in big colonies hanging from tall trees by day and help spread fruit seeds across the forest at night.
A mother flying lemur carries her baby clinging to her belly even while she glides through the air. She can fold the skin near her tail into a kind of pouch or hammock to hold the little one safely.
The flying lemur prefers young leaves because they are softer and have more nutrients than old leaves.

Both the flying lemur and the flying squirrel glide, but the flying lemur's skin membrane reaches all the way between its fingers and out to its tail, giving it a wider 'sail.' They also belong to different animal families even though their gliding looks similar.
The flying lemur is very awkward and weak when walking on the ground, so it stays up in the trees. Up there it is safer from ground predators and can move around by climbing and gliding instead.
Even though it is famous worldwide, the Venus flytrap grows naturally in only one small area in the eastern United States — it is not found wild anywhere else.
Energy is the ability to make things move or change. It comes in different forms: heat, light, sound, electrical, mechanical (motion), and chemical (stored in food and fuel).

Some kids think friction can happen with nothing touching. But friction only happens when two things are in contact and rub. Air resistance is also a kind of friction, because the moving object is rubbing against tiny air particles.
We see color because objects reflect some colors of light and absorb others. For example, an apple looks red because it reflects red light and absorbs the other colors.
Momentum is the strength of an object's motion — it depends on its mass and speed. A heavy, fast object (like a truck) is harder to stop than a light or slow one — which is why it is more dangerous.
Fog is a colloid (an aerosol) because tiny droplets of water are suspended in the air.
In thick fog you can see a car's light beam because the light scatters off the millions of tiny water droplets floating in the air.
The difference is that fog forms in the air itself, while dew forms on surfaces like grass and leaves.
Fog often forms at night and early morning when the ground cools and chills the air just above it, so the water vapor turns into tiny droplets close to the ground.
Fog and dew are part of the water cycle because they come from water vapor turning back into liquid drops.
Fog droplets form around very tiny bits of dust floating in the air, which give the water something to cling to.
Leaf-eaters use two strategies: some ferment leaves in a special stomach called the rumen, while others like the colugo do it in the cecum and large intestine.
A fomite is any object such as a doorknob, cell phone, or utensil that can carry microorganisms and spread disease to people who touch it.
A food chain is one straight path of eating, but in real nature animals eat many kinds of food. So many connected food chains together are called a food web.
Food gives the energy that the body uses to make heat and stay warm.
Food takes about 6 to 8 hours to pass through the stomach and small intestine, and may take up to 36 hours to become solid waste.
Eating spoiled food can cause food poisoning, which gives you vomiting and a sore stomach.
The food pyramid shows that we should eat more grains, vegetables, and fruits, and only a little fat and sweets, to keep a balanced diet.
Removing one species from a food web can cause large changes in many other species — if a species disappears, those that ate it may starve, while those it ate may overpopulate.
A food web is a diagram showing how many food chains link together, where each arrow points from the food to the living thing that eats it.
In a grassland, grasshoppers eat grass, birds eat grasshoppers, and snakes may eat birds, forming a food web that links many living things.
In a Philippine rainforest, insects eat leaves, birds eat the insects, and big predators like eagles eat the birds, forming a food web that links them all.
Air pushes against moving things, so a sheet of paper falls more slowly than a stone.

In physics, acceleration is ANY change in speed OR direction — not only speeding up. So a force causes acceleration: it can speed up, slow down, or turn an object. Even a car turning at constant speed is accelerating, because its direction is changing.

Sometimes you apply a force but the object still does not move — for example, you push a heavy cabinet but it does not budge. That is because friction balances your push, so the net force is zero. There is a force, but no change in motion because the forces are balanced.

Some forces must TOUCH an object before they can change its motion (contact forces) like a push or friction. Others change motion without touching (non-contact forces) like gravity and magnetism. That is why an object falls with nothing holding it — gravity pulls it from a distance.

A single force can change more than one thing at the same time. When you kick a ball, you change its speed, its direction, and even its shape slightly as your foot makes contact. These changes do not have to happen separately.

A question kids often ask: why does a thrown ball not fly straight but curve downward? While the ball flies, gravity keeps pulling it down. So the direction of its motion changes little by little until it lands — a force is always doing this.

For the same strength of force, a heavier object's motion changes less. An empty cart is easy to push, but a fully loaded cart is hard to push with the same effort. The more mass an object has, the more it resists a change in motion.

It is a common misconception that an object needs a constant force to keep moving. In truth, a force is only needed to CHANGE motion, not to maintain it. Where there is no friction (like outer space), an object keeps moving even when you no longer push it.

In a crash, the car stops suddenly but your body wants to keep moving at the old speed. The seatbelt applies a force on your body so it stops more slowly and safely, instead of being thrown forward. This is a real-world use of force to change motion safely.
Forces do not only change motion — they can also change the shape or form of an object, such as squeezing rubber or bending metal.
A force can make a moving object speed up or slow down.

Force and energy are easy to confuse, but they are different. A force is the PUSH or PULL itself that changes motion; energy is the ABILITY to cause change. When a force acts over a distance (work), energy is transferred. So they are linked: you use energy to apply a force and change motion.
By Newton's second law, force equals mass multiplied by acceleration: Force = mass × acceleration (F = m × a).

Many kids think friction is always bad because it slows things down. But that is not true — without friction we could not walk, cars could not brake, and we could not hold a pencil. We need friction for many everyday things.

There is much less friction with wheels than when you drag something. That is why a cart with wheels is easier to pull than dragging a box on the ground. A rolling object does not rub against the ground as much, so it moves more easily.
Friction is a force that resists motion and slows down a rolling or sliding object.
When you sit at the top of a slide, gravity pulls you downward so you slide all the way to the bottom. Nobody is pushing you—it is gravity alone that brings you down.
Opposite magnet poles pull together, but like poles push apart.
Only the part of a force that points along the direction of motion does work.
A force can make a moving object stop.
The stronger the push, the faster or farther the object moves.
Most forces need touch, but magnets and gravity can act without touching.
A forecast is not always right because the weather changes fast, so it is a smart guess — the best estimate, not a certainty.
Forests play a vital role by removing carbon dioxide from the air — trees absorb CO2 and store it in their bodies and the soil, helping slow climate change.
The forest floor receives very little sunlight because the canopy shades it, so mainly fungi and shade-tolerant animals live there.
Lipote is a native Philippine forest fruit with small purple berries that taste sweet-sour. It is often made into jam or juice, and it grows wild in our forests.
A forest fruit is a fruit that grows on its own in the wild, not planted by people. It comes from wild trees and plants, and it is the part of the plant that holds the seeds inside.
Trees race upward because sunlight is the energy they compete for, so a forest's shape is another sign of the Sun's importance.
The chemical formula of ammonia is NH3, one nitrogen and three hydrogen.
The chemical formula of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) is NaHCO3.
In CO2, the C means 1 carbon atom and the O2 means 2 oxygen atoms, so one carbon dioxide molecule has 1 carbon and 2 oxygen.
The chemical formula of glucose (a simple sugar) is C6H12O6.
The chemical formula of methane is CH4.
The chemical formula of the oxygen gas we breathe is O2.
The small lowered number in a formula, like the 2 in H₂O, tells how many atoms of that element are in the molecule.
In NaCl, the Na means sodium and the Cl means chlorine, so salt is made of sodium and chlorine.
Sometimes tiny insects get trapped in sticky tree resin that hardens into amber, preserving them whole.
Finding coral fossils in a place is a clue that the land there was once covered by a warm, shallow sea.

Fossils of ancient ferns and trees are found inside coal deposits; this confirms that coal comes from large tropical swamp forests that lived hundreds of millions of years ago; these fossils show the shapes of ancient plant leaves.
Most fossils are found in sedimentary rock, which forms when mud, sand, and silt pile up in layers and harden over time.
Some animals like mammoths have been found frozen in the ground, so even their skin and fur were preserved.
When fossil fuels are burned, they release carbon dioxide that causes pollution and global warming.
Before industry, carbon dioxide in the air was balanced, but human burning of fossil fuels has added far too much of it.

Why is burning fossil fuels a problem? It took millions of years to lock carbon inside them, but we release it back into the air in just a few years. The release is far faster than the storing, which upsets Earth's carbon balance.
Fossil fuels formed from the remains of plants and tiny sea creatures that died millions of years ago, got buried underground, and were pressed by heat and weight over a very long time.
Many people think fossil fuels come from dinosaurs, but that is not true. Most oil and gas came from tiny sea creatures and plants, not big dinosaurs. Some oil is even older than the dinosaurs.
When oil leaks from a ship or tanker into the sea, it is called an oil spill. It coats the water and sticks to birds' feathers and fish gills, causing serious harm to sea life and coastlines.
Oil is not stored in big underground lakes. Instead, it collects in the tiny spaces inside rocks, like water soaking into a sponge. That is why deep wells must be drilled to reach it.
How can we help? Every time we save energy, like turning off unused lights or walking instead of riding, less fossil fuel gets burned. Small as it seems, it helps our limited supply last longer.

Where does the energy in fossil fuels come from? Long ago, plants captured energy from the sun through photosynthesis. That energy got stored inside them, so when we burn coal or oil, we are really releasing ancient sunlight.
There are three main types of fossil fuels: coal (a solid), oil or petroleum (a liquid), and natural gas. They look very different, but all three formed from ancient living things buried long ago.
Hard parts like bones, teeth, and shells fossilize more often than soft parts like skin and muscle.
Some fossils that were widespread but lived only for a short time are used as markers to tell the age of the rock they are found in.
Some animals like the coelacanth are called living fossils because they have barely changed since ancient times.
Over time, mineral-rich water fills the tiny spaces in a buried bone, slowly turning it into stone.
It is rare for an animal to become a fossil, because it must be buried quickly before it rots or is eaten.
Scientists piece together fossil bones to rebuild an animal's skeleton and display it in a museum.
The fossil record in successive rock layers shows that the kinds of life changed over time — some organisms appeared and others disappeared.
Fossils tell us about animals and plants that once lived but no longer exist today, such as the dinosaurs.
Scientists use fossils found in rock layers to learn what life existed and how old the layers are.
Fossils can tell us what an environment was like in the past — for example, seashell fossils on a mountaintop show that the area was once under the sea.
Fossils tell us what plants and animals lived in the distant past, including dinosaurs, and how life on Earth has changed.
When you can say the problem, the materials, the steps, and the finding, the simple investigation has gone all the way around.
There are four fundamental forces in nature: gravity, electromagnetic, strong nuclear, and weak nuclear force.
Earth's geologic time is divided into four big spans: the Precambrian, Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic.
A simple science plan can fit on one page: the problem, the materials, the steps to do, and what you found out.
The method used to split crude oil is called fractional distillation, where the oil is heated and separated according to the different boiling points of its parts.
From a single batch of crude oil we get many useful products such as gasoline, diesel, and kerosene.
Benjamin Franklin showed that lightning is a form of electricity.
Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod, the metal that draws lightning safely down to the ground.
A free-body diagram is a drawing that shows all the forces acting on an object, using arrows that point in the direction and size of each force.
In free fall with no air resistance, all objects speed up downward at the same acceleration due to gravity, about 9.8 meters per second each second near the ground.
Without air resistance, heavy and light objects fall at exactly the same rate because gravity gives every mass the same acceleration.
With no air resistance, all objects — heavy or light — fall with the same acceleration, because a larger mass has a larger weight but also a larger inertia (F = ma).
When a free throw is shot, the ball follows a curved arc because gravity pulls it downward while it flies forward.
A freezer makes ice by taking heat away from water until it gets so cold that it turns solid — water becomes ice when it is cold enough.
Not everything melts at the same temperature. Ice melts at zero degrees Celsius, but candle wax and chocolate melt at higher heat, and metal needs very high heat to melt.
When ice melts, it absorbs heat from its surroundings. That is why your hand feels cold holding ice, the ice is pulling heat out of your skin to melt.
When you make ice candy, you put sweet juice in the freezer until it hardens. That is freezing! And when you take it out into the heat, it slowly melts back into liquid.
In the Philippines we almost never see natural ice or snow because it is warm here all year. The outdoor temperature does not reach zero degrees Celsius, so we need a freezer to make ice.
Freezing and melting can happen over and over to the same water. You can freeze water, melt it back, and freeze it again, nothing is destroyed; it is still the same water.

Slush, crushed ice mixed with water, is right between freezing and melting. Some solid ice is still there while some has turned to liquid. It is like a favorite ice scramble, half-melted and still cold.
While ice is melting, its temperature does not rise even though heat is being added. All that heat goes into breaking apart the ice, so it stays at zero degrees Celsius until all the ice is gone.
Freezing is liquid turning solid as it cools. This is different from evaporation, where liquid turns into gas as it heats. Both are changes of state, but the heat moves in opposite directions.
Water is unusual: it expands when it freezes. That is why a full bottle of water can crack in the freezer, the ice needs more space than the liquid water did.
Melting absorbs heat, while freezing releases heat.
Water grows bigger in size when it turns into ice, which is why a full bottle can overflow in the freezer.
A faster vibrating dipper makes more crests each second, so the pattern looks tighter even if the tank size stays the same.
Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), where one hertz means one vibration per second.
Pitch goes up when more sound waves reach your ear each second, which is what a moving-closer source does to the wave train.
The SI unit of frequency is the hertz (Hz), named after Heinrich Hertz.
A volcano that erupts often, like Mayon, is not safer just because people are used to it; each new unrest still needs watching.
Fresh lumpiang ubod is wrapped in a thin crepe and filled with ubod, the soft white heart taken from inside the stem of the coconut palm.
The freshwater eel (palos) is a snake-shaped fish with slippery skin that lives in rivers and streams before swimming to the sea to lay eggs.
Fresh water freezes more easily; salt water must get colder before it turns to ice.
Only a tiny share of Earth's water is fresh water people can use, so it should be saved and not wasted.
A freshwater lake is a large body of fresh water that is home to fish, water plants, and birds that all depend on one another to live.
When a river or groundwater is polluted with trash and chemicals, it becomes unsafe to drink, and it is very hard and costly to clean it again.
Some marshes are freshwater marshes near rivers and lakes, while others are saltwater marshes near the coast.
Crops like rice need fresh water; salty water harms most plants.
Almost all of Earth's water is salty seawater — less than 3 percent is fresh water, and most of that is locked away in ice and glaciers.
Basketball dribbling relies on friction between the rubber ball and the court floor — friction causes the ball to bounce predictably and stay under the player's control.
Brakes use friction to stop a bicycle or car when they press against the wheels.
When two objects rub together, friction turns some of their kinetic energy into heat, which is why a car's brakes and rubbed hands get warm.
How much friction there is depends on what kinds of surfaces touch: rubber on concrete has lots of friction, but ice on metal has very little.
Besides slowing things, friction also makes a car go: the friction between the tire and the road is what pushes the car forward.
Because of friction, some of a moving object's kinetic energy turns into heat.
Over a long time, friction from rocks rubbing in a river slowly wears them down until they become sand.
Friction comes from tiny bumps and dips on surfaces that catch on each other when they rub, even when the surfaces look smooth to the eye.
Too much heat from friction can damage a machine, so its moving parts are oiled to keep them from overheating.
Because of friction we can hold a pencil or a glass without it slipping out of our hand.
Friction helps us walk without slipping because it grips our feet to the ground.
On Earth, moving things stop because of friction and air resistance, not because Newton's law is wrong.
Oil or grease reduces the friction between machine parts so they move more smoothly.
Friction always points opposite to the direction of motion, so if you run forward, friction pushes backward to slow you down.
Ball bearings are small metal spheres placed between a shaft and its housing to replace sliding friction with rolling friction, making rotation smoother and more efficient.
Asphalt roads are not perfectly smooth — the rough texture is intentional to increase friction between vehicle tyres and the road, especially when wet.
Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction, which is why a box with wheels is easier to move.
Sandpaper uses friction to scrape and make rough wood smooth.
Friction is a force from two surfaces rubbing, and it slows motion down.
Static friction that keeps a stationary object still is greater than kinetic friction acting on the same object once it is already moving.
Because of friction, part of the work we do is wasted as heat.
Because of friction, some of the work turns into heat and seems wasted.
Friction goes down when a floor is wet, so it becomes slippery and risky to walk after rain.
Overall, fridges and air conditioners warm their surroundings because they release the heat removed plus the heat from the electricity used.
The coils at the back of a fridge feel warm because that is where the heat removed from inside escapes.
A fridge acts like a heat pump that forces heat from the cold inside out to the warmer outside.
A fridge has thick walls that act as insulation to keep outside heat from getting in.
A safe refrigerator is kept at about 4 degrees Celsius, cold enough to slow microbe growth.
A sitting friend hears less pitch shift from the same bell, because that friend's ears are not moving into the waves.
A fringing reef grows attached right along the shore of an island or coast.
Besides using lungs, a frog can breathe through its wet skin — oxygen passes through the skin into its blood, which lets it stay underwater for a long time.
A frog has big, bulging eyes on top of its head so it can see around even while in water.
Some frogs in cold countries can survive even when most of their body freezes in winter — their heart stops, and when the ice melts they come back to life.
Frogs lay many eggs together in jelly-like clusters in the water.
One main reason frogs jump is to escape predators like snakes or birds. With one strong, sudden jump, a frog can get far away before it gets caught.
Many kids ask how high a frog can jump. A frog can leap higher than its own body, so for a moment it looks like it's flying before coming back down to the ground.
A frog's jumps are not all the same. Sometimes it makes small hops when moving slowly, but when scared or escaping it makes much bigger, longer leaps.
Tadpoles turn into frogs faster in warm water, so in the warm ponds of the Philippines their change often happens quickly.
A frog can breathe through its moist skin, not just with its lungs.
A frog does not drink water with its mouth; instead, it soaks up water through its skin.
Not only insects go through metamorphosis; frogs also change from tadpoles into legged adults.
When a tadpole turns into a frog, its tail does not fall off — its own body absorbs the tail and uses it as nourishment while its legs grow.
Male frogs use vocal sacs — pouches of loose skin under the mouth — to amplify their calls so they reach females farther away.
Front-view diagrams show left and right testes or ovaries as a pair, while side-view diagrams show depth from front to back.
In high, cold places like Benguet, frost sometimes forms on crops at dawn, and it can damage vegetables when it gets very cold.
Frost looks like a thin white coating, almost like powdered sugar or flour, on grass and objects. When you touch it, it feels cold and quickly melts from the warmth of your finger, turning wet.
In very cold weather dew can freeze into frost, as sometimes happens in the high parts of Baguio.
To keep frost from harming crops, farmers cover their vegetables with plastic or cloth at night. This traps a little heat from the ground and keeps the leaves from getting cold enough to freeze.

Frost is part of the water cycle: water vapor in the air freezes into frost on cold surfaces, and then when it warms up it melts and becomes wet, or turns back into vapor that returns to the air. This is how water moves through its different forms.
Fruit bats sleep during the day and fly out at night to find fruit to eat.
Unlike many other bats, large fruit bats use their sharp eyesight and sense of smell to find food rather than echolocation.
By scattering seeds and carrying pollen, fruit bats help forests regrow and stay healthy.
A bat is a mammal, not a bird, even though it can fly with its wings.
As fruit bats drink nectar, pollen sticks to their fur and is carried to other flowers, so they help pollinate plants.
Fruit bats rest and sleep hanging upside down from tree branches.
When fruit bats eat fruit, they carry and drop the seeds far away, helping new trees grow in the forest.
The fruit dove is a kind of pigeon with very colorful feathers.
True to its name, the fruit dove eats mostly fruit.
Most monitor lizards eat meat, but the butaan (Varanus olivaceus) of Luzon and Catanduanes is one of the very few monitor lizards in the world that eats fruit. It is rare and lives in forests.
Fruit first ripens, but if it sits too long it rots and gets attacked by mold.
Santol, atis, and guyabano first grow flowers, which then turn into fruit.
Vegetables and fruits contain fiber, which helps food digest well and makes going to the toilet easier.
Fuel is any material that can burn, such as wood, paper, or gasoline.
Coal and oil store energy that plants captured from sunlight long ago, so even some fuels in engines began as solar energy.
The Fujita scale rates a tornado's strength based on the damage it causes.
When the bladder gets full, it sends a signal to your brain so you know it is time to pee.
It saves electricity to run a full washing machine load instead of many small loads.
At full moon we see its entire sunlit face, so it looks round and bright.
A bright full moon can make evening outdoor games possible, because that sky object reflects enough sunlight to light a yard.
Fungi feed by absorbing nutrients from their surroundings instead of eating with a mouth like animals.
Amanita phalloides, the death cap, is one of the world's most deadly mushrooms; it looks similar to edible mushrooms and can cause liver failure and death.
Fungi are called decomposers because they break down dead things and return nutrients to the soil.
Many people think fungi are plants, but unlike plants they do not make their own food from sunlight. They have no green chlorophyll, so they must digest and take their food from other things.
Fungi can digest even tough materials like wood and leaves that most animals cannot break down. They have special enzymes that cut apart the hard parts of plants to turn them into food.
People and animals swallow their food first and digest it inside the stomach. Fungi do the opposite: they digest the food outside first, then soak it up, so they need no stomach.
Yeast is a kind of fungus used to make bread. It digests and feeds on the sugar in the flour, and in this process it releases a gas that makes the bread rise and turn soft.
Some mushrooms are safe and nutritious to eat, like the oyster mushroom often cooked as a dish.
Claviceps purpurea (ergot) is a dangerous fungus that grows on rye and wheat grains; ergot poisoning caused serious illness and hallucinations historically.
Fungi are called heterotrophs because they cannot make their own food and must get it from other living things.

In the Philippines, farmers grow mushrooms (like oyster mushrooms) by placing hyphae into damp rice straw or sawdust bags. The mycelium first spreads inside, and then mushrooms sprout that can be eaten or sold.

The mushroom we see is only the FRUITING part of the fungus — its real body is the long hyphae (mycelium) hidden underground or inside wood. The mushroom pops up to release spores that become new fungi.

Looked at under a microscope, a hypha is often divided by thin inner walls (septa) that make it like boxes lined up in a row, like a train. There are tiny holes in the walls so nutrients and other things can pass from one cell to the next.

Have you ever wondered why mushrooms pop up suddenly after rain? It is because the hyphae (mycelium) were already there, hidden in the soil, just waiting. When rain comes and there is enough moisture, they quickly grow and push up as mushrooms.
Not all fungi make hyphae! Yeast, used to make bread rise, is also a fungus, but it is just a single round cell and does not form long threads. This shows that fungi come in different forms.
Fungi are not plants or animals but belong to their own separate group of living things.
A mushroom has three main parts: the cap (pileus) on top, the stalk (stipe) below it, and the gills on the underside of the cap where spores are made.
Many fungi help plant roots: they give the plant water and nutrients, and the plant gives them sugar in return.
Mycoprotein is a fungal protein used as a meat alternative; the best-known is Quorn, made from Fusarium venenatum grown in large fermentation tanks.
Some fungi grow on tree roots and help the trees take in water and nutrients from the soil.
Penicillin, a medicine that kills disease-causing bacteria, comes from a mold fungus.
During World War II, scientists developed large-scale production of penicillin using Penicillium chrysogenum in large fermentation tanks, making penicillin available for millions of wounded soldiers.
Ringworm and athlete's foot are skin infections caused by fungi, not worms; they spread easily by skin contact or sharing footwear.
Tinea versicolor (an-an) is a common skin fungal infection in the Philippines that worsens in hot and humid climates, causing patches of discolored skin.
Truffles are expensive edible fungi that grow underground near tree roots; they are prized in cooking for their strong aroma and flavor.
In warm, humid climates like the Philippines, things rot faster because fungi grow quickly.
Bird feathers and animal fur trap a layer of air close to the body — this trapped air layer prevents body heat from escaping to the surroundings.

When a breaker keeps tripping right after you switch it on, it isn't broken — it's telling you there's still a problem. The right move: unplug some appliances or check for a short first, before switching it back on. You shouldn't just keep forcing it on, because that's dangerous.

In a breaker panel there is one large 'main breaker' that cuts power to the whole house, plus many small 'branch breakers' for separate lines — one for the kitchen, one for a bedroom, and so on. So when there's a problem in just one room, only that line shuts off, not the whole house.

In most Filipino homes, there is a box of circuit breakers near the door or outside the house. When the lights suddenly go out in just one part of the house, often a breaker there has tripped — you can switch it back on after unplugging the extra appliances.

A big difference: when a fuse blows, you must replace it with a new one because its wire has melted. A circuit breaker, though, you can simply switch back on (reset) after fixing the problem — you don't need to replace it.

One reason a fuse or breaker trips is a short circuit — when two bare wires touch, a very large current suddenly rushes through a short path. The fuse or breaker senses this fast and immediately cuts the flow.

A fuse and a grounding wire are different kinds of protection. A fuse cuts the current when too much flows. A grounding wire gives stray electricity a safe path into the earth, so you don't get shocked when you touch an appliance. They work together to protect you.
A fuse melts and cuts off the current when too much electricity flows, to prevent fire.
Nuclear fusion inside a star releases great amounts of energy over millions of years, and this is why stars like the Sun shine and give off heat.
The devastating 1990 Luzon earthquake was triggered by a sudden tectonic slip along the Digdig Fault of the Philippine Fault Zone.
Weaving abaca fibers into a Manila hemp rope is a physical change because the abaca's chemical composition remains unchanged.
Adding baking soda to vinegar causes an acid-base reaction that rapidly produces carbon dioxide gas, creating the bubbling foam you see.
Mixing solid baking soda with liquid stomach acid produces carbon dioxide gas, which you burp out to relieve indigestion.
Dropping chalk into vinegar causes an acid-base chemical reaction that produces bubbling carbon dioxide gas and dissolves the solid calcium carbonate.
The tamarind tree produces fruits containing tartaric acid, which gives liquid sinigang its sour chemical property.
Calamansi juice tastes sour and turns blue litmus paper red because it contains citric acid, showing its chemical property.
The Texas horned lizard can shoot blood from the corners of its eyes to deter predators.
Cooking chicken adobo involves a chemical change because the acetic acid in vinegar reacts with the meat proteins to alter their chemical structure and flavor.
The Aedes aegypti mosquito transmits the dengue virus to humans, making eliminating its breeding grounds crucial for public health.
Scientists remove almost all the liquid from a silica gel mixture to create aerogel, a solid material that is 99 percent air.
Aerogel is a solid material made mostly of air, making it so light it can balance on a delicate flower without crushing it.
Silica aerogel is 99.8 percent air, making it an incredibly light solid material that can rest delicately on a flower petal.
Silica aerogel is a solid material made of 99 percent empty air, making it one of the lightest solids known.
Aerogel is a synthetic solid material composed of 99.8 percent air, yet it is strong enough to support thousands of times its own weight.
Aerogel is a synthetic solid material made by replacing the liquid in a gel with gas, making it 99 percent air and incredibly lightweight.
Never leave an aerosol spray can in a hot car because heating the gas inside increases pressure and can cause the can to explode.
Heating a sealed aerosol spray can increases gas pressure inside, which can cause the metal container to explode.
Aerosol spray cans contain gases under high pressure, so leaving them in a hot car can cause the metal can to explode.
Never throw aerosol cans into a fire because the heated gas inside expands and causes the metal can to explode.
The Agusan River flows northward into Butuan Bay, draining rainwater from the Caraga region back into the Bohol Sea.
Air is a mixture of 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen, meaning it contains nearly four times more nitrogen than oxygen.
Earth's atmosphere contains about twenty-one percent oxygen gas, which is necessary for combustion and rusting.
Compressing air into a standard scuba tank reduces its volume by about 200 times compared to normal atmospheric pressure.
HEPA air filters trap solid dust particles and pollen from the gas mixture we call indoor air.
N95 masks filter solid dust particles from the air we breathe, protecting our lungs from pollution.
The streamlined, pointed nose of the MRT-3 train in Manila reduces air friction, allowing it to move faster and use less energy.
Air is a mixture of gases that has measurable mass and takes up physical space.

A gecko's feet use no glue; they are dry yet still grip a smooth wall.

Grip is stronger when the contact is split into many tiny hair-tips than when it is one big flat patch. That is the gecko's secret: instead of one sticky surface, millions of tiny tips grip the wall together.

To let go, a gecko simply changes the angle of its toes and peels them upward, much like lifting tape off a surface. At the right angle the stickiness instantly switches off, which is why a gecko can lift each foot so quickly while climbing.

A gecko sticks because of an extremely weak attraction between molecules called van der Waals forces. The pull from one hair is tiny, but with millions of hairs working together, the total force is strong enough to hold the gecko's whole body.

It is harder for a gecko to cling to a soaking wet or slippery surface because water gets in the way of the hairs' pull on the wall. Still, some geckos are adapted to damp places and can grip even on a wet wall.

There are several reasons DNA changes or mutates: sometimes from a mistake while it is being copied, and sometimes from too much sunlight (UV), cigarette smoke, or certain chemicals. That is why protecting yourself from the sun matters.

When an organism's two alleles differ, the dominant allele shows up in the appearance while the recessive allele stays hidden and shows only when two recessive alleles are present together.
Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk, is known as the "Father of Genetics."
When two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb) are crossed, the expected phenotype ratio of the offspring is 3 to 1 — three with the dominant trait for every one with the recessive trait.

Kids ask whether you can feel a mutation when it happens. You cannot. Cells and DNA are so tiny that you feel no pain and notice nothing at the exact moment a mutation occurs. Usually there is no sign at all, and many of us carry mutations we never even know about our whole lives.

Cells normally follow instructions about when to divide and when to stop. If certain mutations build up in the genes that control dividing, it is like the brakes break, and the cell starts dividing out of control. This unstoppable growth is what we call cancer.
A mutation is a change in the sequence of DNA; a part of the DNA may be altered, deleted, or added, and this can change how a gene works.

The body does not leave every DNA mistake alone. There are special proteins that act like a spell checker, finding and fixing many errors before they become permanent mutations. Because of this repair system, we end up with far fewer mutations than we otherwise would.
A mutation's effect can be helpful, harmful, or neutral — some mutations help an organism survive better, some are damaging, and many have little or no effect at all.
