Germs travel through air in two ways: droplets that are heavier and fall quickly nearby, and airborne particles that are very tiny and float a long time and far. Some diseases like tuberculosis and measles are airborne, so good ventilation and fresh air are important.
Germs can spread through tiny droplets of spit when someone coughs or sneezes.

Germs spread faster in crowded places like schools, markets, and rides like jeepneys or trains. Because people are close together and the air is sometimes trapped, germs move more easily from one person to many. That is why fresh air and, when sick, wearing a mask matter.

When germs enter the body, they must multiply first before you feel sick — this is called the incubation period, which can be several days. Surprisingly, you can already spread it to others even before you have symptoms. That is why illness spreads even when a person still looks healthy.

Not all germs spread through air or hands — some are carried by mosquitoes. When a mosquito with a virus or parasite bites, it passes germs into the blood, as with dengue and malaria. In the Philippines, avoid standing clear water because that is where the Aedes mosquito lays eggs.

It is a misconception that all germs are bad and cause sickness. Most bacteria are harmless, and some are even helpful — like the good bacteria in our gut that help digestion. Only 'pathogens,' a small portion of germs, actually cause disease.

Quarantine is keeping a sick or exposed person separated from others for a while. When the germs have no one nearby to reach, the chain of transmission is broken and spreading slowly stops. The whole world did this during COVID to slow the spread of the virus.

A vaccine teaches the immune system to recognize a germ before it can make you sick, using a dead or weakened part of it. When many people are vaccinated, germs have a harder time finding new people to infect, so spread slows down — this is called herd immunity. This is how polio and measles were controlled.
Germs can survive on doorknobs and other things that many people touch.
Many germs spread through dirty water and unclean toilets. That is why clean water and proper toilets are important to keep children from getting diarrhea.
Germs are also why food spoils. They multiply in food and break it down, so it turns sour or gets moldy. That is why we keep food in the fridge to slow the germs down.
Not all germs are the same. There are different kinds: bacteria, viruses, fungi (like molds), and others. Each kind has its own way of living and spreading.
We also use some helpful germs to make food. For example, certain bacteria turn milk into yogurt and cheese. So not all germs are our enemy.
Not all germs are bad. There are helpful bacteria inside our gut that help us digest food. So it is wrong to think every germ is something to fear.
Germs are so tiny that we cannot see them with our eyes — you need a microscope to see them. Even if a hand or table looks clean, there may still be germs on it, so washing and cleaning matter.
The germs that make us sick include bacteria and viruses that are far too tiny to see with the eye.
A geyser is a spring that repeatedly shoots hot water and steam into the air, because heat from inside the Earth boils underground water until it bursts out.
A geyser erupts when water in a narrow underground channel gets so hot it turns to steam. The steam's pressure forces the water upward, so it shoots out.
True geysers are rare in the world — they are found in places like Iceland and Yellowstone in America. The Philippines has many hot springs, but almost no true geysers.
Fishing nets lost or left in the sea are called "ghost nets" — they keep trapping and tangling fish and sea turtles even though no person is holding them anymore.
A giant clam holds tiny algae inside its body that make food from sunlight for both of them to share.
A giant clam has two thick, heavy shells that close to protect its soft body inside.
By filtering water, giant clams help keep the water around the coral reef clean.
Large giant clams give shelter and a home to small fish and other animals on the reef.
Even though giant clams are huge, they are not dangerous to people and close their shells only slowly.
Even though the shell is big and hard, a young giant clam and its soft mantle can be eaten by certain fish, sea snails, and turtles, so closing the shell is important for them.
The giant clam has openings called siphons where water flows in so it can take oxygen and food, and used water and waste flow back out.
The giant clam (Tridacna gigas) — the largest living bivalve — can grow over 1.2 meters and weigh over 200 kilograms; it can live more than 100 years and does not move after settling.
The giant golden-crowned flying fox flies at night and uses its sharp eyesight to find fruit in the dark.
A newborn panda baby is very tiny, about the size of a stick of butter.
Pandas do not sleep through winter; instead they move to warmer parts of the mountain where bamboo still grows.
A panda often sits upright while eating, using its hands to hold the bamboo.
The giant squid has the largest eyes of any animal, about 27 centimeters wide—as big as a dinner plate.
Giant squid suckers have sharp teeth around their rims — evidence of battles between sperm whales and giant squid can be seen as large circular scars on whale skin, left by the squid's suckers.
Giant tortoises commonly live for more than 100 years.
A giant tortoise can live more than 100 years, one of the longest-living animals.
Giant tortoises can live more than 100 years, making them one of the longest-lived animals.
A hard flap called the operculum on each side of a fish's head protects the gills.
Gills look red because of all the blood flowing inside them to pick up oxygen.
Ginataang mais is a warm or cold dessert made from corn kernels and glutinous rice cooked in sweet coconut milk.
Ginger, such as in ginger tea, is often used to calm an upset stomach or queasy feeling.
The giraffe has a long, strong tongue to pull leaves from the thorny branches of acacia trees.
The giraffe is a herbivore, meaning it eats only plants and leaves.
The giraffe has a large, strong heart to push blood all the way up its long neck to its brain.
Giraffes live in the grassy, tree-dotted savannas of Africa.
The giraffe uses its long neck to reach leaves on the high branches of trees.
Male giraffes fight by swinging their long necks against each other.
The patches on a giraffe's coat help it hide among the shadows of trees and grass.
Because the giraffe is so tall, it can see danger from far away before it gets close.
If a full ring of bark is stripped all around the trunk, the tree can die because food can no longer flow down.

U-shaped valleys form by glacial erosion: when a large glacier passes through a valley, it carves the sides and creates a smooth wide bottom instead of the narrow, sharp V-shaped valley that rivers create.
In cold places, thick moving ice called a glacier slowly scrapes and digs the land, carving wide valleys.
Thick glacier ice looks blue because it soaks up the red light and sends the blue light back to our eyes.
Deep inside thick glacier ice are tiny bubbles of ancient air, so scientists use it to learn what the climate was like long ago.
Endocrine glands release their hormones straight into the blood without a duct. They differ from glands like sweat and salivary glands, which use ducts to release sweat or saliva.
Glass is clear because its atoms are arranged in a jumbled, non-crystal way, so it does not scatter the light passing through.
Benjamin Franklin's glass armonica makes sound when wet fingers rub the rim of spinning glass discs — friction sets up standing waves in the glass producing musical tones.
Glassblowing began in the Syria region during Roman times.
Borosilicate glass (like Pyrex) resists thermal shock better than ordinary soda-lime glass because it expands less when heated, so it is used in labs and bakeware.
Glass cannot bend or stretch when forced, so instead of bending it suddenly cracks and breaks.
Optical fibers are thin glass fibers that carry light signals over long distances with minimal loss; they are used for internet and telecommunications connections in the Philippines.
Glass is made from sand that is melted at very high heat.
Sand must be heated to over 1,700 degrees Celsius to become glass.
There is a natural glass called obsidian, which forms when lava from a volcano cools very quickly.
Glass was first made in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt.
Glass can be recycled over and over endlessly, because it can be melted and reshaped again without losing its quality.
Crushed recycled glass called cullet melts faster than raw materials for making new glass, saving energy and reducing emissions at glass factories.

Even though it is made from sand, glass is clear because when it cools quickly from melting, its tiny parts do not line up in a neat pattern like a crystal. This lets light pass through, so we can see through it.
Soda is added to the sand to lower the melting temperature, and lime is added to make the glass stronger.
Kids often ask: will a glass cup melt if left in the sun? No! The heat needed to melt glass is very high, hotter than the hottest sunny day. So your glass is safe.

Many kids think the 'soda' in glass is the soft drink we drink. It is not! The soda here is a different chemical (sodium carbonate, like washing soda), a white salt-like powder. They just share a name.
A great thing about soda-lime glass is that it can be melted down again and again to make new glass. That is why old bottles can be recycled, the glass is never wasted.
Lime is added because glass made from just soda and sand could slowly dissolve in water. The lime makes the glass stable and durable so it lasts a long time and resists water.
Ordinary glass softens and melts at about 1400 to 1500 degrees Celsius.
At normal temperature, glass is hard and solid, and it turns into a liquid only when heated very strongly.
Ordinary glass can shatter under sudden temperature change (thermal shock) — for example, placing hot food in a cold glass — because the outer surface expands faster than the inner part.
Some geckos have skin flaps along their body and between their toes that help them glide.
Gliding has no wing flapping; the animal simply descends slowly as it moves through the air.
The flying lizard, gliding snake, and gliding gecko are not closely related but each learned to glide separately.
Gliding reptiles often live high in the tops of tall trees in dense rainforests.
All the surface and deep currents connect into one giant loop called the global conveyor belt that circles the whole planet.
A GMO, or genetically modified organism, is a plant or animal whose genes have been deliberately changed using genetic engineering to give it a useful trait.
Go foods provide energy for the body; these are carbohydrate-rich foods such as rice, bread, corn, and sweet potato.
Some examples of go foods are rice, bread, sweet potato, corn, potato, and pasta. Most of them come from plants and are full of energy.
Kamote (sweet potato) is a healthy go food common in the Philippines. Besides energy, it also gives fiber that helps your tummy digest food well.
During a flood, it is safest to move to higher ground away from rushing water.
Many goats have hair on their chin that looks like a beard.
A male goat (billy goat) has hard horns it uses to fight and protect itself, and it eats grass and leaves.
The goat is a herbivore that prefers leaves and small shrubs, not just grass. It can even climb to high places to reach leaves.
A goat is a ruminant; it brings back partly digested food to chew again, called cud.
Many Filipinos raise goats in the backyard because they are easy to feed with grass and not costly.
Goats are good climbers, so they sometimes climb rocks or lean on trees to reach and eat leaves that are too high to get from the ground.
Even though goats eat plants, not all plants are safe — some are poisonous and can make a goat sick, so farmers watch where their goats graze.
At first a baby goat drinks only milk, but as it grows it copies its mother to learn how to pick and graze on grass until it can feed on its own.
Goats are commonly raised on farms in the Philippines because they are easy to keep and eat grass.
Goats and sheep are different: a goat has an upright tail and flat hair, while a sheep has curly wool.
Goats and sheep are mammals, so they give birth to live young and feed them milk.
Goats are given vaccines and deworming medicine to prevent disease and stomach worms.
Like all animals, goats and sheep need clean water to drink every day to stay healthy.
Goggles are protective glasses worn over the eyes to shield them from chemical splashes or small flying bits during experiments.
Goiter was more common in inland and mountain areas far from the sea, where soil and food have less iodine.
Gold boils at a very hot 2,856 degrees Celsius.
Tiny amounts of gold are used inside cellphones and computers because it conducts electricity and does not rust.
In the Philippines, gold and copper are often found together in the same kind of rock underground.
Gold does not rust or corrode, so it stays shiny.
Gold conducts electricity well, so a little of it is used in cellphones and computers.
Pure gold is soft, so it is mixed with other metals like copper or silver to make jewelry harder and stronger.
Gold jewelry is often mixed with copper or silver to make it stronger; 24-karat is pure gold.
Gold melts at about 1,064 degrees Celsius.
Some miners look for gold in rivers by panning sand in a shallow basin.
Pure gold is a soft metal that can easily be bent and shaped.
Gold is a soft, heavy metal that does not rust, which makes it valuable for jewelry.
Gold is a soft, yellow metal that is shiny and does not rust.
The golden apple snail has a hard door called an operculum that it can close to keep from drying out when water is low.
Farmers lower the water in the field because golden apple snails cannot move and feed well in shallow water.
The giant golden-crowned flying fox is endemic to the Philippines, meaning it is found only on our islands and nowhere else in the world.
The giant golden-crowned flying fox can weigh up to 1.4 kilograms, making it one of the heaviest bats in the world.
The Golgi apparatus is a part of the cell that packages and sorts proteins before sending them to other parts of the cell or out of it.
The Goliath birdeater, the heaviest spider, can weigh about 175 grams.
The goliath frog can weigh up to about 3 kilograms.
Helpful 'good' bacteria live in our gut and aid defense by crowding out harmful germs.

When you stand tall with your head up, you look more confident to other people. Scientists even say good posture can help you feel better, too. Try it: stand tall before speaking in front of the class.

When you sit upright after eating, your stomach has more room to digest your food. When you slouch, the belly gets squeezed and you may feel uncomfortable. So it helps to sit up straight for a while after your meal.

In offices and schools, some chairs are made to support your back while you sit. Their backrest follows your spine's natural curve so you don't tire or slouch. Even at home, a chair with a firm backrest helps good posture.
When your back is straight, your lungs have more room to fill with air. When you slouch, your lungs get squished and your breaths are shallow. So good posture helps you breathe more deeply.
Good posture, like sitting and standing up straight, helps keep the spine healthy and strong.

Some kids think good posture is only for sitting. But you need it while walking too: keep your head up, back straight, and don't slouch as you move. Even while playing or just standing, good posture still helps.
Good posture protects our spine and helps prevent back pain.

Your spine is not perfectly straight like a stick. It has gentle S-shaped curves that help you balance and absorb shock when you walk. Good posture means keeping these natural curves, not flattening them out.
Good posture means keeping our back straight when we sit or stand.
Larry Page and Sergey Brin founded Google in 1998.
Tiny muscles in the skin make body hair stand up, giving us goosebumps when we are cold or scared.
Goosebumps are a leftover from our furry ancestors — in thick-furred animals the same reflex fluffs up the hair to trap warmth, but on our smooth skin it does almost nothing useful.
In furry animals, raised hair traps a layer of warm air to keep the body warm.
Using GPS and satellites, scientists can measure how fast and in what direction the plates are moving.
In grafting, the upper fruit-bearing part is called the scion, and the lower rooted part is called the rootstock.
The gram is a unit for measuring mass or weight.
A simple graph is more trustworthy after you have at least three careful trials, because two points can make a line that is only luck.
A bar graph shows data using rectangular bars whose length or height stands for an amount, making it easy to compare which is more.
A difference: a graph of pressure versus time can look like a transverse drawing even when the real wave is longitudinal, so the picture needs a label.
A pictograph is a graph that uses small pictures or symbols to stand for numbers, where each picture equals a certain amount.
Graphite, the material inside a pencil, conducts electricity even though it is not a metal.
Graphite, used in pencils, is very soft at only about 1 to 2 on the Mohs scale, even though it is also pure carbon.
Grasshoppers and crickets are insects with six legs and three body parts.
Grasshoppers eat plants such as leaves and grass.
Usually the whole cycle from egg to adult grasshopper takes a few months. The nymph grows faster when it is warm and there is plenty of food.
A grasshopper nymph usually molts about five to six times before it becomes a full winged adult.
Grasshoppers have no pupa because their body changes only gradually with each molt. Unlike a butterfly that must transform greatly inside a cocoon, the grasshopper just grows little by little.
Farmers know that the wingless nymph cannot yet fly, so it is easier to control at that stage before it grows and multiplies in the rice fields.
A grasshopper differs from a butterfly: the butterfly has four stages including a caterpillar and pupa (complete metamorphosis), but the grasshopper has only three stages and no pupa.
Grasshoppers can jump up to 20 times their body length—made possible by the very powerful muscles in their hind legs.
Birds and frogs eat grasshoppers and crickets.
Many grassland animals like deer and horses can run very fast. Because the land is open with nowhere to hide, they must run to escape predators.
Many small grassland animals dig burrows underground. There they hide from the heat and from predators.
Grasslands help nature because their deep roots and soil store carbon. This helps keep the air cleaner.
In a grassland, a grasshopper eats grass, a bird eats the grasshopper, and a snake or hawk eats the bird. This is a food chain.
Grasslands have different names around the world, such as prairie in North America and savanna in Africa.
Some think a grassland is useless because it is just grass. But it is home to many animals and a source of food and fresh air.
A grassland changes its look with the seasons. In the wet season the grass is green and fresh; in the dry season it turns brown and dry.
Grassland soil is very fertile because dying grasses rot and turn into nutrients. That is why it makes good farmland.
A grassland gets more rain than a desert, so grass can grow there. A desert gets so little rain that you mostly see sand and only a few plants.
Graupel is soft pellets of ice that form when tiny supercooled water droplets freeze onto a snowflake as it falls.
Gravel on a barangay road is an earth material: broken rock pieces used because they are hard, non-living, and easy to spread.
An object's gravitational potential energy increases when it is heavier or placed higher up, because more energy is stored for it to fall with.
A heavier object has more gravitational potential energy at the same height.
Gravity acts on every mass near Earth, light or heavy, which is why both a pebble and a mango are pulled downward when you let go.
Every object with mass pulls on every other object through gravity, but the pull is so weak for small things that we only notice it with huge bodies like the Earth.
The more mass an object has, the stronger its gravity is.
Every object on Earth, big or small, is pulled by gravity, so they all have weight.
Without air to slow them, a heavy object and a light object fall at the same speed.
Isaac Newton explained that gravity is the force that holds the planets in their orbits around the Sun.
Gravity is a force we cannot see but we can feel its pull.
The Sun's gravity ties the whole solar system—planets, moons, asteroids, and comets—together as one family.
Gravity pulls weathered rock and soil downhill along mountain slopes, which is why landslides happen.
The Moon's gravity is only about 1/6 (one-sixth) of Earth's gravity, so you feel much lighter there.
A book resting on a table stays still because the downward pull of gravity is balanced by the upward push of the table.

A planet stays in orbit because of the balance between two things: the Sun's gravity pulling the planet inward, and the planet's sideways motion. Without the motion, the planet would fall into the Sun; without gravity, it would fly off in a straight line.
A ball rolls down a slope because gravity pulls it downward.
A helium balloon rising does not mean gravity turned off; a larger upward force from the air is winning for a while, which is a different comparison.
Of the four fundamental forces, gravity is the weakest, while the strong nuclear force is the strongest.
The Moon's gravity pulls on the ocean water and causes high and low tides.
The Moon's gravity pulls on ocean water on the side of Earth closest to it, causing high tide there and on the opposite side, with low tides in between.
Water in rivers and waterfalls flows downhill because gravity pulls it down.
Astronauts on the International Space Station feel weightless not because there is no gravity — there still is — but because they and the station are both in freefall around Earth at the same time.
Gray's monitor disperses tree seeds by eating fruits and excreting intact seeds in different parts of the forest.
Gray's monitor lizard is endemic to Luzon and is commonly found in the forests of the Sierra Madre and other Luzon mountain ranges.
Grazers eat grass on the ground, while browsers eat the leaves of taller plants and trees.
Moderate grazing by animals helps keep grasslands open by stopping shrubs and trees from taking over.

Although Australia's Great Barrier Reef is larger in area, Philippine reefs have more coral and fish species per unit area because the Philippines sits at the centre of the Coral Triangle — the world's most marine-biodiverse region.
The Great Barrier Reef stretches over 2,300 kilometers long — it is the largest living structure on Earth.
The Great Wall of China is about 21,000 kilometers long in total.
Greenhouse gases act like a blanket around the Earth that keeps its warmth in.
When people burn coal, gasoline, and oil, more carbon dioxide is added to the atmosphere.
Scientists measure carbon dioxide in the air and have found it is higher now than it was a hundred years ago.
In the greenhouse effect, certain gases like carbon dioxide trap some of the sun's heat near Earth, like a blanket. We need some of it to keep Earth warm, but too much causes global warming.
Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation (heat) emitted by Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions, including back to Earth; this keeps heat in the atmosphere.

In the greenhouse effect, sunlight passes into the atmosphere and warms the ground, but certain gases like carbon dioxide and water vapor absorb the heat (infrared) radiating back out, which keeps the Earth warm.
The natural greenhouse effect is important and helpful, because without it the Earth would be too cold and frozen for most living things to survive.
The greenhouse effect occurs when Earth's atmosphere lets sunlight in but absorbs and re-emits outgoing infrared radiation — keeping the planet warm enough for life.
Water vapour is the most powerful natural greenhouse gas; its concentration in the atmosphere increases as Earth warms, amplifying the greenhouse effect as a feedback mechanism.

Why does adding more greenhouse gas make things warmer? Think of greenhouse gas like a blanket. A thin blanket keeps in only a little heat. A thicker blanket keeps in more heat and makes you warmer. The same goes here: as greenhouse gas increases, Earth's 'blanket' gets thicker and the world warms up.

We breathe out carbon dioxide — is that the cause of global warming? No. The carbon dioxide we exhale comes from food made by plants that first absorbed carbon dioxide — so it balances out. The problem is carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels that were buried underground for a very long time.

Are there natural sources of greenhouse gases too? Yes — volcanoes, dying plants, and animals also release carbon dioxide naturally. But there used to be a natural balance. The problem now is the extra carbon dioxide humans add by burning fossil fuels, faster than nature can take it back.
The natural greenhouse effect is important—without it, Earth would be far too cold for life to survive easily.
Trees and plants absorb carbon dioxide, so they help reduce greenhouse gas in the air.
Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas in the atmosphere and plays a big part in warming the Earth.
Many leafy greens contain calcium that helps build strong bones and teeth.
Gregorio Zara was a Filipino inventor who created the videophone, a telephone that shows a picture of the person talking.
Because the sun and wind come and go, large batteries or other storage are needed to save the extra electricity so it can be used at night or when the wind is still.
Sunlight can react with vehicle exhaust to form ozone near the ground — unlike the helpful ozone high above us, this low-level ozone is harmful to our lungs.
Unlike the dinosaurs, the giant ground sloth lived at the same time as early humans and only went extinct a few thousand years ago.
Before some eruptions the ground slowly swells as magma rises, then sinks after the event, a rise-and-fall pattern instruments can track.
An aquifer is a layer of rock or sand underground whose tiny spaces are filled with water, and it stores most of the water we draw from wells.
Some groundwater is very old and has been stored underground for thousands of years.

Much of the bottled and mineral water we buy comes from groundwater. As water passes through rocks, some minerals like calcium dissolve into it, giving it flavor and nutrients. So "mineral water" is really water from underground.
If people pump too much water from wells, the groundwater can run out and the aquifer can dry up.
Groundwater can become polluted by garbage and chemicals that seep down through the soil.

There are places called recharge areas where rain easily soaks down and refills the groundwater, like forests and fields with loose soil. That is why protecting forests is important so the underground water does not run out.

A spring is groundwater that naturally comes out at the surface, often on the side of a hill or mountain. This is where we directly see the water hidden underground, which is why it is usually clean and cool.

Surface water is water we can see, like rivers, lakes, and the sea. Groundwater is hidden underground. Surface water dries up and gets dirty faster, while groundwater lasts longer and is usually cleaner.

The water table is the top level of groundwater, where all the spaces in the soil are completely filled with water. It rises in the rainy season and drops in the dry season. When it gets too low, plants struggle and wells dry up.
Groundwater can slowly dissolve soft rock such as limestone, and over long ages this carves out large caves underground.
During the dry season, groundwater keeps some rivers flowing even when there is no rain.
Underground water sits in tiny spaces between grains of sand, gravel, and rock.
As water soaks through sand and soil, some dirt is filtered out, so groundwater is often cleaner.
A lot of fresh water is stored underground, and this is what we draw from wells.
Most of the fresh water people can use is hidden underground as groundwater.

Groundwater in karst limestone areas is usually high in calcium because the water dissolves calcite as it passes through the rock; this is called 'hard water' and can leave white deposits in glasses and buckets.
Groundwater is recharged when rainwater soaks back down into the ground, but if we pump it out faster than it refills, it runs low.
A spring forms where groundwater naturally flows out at the surface, giving clean flowing water even when it has not rained.
A male bee in a colony is called a "drone."
A group of flying geese is called a "skein."
A group of geese on the ground is called a "gaggle."
A group of birds is called a flock.
A group of cows is called a herd.
Sort your notes into three piles: eclipses, night-sky patterns, and timekeeping, matching the three questions this competency asks you to investigate.
A group of whales is called a "pod."
A baby wolf is called a "pup."
The grouper (lapu-lapu) is an ambush predator that waits among rocks and coral before lunging at passing fish; all are born female and some change to male as they age.
The vertical columns of the periodic table are called groups, and elements in the same group have similar properties.
Grow foods help the body grow bigger and build strong muscles. Examples are fish, meat, eggs, milk, and beans (munggo).
Grow foods like fish, eggs, meat, and beans are rich in protein that helps build and repair our bodies.
Some stomach noises are part of cleaning, where waves of muscle push leftover food along the gut.
Not only insects go through metamorphosis — frogs and other amphibians, and even starfish and sea urchins, transform from a larval form to an adult form as they grow.
The human brain grows most rapidly in the first three years of life — during this time millions of nerve connections form every second, building the foundation for all future learning.
Some plants go through dormancy during the dry season — the plant's activities slow down to conserve water and energy, and when rain returns the plant resumes growing.
Guano is useful as fertilizer, but it should be collected carefully so the bats that make it are not disturbed.
The guava fruit contains fiber that helps with good digestion of food.
Guava leaves are boiled to make a wash for cleaning wounds and the skin.
In old practice, guava leaves are chewed or gargled for a sore tooth or gums.
Guava leaves are oval-shaped, green, and have clear veins on the surface.
Even though guava is used as a remedy, it is still important to see a doctor when an illness is serious.
A guava is green when unripe and turns yellowish when it is ripe.
A plucked guitar string is a transverse wave example, because bits of the string move across the string while the wave runs along it.
Gulaman is made from agar, a substance from certain seaweeds that dissolves in hot water and sets into a jelly as it cools.
When rainwater rushes fast over bare soil, it digs deep channels called gullies.
Plaque is a thin film of bacteria on teeth; when not removed it hardens into tartar and can cause gingivitis (inflamed gums) and more severe gum disease.
A single gumamela flower often opens for only one day before it wilts.
Gumamela leaves are shiny, green, and have edges that look like little teeth.
At the tip of each gumamela stamen is a tiny part called the anther. The yellow powder called pollen sticks here.
In a santan flower, the stamens are separate inside the bloom, but in a gumamela they are joined into one tube. This is one easy way to recognize a gumamela.
Each stamen has a thin stalk called the filament. It holds up the anther so the pollen can spread easily.
In a gumamela, the stamens are joined together into one long tube in the center of the flower. This is different from many flowers that have separate stamens.
The stamen sits in the center of the gumamela, surrounded by colorful petals. This helps because the petals attract insects toward the stamen where the pollen is.
Gumamela pollen is sticky and has tiny spikes, so it clings easily to an insect's body. This way the pollen is more easily carried to another flower.
In the center of the gumamela flower is a long tube that holds the stamens, the male part of the flower.
Gunpowder was discovered while Chinese alchemists were searching for an elixir of eternal life.
Gunpowder was invented in China during the 9th century, in the Tang dynasty.
Gunpowder was first invented in ancient China.
Helpful bacteria live in the human gut and help digest food and make some vitamins, while they get food and shelter inside us.
The intestines are home to billions of helpful bacteria that assist digestion, produce some vitamins, and protect against harmful germs.
Not all bacteria are bad — most of those living in our gut are helpful and we need them.
Besides bacteria, fungi and viruses also live in our gut as part of the microbiome.
The number of microbes in our body is about as many as our own body cells.
When bacteria break down fiber, they make acids that feed and keep healthy the cells lining our gut.
Greater diversity of bacteria in the gut is generally associated with better health; eating a variety of vegetables and fruits helps increase gut microbiome diversity.
The Gutenberg Bible was one of the first books printed using movable type.
Of the three fruits, the guyabano is the largest and can weigh several kilograms.
The spines on the guyabano's skin are soft and do not prick the hand.
The guyabano, or soursop, is a tree that grows large green fruit with soft spines on its skin.
A gyre is a large system of currents that flow in a big circular pattern inside an ocean.
An aerial habitat is the air, where animals like birds, bats, and winged insects spend much of their time flying.
Breaking forests into small habitat patches (habitat fragmentation) isolates small animal populations, leading to inbreeding and reduced genetic diversity.
When planning habitat restoration, connecting remaining forest fragments is often more effective than only planting in new areas, because it allows animals to move between patches.
A habitat is the place where an animal lives, while its niche is the role or job it plays in the ecosystem, like what it eats.
A haboob is a huge wall of dust pushed forward by strong winds coming out of a thunderstorm.
The hadal zone is the deepest ocean layer, found inside deep trenches from about 6,000 meters down.
Inside the ear are tiny hair cells that sense sound, and loud noise can damage them permanently.
Hair grows from a living root under the skin called a follicle.
Sometimes doctors look at your nails because they can give clues about your health. For example, if the nails look pale or dull, it can be a sign that the body is low on enough blood or nutrients.
Hair color comes from a natural coloring called melanin. Most Filipinos have black hair because they have a lot of melanin. When there is less melanin, the hair is a lighter brown or blond color.

Whether your hair is curly or straight depends on the shape of the follicle it grows from. A round follicle makes straight hair, while a flatter, oval follicle makes curly hair. You inherit this from your parents.

Your eyebrows and eyelashes are special hairs with a job to do. Eyebrows stop sweat and rainwater from running into your eyes, while eyelashes catch dust and tiny things so they do not get into your eye.

Not only liquids or gases can be homogeneous — some metals can too. An alloy like bronze is two metals melted and mixed evenly while hot. Once it hardens, it looks the same in every part, so it is a solid homogeneous mixture.

When you put sugar in coffee and stir, it becomes homogeneous — equally sweet in every sip. But if you do not stir, the sugar sinks to the bottom and it stays heterogeneous for a while, sweet below and not on top. That is why you stir, to make it even.

Many liquid medicines are made homogeneous to be safe. If the mixing is even, every spoonful has the same amount of medicine. That is why some medicines say 'shake well' — to make it even again in case some parts sink and it becomes heterogeneous.

Muddy water from a river is a heterogeneous mixture because you can see the mud particles floating in it. If you leave it still, the mud slowly settles to the bottom and the water clears at the top. This is a sign that the mixing is not even.

Some kids think that once things mix, they all become a brand-new substance. But in a mixture, whether homogeneous or heterogeneous, the parts do not change — salt is still salt even when dissolved in water. That is why you can get them back, for example by evaporating the water.

The reason some mixtures are homogeneous is that the dissolved particles are extremely tiny — too small to see. In heterogeneous mixtures, the pieces are larger so you can still see them. So particle size is one key to whether a mixture looks uniform or has visible parts.

It is easier to separate the parts of a heterogeneous mixture because you can see them. You can filter sand out of water using a strainer, or pick fruit pieces out of a salad by hand. The larger size of the pieces is what makes this easy.

A suspension is a kind of heterogeneous mixture where tiny pieces float for a while but eventually sink. For example, when you mix flour in water it turns cloudy, but if left alone the flour settles at the bottom. This differs from a solution, which never separates.

Hundred Islands National Park in Alaminos, Pangasinan is made of hundreds of small islands that were once ancient coral reefs lifted up out of the sea thousands of years ago.

The Hundred Islands in Pangasinan are small chunks of coral limestone that stand out of the sea; they formed over thousands of years as ocean waves and rain dissolved and carved the limestone; each one has a unique shape sculpted by nature.
We feel hungry when our body needs food to get energy.
The feeling of hunger comes in waves, so sometimes it goes away even before you eat.
Hunger is an important survival signal that helps animals and people stay alive by looking for food.
Hunger and thirst are like warnings from the body so we take care of it by eating and drinking.
Huygens proved that a pendulum should follow a curve called a cycloid to keep perfect time.
A hydra can reproduce by itself through budding: a small bump grows on the side of its body, slowly becomes a new hydra, and then breaks off.
During hydration, water bonds with the cement and forms tiny crystals that link everything together.
Hydraulic car brakes use brake fluid to carry pressure from the brake pedal to the brake pads at each wheel, which then clamp the discs to slow the car.
In a hydroelectric dam like the Magat in the Philippines, water's potential energy at the top becomes kinetic energy as it falls, spins a turbine, and turns into electricity.
The water held high behind a dam is like a giant battery: as long as it stays up high it stores energy, and that energy is released when the water is let fall onto the turbine.
A dam blocks a river so water collects in a high place. When the water is released downward, it moves with great force and spins a turbine to make electricity.
Hydro energy comes from the power of flowing or falling water.
Even though a dam makes clean energy, it can block fish from swimming up the river, so people sometimes build a "fish ladder" — steps of water the fish can climb past it.
Height is not the only thing that matters; the more water that flows past each second, the more electricity a hydro plant can make.

Of all the renewable sources of electricity in the world, hydroelectric power from flowing water makes the most and is one of the oldest, because people have harnessed the force of water for a very long time.
Long before electricity was invented, people used water wheels to grind grain and run machines using the force of flowing water.
Water from the dam flows down through a big pipe called a penstock, which carries the water with force straight to the turbine.
The water flow in a hydro plant can be opened or shut quickly, so it can respond fast when electricity demand suddenly rises.
In the Philippines, hydro plants make more electricity during the rainy season when the dams are full, and less in the dry season when water is low.
Even though hydro is clean, plants drowned and rotting under a large reservoir can release methane, a greenhouse gas, especially in warm places.
Over time, mud and silt carried by the river slowly fill a dam's reservoir, reducing how much water it can store for electricity.
Hydropower is renewable because rain and the water cycle keep refilling the dam's reservoir after the water flows out.
In hydroelectric dams like Magat in Isabela, the power of flowing water spins the turbine and generator to make electricity.
The chemical symbol for hydrogen is H.
Hydrogen (symbol H) is element number 1 on the periodic table because it is the lightest.
Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe; it is the primary fuel in stars like our sun, where nuclear fusion of hydrogen produces the heat and light we receive.
Hydrogen is the lightest and first element in the periodic table, with an atomic number of 1.
Hydrogen has just one (1) proton, making it the lightest and simplest element.
Hydroponics is a farming method where plants grow in nutrient-rich water without soil; it is used in urban farms in the Philippines to grow crops like kangkong and lettuce in limited spaces.
In dams like Magat and Angat, the potential energy of stored water is turned into electricity as it falls.
Worldwide, hydropower is the largest source of renewable electricity.
At deep-sea hydrothermal vents, bacteria make food from chemicals instead of sunlight, a process called chemosynthesis.
A hygrometer is a tool that measures humidity — how much water vapor is in the air, usually shown as a percentage.
High blood pressure is one of the leading causes of heart disease and stroke worldwide, including in the Philippines.
If body heat drops too low, it becomes dangerous and is called hypothermia.
Ice does not give off cold; instead it takes heat from its surroundings, which is why a drink cools as the ice melts.
Ice floats on water because solid ice is less dense than liquid water.
Ice floats on water because it is less dense (lighter) than liquid water.
Ice floats in water because it is less dense than liquid water.
Ice on a mountain or in a freezer is still the earth material water, only in solid form, not a living thing.
The melting point of ice is the same as the freezing point of water — both are 0 degrees Celsius (0 C).
Water turns to ice (freezes) at 0 degrees Celsius, the same temperature at which ice melts.
Ice melts at a temperature of zero degrees Celsius (0 °C).
Ice melts when it absorbs heat, so good insulation makes ice last longer in a cooler.
Ice left in sunlight melts faster than ice in shade, a home test that the Sun delivers heat living things and people then use.
In the warm Philippine weather, ice melts quickly because the air is hotter than its melting point.
While ice is melting, it stays at 0 degrees Celsius until it is fully melted.
Melting ice on land raises the sea, but melting floating sea ice does not add to the level.
Because ice is only slightly less dense than water, most of an iceberg stays hidden underwater and only a small tip shows.
Even though large icebergs float, almost all of the ice is underwater — only a small part shows above the surface because ice is just slightly lighter than seawater.
Science begins with good questions like "Why?" and "How?", which push us to investigate and look for answers.
We can see because light enters our eyes, and the eye sends a message to the brain so we can understand what we are looking at.
The gas constant R is about 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), or 8.314 J/(mol·K) in SI units.
An ideal gas is a theoretical gas whose particles have no attractive forces and no volume of their own — it follows the gas laws perfectly.
When the glass eel gains color in the river, it is then called an elver, or young eel.
The eel has one long continuous fin running along its back to its tail, and it has no pelvic fins.
The eel is usually active at night, when it hunts for food.
Tiny eel larvae are carried by ocean currents for many months before they reach land.
Most eels spawn only once in the deep ocean, and then they die.
Granite and basalt are examples of igneous rock; basalt often comes from volcanoes.
Igneous rock that cools underground is called intrusive, like granite, while rock that cools at the surface is extrusive, like basalt.
Intrusive igneous rocks (like granite) cool slowly underground and have large crystals, while extrusive rocks (like basalt) cool quickly at the surface and have small crystals.
Igneous rock forms when hot melted rock called lava or magma cools and hardens.
Many igneous rocks in the Philippines come from volcanoes like Mayon, Taal, and Pinatubo.
The illegal wildlife trade reduces populations of endangered species like pangolins and tarsiers, making it harder for them to recover in the wild.
Some vaccines need a booster because protection slowly fades, and the booster reminds the immune system how to fight.
A fever is the body deliberately raising its temperature; it slows some germs from multiplying and speeds up the defending cells.
When most people in a community are vaccinated, a disease can hardly spread, so even those who cannot yet be vaccinated are protected too.
The skin is the body's largest barrier; it keeps germs out as long as it has no cut or scrape.

Many vaccines must be kept cold all the way from the factory to the health center — this is called the cold chain. If they get warm they can spoil and lose their power, so they are stored in refrigerators and ice-packed boxes.

In the Philippines there is a free vaccine program for babies and children at health centers and barangays, run by the Department of Health. It follows a schedule so every child can be protected against common diseases.
Some diseases like the flu have a virus that changes every year, so a new vaccine is needed yearly to match the latest version. The old vaccine is not enough because the germ now looks different.

When most people in a community are vaccinated, a disease has a hard time spreading, so even those who cannot be vaccinated yet — like tiny babies — are protected. This is called herd immunity or group protection.

People often think a vaccine is a medicine, but they are different. A vaccine is meant to prevent a disease before it arrives, while medicine like an antibiotic is given once you are already sick to fight it. Prevention versus cure is the difference.
We catch colds again and again because many different viruses cause them and they keep changing, so old memory cells are not enough against a new one.
A person who recovers from measles or chickenpox usually gains lifelong protection against it.
Impetigo is a skin infection caused by bacteria that makes sores with a yellowish crust.
Impetigo spreads easily when the sores are touched or scratched and then other parts of the skin are touched.
Impulse is force multiplied by the length of time it acts, and it is what produces a change in an object's momentum.
In-situ conservation protects endangered species within their natural habitat by establishing protected areas and employing park rangers.
In the old kind of light bulb (incandescent), electricity passes through a very thin wire called a filament; it heats up so much that it glows and gives off light.
LED in modern lights stands for 'light-emitting diode' and uses less electricity than old bulbs.
The flat front teeth, called incisors, are used to cut or bite off food.
The front teeth, called incisors, are sharp and are used to cut or bite off food.
An inclined plane is a simple machine made of a flat surface that is tilted, like a ramp.
An inclined plane raises a load with less force, but you must push it over a longer distance.
The mechanical advantage of an inclined plane equals the length of the slope divided by the vertical height it rises.
Every inclined plane has a mechanical advantage greater than 1 — meaning less input force is needed than the full weight of the object being lifted, at the cost of a longer travel distance.
Put a notebook or data table in the materials, because 'what you need to do' includes a place to catch the numbers.
When there is not enough oxygen, burning is incomplete and can make poisonous carbon monoxide.
A yellow, smoky flame is a sign of incomplete combustion — there is too little oxygen, so it makes a lot of soot and smoke.
Plant breeders use incomplete dominance to create new in-between flower colors—for example crossing red and white to get the pink varieties admired in gardens and flower markets.

Besides snapdragons, incomplete dominance shows in other plants too: in some carnations the colors blend, and in radishes an in-between shape between long and round appears in offspring of differing parents.
When two pink plants are crossed, the offspring appear in a 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white ratio—three different looks, unlike the usual 3:1 seen with full dominance.
Why do the colors blend? In incomplete dominance only one allele makes pigment, so an offspring with just one of that allele makes only about half the pigment—giving a paler, in-between color.

It is a misconception that the blending in incomplete dominance is about mixing male and female. Really, it is about two alleles of the SAME trait (like color) giving an in-between form, not about the parents' sex.
To predict offspring in incomplete dominance you still use a Punnett square—but each genotype has its own look: RR=red, RW=pink, WW=white, so the genotype and phenotype counts match.

Not just in flowers: in people, someone with a single sickle-cell allele has an in-between condition (sickle cell trait)—milder than having two alleles—an example of incomplete dominance in human inheritance.
In snapdragons (a kind of flower), crossing a pure red plant with a pure white plant gives all pink offspring—a classic textbook example of incomplete dominance.

In complete dominance, the dominant allele masks the other, so the offspring looks like one parent. In incomplete dominance, neither wins, so a new in-between form appears that matches neither parent.
Cockroaches, grasshoppers, dragonflies, and crickets go through incomplete metamorphosis with three stages.
Grasshoppers, crickets, cockroaches, and dragonflies all go through incomplete metamorphosis.
Before you start, name the one thing you will change, such as the kind of salt, so the rest of the plan can stay fair.

An index fossil belongs to an organism that: (1) was geographically widespread, (2) evolved quickly (lived for a short time), and (3) is easy to identify; geologists use them to match the age of rocks from different places around the world.

Index minerals such as chlorite (low grade) and sillimanite (very high grade) are used by geologists to determine how high a temperature and pressure a metamorphic rock experienced when it was changed.
The index of refraction of water is about 1.33 and of glass about 1.5 — meaning light travels more slowly in glass than in water.

There is an indicator called bromothymol blue that is blue when neutral but turns green or yellow when you blow into it through a straw. This happens because the carbon dioxide in your breath forms a weak acid in the water.
An indicator is a substance that changes color to show whether something is an acid or a base.
You can make your own indicator paper: boil red cabbage, soak white paper in the juice, and let it dry. Once dry, use it like litmus paper to test liquids at home.
If a liquid is neutral like pure water, litmus does not clearly change because it is neither clearly acidic nor basic. With universal indicator, an in-between green color shows up.
It is a mistake to think every color change is an acid-base indicator. Some color changes have other causes, like rusting or fruit rotting, which have nothing to do with testing for acids or bases.

With universal indicator, it tells you not only whether something is an acid or base; the depth of color also hints at how strong it is. A strong acid shows red, while a weaker acid shows orange or yellow.
We can make our own indicator from flowers or turmeric to test whether a liquid is an acid or a base.
Litmus only shows whether something is an acid or a base, but it does not tell the exact pH; a universal indicator or a pH meter is needed for the number.
Philippine indigenous peoples like the Igorot, Lumad, and Mangyan have deep traditional knowledge of medicinal plants and plant uses in daily life passed down through generations.
Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, where a moving magnet creates electric current.
Mass measures how much matter or how many particles an object has. The more particles there are, the more there is to 'convince' to move, so the inertia is greater.
Kids ask: can anything have zero inertia? Everything that has mass has some inertia, no matter how small. Only light, which is massless, is considered to have no inertia in the ordinary sense.

Inertia is the natural 'resistance' of an object to any change in its motion. If it is at rest, it resists moving; if it is moving, it resists stopping or turning. It is not a force but a property of every object that has mass.
An object has more inertia when it has more mass, so a loaded cart is harder to start moving or to stop than an empty one.

An object's inertia depends only on how much mass it has, not on its size or shape. A small iron ball can be harder to get moving than a big beach ball, because the iron has more mass even though it is smaller.

In the tablecloth trick, the cloth is yanked out fast but the plates stay in place. Because of inertia, the plates resist moving; if you pull fast enough, there isn't enough time for the friction to drag them along.
The greater an object's mass, the greater its inertia, so it is harder to start moving or to stop.
Inertia is not a force but a property of an object that depends on its mass.
Inertia is an object's tendency to keep doing what it is already doing. When a car stops suddenly, your body keeps moving forward — which is why a seatbelt protects you.
Inflammation is a normal immune response to infection or injury; its signs — redness, heat, swelling, and pain — show the body is fighting back.
Infrared is light with a wavelength longer than red, and we often feel it as heat.
William Herschel discovered infrared light in 1800.
Infrared light was discovered in 1800 when Herschel noticed the spot just beyond the red color of a prism was warmer.
Infrared is the band of the electromagnetic spectrum that we feel as heat.
Infrared lies just beyond the red end of visible light, so its wavelength is longer than red.
A TV remote sends invisible infrared light pulses to control the television.
A thermal camera can detect infrared, so it can see the heat of a body even in the dark.
When we feel warmth from a fire or the sun without touching it, infrared is reaching our skin.
Infrasound is sound with a frequency below 20 Hz, which humans cannot hear.
Some traits are inherited through genes, like eye color, while others are learned during life, like speaking a language — the latter is not inherited.
One bite of inland taipan venom carries enough poison to kill more than 100 adults.
Innate immunity is the body's fast, non-specific first defense against any pathogen; adaptive immunity is slower but specific and creates memory cells that remember past infections.
An insect's abdomen contains the digestive and reproductive organs and may have up to ten segments.
Insects use their antennae to smell, touch, and sense their surroundings.
The sounds bats use for echolocation are too high-pitched for people to hear.
Many insects like flies and dragonflies have compound eyes—eyes made of thousands of tiny lenses, which makes them very good at noticing fast movement.
An insect's eyes are on its head and are made of many tiny parts.
Insects have compound eyes, which are made of hundreds of tiny lenses working together.
Some insects like certain beetles and ants feed on dead animals, plants, or waste, so they help clean nature and return nutrients to the soil.
Diapause is a form of insect dormancy in which they lower their metabolic rate to survive dry or cold seasons—they remain inactive until conditions improve.
The world silk industry depends on silk moth (Bombyx mori) larvae—each cocoon yields a single continuous silk thread over 300 meters long when carefully unwound.
An insect's flight muscles are in the thorax and power rapid wing beats—bees beat their wings over 200 times per second.
An insect uses its six legs to walk, climb, and hold on.
Research shows insect populations are declining worldwide due to habitat destruction, pesticide use, and climate change—the loss of insects could severely damage ecosystems that depend on them.
Order Coleoptera (beetles) is the largest insect order with over 400,000 known species; all beetles have hard elytra protecting their flight wings.
When a new queen bee emerges from her cell, she quickly seeks out rival queens—including those still in their cells—and stings them to death; only one queen can live in a hive.
All true insects have six legs.
An insect has six (6) legs and three (3) body parts: head, thorax, and abdomen.
An insect's wings are very thin and light, so it can fly easily.
Many insects survive cold weather as eggs or larvae in a deep resting state until warmth returns.
People riding with the horn usually do not hear that sliding pitch, because they are moving with the source instead of past it.
Some substances are insoluble, like sand in water; they stay solid and sink or settle at the bottom.
Instantaneous speed is the speed of an object at one exact moment, like what a speedometer shows at that instant.
The hollow body of a guitar makes the air inside vibrate, which makes the sound louder.
Seismometers, gas sensors, and satellites help PHIVOLCS see repeating signs of unrest that people on the ground might miss at first.
Foam insulation traps many small air pockets; the trapped air is an excellent thermal insulator because air does not conduct heat well, which is why it is used in refrigerators and building walls.
The same insulation keeps hot things hot and cold things cold, because it slows heat moving in either direction.
Good insulators like foam, fur, and clothing trap tiny pockets of air — the trapped air is a poor conductor of heat and reduces heat transfer.
An insulator is a material that does not let electricity flow through it easily, like rubber and plastic.
Insulators like wood, plastic, and rubber move heat slowly. That is why a pan's handle is often made of plastic or wood so your hand does not get burned.
Frederick Banting and Charles Best discovered insulin in 1921, the treatment for diabetes.
When there is too little insulin or it does not work well, blood sugar rises and a person can develop diabetes.
Insulin is a hormone that helps lower blood sugar by letting glucose move into the body's cells.
When two waves meet, they can add together (constructive interference) or cancel out (destructive interference) depending on their phase — noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference.
The internet grew from the first network called ARPANET.
Every website you open is stored on a powerful computer that is always on, called a server, and when you click, your phone asks that server for the information.
Most of the internet that reaches other countries does not go through satellites but through thick cables resting on the ocean floor, where information travels as fast flashes of light.
To interpret an alert level is to turn the number into an action: stay, pack, leave, or stay away, matching what PHIVOLCS and the barangay ask.
Rocky shores are divided into horizontal zones based on how long they are submerged — barnacles occupy the high zone, crabs the mid zone, and corals only the lowest zone.

The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a band near the equator where winds from the north and south meet and rise, cooling and bringing thick clouds and heavy rain, including to the Philippines.

Worms are more common in parts of the Philippines where clean water and toilets are limited, especially in the countryside. Because of this, the government runs programs that give free deworming medicine to schoolchildren.
Some worm eggs cannot infect you right after they come out; they first need time in warm, moist soil to become ready. This is one reason worms are more common in hot, humid places.
Worm eggs leave the body in stool, develop in the soil, and return to the body when contaminated things are eaten or touched.
Most intestinal worms live inside your intestines, the long tube where digested food passes. There they cling to the wall of the intestine and soak up nutrients before your own body can absorb them.
Some people believe you get worms from eating too many sweets or candy, but that is not true. You get worms from swallowing worm eggs found on dirty hands, food, or water, not from sugar.
You will not get worms just by touching or hugging a friend who has them. Only worm eggs that reach your mouth, for example from dirty hands, can give you worms.
It is not true that worms come from eating sweets; they come from eggs that get into the body.
Using a proper toilet stops worm eggs from spreading from waste into the soil.
Intestinal worms can be easily treated with medicine and prevented through cleanliness.
A child can get worms by eating vegetables or fruit that were not washed or by drinking dirty water.
Sometimes an invasive species breeds with a closely related native species. The offspring are mixed, so the pure native line is slowly lost.
Islands like the Philippines are easily harmed by invasive species. They have many endemic species that are unique and isolated, so they have no defenses against newly arrived animals.
The janitor fish is an invasive fish in the Philippines, such as in the Marikina River. It digs burrows in the banks and competes with native fish for food, so the native fish decline.
An invasive species often succeeds in a new place because it has no natural enemies there — this gives it a major competitive advantage over native species.
Some invasive vines grow very fast and cover other plants. They block out the sun, so the native plants underneath are smothered and die.
Invasive species are animals or plants from another place introduced to a new area where they out-compete native species and disrupt the ecosystem.

There is a natural way to control water hyacinth: using special tiny insects (weevils, a kind of beetle) whose only food is this plant. As they nibble the leaves, the water hyacinth weakens and spreads more slowly, without harming the other plants.

Water hyacinth is one of the fastest-growing water plants—in warm weather and slightly dirty, nutrient-rich water, it can double the area it covers in just a few weeks. That's why a small patch can end up covering a large part of a lake.

A thick cover of water hyacinth stops the water from moving and creates hidden, still corners. This kind of standing water is a favorite breeding spot for mosquitoes, so mosquitoes that carry diseases like dengue can multiply.
Insects make up roughly half of all known animal species on Earth—over a million insect species have been described, and many more remain undiscovered.
Some kinds of light cannot be seen by our eyes, such as infrared beyond red and ultraviolet beyond violet.
Io, a moon of Jupiter, has the most active volcanoes in the solar system.
When the diet lacks iodine, the thyroid grows larger and a goiter can form.
A lack of iodine can cause goiter, which is why salt with added iodine is important in food.
Iodine added to salt (iodized salt) and found in seafood is needed by the body; a lack of it causes goiter, a swelling in the neck.

If the thyroid works too fast (overactive), the heart may pound and the person may lose weight; if it works too slow (underactive), they may gain weight, feel tired, and feel cold. The right amount of iodine helps keep it balanced.
Iodine does not come only from iodized salt; it is also found in milk, eggs, and various fish. So eating a balanced diet helps make sure we get enough iodine.
More is not always better: too much iodine can also harm the thyroid, so the body needs just the right amount, not too much. A balanced diet usually gives enough.
In the Philippines, the ASIN Law requires that food salt be iodized with iodine.
Iodized salt is a mixture because a little iodine is added to the salt to help prevent goiter.
In the Philippines, much of the salt has iodine added (iodized) to help prevent goiter in people.
What holds an ionic bond together is the force of attraction between a positive ion and a negative ion, which have opposite charges.
Even though it is made of ions, a whole ionic compound is neutral because the amounts of positive and negative charge are equal and balance out.
Why do ions stick together? Because positive (+) and negative (-) attract each other, like magnets. This pulling force holds the ionic compound together so it does not fall apart.
Salt is hard but easily shatters when struck. Why? When the ions are forced to shift, the same charges (+ and +) suddenly line up and push each other away, so the crystal cracks apart.
There are ionic compounds inside your own body! Calcium compounds help make your bones and teeth strong. That is why it is important to drink milk that has calcium.
In an ionic compound, the ions are not scattered randomly. They arrange in a repeating pattern called a crystal lattice. That is why if you look at a grain of salt, it looks like tiny cubes.
Why does salt disappear when put in water? The water molecules pull on the ions and separate them. So the salt 'disappears' from view, but its ions are still there in the water.
On farms in the Philippines, farmers use fertilizers that are often ionic compounds. These provide nutrients like potassium and nitrate that plants need to grow.
Ionic compounds usually form from a metal and a nonmetal, such as sodium (a metal) and chlorine (a nonmetal) forming table salt.

Why does it take a LOT of heat to melt salt? Because the pull between the ions is very strong. You need a huge amount of heat to break these bonds. That is why ionic compounds have high melting points.
When naming a simple ionic compound, the metal's name comes first and the nonmetal's name comes next ending in '-ide', as in sodium chloride.
It is wrong to think a piece of iron or metal is an ionic compound. A pure metal alone is an ELEMENT, not a compound. A nonmetal must join and exchange electrons first before an ionic compound forms.
Why do some compounds have two nonmetals for one metal? For example, magnesium is +2 but chlorine is only -1. So you need TWO chlorines (-1 and -1) to match the +2 and stay balanced (MgCl2).

What is the difference between ionic and covalent? In IONIC, electrons are GIVEN away (metal + nonmetal). In COVALENT, electrons are SHARED (nonmetal + nonmetal, like water). They join in different ways.
When an ionic compound like salt dissolves in water, its ions move freely and let the water conduct electricity.
The main difference between the two kinds of bond is this: in an ionic bond electrons are transferred, but in a covalent bond electrons are shared.
An atom is neutral with no charge, but it becomes an ion when its number of electrons changes so the electrons and protons no longer match.
The ipil is another strong Philippine tree whose wood is used for building.
Because ipil-ipil spreads so quickly, it can sometimes crowd out the native plants in an area.
Ipil-ipil is planted in rows on hillsides to prevent soil erosion, because its roots hold the soil in place.
Ipil-ipil is planted as a living fence on farms to give shade and hold back soil.
Ipil-ipil contains a chemical called mimosine, so animals should not be fed too much of it.
The ipil-ipil enriches the soil because its roots can capture nitrogen from the air.
The ipil-ipil produces flat pods that hold many seeds that can be planted again.
Iron is needed to make healthy blood, and a lack of it causes anemia.
Iron boils at about 2,862 degrees Celsius.
Cast iron contains more carbon (2-4%) than steel, making it more brittle but excellent at retaining heat; cast iron pans are prized for their even heat distribution.
The chemical symbol for iron is Fe.
Iron deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis in young leaves—the tissue between the veins turns yellow while the veins stay green; this occurs because iron cannot move from old to new leaves.
Tiny pieces of iron cling to the magnet when it is brought near the mixture.
Hemoglobin contains iron, and it is this iron that grabs onto oxygen.

Even though iron is very important, the total amount of iron in a human body is tiny — only a few grams, about the weight of a small nail. Yet without even this small amount, our cells could not get oxygen properly.

Why do you get tired when iron is low? With too little hemoglobin, less oxygen reaches the cells. Cells use oxygen to make energy, so when oxygen is short, the body cannot produce enough energy and tires easily.
Iron is pulled by magnets, which is why it is used in the magnets that stick to fridge doors.
Iron is mainly used to make steel, which builds buildings, vehicles, and bridges.
In iron mining, magnets are used to separate the iron mineral from useless rock.
Leafy greens like malunggay and kangkong are rich in iron, which the body needs to make healthy red blood cells.
Iron rusts when it stays wet and exposed to air for a long time.
Iron sinks in water because its density (about 7.9 g/cm³) is higher than water's.
The Irrawaddy dolphin is an endangered dolphin species with a blunt, rounded snout found in Malampaya Sound, Palawan.
Island biogeography states that larger islands generally have more species than smaller ones because greater area can support more species and more varied habitat.
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon — both have 6 protons but a different number of neutrons.
An isotope is an atom of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers; carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon atoms but have different masses.
There is no air in space, so machines on the ISS make the oxygen astronauts breathe, often from water.

The International Space Station has been continuously crewed since 2 November 2000 when the Expedition 1 crew arrived; this represents the longest continuous human presence in space. Astronauts typically stay for about 6 months before being replaced by a new crew.
You cannot pour water into a cup in space, so astronauts drink through a straw from a sealed pouch.
In space, body fluids drift upward, so astronauts' faces look a little puffy and they even grow slightly taller.
The International Space Station was built and is run by many cooperating nations, and astronauts live aboard it while it orbits Earth.
The space station orbiting Earth today is called the International Space Station (ISS).
The space outside the ISS has no air or oxygen, so a person cannot breathe there without a spacesuit.
There is no sound outside the ISS because sound needs air to travel, and space has no air.
The ISS moves so fast that it circles Earth once about every 90 minutes, so astronauts see roughly 16 sunrises and sunsets each day.
The International Space Station travels around Earth at about 28,000 kilometers per hour.
On the ISS, water from sweat and urine is cleaned and turned back into drinking water because fresh water is hard to bring from Earth.
The International Space Station (ISS) is a large laboratory that orbits Earth where astronauts live and work.
The itak is made of hard metal with a thin, sharp edge that focuses force on one line, so it can easily cut wood or coconut.
Female ducks lay eggs, and their eggs are made into balut and penoy.
The huge jackfruit grows attached directly to the trunk and branches of the tree.
When a jackfruit is ripe, it gives off a strong, sweet smell. This is one sign that it is ready to eat.
Inside each yellow part of the jackfruit is a big seed. If you plant this seed, it can grow into a new jackfruit tree.
One jackfruit is made of hundreds of tiny flowers that join together to form one big fruit.

Even though a jellyfish has no brain, it has a web of nerves spread across its whole body, called a nerve net. This lets it sense touch and light and react right away.
Jellyfish have no brain, heart, or blood — they only have a simple network of nerves called a nerve net that sends signals throughout their body to control contractions and movement.
Even with the word fish in its name, a jellyfish is not really a fish because it has no backbone.

Jellyfish have two stages in their life cycle — the polyp stage (attached to rock, reproducing asexually) and the medusa stage (the floating bell that reproduces sexually); the polyp releases small medusae through a process called strobilation.
If a jellyfish stings you, it is better to rinse with seawater than with fresh water.

Europa Clipper is a NASA mission launched in 2024 to study Jupiter's moon Europa in detail; its goal is to determine whether Europa's subsurface ocean could support conditions suitable for life.
At the top of Jupiter's clouds it is extremely cold because Jupiter is so far from the Sun — colder than the coldest place on Earth. But deeper inside, it actually becomes very hot.

In 1994, a comet called Shoemaker–Levy 9 broke into pieces and crashed into Jupiter. It left big dark marks in Jupiter's clouds that telescopes on Earth could see — real proof that Jupiter catches objects heading its way.

Jupiter is so far away that even light — the fastest thing there is — takes more than 40 minutes to travel from the Sun to Jupiter. So when we look at it, we are seeing something extremely far from us.
Jupiter is the first planet you reach after crossing the asteroid belt. It sits right between the small rocky inner planets and the giant gas planets outside, so it leads the gas giants.
Jupiter is so massive that it weighs more than all seven other planets put together. That is why it is truly the 'king' of size and mass in our solar system.
We know a lot about Jupiter because robotic spacecraft have been sent there, like Juno, which is orbiting Jupiter now. It takes close-up pictures and measures Jupiter's gravity and clouds.
Jupiter has a magnetic field, like a giant magnet wrapped around it — the strongest of all the planets. It is even much stronger than Earth's magnetic field, the one that makes our compass work.
Io, one of Jupiter's moons, is the most volcanically active body in the solar system; it has hundreds of active volcanoes spewing sulfur, which gives it a mottled yellow-orange colour.
Jupiter, which Galileo studied, is the largest planet in our solar system.

The kagwang glides to find food and to escape enemies without having to come down to the ground.
The kagwang has the largest and most complete gliding membrane of any mammal, reaching even between its fingers and toes.
The kagwang is a skilled glider because it can travel far while losing only a little height.
The kagwang is one of the main foods of the Philippine eagle, our national bird.
Even the kagwang's tail is part of its wide gliding skin, which helps steer it while gliding.
The kakawate, also called madre de cacao, is a tree found in many farms and yards across the Philippines.
The kakawate grows fast and provides shade, making it useful on farms even as it enriches the soil.
Kakawate wood is also used as firewood because the tree regrows easily after it is cut.
The kakawate is a legume that adds nitrogen to the soil through its roots, making the soil more fertile.
On the roots of the kakawate are small nodules where Rhizobium bacteria live and take nitrogen from the air.
Some parts of the kakawate are toxic to rodents and other animals, so care is needed when using it.

The hornbill eats forest fruits, especially figs.
Many people think hornbills eat only fruit, but that's not true. Besides fruit, they also eat insects, lizards, and small animals, especially when they are feeding their chicks.
A parrot cracks open and eats the seed of a fruit with its strong beak. The hornbill is different: it swallows the whole fruit and does not destroy the seed, so it helps plant new trees.
The rufous hornbill is threatened because of forest loss and hunting.

The kalaw calls loudly to communicate with other hornbills far away. They use the call to find a mate, gather their family, or warn others when there is danger. It is their way of 'calling out' across the wide forest.

The kalaw calls most often in the morning and late afternoon, especially as it flies to and from the fruit trees where it feeds. These are the times you will most often hear its loud cry ringing through the forest.

In the Philippines, some indigenous people call the kalaw the 'clock bird' because it used to call at the same time each day, such as at noon. Forest dwellers once used this to tell the time even without a watch.
The Philippines has several different kinds of hornbills, and some are found on only one island.
The kalaw lays its eggs inside holes in old trees, so it needs large trees in the forest.
The hornbill is protected by law in the Philippines, so it is illegal to catch or kill it.

Around the kalaw's eye there is a patch of bare, featherless skin that looks red or pink. Because the skin there has no feathers, the color of the blood underneath shows through, making it look reddish.
The kalaw has a bright red beak, a yellow throat, and a black body, which makes it easy to recognize.
On top of the kalaw's bill there is a helmet-like part called a casque, colored red. It sits on top of its big beak almost like a crown.
A young kalaw does not yet have colors as vivid as an adult's. As it grows up, its red skin and bill become brighter until they match the colors of a grown bird.
Many people think the red on the kalaw's face is red feathers, but it is not. The red parts on its face and throat are bare skin, not feathers. Its body feathers are black and brown.
When the kalaw flies, its wingbeats make a loud whooshing sound that can be heard from far away.
