Kapok comes from the large seed pods of the kapok tree. When the pod ripens, it splits open and the soft white fibers come out together with the seeds.
Long ago, kapok was used to fill life jackets and floats because it floats and does not get wet easily. It helped keep a person afloat in the water.
Kapok is a natural fiber that comes from a tree, not made by people like plastic or foam. Because it is natural, it breaks down more easily and is gentler on the environment.
The light kapok fibers help its seeds fly with the wind to faraway places. In this way, new kapok trees can grow in other ground.
Kapok flowers open at night and are pollinated by bats.
Kapok seeds can be pressed to get oil used for cooking and making soap.

The carabao is a large mammal that farmers use to plow rice fields, and it loves wallowing in mud to cool itself down.

Karst caves are home to dark-loving animals like bats and swiftlets, which help spread plant seeds and eat insects.
Karst caves are often cool with a steady temperature all year because the thick rock protects them from the heat of day and cold of night.
It is a mistake to think big animals dug out the large karst caves, but in truth it was water dissolving the limestone over a very long time that made them.
Limestone does not dissolve evenly, the water follows the cracks and joints in the rock, so that is where holes, caves, and passages form.
A landscape called karst forms when limestone dissolves, creating caves, sinkholes, and hills.
In karst, some streams suddenly vanish into the ground because the water enters a hole in the limestone and keeps flowing underground.
The limestone that karst is shaped from comes from millions of years of piled-up sea shells, coral, and tiny animal skeletons that hardened into rock.
Land shaped by water dissolving limestone is called karst.
Not every land becomes karst, it needs rock that dissolves easily in water like limestone, so in places with granite or hard insoluble rock it does not happen.
Many think karst hills and caves formed suddenly, but in truth it is extremely slow, taking thousands to millions of years to be shaped.
Beautiful karst landscapes in the Philippines like the islands of El Nido and the caves become popular tourist destinations, providing livelihoods for local communities.
In karst, water easily seeps into cracks and holes in the limestone, so many rivers flow underground, like the famous underground river in Puerto Princesa, Palawan.
Karst is shaped by water dissolving rock from the surface downward, while volcanic landforms are built up by heat and lava coming out from inside the Earth.

In a karst landscape, rain rapidly sinks underground and flows through underground river systems; when the water reaches lower ground, it emerges as a resurgence spring — often as a clear, cold gushing water source.
Water that sank into karst often reappears lower down as a spring.

El Nido, Palawan is famous for dramatic karst towers: tall vertical limestone walls rising from the sea and lagoons; they formed over millions of years as rainwater dissolved the limestone and left behind the more resistant parts.
Natural arches and bridges in karst landscapes are remaining portions of a former cave ceiling whose rest has collapsed; they can become large scenic features with rivers passing underneath.

Fig trees are keystone because they bear fruit even when no other fruit is available in the forest, so birds and bats still have food during lean times.
To find out if a species is a keystone, scientists study what happens when it is reduced or removed—if many parts of the ecosystem collapse, it is likely a keystone.
Mangroves are keystone along Philippine coasts because their roots form the nursery where young fish and shrimp shelter before they grow up.
It is a misconception that the biggest or strongest animal is always the keystone; even a small species like a bee or starfish can be a keystone if its effect is large.
The parrotfish is a keystone on coral reefs because it eats the algae that could smother and kill coral, keeping the reef clean and alive.
Why does losing one keystone affect so many? Because many species are linked to it in the food web, so removing one is like cutting a central thread that holds many others together.
When wolves were brought back to a large park, the over-large deer population dropped, trees grew back, and even the rivers changed course, showing how powerful a keystone species can be.

Sometimes minerals in the urine harden into small solid pieces called kidney stones.
Kidney stones are hard mineral deposits (usually calcium) that form inside the kidney when there is not enough water intake or too many minerals in the urine.
On hot days when we sweat a lot, we make less urine because much water leaves through sweat instead.
If kidneys fail and can no longer balance water or remove waste, a machine called dialysis does that job for the patient in the hospital.
Kidneys do not just balance water, they balance salt too. The two work together: too much salt pulls water along, so kidneys adjust both at the same time.
What if you drink way too much water? Healthy kidneys usually handle it by getting rid of the extra through more urine, keeping your body balanced.
Some think all the water passing through the kidneys becomes urine. Not true. Most of the water is returned to your blood; only the extra becomes urine to keep you balanced.
The kidneys help regulate blood pressure by controlling the amount of water and salt in the body and releasing hormones that affect blood vessel tone.
The kidneys clean the blood by filtering out wastes and extra water from it.
Each kidney is about the size of a person's fist.

The kidney's filter holes are so tiny that big things like blood cells cannot pass through. So in a healthy person, there are no red blood cells in the urine. If there's blood in the urine, it's a sign to have a doctor check.

The color of your urine is like a hint of how your kidney keeps water. When it's clear or pale yellow, you have enough water. When it's dark yellow, the kidney is trying to keep water because you're low—a sign you should drink.

When a person's kidneys stop working, a machine called dialysis helps. It tries to copy the kidney's job—removing waste from the blood while keeping the useful substances. This shows how important the kidney's work really is.

Even while you sleep, your kidneys keep working—filtering the blood and keeping useful substances without rest. They do this all day and all night so your blood stays clean and your body stays steady.

We have two kidneys, one on each side of the back. This is good because if one has a problem, the remaining one can still keep important substances. That's why some people are able to donate one kidney to someone who needs it.

Besides sugar and water, the kidney also helps so that some vitamins and nutrients the body needs aren't lost too quickly. When the body still has enough, the kidney slows their loss in urine so we don't run short right away.

The kidney is great at two jobs at once: it throws out the body's waste as urine, but it chooses to keep the important substances. It's like a smart sorter that knows what to throw away and what to keep.

Kidneys don't just handle waste—they also keep the right amount of water in your body. When you're low on water, your urine is less and darker because the kidney keeps water back. When you have too much, your urine is more and clearer.
The kidneys release a chemical that tells the body to make more red blood cells.
One waste the kidneys remove is urea, which forms when the body uses protein.
The kidneys control how much water is in the body—when water is short, they make less and more concentrated urine.

Because kinetic energy equals ½mv², doubling the vehicle speed quadruples its kinetic energy — which is why high-speed crashes cause so much more damage than low-speed ones.

Kinetic energy has a formula: half the mass times the speed multiplied by itself (KE = 1/2 x m x v x v). So a heavier or faster object gives a bigger number. The answer comes out in a unit called the joule.
When you swing a hammer, it gains kinetic energy. When it hits the nail, that kinetic energy pushes the nail into the wood. The faster you swing, the deeper the nail goes in.

It is a common mistake to think a heavy object always has kinetic energy. Not true! If the object is still and not moving, it has zero kinetic energy no matter how heavy. It must move first to have kinetic energy.
A moving object has energy called kinetic energy, which can do work.
Any moving object, like a rolling ball, has kinetic energy, the energy of motion.

In some modern electric cars, a technology captures kinetic energy when braking. Instead of being lost as heat, it is turned into electrical energy and stored in the battery to be used again. This is called regenerative braking.
An object has more kinetic energy when it moves faster.

Even you have kinetic energy when you move! While walking, you have a little kinetic energy. But when you run fast, your kinetic energy is bigger. That is why you get tired running fast, because you use more energy.

It is not only solid objects that have kinetic energy; moving air does too! That is why strong wind can spin the giant wind turbines like those in Bangui, Ilocos, to make electricity. It is also why typhoons can cause damage.

The Komodo dragon is a cold-blooded reptile, so it basks in the sun to warm up.
The largest lizard in the world is the Komodo dragon of Indonesia, a giant kind of monitor lizard. It is a relative of our bayawak but is not found in the Philippines.
The Komodo dragon can weigh up to about 150 kilograms.
The Komodo dragon can ambush and eat large animals such as water buffalo and goats.
A large Komodo dragon can reach about 3 meters long and weigh up to around 70 kilograms.
Despite its size, the Komodo dragon can run fast over short distances to chase prey.
The Komodo dragon has sharp, saw-like teeth for tearing flesh.
The Komodo dragon has a strong, long tail that it uses for defense.
The Komodo dragon's venom is stored in tiny glands in its lower jaw, not in fangs like a snake's; the venom seeps out between its teeth when it bites.
Yes, a Komodo dragon's bite is dangerous even to people — the wound swells, hurts, and keeps bleeding because of the venom, so medical help is needed right away.
The monitor lizards in the Philippines are relatives of the Komodo dragon but smaller; studies show some monitor lizards also have a little venom, but not as strong as the Komodo's.
The venom helps the Komodo dragon hunt large animals like deer, wild pigs, and even water buffalo bigger than itself, because it weakens them.
When the Komodo dragon bites, its venom mixes with its saliva and enters the prey's wound; that is why it drools a lot while hunting.
Komodo dragons often fight and bite each other, but usually they don't quickly die from one another's venom; it is believed their blood has some protection against it.
The Komodo dragon lives only on a few islands of Indonesia, such as Komodo Island.

When you flick a kubing, the energy from your finger's movement transfers to the instrument's tongue. The tongue holds this energy as vibration, and the vibration then passes the energy to the air as sound. So energy flows: finger → tongue → air → your ear.

If the kubing tongue has a crack or split, it cannot vibrate well and the sound comes out bad. The tongue must be whole and even so it can move back and forth cleanly. This is why a kubing is cared for — the shape of the tongue directly affects the sound.

The word Kuroshio means "Black Current" in Japanese because of its dark blue water color.

Kwek-kwek is a popular street food in the Philippines. It is often sold from carts or stalls near schools and markets. It is a cheap snack that students love after class.
Kwek-kwek and tokneneng are like siblings. Kwek-kwek uses small quail eggs, while tokneneng uses larger chicken or duck eggs. Both are coated in orange batter and fried, but tokneneng is bigger.

It is not only the Philippines that La Nina affects. Weather changes around the world: it gets rainier in Australia and Southeast Asia, but drier in parts of South America and the southern United States. The whole planet's climate is connected.
During La Nina, the amihan may strengthen and bring more rain than usual to northern Luzon and the Visayas.

La Nina and El Nino are like two sides of the same coin. In El Nino, Pacific water is warm and the Philippines often gets drought. In La Nina, the water is cool and it rains more. They are two ends of the same cycle.

It matters to farmers to know if it is a La Nina year. Because it rains more, rice fields can flood and crops can rot. So they prepare good drainage canals and choose the right planting time so the harvest is not drowned.
During La Nina, Australia typically experiences above-normal rainfall while parts of North America may experience a drier-than-normal winter.

During La Nina, more typhoons may form near the Philippines. Because warm water piles up in the western Pacific, storms can gain strength more easily as they head toward us. So we must be more prepared during La Nina.

Scientists know La Nina is happening when the sea surface in the central Pacific cools by at least half a degree Celsius below normal and stays that way. They use floating buoys in the ocean to measure this.

Deep in the ocean there is a boundary that separates warm water on top from cold water below, called the thermocline. During La Nina it tilts more: it sits shallow in the eastern Pacific (closer to the cold) and deep in the west (where warm water piles up).

La Nina begins when the trade winds get stronger. These winds blow westward along the equator and push warm surface water away from South America toward Asia, letting cold water rise up in the eastern Pacific.
During La Nina, a process called upwelling happens. Wind pushes surface water away, so cold water rises from the deep ocean. This deep water carries nutrients that feed small fish.

During La Nina, a huge amount of warm water piles up in the western Pacific near the Philippines and Indonesia. In fact, the sea level here is a bit higher than in the east because so much warm water gathers. This brings more clouds and rain.

The ladybug is a small red, spotted insect that helps farmers because it eats the tiny pests that damage plants.
Even the larva of a ladybug eats many aphids before it grows up.
A mother ladybug lays her eggs near aphids so the larvae have food right away.
Some farmers purposely release ladybugs into a field to fight pests.
A ladybug is an insect with six legs and two antennae.

A lahar is a flowing mix of volcanic ash, mud, and water that rushes down a volcano, especially during rain.
Lahar is a fast and dangerous flow of volcanic mud and ash set in motion by heavy rain, and it caused great damage after Pinatubo erupted.
After Pinatubo, lahars kept flowing in rainy years, showing that the danger pattern can last long after the volcano grows quiet again.
Laika the dog went to space aboard the satellite Sputnik 2 in 1957.
Lake Baikal in Russia is the deepest lake in the world, and it holds more fresh water than any other lake.
Laguna de Bay is the largest lake in the Philippines, and it is an important source of fish and water for the communities around it.
Land heats and cools faster than the sea because land has a lower specific heat capacity — this is why coastal areas are cooler in summer and warmer in winter than inland areas.
Some land tortoises have been recorded living nearly 180 years, among the oldest animals ever.
After a severe wildfire on a hillside, landslides happen more easily. The plants that held the soil die, and burned ground soaks up less water, so rain runs downhill faster and triggers slides.
Sometimes soil sits on top of a layer of clay. When the clay fills with water, it becomes slippery like soap, so the soil resting on top slides downhill easily.
Not only rain can cause landslides — earthquakes can too. Strong shaking of the ground loosens soil and rock on steep mountains, so they can suddenly slide even without rain.

The roots of plants and trees hold the soil together like a net, so it does not easily slide. When trees on a mountain are cut down (deforestation), nothing holds the soil and it slides more easily when it rains.

There are different kinds of slope failure: a rockfall is the sudden drop or roll of large rocks from a steep cliff, while creep is a very slow downhill drift of soil that you can barely notice over many years.
To stay safe, listen to PAGASA warnings and evacuate when told. Avoid living or building at the foot of steep slopes, and when heavy rain keeps falling, move away from places that slide easily.
There are ways to prevent landslides: plant trees and grass to hold the soil, build step-like terraces on slopes, and put in drains so water does not collect in the ground.
In dry ground, grains of sand and mud cling together and grip one another. When water fills the spaces between the grains, their grip loosens and the ground weakens, so it slides more easily.
The light of some fish like the anglerfish comes from glowing bacteria that live inside their light organ.
Lanternfish are among the most abundant fish in the deep sea anywhere in the world.
In Camiguin, Philippines, a yearly Lanzones Festival celebrates the harvest of this fruit.
Lanzones and rambutan contain vitamins that help keep our bodies healthy.
Lapis lazuli is a gem rock with a deep blue color.
In the large intestine the body absorbs water from the leftover food, making the waste more solid.
Ceres is the largest asteroid in the asteroid belt, and it is also counted as a dwarf planet.
The Bay of Bengal in the Indian Ocean is the largest bay in the world.
The largest bone in the human body is the femur (thigh bone).
The Great Barrier Reef in Australia is the largest coral reef system in the world, stretching about 2,300 kilometers.
The largest dinosaur ever found is Argentinosaurus, a giant plant-eater.
The whale shark is the largest fish, reaching about 12 meters long.
The largest frog in the world is the goliath frog.
The largest and heaviest seed in the world is the coco de mer (double coconut), which can weigh up to about 25 kilograms.
The polar bear is the largest meat-eating predator that lives on land.

The largest fruit that grows on a tree is the jackfruit, which can weigh up to about 55 kilograms.

The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of any bird, almost 3 meters from tip to tip.
The larynx sits at the top of the windpipe, or trachea, the tube that carries air down to the lungs.
A laser produces light of a single colour and wavelength all travelling together, which keeps its beam narrow and able to reach far distances.
The last month of the year is December.

Bauxite is the main ore of aluminium; it forms through intense weathering of rocks in hot, humid tropical climate, leaving behind aluminium oxide (the main mineral) after other minerals have dissolved; the Philippines has some bauxite deposits.

Laterite is a red, crumbly tropical soil that forms in hot, humid places like the Philippines; heavy rain leaches away nutrients but concentrates iron and aluminum oxides, making it poor for farming but rich in metal ores (like nickel and bauxite).
Latex—the milky sap that oozes from wounds in some plants—acts as a defense against insects and fungal infections; it also helps seal plant wounds.
When washing clothes by hand in a basin, soap helps grab oil and dirt and mix them into the water so they wash out of the cloth.
Laundry detergents are usually slightly alkaline (pH about 9 to 11) to help remove acidic stains like grease and oil from clothes by neutralizing them.

Antoine Lavoisier is called the "Father of Modern Chemistry."
Antoine Lavoisier was a French chemist.
Antoine Lavoisier gave oxygen its name in 1777.
Newton's first law is also called the law of inertia because it describes how inertia behaves.
When light reflects, the angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence — this is the law of reflection.
Leachate is the contaminated liquid that percolates through decomposing waste in a landfill; it can seep into the ground and contaminate groundwater sources.
Old paint in older buildings may contain lead, which is toxic — lead causes brain damage in young children, so it is now banned in modern paints.
Some trees drop their leaves during the dry or cold season. They do this to save water when it is hard to get. When the rainy or warm season comes, new leaves grow back.
If you want to find a leaf insect, do not look for the insect — look for the leaf that moves or sways on its own. That is often where you discover the hidden bug.
The palisade mesophyll is a layer of cells near the top of the leaf that contains many chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

The photosynthesis rate can be limited by light intensity, temperature, or CO2 concentration—any of the three can be the limiting factor; raising one increases the rate until the next factor becomes limiting.
Leaves release water into the air through their tiny holes. This is called transpiration. It is like the plant sweating, and it helps pull water up from the roots all the way to the leaves.
If the veins get blocked or cut, water can no longer reach the leaf and it wilts or droops. That is why a leaf snapped off its stalk wilts quickly, with no water climbing up to it anymore.
Try picking a leaf and running your finger over its back. You will feel raised lines, those are the veins sticking out a little. They show up even more clearly when you hold the leaf up to the light.
When a caterpillar or insect eats a leaf, it usually munches the soft green part and leaves the tougher veins behind. That is why you sometimes see a chewed leaf with only a net of veins remaining.

It is fine to call them 'veins,' but they are not like our blood vessels with blood flowing through. Inside a leaf's veins flow water and dissolved food, not blood, and there is no beating heart pumping them.
In banana, cogon grass, and coconut leaves, the veins run side by side in parallel lines from end to end, without branching. That is why a banana leaf tears easily downward, following the vein lines.
Many leaves have a thin waxy coating on top. It protects the leaf and stops it from losing too much water. That is why some leaves look shiny and feel waterproof.
Leafy green vegetables like malunggay and kangkong are rich in iron, calcium, and vitamins.
Earth's trip around the Sun is not exactly 365 days but about 365 and a quarter days; so every fourth year we add one extra day (February 29) — a leap year.
A leap year happens every 4 years, when an extra day, February 29, is added.
What you found out can surprise you; an honest investigation reports the surprise instead of changing the numbers to match the first guess.

When chlorophyll fades in an old leaf, other colors like yellow and orange that were always there become visible.
In cold countries, leaves change color in autumn before they fall.
The broad green banana leaves we use to wrap suman or food are green because of chlorophyll. They are a familiar example of green leaves here in the Philippines.
Leaves are green because of chlorophyll, a coloring that helps the plant make food from sunlight.
The chlorophyll sits inside tiny parts of the leaf cells called chloroplasts. They are like little green factories where the plant makes its food.
If you pick a green leaf and leave it, it slowly loses its green and turns yellow or brown. That is because the chlorophyll slowly breaks down once it is off the living plant.
Many think a plant eats its food from the soil. But the green leaf itself makes the food using chlorophyll and light; from the soil it only takes water and a few minerals.
There are other colors (like yellow and orange) inside the leaf, but they are hidden by lots of green chlorophyll. So a leaf is green while healthy, and other colors show when the chlorophyll fades.
Some plants have red leaves, but they still have chlorophyll inside hidden under a red pigment. They keep making food because the green chlorophyll is still there, just covered.
The tiny lines or veins in a leaf carry water to the green parts. The chlorophyll needs this water to make food from light.
Leaves are green because they are full of chlorophyll, but flowers are colorful because they hold different pigments. Bright flower colors attract bees and butterflies, not to make food.
Some leaves have defense chemicals against animals that eat them, and gut microbes help break these chemicals down.
Yellow and orange colors are already hidden inside a leaf, but the strong green covers them while the plant is healthy.
Leche flan was brought to the Philippines during Spanish times; the word 'leche' is Spanish for milk, so the name means 'milk flan'.

A common question: do LEDs ever fail? Yes, but only after a long time. Instead of suddenly going dark like an old bulb, an LED slowly dims over many years. The heat inside is what slowly wears it out.

A single LED gives off light in one direction, not all around like an old bulb. That makes it great for flashlights and spotlights. In home LED bulbs, a special design is used to spread the light out.

LEDs are not only used in bulbs. They are in the screens of phones and TVs, in flashlights, in remote controls, and even in traffic lights. They are small, energy-saving, and durable, so they are everywhere.
When you flip the switch, an LED bulb instantly lights up at full brightness, unlike some old lights that slowly warm up first. This is because the LED responds quickly to electricity.

Many LEDs run on a small amount of power, so a battery or powerbank can light them. That is why you see LEDs in toys, flashlights, and battery gadgets. But a home LED bulb has a part that changes the power coming from the wall socket.

Some old fluorescent or CFL lights contain mercury, a poisonous substance that is dangerous if the bulb breaks. LED bulbs do NOT contain mercury, so they are safer when broken and better for the environment.
An old bulb has a tiny wire inside called a filament that heats up until it glows. An LED has NO such wire. It uses a solid material to make light, so it does not produce a lot of heat.
An LED bulb has several parts: the LED chip that makes the light, the base that screws into the socket, and a small part inside that controls the electricity so the right amount flows to the chip.
Because LEDs need only a little electricity, they pair perfectly with a solar panel and battery. In places in the Philippines without regular electricity, solar LED lamps provide light at night.
An LED makes light directly from electricity when tiny particles (electrons) inside it release light as they pass through — unlike an old bulb that must first glow hot to shine.
Some leeches have many tiny teeth they use to break the skin and drink blood.
Many kids ask if leech therapy is dangerous. It is safe when a medical leech is used by a doctor in a clean way. It is only risky if a wild leech or dirty equipment is used.
The special substance in a leech's saliva is called hirudin. It is what blocks blood from clotting. That is why the blood keeps flowing while the leech feeds.
In the past and even today, some doctors use leeches in medicine to help blood flow after certain surgeries.
Sometimes, when a finger or ear is cut off and a doctor reattaches it, blood pools up and swells. A leech is placed there to suck out the extra blood, so the reattached part can stay alive.

A leech's saliva is like a tiny medicine kit because it holds many kinds of substances. There is one to numb pain, one to stop clotting, and one to widen blood vessels. All of these help while it feeds.
Like leeches, some doctors also use maggots to heal wounds. But their jobs differ: a leech drinks blood to improve flow, while a maggot eats dead flesh to clean a wound.
Not all leeches suck blood; some instead eat small animals in the water.
A leech uses its rear sucker to anchor down while its front sucker does the blood-feeding.
To remove a leech, gently slide its end loose with a fingernail until it lets go of the skin.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first discovered bacteria, which he saw in his own saliva in 1676.
The brain is divided into left and right hemispheres; the left hemisphere typically controls language and logical thinking, while the right is more involved in creativity and spatial thinking.
Leftover food should be reheated until hot before eating to kill bacteria.
The strong muscles in our legs pull the bones so we can walk and run.
The bacteria in the nodules change the air's nitrogen into a form the plant can use as nutrient.
Each legume pod starts as a flower that slowly turns into a seed-filled pod.
Some legumes are grown and then plowed into the soil to serve as natural fertilizer.
Plants need nitrogen to grow healthy and to make green leaves.
Legume roots have tiny lumps called nodules where helpful bacteria live.
Legume seeds like mung beans are rich in protein that helps build the body.
When planted next to crops like corn, the kakawate helps them grow better because the soil becomes more fertile.
In a lemon battery, the lemon's juice and two different metals make a chemical reaction that produces a small flow of electricity.
Lemon and calamansi taste sour because they contain citric acid.
Squeezing lemon or calamansi juice on cut fruit slows down its browning.
The more curved and thicker a lens is, the more strongly it bends the light.
Eyeglasses use lenses to correct blurry vision.
A convex lens can make a real image that can fall on a screen, or one seen only through the lens like in a magnifying glass.
A convex (converging) lens bends light to a single point, while a concave (diverging) lens spreads the light outward.

The focal length of a lens depends on two things — the curvature of its surfaces (more curved means shorter focal length) and the refractive index of the material (higher index means shorter focal length).
If untreated, severe leptospirosis can damage the kidneys and liver and cause yellowing of the skin.
In the Philippines, more people get leptospirosis during the rainy season and times of flooding.
You can catch leptospirosis when you wade in flood water or water that has the Leptospira bacteria.
Do not drink floodwater or let it get into your mouth, because it can carry the leptospirosis bacteria.
After heavy exposure to floodwater, a doctor may prescribe preventive medicine against leptospirosis.
If untreated, leptospirosis can become severe and damage the kidneys and liver.
Leptospirosis can be treated with antibiotics, so it is important to see a doctor quickly if you get a fever after a flood.
Leptospirosis is a disease that can spread from animals such as rats, pigs, dogs, and cattle to people.
Alert Level 2 is already a watch, not a time for picnics on the slope; interpreting it means extra caution even before evacuation is ordered.
Place a balance on a level table before you weigh, because a tilted scale can make every trial read a little high or low.

Alert levels can rise or fall as the instruments change, so a family plan should work both for going away and for a later return.
The ancient scientist Archimedes said that with a long enough lever and a place to stand, he could lift the whole world.
The human arm is a third-class lever: the elbow is the fulcrum and the muscle provides the effort.
A catapult uses a long first-class lever: the long effort arm swings down and the shorter load arm flings the projectile far.
A boat oar is a first-class lever: the water is the fulcrum, the rower's hand provides effort, and the boat is the load being moved.
A baseball bat is a third-class lever where the bottom hand is the fulcrum, the top hand provides effort, and the ball is the load.
In a first-class lever, the fulcrum is in the middle, between the effort and the load, like a seesaw or scissors.
When you use a stick to lift a heavy coconut frond off the ground, you are using the stick as a lever.
A lever is a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point to help us move something more easily.
Your arm is a lever inside your body! The elbow is the fulcrum, the muscle pulling the bone gives the effort, and the object in your hand is the load. That's how you lift things with your hand.

There are many levers around us every day! Scissors, a seesaw, a bottle opener, and even a spoon you use to scoop are levers. When you see a bar that turns on a point to lift or move something, it's probably a lever.
A one-wheeled wheelbarrow is a lever. The front wheel is the fulcrum, the load you carry sits in the middle, and you lifting the handles give the effort. So heavy things become easier to move.
The turning effect of a force on a lever depends on how strong the force is and how far it is from the fulcrum. The farther from the fulcrum the force acts, the bigger its effect.
Torque is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot (lever arm) — a longer lever arm produces greater torque for the same force.
A Lewis dot structure is a diagram that uses dots to show an atom's valence electrons and how those electrons are shared to form chemical bonds.

The Tongonan geothermal field in Leyte is a major geothermal resource that supplies a large share of the Visayas electricity; it shows how the Philippines' volcanic nature can be used for clean and renewable energy.
Lianas are long woody vines that use trees as support to reach sunlight at the forest canopy; they are an important part of tropical forest ecology and provide pathways for animals.
Many lichens are sensitive to dirty air, so when many of them grow in a place, the air there is usually clean.
Some birds use lichens to build their nests, and small animals also hide among them.
Lichens come in many colors such as green, yellow, orange, and gray.
Lichens are food for some animals, such as reindeer and caribou in cold places.
In a lichen, the fungus provides the structure, shelter, and moisture that hold it together.
Lichens grow on rocks, tree bark, and other bare surfaces where other plants cannot easily grow.
Lichens can survive in places where almost nothing else can live, like bare rock and very cold lands, because the fungus and the alga help each other.
Long ago, people used some lichens as natural dyes for cloth.
Lichens spread when small pieces containing both the fungus and the alga break off and are carried by wind to new places.
Some lichens contain cyanobacteria that can take nitrogen from the air to enrich the soil.
Lichens can survive in harsh places such as the freezing tundra and the dry desert.
Lichens have different shapes: some are flat and crusty, some look like leaves, and some look like tiny branches.
Clean water, sanitation, and vaccines are among the main reasons human life expectancy has greatly increased over the past 150 years.
Some bacteria like E. coli double every 20 minutes under perfect conditions — meaning one bacterium could produce over a billion bacteria after about 10 hours of doubling.
Some bamboo species flower only once after 60 to 120 years — after mass flowering, all the plants set seed, reproduce, and then die.
Birds keep their eggs warm by sitting on them so the parent's body heat reaches the embryo growing inside the egg during incubation.
Different birds have different incubation periods — the sparrow incubates for about 14 days, the chicken for 21 days, and the Philippine eagle for about 62 days.
A chicken begins as an egg kept warm by the hen, and after about three weeks a chick hatches that slowly grows into a full-grown chicken.
Ferns produce spores on the underside of their fronds in tiny brown sacs called sori — when mature, spores are released and can grow into a new fern if they land in the right place.
Fish lay their eggs in water, and from the eggs hatch tiny young fish that slowly grow until they become full-grown fish.
Butterflies and moths lay their eggs specifically on the leaves of plants that their caterpillars eat — they do this to ensure that newly hatched caterpillars have food close by.
The length of pregnancy varies with animal size — a mouse is pregnant for only 3 weeks, humans for 9 months, and elephants for about 22 months.
Because mosquito larvae live in standing water, the best way to control mosquitoes is to remove water containers like old tires and cans around the home.
Mosses go through two different generations in their life cycle: the gametophyte generation that makes sex cells, and the sporophyte generation that makes spores for asexual reproduction.
Annual plants like rice complete their life in one growing season, biennial plants like carrots take two years, and perennial plants like mango trees live for many years.
Most plants begin as a seed that sprouts and grows roots and leaves, then forms flowers and fruit holding new seeds that start the cycle again.
Many animals help disperse seeds by eating fruit — the seeds pass through the animal's body unharmed and are dropped far from the parent plant in the animal's droppings.
A wing pushes air downward, and in return the air pushes the wing upward (action-reaction). Tilting the wing more pushes more air down and makes more lift.
An airplane wing is curved so air flows faster over the top than the bottom. This makes the pressure on top lower, creating lift that pushes the wing upward.
Combining colors of light is called additive mixing because each added light adds more brightness.
In just one second, light can travel about seven times around the Earth.
Diffraction is the bending of light around edges and through small openings — it demonstrates the wave nature of light and is why shadows have slightly blurry edges.
Light takes only about 1.3 seconds to travel from the Moon to Earth, which is 384,400 km away.
The eye has three kinds of cells sensitive to red, green, and blue, which is why light has just three primary colors.
Light is much faster than sound, which is why we see lightning before we hear the thunder.
Light travels fastest in a vacuum (empty space), such as outer space.
Light from a classroom lamp is a transverse wave example that does not need a slinky, a rope, or air to travel across the room.
When green light and blue light mix, they make a blue-green color called cyan.
Turning a room light on or off can mean 'I am home' to a family member watching from the yard, a simple light message after dark.
Light from the Moon takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Earth.
When there is no light at all, we see black, so black is the absence of light.

Newly hatched pawikan (sea turtle) hatchlings in the Philippines follow the brightest night sky toward the sea — but artificial light from resorts and roads disorients them and leads them away from the sea.
The three primary colors of light are red, green, and blue.
In the light reactions of photosynthesis, chloroplasts use sunlight energy to split water, releasing oxygen as a byproduct and producing ATP energy.
When red light and blue light mix, they make magenta, a color like deep pink.
When red light and green light mix, our eyes see yellow light.
Yellow, cyan, and magenta are called secondary colors of light because each is made from two primary colors.
Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second in a vacuum — the fastest anything in the universe can travel.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
Light from the Moon takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Earth.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
Light travels as waves, and the color we see depends on the wavelength of the light.
A light-year measures distance, not time—it is how far light travels in one year.
One light-year is equal to about 9.5 trillion kilometers.
A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers.
One light-year is about 9.46 trillion kilometers — the distance light travels in one year.

The lightest gas is hydrogen, which is also the lightest element of all.

Many people think a car is safe because of its rubber tires, but that is not true—the real reason is the metal body that channels the electricity around the outside; lightning is far too powerful to be stopped by thin rubber.
Lightning is the flash we see, and thunder is the sound we hear caused by the air suddenly heating and exploding around the lightning—both come from the same single event.
If your hair suddenly stands up and your skin tingles during a storm, that is a warning that a lightning strike is about to happen nearby—you should crouch low and make yourself small at once.
Many people think electricity stays in the body of a person struck by lightning, but that is not true—it is safe to touch and help them, so you should get help right away and call for emergency aid.
Even when you are inside the house, stay in an inner area and keep away from windows and doors during lightning, because electricity can travel through their metal parts.
Do not shelter under a tall tree during lightning because the tallest object is often struck.

Why is such intense heat needed to break nitrogen apart? The two nitrogen atoms in N2 are joined by an extremely strong bond, one of the strongest in nature. Ordinary heat is not enough to break it. Only the very high temperature of lightning, or the help of special bacteria, can do it.

Some people wrongly think lightning is the main source of nitrogen in the soil. It does help, but the larger share of nitrogen fixing is done by bacteria living in the soil and plant roots. Lightning only contributes a small part.

Right along the path of a lightning bolt, the air reaches an extremely high temperature. In this heat, nitrogen and oxygen in the air combine and form nitrogen oxides. These are the first products before they become nitrates. These gases are the start of the help that reaches the soil.

After lightning splits nitrogen, it combines with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides. When it rains, these dissolve and become nitrates that get carried down into the soil. Plants use nitrates to grow, so a thunderstorm brings something like free fertilizer!
Lightning heats the air around it so fast that the air explodes outward, and that burst of air is thunder.

After a lightning flash, the air in its channel cools extremely fast because the heat lasts such a short time. That is why the air does not stay hot even though it was incredibly hot an instant before.
Lightning glows blue-white because it is so hot. When something is extremely hot, its glow turns from red toward white or blue—a sign of how intense the heat is.
Yes, lightning's heat can melt small spots of metal it strikes, like the tip of an antenna or a roof. It is hot enough to pass the melting temperature of some metals.
When lightning hits sand, it is so hot it can melt the sand into a glassy material. The hollow glass tube left behind is called a fulgurite.
If lightning strikes a person, its intense heat can burn the skin. That is why it is so important to take shelter during a storm and never stand in the open or under a tall tree.
A bolt of lightning can become nearly five times hotter than the surface of the sun.
Because lightning is so hot, the air around it suddenly expands and bursts outward. That sudden burst of air is what makes the sound we call thunder.
When lightning strikes a tree, its heat instantly boils the water inside. The water flashes to steam and bursts, which is why a tree can split apart or catch fire.
To picture how hot lightning is: a kitchen stove is hot enough to boil water, but lightning is thousands of times hotter than a stove flame.
A lightning rod is a metal bar on top of a building that safely guides lightning down into the ground.
When lightning strikes sand, its extreme heat can melt the sand in an instant and fuse it into a glassy tube called a fulgurite — a rock made by lightning.
When there is lightning, it is safer to stay inside a building than to be outdoors.

Not all lightning hits the ground. Most lightning actually stays up in the sky traveling from one part of a cloud to another, or from one cloud to a neighboring cloud. The cloud-to-ground strikes we fear are only a fraction of all lightning.

Why does lightning come in different colors? The lightning channel is so hot that its natural light is bluish-white. But the color we see is changed by air, rain, or dust between us and the bolt distant lightning can look orange or red, while nearby lightning looks white or blue.

When you see a lightning flash, count the seconds until you hear the thunder. Light travels faster than sound, so every three seconds of counting means the lightning is about one kilometer away. If the flash and boom come together, it's very close take shelter.

Before the bright flash, a dim, invisible path creeps down from the cloud in little jumps, which is why it's called a 'stepped leader.' It carves a channel through the air for electricity to follow. The bright spark simply races back up along this path.
A single lightning bolt can carry billions of volts of electricity.
Even though it looks bright, a lightning bolt is only about 2 to 3 centimeters wide.
A light-year measures distance, not time — it is how far light travels in one year (about 9.46 trillion kilometers).
A rule called 'like dissolves like' means substances of similar type dissolve more easily in each other.

Quicklime (calcium oxide, CaO) is made by heating limestone at high temperatures; when quicklime is mixed with water, it produces slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) and releases a large amount of heat.
Many old churches in Bohol and Cebu were built from blocks of limestone and coral stone during the Spanish period.
Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, the same chemical that makes up seashells and snail shells.

Limestone is the main ingredient in cement (Portland cement): limestone is heated to high temperature to produce calcium oxide, which mixed with sand and water becomes cement; the Philippines has large cement factories using local limestone.
The main chemical in chalk and limestone is calcium carbonate, with the formula CaCO3.
Many unusual Philippine landforms, like the Chocolate Hills in Bohol and the caves of Palawan, formed as water dissolved limestone rock.
Limestone is a sedimentary rock that often forms from the built-up shells and skeletons of sea animals.
Limestone is only slightly soluble and dissolves very slowly in water; that is why it takes thousands of years of flowing water to carve out caves.
It took millions of years for thick limestone to form as the remains of sea animals piled up layer upon layer.
Limestone is used to make cement, so it is important for building houses and buildings.
Old lime mortar hardens slowly over time as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air.
A limpet is a kind of sea snail with a cone-shaped shell that looks like a tiny hat.
Unlike a barnacle, a limpet can slowly move to find food when the rock is wet or at night, so it does not dry out.
Charles Lindbergh made his solo flight across the Atlantic in 1927.
The lionfish eats small fish and shrimp, herding them with its wide fins before swallowing.
The lionfish has colorful fan-like fins and dorsal spines loaded with venom — its bright colors warn predators that it is dangerous to approach.
Fats are solid at room temperature (like butter) while oils are liquid; the difference is the type of fatty acids they contain — saturated fatty acids tend to make fats solid.
You can pour and stir a liquid like water or milk; it splits apart when poured and joins back together in a container.
A liquid thermometer works on the property that liquids expand when heated — the liquid inside the tube rises as temperature increases and falls as it decreases.

A complete answer can list three measures: shade or an umbrella, covering clothes or a hat, and never looking straight at the Sun.
If you cannot see clearly, listen: two compact objects dropped together often make one shared sound, evidence they arrived together.
If you walk away from a ringing bell, you meet fewer waves each second, so the same bell sounds a little lower.
If you walk quickly toward a ringing bell, you meet more waves each second, so the bell sounds a little higher.
The abbreviation for liter is "L".
There are 1,000 milliliters in one liter.
We use a measuring cup or graduated cylinder to measure liquids in liters or milliliters.
Tectonic plates are made of the lithosphere (the rigid crust and upper mantle) resting on the asthenosphere, a hot, partly soft part of the mantle that can slowly flow.
Litmus paper turns RED when it is placed in an acid.
Litmus paper turns BLUE when it is placed in a base.
Litmus paper turns red in an acid and blue in a base.
Litmus paper turns red in acid and turns blue in a base.
A live attenuated vaccine uses a weakened version of the microbe; because it is still alive, it creates a stronger immune response, but it cannot be given to people with weakened immune systems.
The liver is the only human organ that can regrow even after a large part of it is removed.
The liver changes the body's poisonous ammonia waste into urea, which leaves the body in urine.
We can keep our liver healthy by eating nutritious food and avoiding harmful substances.
The liver makes bile, a fluid that helps break down the fat in the food we eat.
The liver makes bile, a fluid that helps break down the fat in food.
The liver makes proteins that help blood clot so bleeding stops when you get a wound.
All our blood passes through the liver to be cleaned. The liver removes poisons and waste from the blood, then helps send them out of the body. It works like a filter running 24 hours a day.

The liver is the largest solid organ inside the body. It sits on the right side, just under the ribs, and weighs more than the heart or a kidney. That is partly why it can handle so many jobs at once.

We cannot feel the liver while it works, which is why it is sometimes called a silent organ. Because of this, the liver can have a problem for a long time before any pain is felt—so taking care of it and regular check-ups matter.

The blood carrying nutrients from the intestines passes through the liver first before spreading to the rest of the body. There, the liver checks and processes everything—keeping what is useful and removing what is harmful.
The liver is special because it can grow back even if part of it is removed or damaged. If a piece is taken out, it slowly grows back. It is one of the only organs that can do this.
Besides sugar, the liver also stores vitamins and iron that the body needs. That is why eating liver as food is nutritious—it is rich in iron, which helps keep our blood healthy.
The liver can regenerate, growing back even after a large part of it is removed.
When blood sugar is low, the liver releases stored sugar to bring the level back up.
The liver's constant work makes heat that helps keep the body warm.
Before a high alert becomes an eruption, farmers in mapped zones are often asked to move animals, because ash and flows can arrive faster than a herd.
To live, animals need food, water, air, and a place to live. Plants need water, air (carbon dioxide), sunlight, and nutrients from the soil.

Biodiversity is the number and variety of living things in a place. It matters because each species has a role in the ecosystem, and the more varied the life, the more stable and healthy the environment. The Philippines is one of the most biodiversity-rich countries.
The cell is the smallest unit of life — all living things are made of one or more cells. Some organisms are a single cell (like bacteria), and many, like humans, are made of trillions of cells.

Dinosaurs were ancient reptiles that lived on Earth from about 230 to 66 million years ago. They were NOT mammals — they are most closely related to modern reptiles and birds. They ranged in size from small to enormous.
DNA is like an 'instruction manual' inside every cell that tells the body how to build and work. Genes are small sections of DNA that carry particular traits, like eye color.

Some animals are endangered — at risk of disappearing forever (extinction) because of habitat loss and hunting. In the Philippines these include the Philippine eagle and the tamaraw. We help them by protecting their habitats.

'Living fossils' are organisms that have barely changed for millions of years; the nautilus is one example found in Philippine seas — their chambered shells look the same as their ancestors from the Paleozoic era over 400 million years ago.
A frog is an amphibian — it can live both in water and on land. It can breathe through its thin skin, so it must stay moist.

Fungi (like mushrooms and mold) are not plants or animals — they are their own group. They do not make their own food; they take nutrients from dead or rotting matter, so they are important decomposers.
The golden apple snail is a foreign snail that became a pest in Philippine rice fields because it eats young rice seedlings. It is easy to spot by its pink eggs stuck on stems.

In heredity, parents pass their traits to their offspring through genes. That is why offspring inherit traits like eye color or leaf shape — so parents and offspring resemble each other but are not identical.
A hermit crab has no hard shell of its own on its tail, so it lives inside an empty shell from a dead snail. As it grows, it moves into a bigger shell.

A plant has parts with jobs: roots absorb water and nutrients and anchor it; the stem carries water and supports the plant; leaves make food by photosynthesis; and the flower is the part for reproduction.
Plants respond to their surroundings (tropism): they grow toward light (phototropism) and their roots grow downward because of gravity (gravitropism). That is why leaves always face the sun.
Almost all animals, including people, need oxygen to live. The body uses oxygen to get energy from food — which is why we cannot stop breathing.
Loam is a mix of sand, clay, and humus, and it is the best soil for growing plants.
Lobsters have two long antennae used for touch and two shorter antennules for detecting chemicals in water — helping them find food and sense danger.
Family stories about past eruptions plus PHIVOLCS records together show whether a nearby volcano tends to wake often or rarely.
The famous "Rocket" locomotive was built by the Stephensons in 1829.
Locusts are insects related to grasshoppers that gather in massive swarms; a large locust swarm can eat crops across thousands of hectares in a single day.
Lomi is a thick noodle soup because added starch absorbs water and thickens the broth when heated.
At the same speed, a longer distance takes more time to travel.
The Arctic tern has the longest migration, flying about 70,000 kilometers each year between the Arctic and Antarctic.
The longest bone in the body is the femur, the thigh bone.
The longest bridge in the world is the Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge in China.
Venus has the longest day (about 243 Earth days) because it is the slowest-spinning planet.
Venus is the planet with the longest day—it spins around once in about 243 Earth days.
Venus has the longest day; one rotation takes about 243 Earth days.
The longest suspension bridge in the world is the 1915 Çanakkale Bridge in Turkey, with a main span of 2,023 meters.
Longganisa is meat mixed with salt, sugar, and spices to make it last longer before spoiling, because salt slows the growth of bacteria.
Longitudinal sound can travel in solids, liquids, and gases, a range of media that a simple transverse rope wave does not match.
A longitudinal wave needs the medium to be able to squeeze and spring back along the travel line, which air, water, and solids all can.
Star patterns are easier to check on a moonless night, so plan the outdoor test of a story for when the Moon is not washing out the sky.
Even if a circuit looks complete, the bulb will not light if a connection is loose, dirty, or corroded — because that interrupts the flow of current through the metal contacts.
Lorikeets have very colorful feathers with red, blue, green, and yellow, like a rainbow.
The lotus is a water plant whose flower and some leaves stand up above the water on tall stalks, unlike the water lily whose leaves usually lie flat on the surface.
The lotus spreads by a thick underground stem in the mud (a rhizome) that sends up new leaves and flowers in different parts of the pond.
Lotus seeds are very tough and can stay alive in the mud for a very long time — sometimes hundreds of years — before sprouting when there is enough water and warmth.
Lotus and water lily are different: a lotus holds its leaves and flowers up above the water, while a water lily's leaves and flowers usually rest flat on the water's surface.
A common misconception is that loud sounds travel faster — in reality all sounds in the same medium travel at the same speed, but louder sounds have larger amplitude and more energy.
After it goes quiet following very loud noise like fireworks or a concert, the ears sometimes ring because the tiny hair cells inside were temporarily overworked.
Louis Braille himself became blind because of an accident when he was a young child.
When blood sugar drops too low, a person can feel weak, dizzy, or even faint, so this is also dangerous.
Very low islands and sandbars could go underwater if the sea keeps rising.
When the sea rises, the low coastal areas of the Philippines flood more easily.
As you climb a high mountain, the air gets thinner and there is less oxygen in each breath. That is why people get out of breath and tired more easily at very high places.
An area of low air pressure often brings clouds, rain, and storms, which is why PAGASA watches for a low pressure area.
Low tide is when the seawater drops to its lowest level at the shore.
The lower jaw bone is called the mandible.
Lower pitch means fewer wave crests arrive each second; a source racing away leaves those crests more spread out.
The LPG cooking gas used in many Filipino kitchens comes from the lightest parts of crude oil that collect as gas.
Leaking LPG in the kitchen can easily ignite or explode, so close the tank tightly after use.
The "lub-dub" sound of the heart comes from valves snapping shut to keep blood from flowing backward.
Lumpiang shanghai is ground meat wrapped in a thin wrapper and deep-fried, so the outside turns golden and crisp.
The Moon can look red during a lunar eclipse (a blood moon) because Earth's atmosphere bends red light onto it.
A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon moves into the Earth's shadow, which can only occur at full moon.
A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and Moon — Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, which often turns red from scattered sunlight that still reaches it.
A lunar eclipse happens at full moon, a pattern people could notice without a telescope, which is why full-moon nights were watched closely.
A lunar eclipse can last for a few hours, while a total solar eclipse lasts only a few minutes.
A lunar eclipse can be seen by everyone on the night side of Earth, so far more people can watch it.

Asthma is a condition where the small tubes in the lungs tighten and swell, making it hard to breathe. It can be triggered by dust, cold, or smoke. Many Filipino kids have asthma and use an inhaler to breathe easily again.
To keep the lungs clean, sticky mucus traps dust and germs that get in. Tiny hairs called cilia act like little brooms, sweeping the trapped dirt upward so it can be coughed out or safely swallowed.
Many people think the lungs are like two big hollow balloons. In truth, the lungs are soft and spongy, filled with millions of tiny air sacs. That is why they are light and even float in water.

When you get a check-up, the doctor says 'take a deep breath' while pressing a stethoscope to your back or chest. They listen to the sound of air moving in and out of your lungs to tell whether the lungs are clear or have mucus or an infection.
Coughing helps push out dust or irritants from the airway leading to the lungs.
The lungs are soft and spongy because they are full of air.
The left lung is slightly smaller than the right lung because the heart takes up space on the left side of the chest.

The lymphatic system also helps absorb fat from digested food in the small intestine.
For example, if you get a cut or infection on your hand, the lymph node in your armpit may swell. That's because lymph from your arm passes here first, so this is where germs get caught first.

In the Philippines, illnesses like dengue, flu, or measles can make lymph nodes swell because they work harder to fight the virus. So when you have a fever and swollen nodes, it's a sign your body is defending itself.
No heart pumps the lymph, so the squeezing of our muscles when we move pushes it through the body.
When lymph flows through a node, special cells inside grab and eat bacteria and debris. It works like a checkpoint that stops germs from slipping through to the rest of the body.
A lymph node is home to lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell that acts like a soldier against disease. They gather and get ready here before attacking germs that enter the body.
When you are sick, a lymph node swells because the disease-fighting cells inside multiply and battle the germs. So a swollen node in your neck is a sign your body's defense is hard at work.
Some tubes bring lymph into a node, and different tubes carry it out after cleaning. The flow goes one way so dirty fluid won't go back. This is how lymph traffic is organized at each node.
Inside the node, B cells multiply and begin making antibodies — tiny weapons that stick to a particular germ so it is easier to defeat.
Picture the lymph vessels as roads and the lymph nodes as checkpoints along the way — every bit of lymph passing through is inspected by the guards before it is allowed to continue.
Children's lymph nodes are often easier to feel than adults' because their immune system is busy meeting many new germs, so the nodes swell slightly more often.
After fighting a germ, 'memory cells' are left behind in the lymph nodes like a record — so if the same germ returns, the body recognizes and fights it much faster.
Doctors check swollen lymph nodes as a sign that the body is fighting an infection.
Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped organs that filter out and trap germs when we are sick.
Lymph nodes and tonsils are relatives: both catch germs, but nodes hide inside and filter lymph, while tonsils stand guard at the mouth of the throat to block germs from air and food.
If the lymphatic system cannot return the extra fluid, the part of the body where it builds up swells.
Thin tubes called lymph vessels carry lymph through the whole body back toward the blood.
Lymphocytes are a kind of white blood cell that live in the lymph nodes and fight the things that cause disease.

Macaques make different calls or sounds to warn the others when danger is near.
Macaques are clever and can learn new ways to get their food.
This monkey is active during the day and sleeps at night.
This monkey has fingers and a thumb that help it grab food and hold onto branches.
The macaque is a mammal that has fur and feeds milk to its young.

This monkey is very smart and can use stones to crack open shellfish.
The long-tailed macaque can swim, so it is often found near rivers and coastlines.
Macaques live together in large groups called troops.
A macaw, a large parrot, can live 60 years or more.
Mach 1 means traveling at the speed of sound, about 1,235 kilometers per hour.
An ideal machine has zero friction and 100% efficiency — it does not exist in reality but is used by engineers as a theoretical baseline for calculations.
A machine does not add energy, in exchange for a smaller force you must move it over a longer distance.
Machu Picchu was built by the Inca under Emperor Pachacuti in the 15th century.
Macrophages are white blood cells that engulf and digest bacteria and other pathogens through phagocytosis; they are the immune system's cleanup crew.
Ferdinand Magellan named the Pacific Ocean because it seemed calm and peaceful.
When a plate sinks, rock deep underground melts into magma that feeds the volcanoes above.
Magma rises because it is less dense than the solid rock around it, so it slowly pushes upward toward the surface.
Magma and lava are extremely hot, about 700 to 1,200 degrees Celsius.
A magnet can lose its strength if it is often dropped, heated, or hit hard.
The needle inside a compass is a small magnet that can spin freely.
A compass points north because the Earth's magnetic field pulls on its magnetic needle.
The whole Earth acts like a giant magnet, which is why a compass points north.
When you press a doorbell, electricity flows and a coil inside becomes a magnet. It pulls a tiny hammer to strike a bell, which is the ringing sound you hear.
The motors inside fans, blenders, and battery toys use electromagnets. The changing push and pull of the magnet is what keeps the motor spinning fast.
A ferrite magnet (also called a ceramic magnet) is made from iron oxide and other minerals — it is inexpensive and widely used in speakers, small motors, and refrigerator magnets.
A magnet's force can pass through thin materials like paper, glass, and water.
Near the Earth's geographic North Pole lies a magnetic SOUTH pole, which is why a compass's north end is attracted there.
Natural lodestone magnets were first recorded by the ancient Greeks, and the word 'magnet' comes from a place called Magnesia in Greece.
There is a natural magnet called lodestone, a rock that has its own magnetic force.

In the Philippines, the magnetic declination — the difference between magnetic north and geographic north — is approximately 1–2 degrees east depending on location. Navigators and surveyors must account for this.
Neodymium magnets are the strongest type of permanent magnet — used in computer hard drives, earphones, EV motors, and wind turbines because of their powerful magnetic field in a small size.
Not every metal sticks to a magnet; copper, aluminum, gold, and silver are not attracted to it.
In recycling plants, big magnets are used to pull iron out of mixed metal trash. Aluminum and other non-magnetic metals are left behind, so they get separated easily.
Opposite poles, like north and south, attract and stick to each other.
Even when iron is mixed in water, a magnet can pull out the iron without taking the water.
A magnet's pull is strongest at its ends, or poles, and weaker in the middle.
Even though a magnet is strongest at its pole, the pull still gets weaker as the iron moves farther away. The closer the clip, the stronger the pull; move it back a little and it suddenly weakens.
When you stick one clip to the pole, it can hold a second clip, then a third, like a little chain. But the pull gets weaker down the line, so the most clips hang nearest the pole.
The loud speakers inside a jeepney or a videoke machine have a strong magnet inside. The strong magnet helps move the part that makes sound, so the audio comes out loud and clear.

There are two kinds: a permanent magnet that stays strong, and a temporary one like a clip that only becomes magnetic while touching a real magnet. Once removed from the pole, the temporary one quickly loses its strength.
When a clip is right on the pole, the magnet's pull beats the downward pull of gravity, so the clip does not fall. But once it is far enough away, gravity wins and the clip drops.
An iron nail can become a temporary magnet when you stroke it repeatedly with a magnet.
A sieve separates by size, but a magnet separates by whether a material is magnetic.
The dark stripe on the back of an ATM or credit card has tiny magnetic bits that store information. When you swipe it, a machine reads the magnetic pattern to learn the card's details.
As the Earth spins, the hot liquid iron in the core flows and swirls, and this moving iron creates electric currents that make the magnetic field. Scientists call this the dynamo.
A magnetic field has a direction: outside the magnet it points from the north pole toward the south pole. That is why field lines are drawn like arrows following this flow.
Around every magnet is an invisible magnetic field, the region where another magnet or piece of iron feels its force.
In junkyards, big electromagnets on a crane lift heavy iron cars. When the electricity is switched on, the magnetic field turns strong and the iron sticks; when it is switched off, the iron drops.
When you put two like poles together (north to north), they push apart. But opposite poles (north to south) pull toward each other. This shows in the shape of their magnetic fields.
Earth's magnetic field is made of invisible lines that run from one pole to the other.
Earth's magnetic field acts like a shield that helps keep our air by blocking the strong wind of particles streaming from the Sun.
Earth's magnetic field traps particles from the Sun and gathers them into belt-shaped regions that circle the planet. These are called radiation belts.
Many times in Earth's long history, the magnetic north and south poles have swapped places. Scientists know this from the way minerals are frozen in old rocks on the ocean floor.

The north a compass points to (magnetic north) is slightly different from the Earth's true north (the North Pole on a map). This is because the magnetic pole is not at the exact spot of the geographic pole.
A magnetic field is strongest close to the magnet, and it gets weaker the farther away you go. That is why you have to bring iron near a magnet to feel its pull.
The strength of a magnetic field is measured in teslas (T), named after Nikola Tesla.
Iron is one of the metals that a magnet can attract (it is magnetic).

How does a piece of iron get a North and South pole? Inside the iron are very tiny parts that act like little magnets, called 'domains.' Usually they point in mixed directions, so it is not a magnet. But when they all line up in one direction, their forces add together and a clear North and South pole appear. That is the secret of how a magnet is made!

Between the two poles run invisible 'field lines' that travel from the North pole to the South pole. You can see them in an experiment: put paper on top of a magnet, then sprinkle fine iron filings (tiny bits of iron). They line up into curved lines going from one pole to the other. That is a picture of the unseen magnetic field connected to the poles!

Magnetic poles are why motors spin in fans, toys, and many machines! Inside a motor, magnets keep attracting and repelling at their poles. Because which side is North and South keeps switching (using electricity), the motor keeps turning. So the simple rule 'opposites attract, likes repel' powers almost every machine in your home.

In hospitals, there is a machine called an MRI that uses a SUPER strong magnet — much stronger than an ordinary magnet at home. Using its powerful magnetic field, doctors get clear pictures of the inside of your body without having to cut you open. So the idea of magnetic poles is not just for toys — it also helps sick people get better.

It looks confusing: a compass North pole points north, yet the rule says 'opposite poles attract.' Why? Because what sits at Earth's north is actually a magnetic SOUTH pole in physics! The north-pointing end of the compass is pulled by Earth's south-type pole up north. We just named that spot 'magnetic north' because compasses point there, not because it is north in physics.

It is easy to mix up magnetic poles with electric charges, because both feel like 'positive and negative.' But they are different! An electric charge (positive or negative) can exist alone. A magnetic pole always comes with a partner — you cannot separate North from South. Magnetism and electricity are relatives, but they are not exactly the same.

The magnetic field coming from Earth's magnetic poles acts like an invisible shield. It protects us from dangerous particles thrown out by the Sun (called the solar wind). Without it, much more radiation would reach us. So the magnetic poles do not just make compasses work — they also help keep life on Earth safe.
Using a magnet to separate iron from a mixture is called magnetic separation.
In magnetic separation the iron does not change, it is only set apart, so it is a physical change.
Valdemar Poulsen of Denmark was the first to record sound on magnetic steel wire in 1898.
Magnetite is an iron ore that is magnetic, so it is attracted to a magnet and is found in black sand.
There is a natural mineral called magnetite that is really a magnet — it can attract iron, and long ago people used it to make a simple compass.
A magnifying glass has a convex lens that bends light so small objects look bigger.
A magnifying glass has a curved piece of glass (a lens) that bends light so small things look bigger when you look through it.
Each earthquake has only one magnitude no matter where it is measured, because magnitude measures the energy at the source of the quake.
When you touch one leaf, nearby leaves may close too. This happens because a fast signal spreads through the plant, like a message passing along the stem to the other leaves.
Closing the leaves uses up the plant's energy. So it does not close for no reason, because it does not want to waste the energy it needs to grow.
In the Philippines, some people use makahiya as a folk herbal plant in traditional medicine. Its parts are boiled for certain ailments, but this should always be guided by an adult or doctor.
Some kids think makahiya closes because it feels hurt. That is not true. The plant has no brain or nerves, so it cannot feel pain. The folding is just a protective movement.
In English, makahiya is called the sensitive plant. Its Filipino name comes from the word hiya, meaning shy, because it seems to shyly close when touched.
You can test makahiya yourself. Gently touch a leaf with the tip of your finger, then watch how fast it folds. Be gentle and do not pull the plant apart.
Both makahiya and the Venus flytrap move, but for different reasons. Makahiya folds to hide and protect itself. The Venus flytrap snaps shut to trap and eat insects.
The makahiya is a plant that quickly folds up its leaves when it is touched.
Touch is not the only thing that closes makahiya. Strong wind, raindrops, or heat can also make its leaves fold. It reacts to any sudden disturbance around it.
The makahiya is easy to find in the Philippines because it grows on its own along roadsides and in yards.
The makahiya moves even though it has no brain, nerves, or muscles like animals do.
Besides its folding leaves, the makahiya has small pink ball-shaped flowers and prickly stems that help protect it.
The makahiya grows small round pink or purple flowers that look like soft fluffy balls.
The scientific name of the makahiya is Mimosa pudica, and in English it is called the sensitive plant.
A signal travels quickly inside the makahiya, so touching one part can make the nearby leaves fold too.
Some people think the makahiya folds because it feels scared or hurt. That is not true. The plant has no brain, so it cannot feel. The folding is just a movement caused by water leaving its cells.
Makahiya is easy to find in the Philippines. It grows along roadsides, in grassy areas, and in yards as a wild plant. Many Filipino children play with it by touching it to watch it fold.
After folding, the makahiya leaf does not open right away. The water has to flow back into the cells first, so it takes several minutes before the leaf opens and straightens again.
The water is not lost when the leaf folds. It just moves into neighboring cells. When one side loses its water and goes limp, the leaf bends toward that side and closes.
The makahiya folds because water quickly leaves the cells at the base of its leaves, making them go limp; this is thought to be a defense against animals that might eat it.
Makapuno is a special kind of coconut with almost no water inside and filled instead with thick, soft, sweet jelly-like meat, caused by a natural change in its seed.
Malampaya supplies natural gas, a cleaner fossil fuel that is turned into electricity.
The Anopheles mosquito that spreads malaria usually bites at night, so bed nets are important.

Most fish do not join their bodies to have babies. First the female releases her eggs into the water, then the male releases a whitish liquid that brings the eggs to life. This all happens outside the body, right in the water.
In some fish, the male keeps the eggs inside his mouth to protect them.
Some male fish have round spots on their bodies or fins that look like eyes or eggs. They use these markings to get noticed by the female. This is one of many ways a male attracts a mate.
Malnutrition happens when the body does not get enough of the right nutrients, so eating a balanced diet with protein, vegetables, and fruit is important for growing up healthy.
Malnutrition happens when the body does not get the right amount or kind of nutrients it needs.
Malocclusion is misalignment of teeth that can cause chewing difficulties and speech problems; it can be corrected with dental braces or other orthodontic devices.
Malunggay leaves contain calcium that helps build strong bones and teeth.
Many Filipino families plant malunggay in their backyard so they have an easy vegetable to pick.
Malunggay is hardy and survives even in hot, dry seasons, making it a valuable crop.
Malunggay is often added to mung bean stew, chicken tinola, and fish soup.
Malunggay provides iron, which helps make healthy blood and prevents anemia.
Malunggay is a Philippine vegetable rich in iron and is often added to soup for nursing mothers.
Malunggay leaves contain protein that helps the body grow and stay strong.
Malunggay leaves are small, rounded, and grow many together along one stalk.
Malunggay leaves are full of vitamins and other nutrients the body needs.
Besides the leaves, the long stick-like pods of malunggay can also be eaten.
A single long malunggay pod can hold many seeds lined up inside. So even one pod is enough to plant several new trees.
Malunggay pods are not poisonous even when they get old, as long as they are cooked. The truth is, old pods are simply not tasty anymore because they turn hard, but they are not harmful.
Malunggay pods are not only tasty but also nutritious, giving vitamins and fiber that help your body digest food well. This makes them a healthy vegetable for the family.
If a pod is left to ripen on the tree, the seeds inside dry out. You can plant these dried seeds in soil to grow a brand new malunggay tree.
A young malunggay pod is soft and good to cook as a vegetable, but as it ages it turns hard and woody. Old pods are no longer tasty to eat and are kept mainly for their seeds.
Malunggay contains potassium, a mineral that helps muscles and nerves work properly.
Malunggay leaves cook very fast, so they are added to soup only when it is almost done.
When crushed malunggay seeds are added to muddy water, they bind small particles together and cause them to settle out—a process called coagulation—used in communities without access to clean water.
Malunggay leaves are also used as food for farm animals like goats, chickens, and pigs because they are nutritious for them too.
Malunggay is easy to grow: if you cut a branch and plant it in the ground, it usually grows roots and becomes a new tree without needing a seed.
Even though malunggay is very nutritious, it is not a 'medicine' that cures every illness; it is healthy food that helps keep the body strong, not a replacement for a doctor.
