Malunggay is a Filipino vegetable that is rich in vitamins and minerals like iron and calcium.
Malunggay produces small white flowers that later grow into long pods.
Most mammals give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
Mammals like dogs and water buffalo and all birds are warm-blooded.
Some manakin birds dance very fast on a tree branch to impress the female.
The mandarin fish is one of the few vertebrates with genuine blue-green skin pigment (cyanophores) and produces toxic mucus instead of having scales.
The sweet carabao mango is made into dried mango, a popular treat that is exported to other countries.
The island of Guimaras in the Philippines is known across the country for its very sweet carabao mangoes, and it even holds a yearly festival for them.
The sweet carabao mango is used in many Filipino foods like mango float, ice cream, halo-halo, and various desserts.
The carabao mango is a famous sweet mango variety from the Philippines.
The carabao mango is a famous kind of Philippine mango known for its sweetness.
Many foods can be made from mango, such as dried mango, juice, and sweets.
A mango is green when unripe and turns yellow when it ripens.
The deep roots of a mango tree hold it in the ground and soak up water and nutrients.
If a mango seed is planted, it can grow into a new mango tree.
A new mango tree can grow from a mango seed.
Some kids think a new mango tree grows from a leaf or twig you plant. Actually, the usual natural way a new mango grows is from its seed.
A newly sprouted mango seedling is still weak, so it needs watering and enough sunlight. With good care, it grows strong and healthy.
To start growing, a mango seed needs water and warmth. When the soil is moist and warm, the seed wakes up and begins to sprout.
A mango tree flowers in clusters of many tiny flowers.
Mango grows on tall trees, and the ripe fruit is harvested using a long pole.
The mangosteen is called the queen of fruits because of its sweet taste.
Mangroves take in carbon dioxide from the air while making food using sunlight.
Bakawan or bakhaw is the Filipino name for trees that grow in salty water along the shore, and many of them are found in the coastal provinces of the Philippines.
People gather food, firewood, and even honey from mangrove forests as part of their livelihood.
Mangroves store what scientists call blue carbon in their roots and soil; they store carbon more efficiently than land forests; preserving mangroves is critical for climate change mitigation.
Mangroves store more carbon per hectare than most tropical forests — their carbon is locked in the soil and underwater roots for thousands of years.
Mangroves store large amounts of carbon in their wood and mud, helping fight the warming of the planet.
Most of a mangrove's carbon is stored in the deep mud beneath the roots, not just in the wood.
Thick mangroves weaken the force of waves before they reach the shore.
When mangrove crabs dig burrows, they let air and water reach into the mud, helping roots and buried animals get oxygen.
Before laying, a female mangrove crab carries thousands of eggs in a spongy mass under its folded belly. It protects the eggs there until they are ready to be released into the sea.

Some think a mangrove crab is an insect, but it is not — it is a crustacean, related to shrimp and lobster. Like insects it has a hard shell on the outside (exoskeleton), but it has ten legs while insects have only six.

Some think a 'soft-shell crab' is a different kind of crab — but it is not. It is a crab that has just molted, so its shell is still soft. Once the shell hardens, it becomes an ordinary hard crab again.
A mangrove crab walks sideways because its leg joints bend to the side, not forward like ours. Moving sideways is faster and easier for it than walking straight ahead.
Mangrove trees block strong waves and water currents. This makes the water inside calm and gentle, which is just right for tiny fish that are still weak swimmers.
Mangroves and coral reefs work as a team. Fish grow up first in the mangrove, then move to the reef when they are bigger. So without mangroves, there would be fewer fish on the reef.
Some think fish get trapped or locked inside the mangrove. That is not true. Fish come and go freely. They simply choose to stay because it is safe and full of food.
It is not only fish that grow up in mangroves. Many shrimp and crabs also begin life here when they are still tiny. Like the fish, they use the mangrove as a safe home.
Many important reef fish like grouper and snapper spend their youth in mangroves before moving to coral reefs as adults — making mangroves essential nurseries for reef fish.
Fallen mangrove leaves rot and become food for shrimp, crabs, and other small animals at the base of the food web.
Mangrove forests are home to many animals such as crabs, shrimp, and birds.
The mudskipper is a fish that can crawl and breathe on the mud when the tide is out in mangroves and mudflats.
Rotting mangrove leaves are the base of the estuary food chain, eaten by bacteria, shrimp, and small crabs.

Milkfish, a famous fish in the Philippines, begins life as tiny fry near shores with mangroves and shallow water. There they safely start to grow before being moved to fishponds. It is a good example of the mangrove's nursery role.

Most grown fish no longer live in the mangrove, but some swim in at high tide to feed on small creatures there. Afterward they return to deeper water. So the mangrove is a home for the young and only a visiting spot for adults.

Fish do not live in mangroves forever. They stay only while they are small and weak. Once they are big and strong enough, they move out to deeper sea or reefs. It is like a classroom they leave when they have 'graduated.'

When mangrove leaves drop into the water they rot into tiny food bits called detritus. Small creatures like shrimp and worms eat them, and young fish eat those small creatures. This keeps the nursery full of food.

In a mangrove the water is cloudy and muddy and shaded by branches and leaves. Big fish find it hard to spot tiny fish in this murky water. So besides the roots, the mud and shade act as extra hiding cover.

Mangroves grow only along warm coasts with salty water, like the Philippines. Cold places have no mangroves, so they lack this kind of nursery. Our country is lucky to have these natural fish nurseries.

Seagrass is grass-like and grows on the sea floor, also giving fish a place to hide, but it is not a tree like the mangrove. Mangroves have tall roots above the mud, while seagrass lies underwater. Both are nurseries, but of different kinds.

In the Philippines, many fish and crabs that fishers catch first grew up in mangroves when they were small. Where there are healthy mangroves, the catch is often larger. Mangroves matter for the livelihood of Filipino families.

Fish are not the only ones raised in mangroves. Many young crabs, shrimp, and shellfish also spend their early stage here before moving to deeper sea. That is why mangroves are called a nursery for many sea animals.

In the open sea a tiny fish has nowhere to hide and is easily eaten by big animals, and food is harder for the small ones to reach. In a mangrove there is shelter and plenty of food, so more survive and grow.
The Philippines has more than 35 kinds of mangrove, making it one of the world's richest places for mangrove variety.
Because wet mud has little air, some mangroves have roots that poke upward to breathe in oxygen.
Some mangrove species have pneumatophores — roots that grow upward from the mud to absorb oxygen from the air, because the waterlogged muddy soil lacks sufficient oxygen for roots.
The mangrove roots that rise from the mud to take in air are called pneumatophores, or breathing roots.
Some mangrove species have special roots called pneumatophores that grow upward from the mud to absorb oxygen, because the waterlogged soil beneath lacks it.
Many mangroves have stilt-like prop roots that arch out into the mud to keep the tree standing in soft ground.
Many mangroves have tall stilt-like roots that prop the tree up in soft mud.
Many communities in the Philippines replant mangroves to bring back the coastal forests that were lost.
Communities in the Philippines replant mangroves to bring back coastal protection and store more carbon.
Because there is little air in the wet mud, some mangrove roots poke above the surface to take in air.
Mangrove roots act like a filter that blocks most of the salt from entering the tree.
Mangrove forests are home to many animals like birds, crabs, oysters, and shellfish that cling to the roots.

Even though a mangrove can 'filter' salt for itself, we still cannot drink the water around a mangrove because it is still a mix of fresh and salty. Only the tree has a special way to remove salt inside itself.
A mangrove is a tree that grows in salty water along the coast, where land and sea meet.

In the past, coastal people used the hard wood of mangroves for firewood, charcoal, and posts. Today, people are encouraged not to cut mangroves carelessly because they are more valuable as protection for the coast.
Mangroves grow on warm coasts near the equator, which is why the Philippines has so many of them. They cannot survive in cold places where it freezes, even if the water there is salty.
A thick mangrove forest acts like a natural wall that weakens the force of large waves and storm surges before they hit homes. Because of this, coasts with mangroves are safer during storms.

Unlike most plants, some mangroves have seeds that begin growing while still attached to the parent tree. After they drop, they float in the salty water until they reach mud where they can stick and sprout.

Both mangroves and seagrasses can live in salt water, but they differ: a mangrove is a tree at the sea's edge with its branches mostly in the air, while seagrass is a grass that lives fully submerged under the sea.
There are three main blue carbon ecosystems: mangroves, seagrass meadows, and salt marshes.
Mangroves are home to many kinds of animals — crabs, fish, snails, and birds — that all shelter among the roots.
Many mangroves have a filter-like barrier in their roots that blocks most of the salt while letting water in. So before the water enters the plant, it is already strained to remove most of the salt.
It is a mistake to think mangroves simply drink salty seawater as it is. They do live in salty water, but they first filter out the salt at their roots before using the water.
Some mangroves do not push salt out but instead store it in old leaves, and when those leaves drop off, the stored salt is removed with them.
Per hectare, a mangrove can store more carbon than a typical tropical rainforest on land.
The dense roots of mangroves slow down strong waves and storm surges, protecting coastal towns during typhoons.
Mangroves help reduce the damage from storm surges along Philippine coastal towns during typhoons.

Some mangroves grow long pencil-shaped seedlings that sprout while still on the tree before dropping. When one falls, it floats on the tide and the current carries it to another part of the coast, until it lodges in the mud and grows into a new tree.

When the tide flows into the tangle of mangrove roots, it slows the water down. Because of this, the mud and sand carried by the water settle around the roots — so the coastal land slowly rises and spreads.

In the Philippines, the mangrove forests along coasts in places like Palawan and Bohol are home to mud crabs and young milkfish (bangus). As the tide rises, these animals move into the shade of the mangroves to feed and hide.

The tide is not the same height every day. Around full moon or new moon the tide is higher (spring tide), so more of the mangrove is flooded. On other days the tide is weaker (neap tide) and the water reaches only a little.
Mangroves grow where the ground is flooded and exposed each day as the sea rises and falls with the tides.
When the tide rises, seawater floods over the mangrove roots.
When it is very salty and very hot, a mangrove closes the tiny pores in its leaves to avoid losing too much water, even though this means it grows more slowly.
Because the mud is wet and has no oxygen, dead leaves and roots rot very slowly, so carbon piles up for thousands of years.
Different kinds of mangroves grow in different parts of the shore: some grow in the saltiest area near the sea, while others grow in the less salty area closer to land.
Manta rays return again and again to certain spots on the reef where small cleaner fish remove parasites and dirt from their skin.
Sometimes a manta ray leaps out of the water and lands with a big splash.
Unlike most rays, the manta ray has no stinging spine on its tail, so it is harmless to people.
The praying mantis eats other small insects such as flies, grasshoppers, and crickets.
Female praying mantises lay eggs inside a foam-like protective case called an ootheca—it can contain hundreds of eggs that all hatch at the same time.
A mantis shrimp's punch is so powerful that some have cracked the thick glass of an aquarium.
The punch is so fast that it makes tiny bubbles in the water that release heat and a flash of light when they pop.
Humans have three kinds of color receptors in the eye, but the mantis shrimp has around twelve.
The mantis shrimp is neither an insect nor a true shrimp—it is a stomatopod crustacean; it is famous for its extremely fast and powerful strike that can crack crab shells.

The mantis shrimp has one of the most powerful punches in the animal kingdom — and its remarkable eyes with up to sixteen types of photoreceptors can see ultraviolet and infrared light invisible to humans.
The mantis shrimp stores energy in a spring-like part of its limb, then suddenly releases it to punch with great force.
Each mantis shrimp eye can judge distance on its own, so a single eye is enough to aim accurately.

Can we see mantle convection directly? No, it is far too deep. But scientists learn about its motion using earthquake waves (seismic waves) that travel through the Earth and act like a scan of the inside.
How do we know the mantle moves? Sometimes the rising rock from convection carries pieces of deep mantle up through volcanoes, so scientists can collect real rock from far below to study.
Two sources of heat power the mantle's motion: (1) leftover heat from when the Earth first formed, and (2) heat from the ongoing radioactive decay of atoms inside the Earth.

These two differ: mantle convection is the broad churning of rock across the whole mantle, while a mantle plume is a narrow column of extra-hot rock rising from very deep — and it makes a hotspot like Hawaii.

Why does the mantle flow if it is solid rock? Because of intense heat and pressure, the rock behaves like very stiff clay or silly putty that slowly bends and flows, even though it is not actually melted.
There are very many plants at the base of the pyramid because they are the starting source of energy for all other living things.
Many parts of the body, like the brain, skin, lungs, and kidneys, work together to keep balance inside the body.
Astronomers use different telescopes—visible, radio, and X-ray—to collect information from across the whole range of electromagnetic waves, including light our eyes cannot see.
Marcotting (air layering) is a propagation method where a branch is wrapped with moist growing medium until roots emerge; then the rooted branch is cut to become a new plant.
Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes — in Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911).
Sometimes seashell fossils are found on mountaintops, proof that the land was once under the sea before being pushed up.

'Marine snow' is a continuous rain of tiny particles of dead phytoplankton, fecal pellets, and other organic matter falling from the ocean surface to the deep — it is the main food source for many deep-sea animals.
The marine toad, or cane toad, is a large rough-skinned toad with poison glands on its body, so it is dangerous for people or animals to handle or eat.
Sea turtles (pawikan) are endangered sea animals in the Philippines. They lay their eggs in the sand on the beach, and their eggs need to be protected.
Before you start waves, mark the still-water level on a side ruler so later you can tell height of crests from that calm line.

Images from Mars orbit spacecraft show extensive networks of ancient valleys and channels clearly carved by flowing water; this confirms that Mars once had liquid water on its surface — probably more than 3 billion years ago before it became dry.
Dark streaks on some Martian slopes may be made by very salty water that appears during the warmer season.

NASA's InSight lander used a seismometer to determine the size of Mars's core in 2021; the study revealed Mars's core is relatively large (1,830 km radius) but lighter than expected — indicating more light elements in it than in Earth's core.
NASA's Curiosity rover landed in Gale Crater on Mars in August 2012; it discovered evidence that Gale Crater was once an ancient lake that may have had conditions suitable for microbial life.
One day on Mars (called a sol) is about 24 hours and 37 minutes — just a little longer than Earth's day.
Mars has dust storms that can sometimes grow so big they cover the entire planet.
Scientists have found water on Mars, but most of it is frozen as ice underground and at the poles.
Because the air is so thin and cold on Mars, liquid water cannot stay liquid and quickly evaporates or freezes.
Rovers have detected small amounts of methane on Mars, a gas often made by living things on Earth, which makes it an intriguing mystery.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano in the solar system — about 22 km high, nearly 3 times Mount Everest.
Some Mars rovers like Perseverance run on the heat of nuclear material rather than solar panels, so they can keep working even at night or in dusty weather.
Because Mars is so far, a command from Earth takes several minutes to reach a rover—so it cannot be driven live like a video game.
The Perseverance rover is collecting Mars rocks and soil that scientists plan to bring back to Earth to study for signs of life.

Mars has a more eccentric (less circular) orbit than Earth; as a result, Mars seasons are not equal in length. Mars's southern summer is hotter and shorter than the northern summer because Mars is closer to the Sun (at perihelion) during southern summer.
Mars has seasons just like Earth because its axis is tilted as it orbits the Sun.
Mars has a very thin atmosphere that is mostly carbon dioxide, so humans could not breathe there without equipment.

Mars has a dramatic geological difference between its two hemispheres: the northern hemisphere is lower and smoother (possibly an ancient ocean floor), while the southern hemisphere is higher and more heavily cratered (older and thicker crust).
One year on Mars lasts about 687 Earth days.
Marsupials like kangaroos have a special pouch on their belly where they carry their young.
A mask stops the virus from leaving a sick person and also helps protect the wearer from other people's virus.
A heavier object feels a stronger pull of gravity, but it is also harder to speed up, so those two effects can cancel in free fall.

Astronauts on the International Space Station feel weightless but they do have mass. Their mass is the same as on Earth — they feel weightless because they are in free fall along with the space station.
In both physical and chemical changes, matter is not lost — the total mass stays the same before and after.
If you went to the Moon, your mass would be the same as on Earth — but your weight would be about 1/6 of your Earth weight because the Moon's gravity is much weaker.
A mass extinction is the disappearance of very many species in a relatively short time; the rock record shows this has happened several times in Earth's history.
The mass number is the total count of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
A bathroom weighing scale actually measures weight (the gravitational force on you) and displays it in kilograms. This is correct on Earth but would give a wrong reading on a different planet.

Mass wasting is the downslope movement of rock and soil due to gravity; types include: rockfall (rock drops freely), slump (a soil block moves as one unit), debris flow (mix of rock and soil moves like a liquid), and creep (extremely slow soil movement).
A class table can list each signal number beside the wind range and the outdoor weather, which is how you describe conditions 'according to' the signal.
The first friction match (struck to light) was invented by John Walker in 1826.
Choose materials the classroom already has, such as spoons, cups, and tap water, so the investigation can actually be carried out.
If you will measure, the materials list should include the measuring tool, not only the water or the powder you will pour.
Put amounts on the materials list, such as 100 milliliters of water, so 'some water' does not mean a different amount each time.
If the problem is about melting, the materials should include something that can melt safely, plus a way to tell when it has melted.
Set materials where every group member can reach them safely, so the doing steps do not become a fight over one spoon.
Write only the materials the test needs, because extra bottles and powders on the table make it easy to use the wrong one.

An acid (like vinegar and calamansi) is sour; a base (like soap and baking soda) is bitter and slippery. The pH scale (0–14) measures how acidic or basic something is: below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic, and 7 is neutral like pure water.

An atom is the smallest part of an element. An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom (e.g., oxygen, carbon, gold). There is a limited number of elements, and they are the building blocks of all matter.

Matter changes state when heated or cooled: a solid melts to a liquid; a liquid freezes back to a solid, evaporates to a gas, and a gas condenses back to a liquid. It is still the same substance — ice, water, and steam are all water.
In a closed system, the total mass before and after any chemical reaction stays the same — matter is neither created nor destroyed; it only changes form (Lavoisier's law).
In an ecosystem, matter like carbon cycles round and round from plants to animals to soil, but energy flows only one way and is gradually lost as heat.
Everything in the world, from air and water to rocks and your own body, is made from combinations of only a few dozen elements.

Plasma is the most common state of matter in the universe — stars are made of plasma. On Earth, plasma occurs naturally in lightning and artificially in neon lights. It is a gas so hot that electrons have separated from atoms.

Storing food in the freezer preserves it much longer. The extreme cold slows down the growth of microbes that spoil food. At lower temperatures, the chemical reactions that cause spoilage also slow down.
Gases spread quickly through air because their particles move fast in all directions. That is why when LPG leaks, the whole room can smell it quickly. This is an important safety warning signal.
All matter has mass, even things we cannot see like air. A balloon filled with air is heavier than an empty balloon.
Even though we cannot see air, we know it exists because: we feel it on our skin when wind blows; it makes a balloon grow when we blow it; and it stops water entering an upside-down glass underwater.

A mixture is two or more substances combined without changing their own properties, and usually can be separated again (e.g., sand and water). This differs from a pure substance, which is only one kind.
By the law of conservation of mass, matter cannot be created or destroyed in an ordinary change — it can only change its form.

All matter is made of extremely tiny, invisible particles (atoms and molecules) in constant motion. In a solid they are packed and only vibrate; in a liquid they are close but slide past each other; in a gas they are far apart and fast. This explains each state's shape and behavior.

Some materials are natural (like wood, cotton, and metal from the earth); others are synthetic or human-made (like plastic and nylon, usually made from oil). Plastic is durable but breaks down very slowly, so it becomes waste.
Recycling many materials uses state changes. Glass, metal, and plastic are melted (solid to liquid) and then reshaped into new products when they solidify again.
Comparing the three states of matter: a solid has a fixed shape and volume; a liquid has no fixed shape but a fixed volume; a gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.
A solution is a mixture where one substance (solute) fully dissolves in another (solvent), like sugar in water. There is a limit to how much can dissolve — once no more dissolves, it is saturated.
We can sort materials by their properties. For example: coloured versus white; magnetic versus non-magnetic; floating versus sinking; hard versus soft.
James Clerk Maxwell showed that electricity, magnetism, and light are one single force, using his equations.
James Clerk Maxwell predicted that light is an electromagnetic wave.
The Eurasian tree sparrow has a black spot on each cheek and a chestnut-brown cap on its head.
The maya bathes in dust to keep its feathers clean and free of pests.
The bird we call maya is a small bird known in English as the Eurasian tree sparrow.
The maya helps gardens by eating insect pests, even though it also likes to peck at seeds.
Both the mother and father maya feed their chicks until the chicks learn to fly.
The maya is a small brown bird commonly seen around houses and fields in the Philippines, and it feeds on grains and seeds such as rice.
The maya is a very small bird, about the size of a child's palm.
The Philippine Eagle was chosen because it is unique and found only in the Philippines, unlike the maya which lives in many countries.
Mayon showed strong unrest in 2018 with lava and ash, one more event in its long pattern of waking many times in a century.
Mayon has erupted about fifty times since 1616, a long record that helps people see how often it tends to wake.
Mayon's deadliest eruption was in 1814, which buried the town of Cagsawa.
Mayon Volcano has erupted many times in the last hundred years, so nearby families often remember more than one eruption.
Mayon Volcano in Albay is famous for its nearly perfect cone shape and is one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines.
Mayon Volcano in Albay is famous for its nearly perfect cone shape.
Mayon has a perfect cone because layers of lava and ash pile up evenly into a steep cone.
Mayon often sends lava slowly down its slopes, a pattern that can give nearby towns more time than a sudden explosion would.
Mayon Volcano in Albay is famous worldwide for its nearly perfect cone shape, and it is one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines.
Mealybugs are white powdery insects that damage calamansi, ornamental plants, and other Philippine crops by sucking plant sap.
Mealybugs often hide on leaf undersides, in stem corners, or near a plant's roots.
After the measles vaccine, your body makes antibodies, which are like tiny shields against the virus. Your body remembers how to make them, so you stay protected even after many years.

The measles vaccine works because it contains a very weakened version of the virus that cannot make you sick. It trains your body's defenses to recognize the virus, so when the real measles comes, your body is already ready to fight it.
The measles vaccine is often part of what is called the MMR, a single shot that protects against three diseases at once: measles, mumps, and rubella. So one vaccine gives three protections.
Measles is not just a rash—it can cause serious problems like lung infections, eye damage, or brain harm. By getting the vaccine, these dangerous complications are avoided.

It is a misconception that the measles vaccine gives you measles. The virus inside it is so weak that it cannot make you sick. Sometimes there is a mild fever or redness at the shot, but that is just a sign your defenses are working, not that you have measles.

The measles vaccine usually needs two doses. The first shot starts the protection, and the second helps almost everyone become fully protected. It does not mean the first one failed—it just makes the defense stronger.
Use the same ruler, balance, or timer for every trial so a change in the number is not just a change of instrument.
With a simple machine, the trade-off for using less force is moving a longer distance — the total work is not reduced.
The first mechanical clocks were developed in medieval Europe.
Mechanical energy is the sum of an object's kinetic energy and potential energy.
A similarity: rope waves and sound waves are both mechanical when they need a material medium, unlike light which does not.

On the label there's something called the 'active ingredient.' This is the actual chemical that does the healing work, like paracetamol for fever. The other ingredients just give flavor or hold the tablet together.

Besides the expiration date, there's a batch number or lot number on the label. This is the number of a group of medicines made together. If one batch has a problem, the company can use it to recall just the affected group.

For liquid medicine, the label says to use the included dropper, syringe, or cup, not a kitchen spoon. Kitchen spoons vary in size, so the amount won't be accurate. The included measuring tool matches the dose on the label exactly.
The 'mg' on a label means milligram, a measure of weight. It tells how much active ingredient is inside each tablet. A higher mg means a stronger dose, so it's important to follow the right number.

It's a mistake to think that because a medicine is sweet or colorful, like a chewable or syrup, it's like candy. The label reminds us it's still medicine and you must follow the right amount, not just eat a lot of it.
For example, on a paracetamol label you'd see: the generic name 'Paracetamol,' the strength '500 mg,' and the use 'for fever and headache.' All of this helps your parent use it correctly.

Some labels use tiny pictures or symbols, not just words. For example, a picture of a car with an X means 'do not drive because it causes drowsiness.' This helps even people who can't read well understand the warning.
The medicine label tells you how to use the medicine safely.

Many medicines have a safety seal on the cap or box. If it's already broken before you open it, you shouldn't take the medicine because it may have been touched or swapped. An intact seal is a sign the medicine is safe and untouched.
The label has warnings about side effects and who should not take it.

If there's an 'Rx' on the label, it means you need a prescription from a doctor before buying it. This is for medicines that are strong or risky if used wrongly. Those without Rx (over-the-counter) can be bought without a prescription.
Medicine is not candy, so it must not be eaten just because it tastes nice.
A difference: sound, a longitudinal mechanical wave, needs a medium, while light, a transverse electromagnetic wave, can travel through empty space.
Meerkats have different alarm calls for different enemies, such as one for a hawk and another for a snake.
In a meerkat group, other meerkats help take care of another's pups while the parents go hunting.
Like sharks today, the megalodon's skeleton was made of soft cartilage that rarely becomes a fossil, so mostly only its teeth are left behind.
Most birds warm their eggs with body heat, but megapodes like the tabon are unusual because they do not.
In meiosis, each sex cell receives only half the number of chromosomes—just one from each pair found in the parent cell.
Meiosis is a special type of cell division that produces sex cells, or gametes, such as sperm and egg cells.
Melatonin is a hormone released at night or in the dark, telling the body it is time to sleep. That is why too much light from a phone before bed can disturb sleep.
When butter or chocolate melts in heat, it is only a physical change — it is still the same substance and hardens again when cooled.

Butter and chocolate melt in heat — even from the warmth of your hand or inside your pocket. Put them back in the fridge and they cool and harden again. Their melting point is much lower than metal's, so they melt easily.
Workers use melting to shape metal: they heat it until it melts, pour the molten metal into a mold, then let it cool and harden into the mold's shape. This is how bells and machine parts are made.
Melting and freezing are opposites: melting is solid to liquid, freezing is liquid to solid.

Sodium is a metal that melts at a very low temperature of about 98 degrees Celsius — you can cut it with a knife and it melts in a pan of hot water. It is also highly reactive, so it must be kept away from water.
When a solid like ice melts, it changes into a liquid like water.
Gregor Mendel is called the Father of Genetics.
Gregor Mendel discovered that traits are passed from parents through "factors" (now called genes).
Gregor Mendel was an Austrian monk and scientist.
Gregor Mendel studied heredity using pea plants.
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist.
Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic mass and by their similar properties.
The Russian scientist Dmitri Mendeleev created the first widely used periodic table in 1869 by grouping elements with similar properties.
Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table and correctly predicted undiscovered elements like gallium and germanium.
Mendeleev left gaps in his table and predicted the properties of elements not yet discovered; when they were found, his predictions matched.
Liquid mercury, which shares the planet's name, was once used in thermometers because it expands and rises when it warms up. But because it is poisonous, it is being replaced with safer kinds.
Some miners use mercury to separate gold, but it poisons the water and the body.
One day on Mercury, from sunset to sunset, lasts about 176 Earth days.
One solar day on Mercury, from one sunrise to the next, lasts about 176 Earth days.
Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature and very dense (about 13.5 g/cm³).
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature; it was used in old thermometers but is dangerous because it is toxic.
Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature; it melts at -39 degrees Celsius.
Mercury melts at a very cold −39 °C, which is why it stays liquid at room temperature.
Mercury has the shortest year because it is closest to the Sun, with a year of only 88 days.

Mercury's surface is heavily cratered because it lacks a thick atmosphere to protect it from meteorites; Mercury's craters are very well preserved because there is no weather or plate tectonics to alter the surface.
Mesozoic means "middle life."
The Mesozoic Era has three periods: the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous.
Metal is a good conductor of heat, so a metal spoon heats up quickly in hot soup.
Metal feels colder than wood because it carries heat away from your hand faster.
Metal feels colder than wood even at the same temperature because metal quickly pulls heat away from our hand.
Metal feels colder than wood even at the same temperature, because metal pulls heat away from your hand quickly through conduction.
Some metals start as minerals in rocks, so the ore in the ground is an earth material before people melt it into a pan or wire.
Metal and wood in the same room are at the same temperature, but the metal feels colder.
A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot even at the handle because heat travels through it fast.
Another example of a metalloid is boron (B).

When you touch metal and wood in the same cold room, the metal feels colder—but they are actually the same temperature! This happens because metal quickly pulls heat away from your hand, so your skin cools faster. Wood carries heat slowly, so it does not steal as much warmth from your hand.

When you cook with a metal pot, heat travels quickly from the flame up to the handle, which can burn your hand. That is why many pots have rubber or wooden handles. Metal is so good at carrying heat that you should never grab a hot metal part without a cloth.
Metals are good conductors of electricity, which is why wires are made of metal.

Usually only metals carry electricity, but there is an exception—graphite, the black core of a pencil. Even though it is not a metal, it also has some free electrons that can move, so it conducts electricity. This is a good reminder that not everything that conducts is a metal, even though most conductors are.
The same free electrons are why metals are great at carrying both heat and electricity.
In a metal, the moving electrons quickly carry heat from the hot part to the cooler part.

Inside cellphones and laptops are pieces of metal (often aluminum) called heat sinks. They soak up heat from hot parts like the processor and spread it away quickly, so the gadget does not overheat. Metal is used here because it is so good at carrying and spreading heat.

Not all metals conduct electricity equally well. Silver is the best, followed by copper, then gold and aluminum. Some metals have fewer free electrons or a more disordered inside, so electricity flows a little more slowly through them.

The same free electrons that carry electricity are also what make metals shiny. When light hits a metal, its electrons catch the light and immediately bounce it back, giving that mirror-like shine. That is why freshly polished metals look bright and gleaming.

Metal carries electricity using free electrons, but water carries electricity in a different way—through dissolved minerals or salt in it. That is why it is dangerous to touch electricity with wet hands or while standing in water. Metal is still the better conductor, but dirty water is enough to give you a shock.

Wood, plastic, and rubber do not carry electricity because their electrons are locked tightly to their atoms and cannot move freely. They are called insulators. That is why wires are coated in plastic and tool handles are made of rubber, so we do not get shocked.
Copper is often used in electrical wires because it conducts electricity very well.
Most metals are dense and feel heavy for their size compared with other materials.
Most metals come from rocks called ore, which are dug from the ground and refined to get the pure metal.
Iron rusts when it is exposed to air and water for a long time.
Most elements are metals, found on the left and middle of the periodic table, and they are shiny and conduct heat and electricity.
Metals are found on the left side and middle of the periodic table.
A bond between a metal and a nonmetal is usually ionic, while a bond between two nonmetals is usually covalent.
Elements can be classified into three types: metals, nonmetals, and metalloids that fall in between.
Old metal can be melted and shaped into new things, so it can be recycled.
Because iron is solid and strong, it is made into hammers, bolos, nails, and other tools. It does not bend easily when used, so it lasts a long time before wearing out.
Most metals need very high heat before they melt, so they stay solid in a house or classroom. For example, a steel spoon does not melt in hot soup because melting it needs far more heat than that.

You should not touch or play with liquid mercury because it is poisonous to the body. Even though the silvery flowing metal looks interesting, it is best to avoid it and tell an adult right away if a thermometer breaks.

Some solid metals are mixed to make them stronger; for example, steel is iron with a little carbon added. The result is harder and tougher than pure iron, which is why it is used in buildings and vehicles.
Three examples of metamorphic rock are marble, slate, and quartzite.
Metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock is changed by intense heat and pressure deep underground, without fully melting.
In metamorphic rock the rock changes form without fully melting, which makes it different from igneous rock.
One advantage of metamorphosis is that larvae and adults eat different foods—so they do not compete for food within the same species.
The change in form and the molting of an insect are controlled by chemicals called hormones inside its body.

A meteor glows because it moves extremely fast as it enters the atmosphere. The rubbing of the rock against the air makes intense heat that burns and lights it up, so it looks like a streak of light in the sky.
Most meteors are only as small as a grain of sand and burn up completely in the atmosphere, so they never reach the ground.
A shooting star is really a meteor — a piece of space rock burning up as it speeds through Earth's air.
A meteor, or shooting star, is the streak of light made when a space rock burns up entering Earth's atmosphere.

A meteor shower happens when Earth passes through the trail of dust left behind by a comet. Many tiny pieces burn up in the atmosphere at the same time, so we can see many shooting stars in one night.
A meteor shower happens when Earth passes through the trail of dust left behind by a comet.
A meteor shower happens when many meteors are seen in the sky on the same night.
A meteorite is a space rock that did not fully burn up and reached the ground; big impacts can dig a pit called a crater.
A meteorite is a space rock that survives burning and lands on the ground.
Some meteorites are made mostly of rock, while others are made of metal such as iron and nickel.
Meteorites and asteroids have changed very little over billions of years, so scientists date them to estimate the age of the Earth and the whole solar system.
Meteors enter the atmosphere extremely fast, often traveling tens of thousands of kilometers per hour.
A meteoroid is a small rock in space; when it enters the atmosphere and glows it is a meteor (shooting star); if it reaches the ground it is a meteorite.
There are 1,000 millimeters in one meter.
The chemical formula of methane is CH4 — one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms.
Methane is another greenhouse gas that comes from cattle, rice fields, and landfills, and it traps heat even more strongly than carbon dioxide.
Methane (CH4) is a more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 over 20 years; it is released by livestock and rice paddies — both significant in the Philippines — and by decomposing organic waste.
Methyl orange turns RED in an acid.
Methyl orange is ORANGE near neutral.
While two astronauts went down to the Moon, the third astronaut, Michael Collins, kept orbiting above and never set foot there.
The symbol for the prefix "micro" is the Greek letter "µ" (mu).
Microbes and mold spores are in the air all around us, which is why exposed food spoils.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutchman, was the first to see living microbes through a microscope.
Microfiber cloths are made of very fine synthetic fibers of polyester and nylon; they trap dirt and oil effectively in their tiny fibers, making them more effective for cleaning than ordinary cloth.
A microphone is a transducer — it converts sound vibrations into electrical signals using a small vibrating membrane (diaphragm) that changes resistance or generates a small voltage.
A microphone on a moving phone is a receiver too; if it races toward a speaker, the recorded pitch can come out a little high.
Microplastics are not only in water — some are light enough to float in the air with dust, and we can breathe them in, especially indoors.

Why are microplastics worrying even though they are tiny? Because plastic acts like a sponge that can soak up and carry harmful chemicals from the water, so it can pass them on to animals that swallow it.
What do microplastics look like? They come in different forms — some are tiny broken bits (fragments), some are thin threads (fibers) from clothes, and some are tiny balls (beads).
There are new tools used to catch microplastics, like special filters on washing machines that strain out plastic fibers, and nets in rivers that trap trash before it reaches the sea.
In the Philippines, scientists have found microplastics in rivers and bays such as Manila Bay. We use many plastic sachets that end up in canals and rivers, so the impact here is large.
Some think microplastics are like dirt that rots or dissolves in water. They do not — plastic is not alive and does not dissolve; it stays as tiny plastic pieces for a very long time.
Microplastics have been found almost everywhere — in rainwater, in table salt, and even in the deepest oceans — because they are small enough to spread far and wide.
How can we reduce microplastics? If we cut down on single-use plastic — like straws, bags, and bottles — there will be less plastic to break down into microplastics one day.
Where else do microplastics come from? As cars drive, their tires wear down and leave tiny bits of rubber and plastic on the road, which rain washes into rivers.
How does plastic become microplastics? Sunlight (UV) weakens the plastic and makes it brittle, then waves, wind, and rubbing slowly crack it apart into tiny pieces.

Is there anything smaller than microplastics? Yes — when microplastics keep breaking down, they become 'nanoplastics' so tiny they can slip into even the smallest parts of the body, unlike the larger microplastics.

Why are microplastics so hard to clean up? Because they are so tiny and almost mixed into the water and soil, they cannot be picked out one by one — so it is easier to stop plastic before it breaks apart than to catch it later.

Microplastics — plastic fragments smaller than 5mm — have been found in the gut contents of fish, zooplankton, and even sea turtles in Philippine seas; they come from the breakdown of larger plastic items in water.
A compound microscope uses two lenses — the objective lens and the eyepiece — to magnify objects hundreds of times, making cells and microorganisms visible.
A microscope is used to see very tiny things invisible to the eye, like cells and microbes.
The first microscope is credited to Zacharias Janssen in the late 1500s.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first person to see microbes (bacteria) with a microscope in the 1670s.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see living microorganisms using his microscope.
A light microscope typically magnifies up to 1000x, enough to see bacteria (1–10 micrometers in size) but not small enough to see viruses, which require an electron microscope.
A microscope uses lenses to magnify very tiny things such as cells.
Through a microscope, students can watch living cells as they grow, divide, and move.
Microscopists use dyes to make cell structures visible; iodine, for example, stains starch blue, while methylene blue reveals the nucleus.
Specimens viewed under a microscope are often stained with special dyes — staining increases the contrast between different parts so they are easier to see under light.
Microwaves in an oven are transverse electromagnetic waves; they are a different example from the mechanical waves on water or a rope.
The Philippines lies on the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, a migration path of birds from Siberia and China to Australia — wetlands like Candaba serve as resting stops.
When it turns cold up north, thousands of birds migrate to the Philippines to spend the season in our lakes and wetlands.
Instead of hibernating, many birds migrate to warmer places to survive the cold season.
Even though it is called 'milkfish,' it does not make or drink milk; the name comes from its white, milky-colored flesh.
Milkfish can survive in both salty seawater and fresh river water, which makes them easy to raise in many different places.
A milkfish swims by sweeping its tail and fins, pushing water backward so its body moves forward.
Milkfish has many tiny bones inside its flesh, which is why 'boneless bangus' has those bones carefully removed so it is easier to eat.
The Milky Way is about 13 billion years old.
Our Sun is one of billions of stars in the Milky Way galaxy; on a very clear, dark night you can see part of it as a faint band of light stretching across the sky.
The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy — it has long spiral arms extending from a bar-shaped centre. Our solar system sits in one of these spiral arms, about 26,000 light-years from the centre.

The centre of the Milky Way galaxy lies in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius; in dark-sky locations, the dense band of the Milky Way can be seen arching across the sky during the northern hemisphere summer.
The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy (a barred spiral with curving arms).
Our Milky Way galaxy is so large that it is about one hundred thousand light-years across, so even light takes thousands of years to cross it.
The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy with long curving arms that wind out from the center; these spiral arms are where many new stars are born.
The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy with curving arms of stars that wind around its center.
The Milky Way contains an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars.
The Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars, roughly 100 to 400 billion in all.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is estimated to have between 100 and 400 billion stars.

At the centre of the Milky Way is a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A* (Sagittarius A-star); it has a mass about 4 million times that of the Sun, and in 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope captured the first image of it.
The abbreviation for millimeter is "mm".
When threatened, a millipede coils up into a tight spiral to protect the soft underside of its body.
A millipede is not a predator; it is a detritivore that eats decaying plants and leaves, making it important for decomposition in nature.
In Philippine farms and compost pits, millipedes help rotting leaves and vegetable scraps break down faster. This turns into rich fertilizer for plants.
A millipede's jaws are weak, so it cannot bite hard or fresh leaves. It eats only soft, already-rotting plant matter that is easy to crush.
Sometimes a millipede eats its own droppings again. It sounds gross, but the droppings still hold leftover nutrients and helpful microbes that aid its digestion.
A millipede is harmless to people and does not bite the way a centipede does.
Some millipedes release a bad-smelling chemical to drive away animals that try to eat them.
Many millipedes release a smelly chemical liquid when attacked, to drive away animals that want to eat them.
The mimic octopus of the Indo-Pacific can change its shape and movements to look like a sea snake, lionfish, or flatfish — copying several dangerous animals to protect itself.
Minatamis na bao is made from the soft flesh of young coconut cooked in sugar until it thickens into a sweet dessert.
The Mindanao Current flows southward along the east of Mindanao toward the equator.
Because minerals are non-renewable, recycling metals like iron and copper is important to reduce the need for new mining.
Minerals grow in different crystal shapes based on their atomic structure; quartz grows in hexagonal (six-sided) crystals and galena in cubic crystals.
Luster describes how a mineral shines in light; it can be metallic (like metal) or non-metallic (such as glassy, silky, or resinous).
Minerals are the building blocks of the rocks that make up Earth's crust.
Minerals are non-living solids that make up rocks, so both minerals and rocks are earth materials in the environment.
Mining and quarrying dig minerals, rock, and metals out of the ground, such as gold, copper, and gravel used in building and industry.
A tailings pond stores the leftover mud and chemicals from mining, and if it leaks it can carry heavy metals that poison nearby water and soil.
There are 1,440 minutes in a day, because 24 hours equals 24 × 60 minutes.
There are 1,440 minutes in one day (24 hours x 60 minutes).
A mirage forms when light refracts downward through layers of hot air near the road — sky light appears to come from the road surface.
A small mirror can flash sunlight toward a partner on a hill, a light signal that works only if both of you watch for the sparkle.
A mirror reverses left and right in an image but not up and down — so when you raise your left hand, your mirror image appears to raise the right hand.
Waterfalls often show a rainbow in their mist on sunny days, because the tiny water droplets split the white sunlight into its colors.
To slow the warming of the Earth, people need to cut greenhouse gas emissions by using clean energy such as solar and wind, saving electricity, and planting trees.
The mitochondria are the cell parts that release energy from food so the cell can use it.
The mitochondria are called the 'powerhouse' of the cell because they make the energy the cell uses from food.
Cancer occurs when cells start dividing uncontrollably due to a mutation in DNA, leading to tumor formation that can damage the body.
Before dividing, a cell first grows and prepares by making more of its parts.
In the last step, the cell body splits in two to form two separate cells.
In mitosis, one cell divides to make two new cells that are exactly alike.
Mitosis is for body cells, not for sex cells like egg and sperm.
Mitosis has four main phases: prophase where chromosomes condense, metaphase where they line up in the middle, anaphase where they separate, and telophase where two new nuclei form.
Skin is constantly renewed — old dead skin cells flake off and are replaced by new cells made through mitosis in the deeper layers of the skin.
When mitosis is not controlled, cells can multiply too much and cause cancer.
In paint, the three primary colours are red, blue, and yellow — mixing two primary colours makes a secondary colour: red + blue = violet, blue + yellow = green, red + yellow = orange.
In a mixture, the substances can be combined in any amounts — a little salt or a lot of salt in water. This differs from a compound, which has a fixed ratio of each element.

Mixtures are classified into three groups based on particle size: (1) solution — invisible particles, transparent, never settle (e.g. salt water); (2) colloid — medium particles, scatter light, do not settle quickly (e.g. milk); (3) suspension — large particles, cloudy, settle over time (e.g. muddy water).

The air we breathe is actually a mixture of different gases. Most of it is nitrogen, followed by oxygen which we need to breathe, plus small amounts of other gases. Even though we cannot see it, air is still a homogeneous mixture.

Because a mixture has no fixed amount of each part, you can change how strong it is. If you add more sugar to coffee, it becomes sweeter; if you add only a little, it becomes weak. The same goes for milk or juice—you control how strong the taste is.

Salt dissolved in water can be recovered using evaporation. When you heat salt water, the water turns into vapor and escapes, but the salt is left behind as white crystals. This is how salt is made at coastal salt farms in the Philippines.

When a mixture has a solid and a liquid, you can use filtering to separate them. The liquid passes through the tiny holes of the filter, but the solid pieces that are bigger than the holes are left behind. This is how we filter coffee or sand from water.

In a heterogeneous mixture, you can still see the separate parts because they are not evenly mixed. Examples are halo-halo, salad, or sand with pebbles—you can clearly see the different pieces. This is different from a solution where it looks like just one thing.

In a mixture, each part keeps its own properties like taste, color, and smell. The salt in a salt-and-sand mixture is still salty and can still be tasted. This is different from a compound, where the parts change and lose their original properties.

If a mixture has iron and something else like sand, you can use a magnet to separate them. The tiny iron pieces stick to the magnet, but the sand does not. This is a clever physical way to separate a mixture.
A mixture is made of two or more substances that are mixed together.
A mixture is made of two or more substances put together that are not chemically combined.

A mixture and a compound are different. In a mixture, the parts are just mixed and can be separated physically. In a compound, the parts join through a chemical reaction and form a new substance with its own properties, like water made from hydrogen and oxygen. A compound is hard to separate again.

In a mixture you can change how much of each part there is — so coffee can be sweeter or more bitter depending on the amount of sugar. This is unlike a compound, whose parts are always in a fixed ratio.
Florence Nightingale is regarded as the founder of modern nursing.
The mineral with Mohs hardness 10 is diamond, the hardest on the scale.
The mineral with Mohs hardness 2 is gypsum.
The mineral with Mohs hardness 3 is calcite.
The mineral with Mohs hardness 8 is topaz.
Ruby and sapphire are both corundum, so they have a Mohs hardness of 9.
The Mohs scale was created by the German geologist Friedrich Mohs in 1812.
The Mohs scale was created by Friedrich Mohs, a German geologist, in 1812.
Scientists use the Mohs scale from 1 to 10 to measure mineral hardness.
The Mohs scale measures the hardness of a mineral, meaning how hard it is to scratch.
The Mohs scale measures the hardness of minerals.
The Mohs hardness scale has 10 levels, from talc (1) to diamond (10).
The Mohs hardness scale was created in the year 1812.
The molars sit at the back of your mouth, near the hinge of the jaw. The jaw pushes hardest there, so it's the perfect spot for crushing tough food.
We use the wide molars at the back to chew and crush our food.
The molave is used as a symbol of the strength and toughness of Filipinos.
Mold is a kind of fungus that grows on old or damp food like bread.
A molecule is a group of two or more atoms bonded tightly together, like the two oxygen atoms in the air we breathe.
An atom is a single smallest piece of an element, while a molecule is two or more atoms joined together.
One molecule of water (H₂O) is made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom joined together.
A nymph molts, or sheds its skin, several times as it grows because its hard outer covering cannot stretch.
The moment magnitude scale was introduced by Thomas Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori in 1979.
The moment magnitude scale (Mw) was developed in 1979 by Thomas Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori for large earthquakes.
For very large earthquakes, scientists now use the moment magnitude scale instead of the Richter scale.
Today scientists mainly use the moment magnitude scale (Mw), not the old Richter scale, especially for large earthquakes.
In a collision, the total momentum of the objects before and after stays the same — momentum is only transferred from one object to another, never lost.
As a coconut falls it speeds up, so its momentum grows larger and it hits harder if it lands on something.
An object's momentum equals its mass multiplied by its velocity (p = mv), and like velocity it has a direction.
In a collision, momentum can transfer from one object to another. For example, in billiards, the moving ball gives its momentum to the resting ball, so that ball then moves.
Momentum is not just an amount; it also has direction, like an arrow pointing where the object is going. So if two objects have the same speed but different directions, their momentum is different.
A fully loaded cart at the market is hard to start pushing, and once it is moving, it is also hard to stop because of its large momentum. The heavier it is, the more momentum it has when moving.
A heavy basketball hurts more to catch than a light tennis ball at the same speed because the heavy ball has more momentum. There is more motion you must stop with your hands.
When an object is at rest and not moving, its momentum is zero, no matter how heavy it is. This is because there is no velocity, and without velocity there is no momentum.
At the same speed, a heavier object has more momentum than a lighter one.
At the same mass, a faster object has more momentum than a slower one.
In a Newton's cradle, when one ball strikes the row, the momentum passes through the middle balls and the ball at the far end swings out.
An object with large momentum is harder to stop, so a heavy or fast vehicle needs a longer distance before it can fully stop.
A truck has much more momentum than a bicycle at the same speed, which is why a truck crash is more dangerous.
The monarch butterfly flies thousands of kilometers from Canada and the United States to Mexico each autumn — so far that it takes several generations of butterflies to complete the full round trip.
A monitor lizard is cold-blooded, so it cannot make its own body heat the way people do. It basks in the sun to warm up before it moves around and looks for food.
Several kinds of monitor lizard are endemic to the Philippines, meaning they are found only here and nowhere else on Earth. This is one reason our islands are so important for studying animal life.
A monitor lizard uses a split, forked tongue to 'smell' the air. It flicks its tongue out to collect scents that help it find food or sense danger — much like a snake does.
The monitor lizard (bayawak) is the largest kind of lizard in the Philippines. It has a long tail, strong legs, and tough scales, and some kinds grow more than one meter long.

The monitor lizard has many local names across the Philippines — such as 'bayawak' in Tagalog, 'bayawan' or 'ibid' among Visayans, and 'halo' in some places. They all refer to the same kind of animal.
The monitor lizard is a large lizard found in the Philippines; they are strong swimmers and tree-climbers, and some kinds live only in the Philippines.
When threatened, a monitor lizard whips its powerful tail like a lash and can also bite. It uses these to defend itself against larger animals.
Scientists watch earthquakes, gas, and ground swelling before many eruptions, but they still cannot name the exact day from the pattern alone.
A forest is healthier when many kinds of trees are planted, not just one kind like ipil-ipil.
The word 'monotreme' means 'one opening' because these animals use a single opening for waste and for laying eggs.
The platypus and echidna are mammals that lay eggs instead of giving birth to live young.
Monotreme eggs are small with a soft, leathery shell like a reptile's egg, not hard like a bird's.
The amihan feels cool because its wind comes from the cold lands of northern Asia before it reaches the Philippines.
Monsoons are not felt only in the Philippines; they are a large wind system that reaches much of southern and eastern Asia, such as India.
The habagat and amihan blow from opposite directions: the habagat comes from the southwest while the amihan comes from the northeast.
The habagat brings rain because its wind passes over warm ocean and carries a lot of moisture or water vapor.
The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a band near the equator where winds converge and heavy rain forms; it migrates over the Philippines seasonally and adds to monsoon rainfall.
Monsoons happen because land and sea heat up and cool down at different rates, so wind blows from the cooler area toward the warmer area.
The monsoon does not affect the whole Philippines the same way because mountains block the wind, so one side can be rainy while the other stays dry.
PAGASA is the government agency that monitors the habagat, amihan, and weather to warn people about rain or storms.
Monsoon wind blows from a place with high air pressure toward a place with low air pressure.
The habagat rains flood the rice paddies and provide the water rice needs; this is why farmers typically plant rice during the habagat season.
Because of the amihan, December and January are usually the coldest months in the Philippines, so people sometimes need a jacket, especially in the morning.
Mountains block the moist monsoon, so the side the wind reaches first is rainy, while the far side stays drier.
During the amihan the weather is drier and sunnier, so it is a good time to harvest crops and hold outdoor festivals.
Many farmers plant rice when the habagat arrives, because its heavy rain gives the water that the fields need.
When the moist habagat air meets mountains or warm land, it is forced to rise; as it rises it cools, so clouds thicken and heavy rain pours down.
The word 'monsoon' comes from the Arabic word 'mausim,' which means 'season,' because this wind returns at a particular time of the year.
There are 12 months in one year.
There are 12 months in one year.

The Moon's maria (dark regions) reflect less light (albedo of about 7%) than the lighter highlands (albedo of about 12-15%); the maria are darker because they are made of basalt, which is darker than the lighter anorthosite of the highlands.

Moon rock samples show that the Moon and Earth originated from the same material (they share very similar oxygen isotope ratios), supporting the giant impact hypothesis; but the Moon has a much smaller iron core than Earth, showing that the impactor added mostly silicate rock material.

NASA successfully landed six Apollo missions on the Moon between 1969 and 1972: Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, and 17; Apollo 13 had a serious emergency and did not land. Apollo 17 was the last and the longest-duration lunar surface stay.
Buzz Aldrin was the second person to walk on the Moon, alongside Neil Armstrong on Apollo 11.
Galileo Galilei was the first to see craters and mountains on the Moon using a telescope.
The Moon completes one full cycle of its phases in about 29.5 days.
People who tracked time by the Moon counted about twenty-nine to thirty nights from one new moon to the next, a cycle you can still check.
One full day on the Moon (sunrise to sunrise) lasts about 29.5 Earth days.
On the Moon it is scorching hot in the daytime and freezing cold at night, so the spacesuit had to protect the astronauts from both extremes.
The Moon's diameter is about 3,474 kilometers.
The Moon is about 1.3 light-seconds away, meaning light from it takes only 1.3 seconds to reach us.
The Moon is about 384,000 kilometers from Earth.
The Moon has 8 main phases: new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, last quarter, and waning crescent.
Europa, a moon of Jupiter, is believed to have a vast ocean of water beneath its thick crust of ice.
Because of tidal locking, there is a side of the Moon (the far side) that is never seen from Earth.
During a solar eclipse, the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth, and only people inside that shadow can see it.
The Moon has a far side we never see from Earth, but it still gets sunlight just like the side we see.
Our Moon is the fifth-largest moon in the entire solar system.
Some night fishing is planned around how bright the Moon is, because moonlight on the water changes what people can see and do.
Scientists think the Moon formed when a huge object smashed into the young Earth, and the pieces that flew off gathered together in space.
The Moon is only about one quarter (1/4) the width of Earth.

According to the most accepted theory, the Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago when a Mars-sized body called Theia collided with the early Earth, throwing up debris that clumped together to form the Moon.
Gravity on the Moon is only about one-sixth of Earth's, so there you feel much lighter and can jump much higher.
An old saying tells that a ring around the moon means rain is near — and it is often true, because the high thin clouds that make the ring usually come ahead of an approaching storm.

The bright areas of the Moon are called highlands; they are older and more heavily cratered than the maria because they formed early and were heavily bombarded by meteorites in the early solar system.
The United States (USA) was the first country to land people on the Moon.
In the early 1960s the leader of the United States challenged the nation to land a person on the Moon before the decade ended, and this was achieved in 1969.
It was not only three astronauts behind the Moon landing; thousands of engineers, scientists, and workers worked together to make it happen.
The first Moon walk in 1969 was watched live on television by hundreds of millions of people around the world.
Humans first landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
The first Moon landing happened on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission.
Light takes only about 1.3 seconds to travel from Earth to the Moon.
The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite—our planet has just one moon.
The Moon has four main phases: new Moon (not visible), first quarter, full Moon (fully lit disc), and third quarter; a complete lunar phase cycle lasts about 29.5 days.
Just as the Sun holds the planets, the Earth's gravity holds the Moon in its orbit.
Collect the local names for new moon, half moon, and full moon, because those words are how people communicated a time cycle you can still observe.
On the same night, everyone on Earth, including us in the Philippines, sees nearly the same phase of the Moon.
At first quarter and last quarter, half of the Moon's visible face is lit, so it looks like a half circle.

The Moon completes one orbit of Earth in 27.3 days (sidereal period), but because Earth itself moves along its orbit around the Sun, the Moon must travel a bit farther before the same phase repeats — so the synodic period (the phase month) is 29.5 days.
We cannot see the stars in the daytime because the bright scattered blue sky is far brighter than their light.

On 23 August 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 mission (ISRO) successfully landed near the Moon's south pole — the first spacecraft to do so; its Pragyan rover explored the region likely to contain large deposits of water ice.
During the day, the Moon's surface heats up to about 127 degrees Celsius.
On the Moon there is almost no air, so the hammer-and-feather thought is that they land together, a clean gravity prediction without air in the way.

The Moon's gravitational pull creates two tidal bulges in Earth's oceans — one on the side facing the Moon and one on the opposite side; as Earth rotates beneath these bulges, most coastal places experience two high tides and two low tides each day.
The Moon is tidally locked to Earth; its rotation period exactly matches the time it takes to orbit Earth (about 27 days), so we always see the same face of the Moon.
It took the Apollo astronauts about 3 days to travel from Earth to the Moon.
When the lit part grows bigger each day it is waxing; when it shrinks it is waning.
On a moonless night, walking a path without a lamp is harder, because the Moon is the night sky object that often lights the ground.
Light from the Moon takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach Earth.
Light from the Moon reaches Earth in only about 1.3 seconds.
The moray eel has a second hidden jaw in its throat that shoots forward to grab prey and pull it down into the throat.
The farther you push an object with the same force, the more work is done.

Samuel Morse created Morse code, which uses dots and dashes to spell out letters.
The international distress signal in Morse code is SOS — three dots, three dashes, three dots (· · · — — — · · ·).
The Aedes mosquito spreads dengue in the Philippines and often bites in the morning and afternoon.
Some mosquitoes can carry diseases like dengue or malaria and pass them to people when they bite.
A female mosquito sucks blood from people or animals for food, and can sometimes spread diseases like dengue.
Only female mosquitoes bite people to drink blood, and some kinds like Aedes carry the disease dengue—so it is important to remove still water around the home.
Some mosquitoes group their eggs together on the water as a tiny floating raft.
Mosquito eggs hatch into larvae when they are wet or in water.
A mosquito's buzz can seem to change as it flies past your ear, because the tiny sound source is moving relative to you.

Not all mosquito larvae hang upside-down. The larva of the Anopheles mosquito (which carries malaria) has no long siphon, so it lies flat, parallel to the water's surface, to breathe. This is one way to tell apart the dangerous kind.
The mosquito larva breathes air through a tube called a siphon that it pokes up to the water's surface.

When there is a shadow or movement above the water, a mosquito larva suddenly dives down to hide near the bottom. After a moment, when it feels safe, it slowly comes back up to the surface to breathe again. That's why they are hard to catch once they notice you.
Mosquito larvae eat tiny things in the water like algae, bacteria, and bits of waste. They have little brush-like bristles near their mouth that they use to sweep food into their mouth.
Mosquito larvae are called wrigglers—they live in water and breathe through a small tube they extend to the water's surface.
The mosquito goes through complete metamorphosis because its body changes greatly from larva to flying adult.
There is air trapped inside the pupa's body near its breathing tubes. This air makes it lighter, so it easily floats back up to the surface.
The pupa absolutely needs water to live. If the water it sits in is poured out or dries up, it cannot survive—which is why removing collected water helps.
The pupa stage is short—usually just a few days before the full-grown mosquito comes out. It goes faster when the weather is warm.
When the time comes, the skin on the pupa's back splits open while it rests at the surface, and the adult mosquito slowly climbs out from there.
The pupa does not eat because it already stored, back when it was a larva, all the energy it needs. It simply uses that stored food to transform into a mosquito.
In the pupa stage the mosquito does not eat and tumbles through the water when disturbed, so it is called a tumbler.
In the warm climate of the Philippines, the pupa stage finishes faster. That is why during the hot and rainy seasons, mosquitoes can multiply quickly.
While sipping blood, the mosquito leaves saliva that makes the bite itchy and a little swollen.
Mosses have no true roots — they use thin threads called rhizoids to hold on, and they soak up water directly through their whole body.

The most abundant element in Earth's crust is oxygen.
