Not only the adult moth knows how to hide. Some moth caterpillars look just like a twig. They hold themselves stiff and straight without moving, so they look like a small branch and birds ignore them.
Many moths are brown or gray, which helps them hide while resting in the day.

People learn from how moths and other animals hide. Broken patterns that match the surroundings are used on soldiers' clothes or outdoor gear so they are not seen right away. This is also called camouflage, taken from the idea found in nature.
Many birds that eat moths are active during the day. So moths fly at night when the birds are asleep, and they hide during the day. The darkness acts like an extra cover that helps them stay unseen.

In Philippine forests, there are large moths whose wing color and shape look like a dry leaf. When they rest among the branches, they are very hard to recognize because they look like a fallen leaf, so they are safe from birds.

A moth hides in different ways at each stage of its life. As a caterpillar, it may look like a twig or leaf. Then it hides inside a cocoon. As a winged adult, it hides on bark. Each stage has its own way of staying safe.
Butterflies form a chrysalis—a hard casing with no silk—while moths spin a silk cocoon around themselves.
Some moths have big eye-like spots on their wings that startle birds.
Flowers pollinated by moths are often white and most fragrant at night so they are easy to see and smell in the dark.
A moth is an insect that usually flies at night and is drawn to light, and it grows from a caterpillar that changes form.
Many moths rest on tree bark during the day, and because their wings are bark-colored, the birds that would eat them can barely see them.
A pregnant mother should avoid smoking and alcohol because they can harm the growing baby.
To tell if something is moving, we need a reference point to compare it against.
Some people get carsick or seasick when the message from the eyes disagrees with the balance center in the ear — the ear feels motion but the eyes see stillness.
Many home appliances have a motor, such as an electric fan, blender, and washing machine.
Inside an electric motor, magnets and electric current push and pull so the motor keeps spinning, running things like fans and toys.
A motor spins because magnets keep attracting and pushing the current-carrying coil over and over.
The first motorcycle, called the Reitwagen, was built by Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach in 1885.
A motorcycle engine often seems to drop in note as it races past, even if the rider did not ease off the throttle at that instant.

Mount Apo is the Philippines' highest mountain (2,954 metres) in Mindanao; although it is an old volcano, it is considered dormant or extinct — not active; hot springs near it show its past volcanic activity.

Although Pinatubo has been quiet since the 1991 eruption, it is still monitored by PHIVOLCS because its magma chamber has not completely solidified; PHIVOLCS has seismographs and tiltmeters around Pinatubo to detect any changes beginning.
When two continental plates collide, neither sinks easily because both are light, so the crust folds and is pushed upward to build tall mountain ranges like the Himalayas.

In a mountain range, plants and animals change with height. Lower down, the forest is warm and leafy; higher up, it gets cooler, with pine and mossy cloud forests full of moss and clouds. So many unusual animals and plants are found only high in the mountains.

Even as mountain ranges rise, they are also slowly worn down by weathering and erosion. Rain, wind, heat, and cold break the rock apart, and water carries it downhill. That is why older mountains are often lower and more rounded than young, sharp mountains.

Most mountain ranges form when two huge pieces of Earth's crust (tectonic plates) slowly push against each other. Over a very long time, the land gets pushed and folded upward, so rows of mountains rise. It is very slow — only a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

When there is a tall mountain range, the rain is different on its two sides. Moist air is forced to rise up the mountain, cools, and rains on the front side (windward). By the time it reaches the far side (leeward), the air is dry — so that side is much drier. This is called a rain shadow.

The Sierra Madre is the longest mountain range in the Philippines, running along the eastern side of Luzon. It is often called the country's 'shield against typhoons' because it blocks strong storms coming from the Pacific Ocean, weakening the winds before they reach the cities.

Why is there no snow on Philippine mountains but there is on other mountain ranges? Even though it is cold up high, our mountains are not tall enough to reach the level where rain always freezes. In very tall ranges like the Himalayas, it is so high and cold that snow stays on the peaks all year.

The longest mountain range on Earth is actually under the ocean, not on land! It is called the mid-ocean ridge, and it stretches thousands of kilometers along the sea floor. It forms where plates slowly pull apart and lava comes up and hardens into new rock.
As you climb a tall mountain, the plants and climate change from tropical at the bottom to cold tundra at the top — it is like traveling from the equator to the pole, but going straight up.
Tall mountains block clouds, so one side gets more rain while the other side stays drier.
Every mountain cools as you go up, but small mountains do not get very cold because they are not tall enough. A mountain must be very tall before it has a truly cold top or ice.
Going up a mountain it gets colder; but going down deep underground (like a mine or deep cave) it gets warmer. The heat inside the Earth is why these go in opposite directions.
The higher you go up a mountain, the colder the air gets, which is why places like Baguio are cool.
Because the high parts of a mountain are cold and misty, they stay wet and damp all the time — so thick moss grows and mossy forests covered in moss form there.
People who have long lived in cold mountains like the Cordillera are used to the cold — they wear thick clothes and keep their homes warm.
Even though the air on a mountain is cold, your skin can sunburn more easily there — because the thin air lets more of the Sun's rays reach you. It is cold, but the Sun is still strong!

High on a mountain, water boils at a lower temperature than in the lowlands because the air pressure is lower there — so food takes longer to cook even though the water looks like it is already boiling.
Mountains form very slowly, usually over millions of years.
When two plates collide, they can push the ground upward and form mountains.

The Philippines has many mountains and volcanoes; Mount Apo in Mindanao is the highest mountain; Mayon in Bicol and Taal in Luzon are active volcanoes that can erupt; they give us beautiful scenery and fertile soil.
A mouse lives only about 1 to 2 years.
The mouth is food's first stop: the teeth crush it (mechanical breakdown) while saliva begins to break some of it down (chemical breakdown).
In exchange for an easier pull, a movable pulley makes you pull a longer length of rope.
Riding a bike toward a playground bell makes you the moving receiver, so the bell can sound slightly higher than to a sitting friend.
It takes several years before a damaged reef fully recovers inside a marine protected area, so patient guarding is important.
An mRNA vaccine gives the body's cells instructions to make one harmless piece of a germ's protein, so the immune system learns to recognize and fight the real germ.
Mount Apo Natural Park encompasses the Philippines' highest mountain and protects forests that are home to the Philippine eagle and other endangered species.
Healthy mucus is usually clear or whitish, and it can change color when you are sick.
Mucus keeps the inside of the nose and throat moist instead of dry.
The sticky mucus in our nose traps dust and germs before they can reach the lungs.
Mud is soil mixed with extra water, so it is still made of earth materials even when it feels messy under your slippers.
In the Philippines, mudskippers live in muddy mangroves and along brackish shores. There they crawl over the mud and breathe air using their wet skin and gills.
Warm, muddy water often holds very little oxygen. So it helps the mudskipper to climb out and breathe air, which has more oxygen than the warm water.
The mudskipper has big bulging eyes on the top of its head.
The mudskipper can live both in water and on land, which is why it is called an amphibious fish.
Even though it feeds on land, the mudskipper still needs a little water in its mouth to swallow and move the food down.
To feed, the mudskipper scoops up mud with its wide mouth to get the algae and tiny animals stuck in it.
In some places in the Philippines, the mudskipper (tambasakan) is caught and cooked as food by people who live near mangroves.
The mudskipper guards its eggs in the burrow and sometimes carries air down so the eggs get oxygen.
Scientists study how the mudskipper's eye can see in both water and air. This has helped inspire special cameras or lenses that can take clear pictures both underwater and above the surface.

The high-set eyes are one of several special features that help a mudskipper survive even out of water. Along with breathing through its skin and walking on its fins, these adaptations make it a fish that lives almost like an amphibian.
A mudskipper's eyes work like a submarine's periscope. While its body rests in the mud or shallow water, the two eyes poking up on top act like little cameras scanning everything above the surface.
The mudskipper is a fish that can walk on mangrove mud using its pectoral fins like legs — it breathes oxygen through its moist skin and specialized air chambers when out of water.
The mudskipper can skip across the mud by curling and quickly snapping its tail.
A mudslide or debris flow is a landslide with so much water that it flows like thick mud. It rushes quickly downhill along channels and streams, carrying soil, rocks, and trees.
In Mullerian mimicry, two or more genuinely dangerous species share similar appearances so predators learn faster to avoid all of them.
Mumps spreads through saliva, for example when a sick person coughs or sneezes.
There is a saliva gland on each cheek, so both can swell and make the face rounder. Sometimes only one side puffs up.
A doctor recognizes mumps by looking at the swelling in front of the ear and other signs like fever. Sometimes a saliva or blood test is done too.
Some think mumps swelling comes from cold or rain, but the truth is a virus causes it. It does not come from cold weather.
A person usually gets mumps only once, because the body learns to fight that virus. So the swelling rarely comes back.
There is no medicine that instantly kills the mumps virus, so rest, plenty of water, and a cool compress help while it is swollen. The body heals itself.
There is a vaccine called MMR that helps stop us from getting mumps. When you are vaccinated, your chance of getting the swollen cheeks is much lower.
The swelling in mumps is caused by a tiny virus that gets into the body. The cheek does not just puff up on its own. A germ too small to see is behind it.
Muro-ami, where fishers pound the reef to drive fish into nets, is also banned because it smashes the coral.
Muscle cells are long fibers that shorten and relax, letting the body move.
When you do work, your muscles change chemical energy from food into the energy of motion and heat.
Our muscles use energy from food to do work like walking and lifting.
Our body moves because muscles contract and pull on bones, like the biceps bending the arm.
Muscles get tired after long use, so they need rest and sleep.
Muscles need energy from food in order to move.

A muscle does not pull on its own — it waits for a signal from the brain. The brain sends a fast signal through nerves to the muscle, and only then does it pull. That is why your arm moves almost instantly the moment you decide to move it.

There are tiny muscles in your face that pull on your skin to make expressions. When you smile, the muscles in your cheeks pull upward. When you raise your eyebrows or frown, muscles are pulling your facial skin too.

Humans are not the only ones with pulling muscles — animals have them too. A fish has strong muscles along its body that pull to swim. A bird has chest muscles that pull its wings down so it can fly. It is all still pulling.

The heart is also a muscle, but instead of pulling a bone, it squeezes itself to pump blood. The pulling-inward of the heart's walls pushes blood out. It is special because it never gets tired even though it beats all day and night.

Muscles grow bigger and stronger when you use them often through exercise or work. When you make a muscle pull hard again and again, it builds up and can pull more strongly later. That is why athletes and laborers have larger muscles.

When muscles pull, they also make heat as a side effect. That is why your body warms up when you exercise. And when you are cold, your muscles shiver — that fast, repeated pulling produces heat to warm your body.
The muscles of the back and stomach help support the spine and keep us standing upright.
Muscles attached to bones by tendons pull on the bones to make a joint move.
Muscovado is a brown sugar made from sugarcane and produced in the Philippines.
The mushroom we see is only the part used for reproduction; most of the fungus is hidden in the soil or wood.
In a musikong bumbong band, the sound comes from air vibrating inside hollow bamboo tubes when the players blow across or into them.
Large mussel beds act as ecosystem engineers — their shells create a three-dimensional substrate for hundreds of other organisms to live in, including algae, worms, and crustaceans.
Mussels attach to rocks and other surfaces using strong byssus threads — silk-like fibers produced by a special gland that are stronger than any synthetic fiber of equivalent thickness.
If a mutation happens in reproductive cells, it can be passed to offspring; but if it happens in other cells, it is not inherited.
Mutations, which are changes in DNA, create new variation that can be passed on to offspring.
Mycorrhizal fungi grow on plant roots and help absorb water and minerals, while the plant gives the fungi sugar.
An N95 mask fits more tightly on the face and filters out more tiny particles than an ordinary cloth mask.
The skin under the nail does have nerves, so it hurts if the nail is cut too short.

Rocks, soil, water, and air can look different, but they share the group name earth materials because they are the non-living environment.
A clear explanation names the sky object and the activity: the Sun for daytime work, the Moon for some night light, the stars for direction.
You can walk a schoolyard and name earth materials: the packed soil, the gravel path, the puddle, and the air you breathe.
A solid answer names three longitudinal examples, such as sound, slinky push-pull, and P-waves, plus three transverse examples such as rope, light, and S-waves.

The hertz is named after Heinrich Hertz, the German scientist who proved that radio waves exist.

When a new kind of living thing is discovered, scientists give it a new scientific name and publish it so it can be recognized worldwide.
Nanosilver particles are tiny pieces of silver (under 100 nanometers) with stronger antibacterial properties than bulk silver; they are used in socks, wound dressings, and medical coatings.
The symbol for the prefix "nano" is "n", so a nanometer is "nm".
The Napoleon wrasse (humphead wrasse) can grow up to 2 meters and is recognized by the large hump on its forehead; it is one of the largest reef fish and is globally endangered.
Some Philippine trees like the narra drop their leaves during the hot, dry season.
The narra (Pterocarpus indicus) belongs to the family Fabaceae, the legume family.
The narra is the national tree of the Philippines, a large tree with strong wood used for furniture, and it blooms fragrant yellow flowers.
Narra wood is hard, strong, and beautifully colored, making it a prized wood for furniture. Because it grows slowly and many were cut down, it is now protected by law in the Philippines.
The narra (Pterocarpus indicus) was declared the national tree of the Philippines in 1934.
The narra is a native tree that grows naturally in the forests of the Philippines.
Yakal is a very strong Philippine hardwood used to build houses and bridges.

The same bacterial cellulose found in nata de coco is also being studied as a material for wound bandages. Because the fiber is clean, moist, and strong, it can help protect and keep the skin damp while it heals.
Nata de coco is a thick cellulose gel produced by the bacterium Acetobacter xylinum as it ferments sweetened coconut water.
Nata de coco and gulaman are different even though both are clear and soft. Gulaman is made from seaweed (agar), but nata is built by bacteria from coconut water, so nata is firmer and chewier.

Besides nata de coco, there is also nata de pina, which is made from pineapple juice instead of coconut water. They are made by the same kind of bacteria; only the liquid the bacteria feed on is different.
Once the nata is thick enough, it is lifted out as one big clear mat. Then it is washed, cooked in water, and cut into the little cubes we see in a dessert glass.
Nata forms on top of the liquid because the bacteria need air (oxygen) to live. So they gather near the surface where the air is, and that is where the floating layer of nata builds up.
You often find nata de coco in desserts like halo-halo, buko salad, and fruit cocktail. It is the clear, little cube pieces that are soft but chewy, mixed into sweet treats.
The bacteria that make nata are called Acetobacter (also now known as Komagataeibacter). This is the same kind of bacteria used to make vinegar, so it is not harmful to people.
The Philippines has native chickens such as the Darag that are raised in backyards and known for their tasty meat.
Wild pigs often live together in small family groups of mothers and piglets.
Pigs communicate with each other using different sounds like grunts and squeals. They have one sound to call their young, another to warn of danger, and another to say they found food.
Native wild pigs have thick, stiff hair, especially on the neck and back, like a mane. This hair stands up when they are angry or scared, making them look bigger.
Wild native pigs, especially the piglets, are food for big predators like large pythons and eagles. In this way, they are an important part of the forest food chain.
Native wild pigs are protected by Philippine law, so hunting them carelessly is against the rules.
When pigs root through the soil, they turn it over and help new plants grow.
Male wild native pigs grow sharp tusks that stick out from their mouths. They use these to fight other pigs and to defend themselves.

The Philippine wild pig is different from the African warthog. Both have tusks, but the warthog has a bigger head and warty bumps on its face. Different kinds of wild pigs live in different parts of the world.
There is a real kind of native pig called the Philippine warty pig. It is called 'warty' because of the wart-like bumps on the male's face. It is found only in the Philippines.
Climate also changes for natural reasons such as shifts in the sun's strength, the Earth's orbit and tilt, and volcanic eruptions, but the rapid warming today is caused by human activity.
A natural dye is a coloring taken from plants, animals, or minerals rather than made from factory chemicals. It is used to color cloth, paper, or food.

Abaca is a strong natural fiber from a plant that looks like a banana, and it grows in the Philippines. Called Manila hemp, it is made into ropes, twine, and paper. The Philippines is famous for abaca because it stays strong even in water.
Natural fibers like cotton, wool, and silk can rot away in the soil because they come from living things, unlike plastic fibers.

Jute is a natural fiber from a plant's stem and is very tough. It is made into sacks for holding rice, coffee, or sugar because it can carry heavy loads. That is why it is often used in storage and markets.

Some kids think all natural fibers are soft like cotton, but that is not true. Some are stiff and rough, like coconut coir and abaca, which are used for ropes and brushes. The softness depends on which plant or animal it came from.

When clothes made of natural fiber wear out, they don't have to be thrown away right away. They can be turned into rags or cleaning cloths so they get used again. This helps reduce waste and save on buying new cloth.
Natural gas is mainly methane (CH4) and burns more cleanly than coal or oil because it produces less CO2 and almost no sulfur dioxide; LPG cooking gas used in Philippine homes is a related product.
After fighting an infection, the immune system creates memory cells that quickly recognize and fight the same microbe if it enters the body again.
Some people are allergic to natural latex rubber because of proteins found in the rubber tree sap; this is why some hospitals use synthetic rubber or vinyl gloves instead.
In natural selection, individuals with traits that fit their environment are more likely to survive and have young, so over time more and more offspring inherit that helpful trait.
Some rubber comes from plants (natural rubber) and some is made by people from oil (synthetic rubber).
The nautilus is a cephalopod, so it is a relative of the octopus and squid even though it has a hard shell.
The nautilus shell is divided into many small chambers, or rooms, inside.
The nautilus has a beautiful spiral shell that is divided into many separate chambers inside.
The nautilus lives only in the newest and largest chamber at the outer edge of the shell.
The nautilus is called a living fossil because it has changed very little over millions of years.
The nautilus has many tentacles that it uses to catch its food.
Unlike the octopus with its eight arms, the nautilus has around ninety tentacles without suckers.
The nautilus is called a living fossil because its body has barely changed for millions of years, longer ago than the dinosaurs.
Unlike the octopus, the nautilus has many tentacles, dozens of them, but they have no suckers. It uses sticky tentacles to grip its food.
The brown and white stripes on the shell help hide the nautilus from predators.
A thin tube called a siphuncle runs through all the chambers. The nautilus uses it to add or remove gas and liquid, so it can control whether it sinks or floats.
As a nautilus grows, it builds new, bigger chambers inside its shell. The animal always lives in the newest, largest chamber, which is why the shell curls in a spiral.
A neap tide, the weakest tide, happens when the Sun and Moon are at right angles, during the first or last quarter moon.
Scientists use telescopes to watch asteroids that come near Earth's path. They calculate the routes of these objects ahead of time to know whether our planet is safe and whether any action is needed.
The lens of the eye changes shape — getting rounder for near objects and flatter for far ones — so light always focuses sharply on the retina.
Apart from the Sun, the nearest star to us is Proxima Centauri.
After the Sun, the next nearest star to us is Proxima Centauri.
The nearest star after the Sun is called Proxima Centauri, and it is so far that its light takes about four years to reach Earth.
The nearest star to Earth is the Sun itself, our own star.
A nearsighted person (myopia) sees nearby things clearly but faraway things look blurry.

If the eyeball is too long, light focuses in front of the retina so distant things look blurry (nearsighted); if too short, it focuses behind so near things blur (farsighted) — the right glasses correct it.
A nebula is a huge cloud of gas and dust in space, and inside some nebulas new stars are born.

Nebulae have three main types: emission nebulae (which make their own light from ionised gas), reflection nebulae (which reflect light from nearby stars), and dark nebulae (whose dust is so thick it blocks light from behind).
When the North Equatorial Current reaches the Philippine coast, it splits into two: the Kuroshio Current going north and the Mindanao Current going south.
Because small birds burn energy fast, they must visit very many flowers in a single day to stay fed.
The small nectar-feeding birds in a garden help pollinate flowers, so they help plants make fruit and seeds.
Light messages need a clear path; a wall blocks the flashlight, so partners must stand where each can see the lamp.
When the Sun is below the horizon, people turn on lamps to keep reading or cooking, an activity change caused by that missing sky light.
A sound message can fail in a very noisy market, so people may switch to a wave or a light when talking cannot be heard.
A movement message only works if the other person is looking; that is why a referee also uses a whistle, a sound, not only an arm signal.

Both kinds need a source of disturbance, such as a vibrating object for sound or a shaken hand for a rope wave.
The gas used in glowing neon signs is neon, which gives off a red-orange light.
Each kidney has millions of tiny units called nephrons that filter the blood.
Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system — reaching about 2,000 km/h.

In 1989 Voyager 2 observed a large storm on Neptune called the Great Dark Spot — about the size of Earth. When the Hubble Space Telescope observed Neptune in 1994, the storm had disappeared, showing that Neptune's storms can change quickly.
Yes, Neptune has rings, but they are faint and hard to see.
Neptune is named after the Roman sea god Neptune.
Neptune has the strongest winds of any planet in the solar system; its winds can reach speeds of 2,100 kilometres per hour — faster than the strongest typhoon on Earth.
Neptune has the strongest winds of any planet, blowing faster than the speed of sound.
Nerve signals can travel up to 100 meters per second along nerves insulated with myelin, allowing very fast reactions.
Messages in the nervous system are tiny electrical signals that travel along neurons. They move so fast that you can feel and respond to things almost instantly.
Nerves are like a network of tiny wires that reach almost every part of the body, from the head down to the tips of the toes.
From the spinal cord, nerves branch out and reach almost every part of the body, all the way to the tips of your fingers. That is why you can feel a touch on any part.
The body is controlled two ways: nerves give fast signals, while hormones act more slowly but last longer.
Inside a neuron the message travels like electricity, but between two neurons there is a tiny gap that a chemical message crosses.
Neurons send messages using fast electrical signals.
A neuron is a nerve cell that carries messages as tiny electrical signals. Billions of connected neurons make up the brain and nerves, and they pass signals through the body very fast.
Neurons carry fast, electric-like signals so the brain can communicate with the body.

Some rivers and lakes near volcanoes in the Philippines, like parts of Taal, have acidic water because of gases and sulfur from the volcano. This acidic water is hard for fish to live in. Scientists study how to neutralize or manage such acid for the environment.

How does neutralization work? An acid has extra H+ (hydrogen ions) and a base has extra OH- (hydroxide ions). When you mix them, the H+ and OH- join together to form water (H2O). That's why the mixture is no longer strongly acidic or basic.

Have you seen 'pH balanced' on shampoo or soap? Our skin is slightly acidic, so products are made to be neither too acidic nor too basic — close to balanced — so they don't irritate the skin. This applies the idea of neutralization to be gentle on the body.

If acid spills in a lab or from a car battery, a safe response is to pour baking soda (a mild base) on it. This neutralizes the acid so it can no longer burn or damage things. It lowers the danger before you fully clean it up.
In neutralization, the H+ from the acid and the OH- from the base join to form water, and the leftover ions form a salt.
A neutron has no charge (it is neutral, or zero).
Neutrons have little effect on how an atom reacts, but the number of neutrons does affect the mass and the stability of the nucleus.
Never look straight at the Sun even during a solar eclipse — it can damage your eyes. You need special eclipse glasses, or just watch its shadow projected on paper.
You should never taste an unknown chemical to find out if it is an acid or base; use an indicator instead.
Some newly grown leaves are reddish at first before they turn green.

Thomas Newcomen built the first practical steam engine in 1712, used to pump water out of mines.
Besides physics, Isaac Newton also helped invent calculus in mathematics.
The scientist Isaac Newton explained that the same gravity that makes an apple fall also holds the planets in orbit.
Isaac Newton is called the Father of Classical Physics.

Not everything follows Ohm's law exactly. 'Ohmic' materials like metal wires obey it, but some things like light bulbs or diodes change as they heat up. It isn't always perfect.

It's a misconception that only high voltage is harmful. Really, it's the current (amperes) flowing through the body that's more dangerous. Static electricity has high voltage but tiny current, so it isn't deadly.
In the Philippines, wall outlets are usually 220 volts. At this higher voltage, less current (amperes) is needed for the same power, which follows from Ohm's law and the power relation.

A resistor is a small part in a circuit made on purpose to have resistance, so it controls how much current flows. Engineers use Ohm's law to choose the right size resistor.

When resistance is almost zero (a short circuit), the current shoots up very high by Ohm's law (I = V / R with tiny R). That's why wires overheat and can catch fire, and why we use fuses and breakers.
A thicker wire has less resistance, so current flows through it more easily. A long, thin wire has more resistance. That's why some cables are made thick.
To picture it, think of water in a pipe. Voltage is like the pressure pushing the water, current is how much water flows, and resistance is like a narrow pipe that slows the flow.

Oresol (ORS) is a special drink that replaces the water and salts lost from the body during diarrhea.
ORS contains sugar because it helps the intestine absorb water and salts more effectively.

Why does ORS taste a bit salty? Because it has the salt the body needs. Sometimes kids dislike the taste. It can help to serve it cold or give it in small amounts. Do not just add sugar to sweeten it, because that ruins the correct balance.

There is a homemade ORS taught by the DOH: in one liter of clean water, mix a little salt and a few teaspoons of sugar, then stir well. But packaged oresol is even safer when available, because the amounts are exactly measured.
How should you drink ORS? Do not gulp it all at once. Drink it slowly, in small amounts, like a spoonful or a sip every few minutes. Drinking too fast can cause vomiting. Steady small sips work best.

Is there a newer kind of ORS? Yes. The WHO improved the old recipe into a 'low-osmolarity' ORS with slightly less salt and sugar. It is gentler on the stomach, more effective at stopping fluid loss, and reduces vomiting compared with the old mix.

Does this relate to osmosis? Yes. Water tends to move toward where there is more salt or glucose. By adding the right amount of sodium and glucose in the gut, water is pulled back into the body through movement similar to osmosis. That is why the correct balance matters.

How do you know ORS is needed? Signs of dehydration include: very strong thirst, dry lips and mouth, little or dark pee, no tears when crying, and sunken eyes. When you see these, give ORS and watch closely.

Is ORS paired with any other medicine? For children's diarrhea, the WHO and DOH recommend giving ORS together with a zinc supplement for several days. ORS handles the fluids, while zinc helps speed up recovery and reduce future diarrhea.

The pancreas has two jobs: it makes enzymes for digesting food, and it also makes hormones like insulin for blood sugar. So it is part of both the digestive and endocrine systems.

When you play or run, your muscles use up sugar, so your body releases glucagon to provide extra sugar as fuel.
The pancreas senses when sugar is low and releases glucagon; once sugar rises, it stops releasing glucagon, like an automatic switch.
The liver stores extra sugar as glycogen; when glucagon arrives, it breaks the glycogen back down into glucose to raise blood sugar.
When blood sugar is low, the pancreas releases glucagon to signal the liver to release its stored sugar back into the blood.
For diabetic people whose blood sugar suddenly drops dangerously low, a glucagon injection is used to quickly bring their sugar back to a safe level.

You might wonder why insulin is injected instead of taken as a pill. It's because insulin is a protein, and if swallowed, the stomach would digest it before it could work. So it has to be injected straight into the body.
Insulin is a hormone — a kind of chemical 'messenger' for the body. The pancreas releases it into the blood, and the blood carries it all over the body to reach every cell.
Some people with diabetes don't make enough of their own insulin, so they have to inject it daily. In the Philippines, you'll find it sold in hospitals and pharmacies for patients.

Blood sugar can also drop too low, not just go too high. When this happens, a person may feel dizzy, shaky, or weak. That's why balance matters — not too high, not too low.

The Philippine duck, also called papan, is a kind of duck found only in the Philippines.

The parent eagles bring food to the nest and feed the chick that cannot hunt on its own yet.
The Philippine eagle is a symbol of the strength and freedom of the Philippines, and its presence in a forest is a sign that the forest is still healthy.
The Philippine eagle is one of the largest eagles in the world, with wings that span almost two meters, and it is the country's national bird.

The Philippine Fault is called an 'active' fault because it still moves and can cause earthquakes in the present. There are old faults that have been quiet for a long time and aren't expected to move. But because the Philippine Fault is active, people living near it must always be ready.

After a strong earthquake on the Philippine Fault, there are often smaller shakes that follow. These are called 'aftershocks'. They happen because the rocks around the fault are still settling after the big movement. Usually they slowly weaken over the following days.

An important use of knowing where the Philippine Fault passes is to decide where it's safe to build homes, schools, or hospitals. Engineers avoid building directly on top of the fault. This way, big damage can be reduced when it moves.

The Philippine Fault exists because our country is squeezed between large tectonic plates that push against each other. The Philippine Sea Plate to the east pushes westward, so the land gets pinched and forced to crack, forming this long fault. It's like paper tearing from being pulled too hard.

Not every part of the Philippine Fault moves suddenly. Some parts slowly creep along little by little, a few millimeters each year, without big earthquakes. This is called 'fault creep'. Here you can see fences or floors slowly bending without the ground shaking.

It's a misconception that when the Philippine Fault moves, the ground opens up and swallows people, like in movies. In reality, the ground shakes and slides sideways; it does not open into a deep mouth. The real danger is buildings collapsing, not the earth eating people.

It's a misconception that every time the Philippine Fault moves, a volcano erupts. This fault causes earthquakes because rocks shift, not because of magma or lava. Volcanic eruptions are a different thing with their own causes, even though both happen in the Philippines' active zone.

The Philippine Fault is very long and crosses many provinces in the country, from northern Luzon, through Quezon, Masbate, Leyte, all the way to Surigao and Davao in Mindanao. Because of this, many Filipinos live near this fault.
The Philippine Fault runs from northern Luzon, through Leyte, down to southern Mindanao.

Many ask why earthquakes happen suddenly. Usually the two sides of the fault are stuck because of friction, so they don't move right away. While stuck, energy builds up, until it can't hold anymore and suddenly slips, which is what shakes the ground.

The Philippine Fault is different from the Philippine Trench. The fault is a crack running through land where two sides slide sideways. The trench is a very deep channel under the sea to the east, where one plate dives beneath another. They differ in form and location.
The giant golden-crowned flying fox is endangered, so we need to protect it.
It is called a flying fox because its face looks like the face of a fox.
Even though its wings are very wide, its body is light—only about one to one and a half kilograms.
There is a saying 'blind as a bat', but bats are not really blind. The Philippine flying fox has big, clear eyes and uses them to see fruit trees even at night.
Flying foxes hang upside down in large trees, and sometimes thousands of them gather in one place.
The Philippine flying lemur, or colugo, is not a true lemur and does not truly fly — it uses a skin membrane called a patagium connecting its limbs to glide long distances between trees.
A flying lemur can glide more than 100 meters from one tree to another while barely losing height. This lets it move tree to tree without coming down to the ground, where it would be in danger.
Unlike the flying fox that loves fruit, the flying lemur mostly eats leaves, shoots, flowers, and buds of plants. So it is a herbivore — an animal that eats only plants.
The Philippine flying lemur (Cynocephalus volans) is a native animal found in the forests of Mindanao and Bohol.

The flying lemur (colugo) has a wide flap of skin (patagium) reaching from its neck to its fingers to its tail. When it leaps and stretches its legs out, this skin becomes like a big 'parachute' or kite that lets it glide through the air.
Many of the Philippines' forest mammals are endemic, meaning they are found only here and nowhere else in the world.
Geothermal energy provides about 10-15% of the Philippines' total electricity supply; this places the Philippines among the leading countries in using geothermal energy as a share of their power mix.

The Irrawaddy dolphin (Orcaella brevirostris) is a small dolphin species found in Malampaya Sound in Palawan — this is one of the very few places in the world where marine dolphins live in semi-enclosed coastal water, and the population is critically endangered.

The Philippines' rich biodiversity and varied landscapes are partly a result of its complex geological history: some islands are volcanic, others are made of limestone, and some have pieces of ancient ocean floor (ophiolite); the different rocks create different soils and habitats for living things.
The Philippine Eagle is one of the largest eagles in the world and is found only in the Philippines. It is our national bird and a great example of a unique animal here.

You might have asked, 'Where can I see these special animals?' Most of them live in forests, mountains, and protected areas. That is why it is important to protect these places so they do not disappear.
Even today, new kinds of animals and plants are still being discovered in the Philippines. This means we do not yet fully know everything living in our forests and seas.
Romblon province in the Philippines is famous for producing high-quality marble; Romblon marble is exported worldwide and used for sculptures, decorations, and building floors.

The Philippines has some manganese ore deposits; manganese is an important metal used in making steel alloys; manganese nodules are also found on the Philippine Trench seafloor but are not yet commercially mined.
The pilandok, or Philippine mouse-deer, is one of the smallest hoofed animals in the world and is found on Balabac Island in Palawan.
Ophiolite complexes in the Philippines, such as those in Zambales, are slices of ancient oceanic crust thrust up onto land by plate collision.
The Palawan pangolin is an endangered animal with unique scales that eats ants and termites; it is among the world's most trafficked animals due to illegal trade.
Many coral reefs in the Philippines have suffered bleaching because of the repeated warming of the oceans from global warming.
Saltmarshes are coastal ecosystems with special plants that can live in salty water — they serve as habitat for birds and small animals and protect coastlines from erosion.
Five sea turtle species are found in Philippine waters: the leatherback, green turtle, hawksbill, loggerhead, and olive ridley — all are endangered.
Much of Philippine lowland soil is ultisol or oxisol — heavily leached by years of tropical rain — red in color due to iron oxides, and may be low in nutrients for crops.
The Visayan spotted deer is found only in the Philippines, on the islands of Negros and Panay.
The edible nest swiftlet builds its nest from its own saliva in caves, and these nests are collected by people for use as food.
The tarsier cannot move its huge eyes in their sockets, so it turns its head almost all the way around to look about.
The Philippine tarsier is found in the forests of Bohol, Samar, Leyte, and Mindanao. It is endemic to the Philippines, meaning it naturally lives only here and nowhere else.
The Philippine tarsier has the largest eyes relative to body size of any mammal — each eye is even heavier than its brain.
Each tarsier eye is so big it is even larger than its brain! These are the largest eyes compared to body size of any mammal.
The tarsier has soft, slightly sticky pads at the tips of its fingers, so it can grip smooth branches firmly. Its long fingers also help it hold tightly onto trees.
The tarsier is nocturnal, meaning it is awake and hunts at night and sleeps during the day. That is why its eyes are so big, to help it see in the dark.
Inside the tarsier's big eyes are many special cells that soak up even a little light. This lets it see clearly in the dark forest at night.
Many people think the tarsier is a monkey, but it is not. It is a primate like monkeys and humans, but it belongs to its own group and looks very different from a real monkey.
The Philippine tarsier (Carlito syrichta) is one of the world's smallest primates, with a body only about 85 to 160 millimeters long.
The Philippine tarsier is a very small animal that belongs to the primates, like monkeys, and can fit in a person's palm.
Like a frog, the tarsier has big, bulging eyes that help it see at night. But they are not related—the tarsier is a primate while the frog is an amphibian.

Animals living in the Philippine Trench must withstand extreme water pressure — over 1,100 times the surface pressure; amphipod crustaceans and sea cucumbers are commonly found at these depths; their bodies have special adaptations to survive such extreme conditions.
The Philippine Trench is one of the deepest ocean trenches on Earth, reaching about 10,540 meters deep.
The Philippine Trench is deeper than Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on Earth, is tall.
The deepest point of the Philippine Trench is the Emden Deep.

The Philippine Trench (Mindanao Trench) is the fourth deepest place in the world's ocean; its deepest point, the Emden Deep, is about 10,540 metres deep — deeper than Mount Everest is tall; it lies east of Mindanao.
As the plate sinks at the Philippine Trench, it produces earthquakes that PHIVOLCS monitors.
The Philippines is surrounded by deep ocean trenches, like the Philippine Trench, where plates sink down.
You cannot just use a tape measure to find the depth of the trench. Scientists use sonar, sending sound down and timing how long the echo takes to bounce back.
The Philippine Trench lies along the eastern side of the Philippines, beneath the Pacific Ocean.

The Philippine Trench in the sea is part of a bigger system of plate movement in our region, along with the Philippine Fault on land. Together they are sources of many of the earthquakes in the country.

At the very bottom of the trench, there is so much water above that the pressure is enormous, about a thousand times stronger than the air around us. That is why only very strong submersibles can reach there.
When the plates at the Philippine Trench suddenly move and cause a strong undersea earthquake, it can push water upward and form a tsunami. That is why people near the coast must stay prepared.
At its northern end near Luzon, the Philippine Trench connects with another deep feature called the East Luzon Trough. Together they form a long line of deep water on the east of the country.

The Philippine Trench is on the east of the country, but there is another trench on the west called the Manila Trench, near the South China Sea. They are in different places and connect to different plates.

The Emden Deep of the Philippine Trench is the third deepest spot in the whole world. The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench and the Horizon Deep in the Tonga Trench are deeper, but all three are quite close.
The Philippine trogon is a colorful bird found only in the forests of the Philippines.
The trogon often sits quietly on a branch and suddenly darts out to catch an insect.

The great Indian Ocean tsunami of December 2004 (from a 9.1 magnitude earthquake off Sumatra) also reached some Philippine coastlines as smaller waves; although it caused little damage here, it showed that tsunamis from other countries can also reach the Philippines.
In the Philippines, the water monitor (bayawak) is a large lizard that is a close relative of the Komodo dragon.
The Philippines has several important wetlands including Agusan Marsh in Mindanao, Candaba swamp in Pampanga, and Liguasan Marsh in Maguindanao — all serving as habitat for many birds and animals.
The Philippines has native woodpeckers, such as the Philippine pygmy woodpecker, found in forests.
According to PHIVOLCS, the Philippines has about 24 active volcanoes that can erupt.
In Bangui, Ilocos Norte, large wind turbines stand along the shore and make electricity.

The Philippines is recognized by Conservation International as a global biodiversity hotspot because of its extraordinary number of endemic species — animals and plants found nowhere else on Earth — demonstrating the country's unique marine and terrestrial diversity.
The Philippines is part of the Coral Triangle, the place in the world with the most kinds of coral and sea fish.
Diwata-1, launched in 2016, was the first microsatellite built by Filipinos to take pictures of our country from space.
To reach enough heat, workers drill very deep wells, often a few kilometers down into the ground. That deep, it is hot enough to turn water into steam.
Kids ask why we do not feel the heat even while standing on the ground. It is because thick rock and soil sit between us and the hot part, so the heat does not reach the surface.
In Tongonan, Leyte there is a large geothermal field that gives electricity to many homes in the Visayas. It is a real example of how the Philippines uses the heat of the earth.
Some think geothermal scoops up lava itself, but that is not true. It uses the heat the ground passes into water, which becomes hot steam, not actual lava.

A geothermal plant has deep wells that bring up heat from the ground. Steam travels through pipes to the turbine and generator that make electricity. Afterward, the water is pumped back underground to be used again.
Geothermal is renewable because the Earth's heat does not run out, it is always there. It is also cleaner than coal because it releases much less smoke.
The Philippines is one of the world's largest producers of geothermal electricity because it has many volcanoes.
When water gets very hot it becomes steam that rushes out fast and strong. The force of this steam spins the turbine, which is why steam, not ordinary water, is used.
Solar power needs sunlight, so it stops at night or when it is cloudy. Geothermal works day and night because it is always hot underground.
The Philippines sits on the Ring of Fire, so we have many volcanoes. Hot magma is closer to the surface here, making it very hot underground. That is why we have enough heat for geothermal energy.
May is usually the hottest month in the Philippines.

Because the Philippines has thousands of islands, its total coastline is very long when you add up the edges of every island. That is why almost no Filipino lives very far from the sea. It is also why fishing, ports, and boats are so important to the lives of many families.

Along the eastern edge of the Philippines is a very deep crack in the sea floor called the Philippine Trench. There, one plate slowly slides beneath the other. This same motion drives the earthquakes and volcanoes that built the islands, which is why very deep sea and high land sit close together.

During the Ice Age the world was colder and much water was locked up as ice, so the sea level dropped. Because of this, some islands that are separate today were once joined by dry land called land bridges. Animals crossed over them, which is why some species are still alike on nearby islands.

Most typhoons form over the wide Pacific Ocean in the east and move toward the west. So the islands on the eastern side of the Philippines, like Samar and Bicol, are often hit first before a typhoon even reaches the inner parts of the country. They act like the first shield against incoming storms.

There are tiny sandbars that you can see only when the sea is low, and that get covered when the sea rises. They do not truly vanish, they just hide under the water at high tide. So some little islands seem to appear and disappear depending on the movement of the sea.

The making of the Philippine islands is not finished, it is still going on. Because the plates beneath us are still active, earthquakes are common and some volcanoes can still erupt. In the language of geology, the Philippines is a young land that is still being shaped today.
Most of the large islands of the Philippines have mountains in the middle, which is why it is called a mountainous country.
The Philippines gets many thunderstorms because its weather is hot and humid, especially during the rainy season.
The Philippines is the country hit by the most tropical cyclones in the world.
There are no icebergs or frozen sea in the Philippines because our seawater is warm all year and never gets cold enough to freeze.
Natural ice or snow is rare in the Philippines because it is tropical and the temperature seldom drops to 0 degrees Celsius — so the ice we usually see is made in a freezer.
In the Philippines cars do not need antifreeze in the radiator because the engine water never freezes — in cold countries it is needed so the water does not freeze and crack the engine in winter.
Roads in the Philippines never need salt or ice clearing because it is warm and roads do not freeze — unlike cold countries that spread salt so roads are not slippery.
Even when we feel cold during the amihan season, it is still far from freezing — 'cold' in the Philippines is often still about 20 degrees, far from the 0 degrees needed for ice.
Because there is no real snow in the Philippines, we make our own 'snow' from shaved ice (like in halo-halo) or from a machine in the mall, not from the sky.
In most of the Philippines, heavy winter coats are not needed because it is warm all year; we wear light clothes, except in cool places like Baguio where a jacket helps.
In high places like Baguio, water boils before it reaches 100 degrees Celsius because the air pressure is lower up there — so sometimes food takes longer to cook.

More than one plate affects the Philippines. It lies between the large Philippine Sea Plate on the east and the Sunda (part of the Eurasian) Plate on the west. Their squeezing is why there are so many earthquakes and volcanoes.

A great example of a Ring of Fire volcano is Mayon Volcano in Albay. It is famous for its nearly perfect cone shape and is one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines. The heat from subduction below keeps it alive.
In the Philippines, many products are sold in small sachets, which creates a lot of plastic waste.
The Philippines is a major player in the global tuna industry, and General Santos is called the 'tuna capital of the Philippines,' but overfishing threatens the sustainability of tuna stocks.
Of the roughly 20 typhoons a year, about 8 to 9 actually cross or make landfall in the Philippines.
The Philippines is one of the countries most affected by climate change because it is an island nation surrounded by sea and often hit by typhoons.

Phloem consists of living sieve tube elements and companion cells—unlike xylem which is dead cells; companion cells actively pump sugars into the sieve tubes for distribution throughout the plant.
Phloem carries sugars made by photosynthesis from the leaves to other parts of the plant such as roots and fruits.

When you turn on airplane mode, the phone stops sending and receiving wireless signals like cellular, wifi, and Bluetooth — which is why it is asked for on a plane so it will not interfere with the plane's equipment.
A mobile phone call travels as transverse radio waves through the air and space around you, then becomes sound only in the speaker.
Many everyday devices, like phones and flashlights, use rechargeable lithium batteries that can be charged again and again.
A phone has a tiny sensor inside that feels how you hold or tilt it, which is why the picture on the screen rotates when you turn the phone sideways.
A phone's buzzing case is a mechanical vibration; the alert you hear across the room is a longitudinal sound wave in air.
Phosphorus is a key plant nutrient needed for root growth and flowering; it is one of the three main nutrients in NPK fertilizer (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) applied to crops.
