A photo of the setup helps you put everything back the same way for trial two and trial three after you wash the cups.
Light is made of tiny packets of energy called photons — it can behave like a wave or like a particle depending on the experiment.
Photoperiodism is a plant's ability to sense day length; some plants (short-day plants like rice) flower only when nights are long, while others (long-day plants) flower when nights are short.
A photo of the materials and of the result can help you remember what you did when you write what you found out later.
Photosynthesis is a chemical reaction that takes in energy from sunlight to combine carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen.
In photosynthesis, a plant uses sunlight, carbon dioxide from the air, and water to make sugar for food and release oxygen.
Chemical changes also happen inside living things, like photosynthesis in plants and digesting food in our stomach.
To make food, a plant needs three things: sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide from the air.
The food made in photosynthesis is a sugar called glucose, which stores energy the plant uses to grow.
Up to a limit, photosynthesis goes faster when brighter light reaches the leaf.
Plants are not the only ones that photosynthesize; algae in the ocean do it too and produce much of the world's oxygen.
The oxygen that plants release during photosynthesis is what people and animals breathe to live.
Most of a tree's mass comes from carbon taken out of the air's carbon dioxide during photosynthesis, not from the soil.
The sugar made in photosynthesis gives the energy for rice and other crops we eat to flower and form their grains.
The roots absorb water from the soil, and it travels up to the leaves to be used in photosynthesis.
Almost all our food comes from photosynthesis — even meat, because animals eat plants.
A leaf has tiny veins that bring water in and carry away the sugar made during photosynthesis.

Scientists copy photosynthesis to make clean energy. An 'artificial leaf' is a device that uses sunlight to split water and make hydrogen fuel — much like how a leaf works, but as an energy source for people.

Because photosynthesis pulls carbon dioxide out of the air, trees and forests help cool the planet. Every time a tree grows in a Philippine forest, it removes carbon dioxide from the air and stores it as wood. That's why planting trees matters against climate change.

In simple words, photosynthesis is: carbon dioxide + water + sunlight → sugar (glucose) + oxygen. The left side is the ingredients (reactants) going in, the right side is the products made. No atoms disappear — they just rearrange.

Many people think a tree's weight comes from the soil, but it doesn't. Most of the plant's solid material comes from carbon dioxide in the air, captured by photosynthesis. So a tree's body is mostly 'built from air'!

Photosynthesis happens in two stages. First, in the light reactions, the plant captures light, makes energy molecules, and releases oxygen. Second, in the Calvin cycle, that energy is used to build sugar from carbon dioxide — even without direct light.
Photosynthesis mostly happens in a plant's leaves, inside tiny cell parts called chloroplasts.
In words, photosynthesis is: carbon dioxide + water, using light energy, become glucose + oxygen.
Phyllite is a metamorphic rock between slate and schist; it is metamorphosed at a higher grade than slate and has a silky or glistening surface due to tiny mica crystals.

A physical change (like cutting or cooling) can usually be reversed because the substance is the same, but a chemical change (like burning or rusting) cannot be reversed because a new substance has formed.
In a physical change, only the form, shape, or size of an object changes, but it is still the same substance.
Physical properties of a material can be observed or measured without changing the material — they include color, mass, density, hardness, and melting point.
While making food, phytoplankton absorb carbon dioxide from the air, which helps control the climate.
Most phytoplankton are so small that you cannot see them without a microscope.
Phytoplankton — the microscopic plants of the sea — produce roughly half of all the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere through photosynthesis.
Like land plants, phytoplankton make food and oxygen through photosynthesis using sunlight.
Pi Day is celebrated every March 14 (3/14) because pi is about 3.14.
Pi (π) is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, and it is always about 3.14.
The decimals of pi (3.14159...) never end and never repeat, so we use 3.14 only as a rounded value.
Drawings look different: a transverse wave is a side wiggle, while a longitudinal wave is drawn as crowded and spread-out patches along a line.
People often feed pigs leftover food from the kitchen.
Pigs make grunting sounds, like oink, to communicate with each other.
A mother pig can give birth to many piglets at once, often eight to twelve.
A pig is a mammal that has hair and feeds milk to its young.
The mud on a pig's skin protects it from the sun and from insects.
A pig uses its strong snout to dig in the soil and search for food.
A pig wallows in mud to cool itself when the weather is hot.
The pilandok (Tragulus nigricans) is an endemic mouse-deer found only on Balabac island and nearby islands south of Palawan.
The pilandok is endangered due to overhunting and forest loss on Balabac island.
In 1991, Mount Pinatubo erupted in one of the largest volcanic eruptions in the world in the past hundred years.
Mount Pinatubo erupted on June 15, 1991.
Mount Pinatubo erupted very powerfully in 1991 after lying quiet for hundreds of years, and it was one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the 20th century.

The 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo released large amounts of sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere — the aerosols formed reflected solar radiation and temporarily lowered global temperature by about 0.5°C.
Mount Pinatubo erupted in the year 1991.
Mount Pinatubo is found in Luzon, at the boundary of Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga.
The 1991 Pinatubo eruption was the second-largest volcanic eruption in the world during the 20th century.
The 1991 Pinatubo eruption was the second-largest volcanic eruption of the 20th century.
The 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption was the second-largest eruption of the entire 20th century.
The Pinatubo disaster grew worse because Typhoon Yunya also arrived, turning the ash into heavy mud that collapsed many roofs.

Mt. Pinatubo's June 1991 eruption was one of the largest of the 20th century (VEI 6); it injected so much ash into the stratosphere that global temperatures dropped by about 0.5°C for a few years; the successful evacuation of over 100,000 people before the eruption saved thousands of lives.
The pineapple grows on a low plant close to the ground, not on a tree.
A single pineapple is made of many small fruits from many flowers joined into one fruit.
The pineapple comes from South America and was brought to the Philippines by the Spanish long ago.
In Pinggang Pinoy, HALF of the plate should be filled with vegetables and fruit, because we need more of these than rice or the main dish.
Pinggang Pinoy is a guide for just ONE meal, so each meal in the morning, noon, and evening should have the right share from every group.
Pinukpok is cloth woven on a loom from plant fibers that are first beaten soft before weaving.
The fiber for piña cloth comes from the long leaves of the pineapple, not from the fruit.
The fibers are removed from the pineapple leaf by scraping it by hand until only the thin threads remain.

The Pioneer anomaly was an unexpected small acceleration toward the Sun observed in the Pioneer 10 and 11 spacecraft that prompted speculation about new physics; in 2012 it was explained as a result of anisotropic thermal radiation from the spacecraft — not new physics.
Pioneer 10 was the first probe to fly past the planet Jupiter.

The pistol shrimp has one oversized claw that snaps shut extremely fast — the snap creates a cavitation bubble that implodes and stuns small fish and shrimp nearby, sometimes briefly producing a flash of light.
A moving horn can also get louder as it comes near, but the Doppler change is about pitch, which is how high or low it sounds.
A smooth slide in pitch as something passes is a clue the source or the listener is moving, not that the object suddenly changed its engine.
Nepenthes or pitcher plants native to the Philippines are carnivorous—their pitcher-shaped leaves contain digestive fluid to trap and digest insects and small animals, obtaining nitrogen.
At the bottom of the pitcher is a liquid with enzymes that dissolves the trapped insect.
A few small creatures, like mosquito larvae, can live inside the pitcher's liquid without being digested.
It grows in soil that is poor in nutrients, so it gets nitrogen from insects instead.
Many Nepenthes are climbing vines, with their pitchers hanging from the leaf tips.
A pitfall trap is a cup buried level with the ground so that small crawling soil animals fall in and can be counted by scientists.
Bubonic plague is caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria spread by rat fleas; in the 14th century, it killed approximately half the population of Europe.
Write the steps and the data table before you mix anything, so you are not inventing a new method halfway through the trials.
A jet high above can change note as it crosses the sky, another moving source, though the boom of a shock wave is a different event.

In 2006 the IAU established three criteria for an object to be called a planet: (1) it must orbit the Sun, (2) it must have enough gravity to pull itself into a roughly round shape (hydrostatic equilibrium), and (3) it must have 'cleared' its orbit of other bodies. Pluto fails the third criterion.
Earth has one moon, but the giant planets have dozens — Jupiter and Saturn each have more than 90 known moons.
The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
The four outer planets are large gas and ice giants: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
Some planets like Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn can be seen in the sky as bright points of light, but they do not twinkle like stars because they are much closer to us.
According to Kepler's third law, planets closer to the Sun orbit faster; Mercury is the fastest (orbital period of 88 Earth days), while Neptune is the slowest (orbital period of 165 Earth years).
Four (4) planets have rings: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune — Saturn's are the brightest and easiest to see.
Plankton form the base of the ocean food web because small fish eat them, and larger animals eat those fish.
Phytoplankton are tiny plant-like organisms floating in the sea, and they are at the base of the ocean food web as the most basic food.
Plankton are very tiny living things that float and drift in the water, and many are too small to see without a microscope.
Many zooplankton make a daily vertical journey — rising to the surface at night to feed on phytoplankton, then descending to colder depths during the day to avoid visually-hunting predators.
Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts, which animal cells do not have.
Often, a bitter taste is a warning to animals that a plant may be poisonous or harmful.
Plants remove CO2 from the atmosphere through photosynthesis and store the carbon in their bodies; this is called carbon sequestration and forests serve as major carbon sinks.
Many plants produce bitter or toxic chemicals like tannins and alkaloids that deter insects and animals from eating them; this is called chemical defense.
Three common ways a plant defends itself are thorns, poison, and a bitter taste.
Inside the gall, the larva or young insect grows safely while feeding on the plant's tissue.
Galls can also be found in the Philippines on different plants such as mango and other trees.
The apical meristem is a zone of continuous cell division at the tip of every shoot and root; primary growth of the plant upward and downward originates here.
Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole full of water that helps keep the plant firm.
The roots are the plant part that absorbs water and nutrients from the soil and holds the plant in place.
Phototropism is a plant's response to light—the stem grows toward the light source to obtain more light for photosynthesis; this can easily be seen by placing a plant near a window.
Even plant roots can break rock—they grow into cracks and slowly widen them until the rock splits apart.

The roots of plants like mung beans and lima beans (legumes) have small lumps (nodules) where helpful bacteria live. The bacteria help the plant get nitrogen from the air, and this naturally enriches the soil for the next crop.

Besides water, roots also absorb minerals (nutrients) dissolved in the soil water. Plants need these to grow, make green leaves, and bear fruit — which is why farmers add fertilizer to give the soil more of these nutrients.

It is a common misconception that roots 'eat' the plant's food from the soil. Really, roots only absorb water and minerals; the plant's actual food (sugar) is made in the leaves using sunlight, by photosynthesis.
Rice has fibrous roots — many small spreading roots. This suits the flooded paddy fields where the soil is watery, because the many roots grip the soft mud and keep the stalk from falling over.
The tips of roots have very tiny hairs called root hairs. They greatly increase the surface that touches the soil, so the plant can soak up much more water and minerals, faster.

Water taken in by the roots rises through tiny tubes (xylem) inside the stem up to the leaves. As water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls more water up from the roots — like drinking through a straw.
Stems are very useful to people. From the hard stems of trees we make wood for houses and furniture, and even the paper we write on comes from tree stems.
On coastal sand dunes, succession starts with special plants able to grow in shifting sand, gradually stabilising the dune and allowing more plants to grow until a stable ecosystem forms.
Thorns, spines, and prickles on plants like roses and bougainvillea serve as physical defenses against herbivores that would eat the plant.
Many plants have sharp thorns or spines so that animals will not eat them.
When water evaporates from the leaves (transpiration), it pulls fresh water up from the roots, so water keeps moving through the plant.
Xylem vessels are formed from dead cells whose cell walls are thickened with lignin; the cell contents break down leaving hollow tubes that efficiently conduct water and minerals.
Farmers needed to know when rains or dry months were coming, and returning constellations were a calendar they could share without a printed book.
Planting trees helps because they take in carbon dioxide from the air.
In photosynthesis, a plant combines water and carbon dioxide to make sugar (glucose), which is its food and energy.
To grow, a plant needs sunlight, water, air, and soil with nutrients.
Besides photosynthesis, plants also respire: they use oxygen day and night to release energy from their food.
Plants use sunlight and store it as chemical energy in the food they make.
A flat iron heats up using electricity, and its heat energy presses out the wrinkles in cloth when you slide it over the fabric.
The sticky plaque on teeth is not leftover food but millions of living bacteria — so brushing is really wiping these germs away before they make acid.
After eating sugar, the bacteria in plaque release acid. This acid slowly damages the tooth and makes a hole, or cavity.
Brushing scrubs the sticky plaque off your teeth. It is important to brush twice a day so it does not build up.
There are special tablets that color the plaque so you can see where it is hiding. The spots with plaque turn red or pink.
If plaque stays on the gums too long, they swell and bleed easily when you brush. This is the first sign of gum trouble.
Some think rinsing with water is enough to remove plaque. But because it is sticky and clings on, you really need to scrub it with a brush, not just rinse.
In some Philippine towns, plastic bags are banned to cut down on plastic waste.
The first fully synthetic plastic, Bakelite, was made by Leo Baekeland.
Leo Baekeland made Bakelite, the first synthetic plastic, in 1907.
A clear plastic bottle is transparent, so you can see the water or contents inside it.
Plastic bottle caps are often made of polypropylene (code 5), a different plastic type from the bottle body (PET, code 1); they usually need to be separated for proper recycling.
When plastic is burned, it gives off toxic smoke that is bad for the air and our lungs.
A coastal cleanup is picking up plastic from the shore so it does not reach the sea and harm animals.
When plastic trash clogs drains and canals, flooding becomes much worse.
Many sea animals get tangled in old nets and plastic, so they cannot move or swim freely.
A lot of plastic floats on the surface of the sea because it is lighter than water.
Sea turtles and fish sometimes eat plastic because they think it is food, and this harms them.
Plastic is a fairly recent invention, becoming widely used only in the 1900s.
A plastic wrapper is made by people from processed materials; it is not a natural earth material the way a stone or a clay lump is.
Plastic is a polymer, meaning it is made of very long chains of small repeating molecules.
Instead of rotting, plastic breaks into very tiny pieces called microplastics.
Tiny units called monomers join together in a process called polymerization to form plastic.
Most plastics do not biodegrade in nature for hundreds of years, so they remain in landfills and oceans for an extremely long time.
Plastic thrown on land is often washed by rain into rivers and finally reaches the sea.
Single-use plastic like straws and bags is used only once before being thrown away, so it quickly becomes trash.
When buried in a landfill, plastic breaks down even more slowly because there is no sunlight and little oxygen underground. So plastic thrown away today may still be there when today's kids are old.
Some kinds of plastic can take hundreds of years to fully break down.
Many think plastic truly vanishes when it crumbles. That is not true — it just becomes very tiny pieces called microplastics, which are still found in water, soil, and even inside fish.
Some think we should just burn plastic to make it go away. But that is wrong — burning plastic releases toxic smoke that is bad for the lungs and the air. Burning is not a safe way.

The styrofoam used for food and drinks is also a kind of plastic. It is very light but takes a very long time to break down — it crumbles easily into tiny pieces but never truly disappears from nature.
Thermoplastics like polyethylene can be melted and reshaped, while thermoset plastics like epoxy cannot be melted again once they have hardened.
There are different types of plastic, and many have a small number inside a triangle that tells how to recycle it.
Plastic and wood are poor conductors, so pot handles are made of them to keep your hand from burning.
Most strong earthquakes happen at plate boundaries where the plates grind or collide.
Earth's outer shell is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates, and along the boundaries where they grind or collide, earthquakes and volcanoes often occur.
Over very long periods, plate motion changes the shape of Earth's oceans, mountains, and continents.
The movement of Earth's tectonic plates buries, pushes, and heats rocks, keeping them moving through the rock cycle.
Where two plates collide, one can slide beneath the other in a process called subduction.
Where two plates pull apart, rising magma cools and forms new crust, often on the ocean floor.
At some boundaries, plates slide past each other in opposite directions, which can cause earthquakes.
Platinum is another precious metal that is even rarer than gold, and it is used in expensive jewelry and some machines.
The platypus uses its bill to sense the faint electricity given off by moving prey underwater.
There are no wild platypuses in the Philippines because they are naturally found only in Australia.
What is in the venom? It is not a single substance but a mix of many kinds of toxins that together cause pain.
Can platypus venom be useful to people? Scientists study it because it may contain substances that could help make new medicines.
Is platypus venom deadly to humans? No. It is extremely painful but it does not usually kill a person.
Does the platypus venom come from its bill? No, it does not bite to inject venom; the venom is in the sharp spur on the back of its leg.
Are venomous mammals common? No; they are very rare, so the platypus is special because only a few mammals can produce venom.
How does the spur work? It is sharp and has a channel through which venom flows from a gland into the body of an enemy.
Does the echidna also have venom? The echidna, a relative of the platypus, also has a leg spur, but it does not release venom.
Playing outdoors in the early morning or late afternoon, and using shade at noon, is a safety measure against the strongest sunlight.
Games like patintero and tumbang preso are a fun way to exercise.

Despite being a distant and cold dwarf planet, Pluto has a thin atmosphere mainly of nitrogen; the New Horizons spacecraft discovered beautiful haze layers in Pluto's atmosphere extending more than 200 kilometres above the surface.
In 2006, Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet, so it is no longer counted among the eight (8) main planets.
Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet, not a full planet anymore.
In the year 2006, Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet.
The International Astronomical Union (IAU), the worldwide group of astronomers, reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006.
John Boyd Dunlop invented the first practical air-filled (pneumatic) tire.
John Boyd Dunlop made the practical air-filled tire in 1888.
Pneumatic tools like air drills and air impact wrenches use compressed air to create power. Compressed air is also used to inflate vehicle tyres.
Pneumonia can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or sometimes fungi that get into the lungs.
In pneumonia, the air sacs fill with fluid or pus, so oxygen cannot pass into the blood properly.
Washing hands often with soap helps prevent the germs that cause pneumonia.
Lung infections are more dangerous for young children because their lungs are smaller and their disease defenses are not yet fully developed.
Pneumonia is a lung infection in which the alveoli fill with fluid, making it difficult for the body to get enough oxygen.
Children with severe pneumonia may need extra oxygen in the hospital to breathe properly.
Pointing your arm at a door sends information with movement: the other person can follow the line of your arm without a spoken sentence.
The polar bear's white fur matches the snow and ice, so its prey cannot easily notice it as it sneaks closer to hunt.
Polaris is in the constellation Ursa Minor, which is also called the Little Dipper.
Polaris, the 'North Star,' is a star that seems to stay still in the sky because it lies almost above Earth's north pole; travelers use it to find the direction north.
Transverse waves can be polarized, which is why polarizing sunglasses cut glare, while a longitudinal sound wave does not polarize that way.
Earth's two poles stay cold because sunlight strikes them at a slant and spreads thin over a wide area, so the warmth is weak — and the white ice reflects much of that light back away too.
When pollen lands on the stigma, a pollen tube grows down through the style to the ovary; it carries the sperm cell to the ovule where fertilization occurs.
Durian is pollinated by fruit bats at night—durian flowers open at night and emit a strong smell that attracts bats, which transfer pollen while feeding on nectar.
Bees and other pollinating insects are essential for food production — many crops like mangoes and melons need insects to form their fruit.
Many pollinators such as bees find flowers by their bright colors.
Pollution, such as plastic and chemicals in the water, harms animals and can put them in danger.
Marie and Pierre Curie discovered polonium in 1898.
Marie Curie named the element polonium after her home country, Poland.
Polyester is a synthetic fiber made from petroleum; it resists wrinkles and dries quickly, making it popular for clothing and sportswear, but it is not as cool to wear as cotton.

Polymers are very large molecules made of many repeating units (monomers) linked together; they include natural polymers like cellulose, rubber, and protein, as well as synthetic ones like plastics and nylon.
Each pomelo segment has its own thin skin or membrane. We peel this off to eat just the tasty flesh, because the membrane is a bit chewy and slightly bitter.
Don't just throw away the thick pomelo rind. In some places, people turn it into candied sweets by cooking it in sugar.
Pomelo does not ripen quickly. After flowering, it takes several months for the fruit to grow big and ripen before it can be harvested and eaten.
A pomelo has a very thick, spongy rind. This thick skin protects the soft juicy parts inside so the fruit doesn't get bruised or damaged easily.
The Pompeii worm is one of the most heat-tolerant animals, living right beside the scalding water that gushes from vents on the deep sea floor.
In a pond, all the plants and animals depend on one another to survive, so balance is important.
Fish such as tilapia eat tiny plants and insects in the pond.
Water plants release oxygen that dissolves in the water, so fish can breathe.
When there is garbage and pollution in the water, the fish and plants in the pond can die.
When there is too much algae in a pond, the oxygen in the water gets used up and fish can die.
Algae are tiny living things in pond water that are green because they contain chlorophyll, so they make their own food from sunlight.
Bacteria are some of the smallest micro-organisms in pond water, and they help break down dead plants and animals.
Most single-celled organisms in pond water reproduce by splitting in two (binary fission): one cell grows, copies its insides, then divides into two identical organisms.

Water keeps seeping into a paramecium because the pond water outside is more watery than its insides. To keep from bursting, it has a special part called a contractile vacuole that acts like a pump, squeezing extra water back out.
Diatoms are tiny algae in pond water with hard, glass-like shells that show beautiful, symmetrical patterns under a microscope.
A single drop of pond water can contain thousands of micro-organisms living in it, so there is a huge amount of life in a tiny space.
A euglena has a red spot called an eyespot that helps it sense where light is. It swims toward the sun using a long tail (flagellum) so it can make food through photosynthesis.
When an amoeba or paramecium eats, it wraps the food inside a tiny bubble in its body called a food vacuole. There the food is digested so the organism can get energy.
The tiny micro-organisms in a pond are food for larger creatures like small fish, so they form the base of the water food chain.
Pond micro-organisms are truly alive—they are not just dirt or dust—because they eat, move, and reproduce like other living things.
Not everything in pond water has the same job. Algae and euglena are producers — they make their own food from sunlight. Amoeba and paramecium are consumers — they eat other, smaller organisms.
The rotifer is a tiny pond animal with a wheel-like ring of hairs (cilia) on its head that spins to sweep food into its mouth.
A population is all the organisms of one kind in a place, while a community is all the different populations living together there.
A population grows quickly until it reaches the limit the environment can support, where its growth slows and levels off.
Porcelain is a high-quality ceramic made from white kaolin clay; it is finer, whiter, and slightly translucent compared to ordinary earthenware.
When pork barbecue is grilled over charcoal, the heat cooks the raw meat to make it safe to eat and gives it a browned color and aroma from its changing ingredients.

Porphyritic texture is when a rock has both large and small crystals; it shows that the magma cooled in two stages: slowly underground forming large crystals, then quickly at the surface forming small ones.
The modern postage stamp was introduced by Sir Rowland Hill of Britain.
A potato is a kind of underground stem called a tuber, and its "eyes" are buds that can sprout into new plants.
Electric power is P = V x I, where power (P) equals voltage (V) times current (I).
In a power plant, other forms of energy such as heat from burning fuel or the motion of flowing water are changed into electrical energy.
Power is the rate at which work is done — it equals work divided by time, measured in watts (one watt = one joule per second).
Power is measured in watts, where one watt is one joule of energy used each second.
Power is measured in watts (W), and one watt equals one joule of energy used or produced each second.
Practice the timing step once with empty cups if the group is new, then do the real investigation with the listed materials.
The black-footed ferret is one of the rarest animals in the world, and it eats almost only prairie dogs. If prairie dogs disappear, the ferret can barely survive.
A prairie dog town is divided into smaller family groups that each have their own section of burrows.
Like other rodents, a prairie dog's front teeth never stop growing. That is why they must keep gnawing on tough grass and roots to wear the teeth down so they don't get too long.
Many animals rely on prairie dogs for food—like eagles, foxes, snakes, and especially the black-footed ferret. This makes prairie dogs very important to the grassland.
Prairie dog burrows are also used as shelter by other animals such as owls, snakes, and other small creatures.
The mounds of dirt around the holes act like raised doorways to the burrow. They help keep rainwater from flowing in and also give the prairie dog a high spot to stand and watch for danger.
Prairie dogs rarely drink water. Instead, they get most of the water they need from the fresh grass and plants they eat.
Though we have no prairie dogs, the Philippines has its own burrowing animals, like field rats. Like prairie dogs, they dig tunnels and hide underground to stay safe from danger.
The praying mantis is the only insect that can rotate its head 180 degrees—giving it a very wide field of view to scan for prey without moving its body.
The Precambrian was the longest span, covering almost 4 billion years from when Earth formed.
The Precambrian covers most of Earth's history, and during it most life consisted of tiny organisms without hard parts, so fossils from this time are rare.
A precipitate is a new solid that suddenly forms when two clear liquids are mixed, showing that a chemical reaction has taken place.
Predators that hunt at night, like owls and tarsiers, tend to have larger eyes. Bigger eyes let in more light, so they can see more clearly in the dark.
Many predators like eagles and cats have forward-facing eyes to judge the distance to their prey.
When light hits a cat's or dog's eyes at night, they seem to glow. There is a mirror-like layer behind their eyes that bounces light back so they can see better in the dark while hunting.
There is a trade-off: forward eyes give sharp depth but a narrow view, so a predator has a blind area behind it. Side eyes on prey give a wide view but less depth.
The Philippine eagle is a predator with forward-facing eyes, so it can accurately judge how far a monkey or snake is while flying over the forest before it strikes.
Some predator snakes do not rely on eyes alone. They have tiny pits near the eyes that sense the body heat of prey — so they can hunt warm animals like mice even in the dark.
Many keystone species are predators that stop their prey from multiplying too much, keeping the ecosystem in balance.
Predator and prey populations often move in cycles — when prey increases so does the predator; as prey decreases, so does the predator.
Examples of predator and prey are a cat that hunts a mouse, and a snake that eats a frog.
If air resistance is small, you can predict that a heavy stone and a light stone dropped together will hit the ground at about the same time.
You may guess what will happen, but the investigation still has to test the guess with materials and steps, not with arguing.
Saying eclipses follow a pattern is not the same as naming the exact clock time; investigate how people talked about 'soon' versus a numbered date.
Write your prediction before you drop anything, then compare the landing with that sentence, or the test cannot change anyone's mind.
Say 'I predict they land together because air will not matter much' or the opposite, so the explanation is inside the prediction, not added later.
The prefix "kilo" means 1,000 (one thousand), so 1 kilogram equals 1,000 grams.
The prefix "pico" means one trillionth (1/1,000,000,000,000).
The prefix "tera" means 1,000,000,000,000 (one trillion).
Many microbes, especially molds, need air to grow. So when the air is removed by sealing tightly (vacuum-sealing), the food spoils more slowly.
If a can is bulging or swollen, it means microbes grew inside and made gas. The food is no longer safe to eat. So some preserved foods give warning signs when they have gone bad.

Long before fridges existed, preserving let people store food and send it to faraway places. So even with no electricity there is lasting food like dried fish and canned goods you can bring on a trip.
In the Philippines we have many foods dried in the sun like daing, tuyo, and dried mangoes. The sun's heat removes the water so they do not spoil easily even without a fridge.
When a leaf is placed between papers and pressed flat, it dries out as the water inside escapes, preserving it for a long time to study.

Blood pressure is the pressure that blood exerts on the walls of blood vessels. The heart pumps blood at higher pressure (systolic) and rests at lower pressure (diastolic). Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mmHg.
Water pressure increases with depth — for every 10 metres deeper in the sea, the pressure increases by about one atmosphere.
Pressure is how strongly a force pushes on each small bit of a surface; it is the force divided by the area it pushes on.
The narrow heel of a high-heeled shoe presses on the floor much harder than a flat sole because all the person's weight lands on a very small area.
If a diver ascends too quickly, nitrogen dissolved in the blood at high pressure can form bubbles in the body — this is called decompression sickness or 'the bends' and is very painful and dangerous.

Suction cups used for phone holders in vehicles work because of air pressure. When you press the suction cup onto glass, air is squeezed out and atmospheric pressure outside holds the suction cup in place.
Tractors and big trucks have wide tires to spread their heavy weight over a large area, so they sink less into soft ground.
Pressure is measured in a unit called the pascal (Pa), which equals one newton of force on each square meter of area.

Airplane cabins maintain pressure equivalent to being at about 1,800-2,400 metres altitude even though the plane flies at about 10,000 metres. Without pressurisation, passengers could not breathe adequately in the thin air.
Some prey like deer run fast to escape from a predator that is chasing them.
The three primary colors of paint are red, yellow, and blue.
The three primary colors of light are red, green, and blue.
Before Gutenberg, the Chinese were the first to print using carved blocks.
When white light passes through a prism, it splits into different colors because each color bends by a different amount.
When white light passes through a prism, it splits into the colors of the rainbow because each color bends a different amount.
Turn the problem into a question you can test, not a story, so the next steps have a real job to do.
Ask 'which dries faster' or 'what happens if', not a huge why that no classroom test can answer in one afternoon.

Write the problem in words a classmate can read once, because a tangled sentence makes the later steps harder to follow.
Pick a problem you can test with school materials in one lesson, not a question that needs a giant laboratory.
