Leave the problem written at the top of the page while you work, so the doing steps do not wander into a different question.
Put fair-test words in the problem when you can, such as 'same amount of water', so the later steps stay honest.
At the same angle, a projectile travels a greater range when its launch speed is faster.
A projectile's path is a parabola — a symmetric curve that rises then falls — because of its steady forward motion combined with gravity's downward pull.
In a projectile's path with no air resistance, the time going up equals the time coming down, and its speed when it lands equals its launch speed.
In projectile motion the horizontal (forward) and vertical (downward) motions are independent of each other, so the forward speed stays the same while gravity changes only the vertical motion.
A projector uses a lens to enlarge an image and cast it onto a distant screen or wall.
Some organisms have no nucleus in their cells like bacteria, while others like animals do.
Prokaryotes such as bacteria lack a true nucleus; their DNA floats freely inside the cell. Eukaryotes such as amoeba, plants, and animals have DNA enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus.
Many farmers prefer cuttings or grafting over seeds because the plant grows faster and the fruit is sure to be the same quality.
To avoid back injury when lifting heavy objects, bend the knees (not the back) and keep the object close to the body; this distributes the weight to the leg muscles instead of the spine.
The prostate wraps around the tube that carries urine out of the bladder, which is why diagrams show it there.
The prostate is a small gland that sits just below the bladder in the male reproductive system.
One job of the prostate is to make a fluid that mixes with sperm and helps the sperm travel.
Prostate fluid is not sperm, but it joins with sperm so the sperm cells can move more easily.
In labeled diagrams, the prostate is often drawn as a small gland about the size of a walnut under the bladder.
Cave formations are fragile and take ages to regrow, so we should not touch or break them.
We can protect our hearing by keeping the volume low and staying away from long, loud noise.
People create protected areas like sanctuaries and parks so that endangered animals have a safe place to live.
Protein from fish, eggs, chicken, and beans builds and repairs body parts such as muscles.
The body needs protein every day because its old cells are constantly being replaced.
Proteins denature — permanently change shape — when exposed to heat, acid, or alcohol. This is what happens when an egg is cooked or when fish is 'cooked' in acidic kinilaw.
Although mainly for building, protein can also be used as backup energy when carbohydrates and fats run low.
Protein comes from fish, eggs, meat, chicken, and beans common in Filipino meals.
Stentor is a very large single-celled protist shaped like a trumpet; it uses waves of cilia to sweep bacteria and algae into its mouth groove for food.
Trypanosoma brucei is a protist that causes African sleeping sickness; it spreads through the bite of the tsetse fly and attacks the brain.
A proton has a positive (+) charge.
Ernest Rutherford is credited with discovering the proton in 1919.
The number of protons in the nucleus determines how many electrons a neutral atom has and how they are arranged, which is why each element has its own properties.
As the solar nebula collapsed it spun faster and flattened into a disk, which is why the planets today orbit in nearly the same flat plane and the same direction.
Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away from the Sun.
The nearest star beyond our Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away.
The Puerto Princesa Underground River in Palawan is a famous river inside a limestone cave in the Philippines.
After the danger passes, the pufferfish lets the water out and shrinks back to its normal size.
Even if a pufferfish is dried or salted, it still does not become safe because its poison stays behind.
If someone eats a pufferfish, they must be taken to a hospital right away because they need fast help from a doctor.
No one should try to clean or cook a pufferfish at home, because the poison is hard to remove unless you are specially trained.
The eggs and inner organs of a female pufferfish are among its most poisonous parts, making them especially dangerous to eat.
Pufferfish eat small hard-shelled animals like clams and crabs.

The Japanese pufferfish (Torquigener albomaculosus) — a relative of the Philippine butete — creates ornate geometric circle designs in the sand on the seafloor using its fins, used to attract females.
Pufferfish live in the ocean, and some kinds also live in rivers and fresh water.
There are many kinds of pufferfish in the world, and some live in fresh water.
A pufferfish gets its poison from bacteria in the food it eats.
Trained chefs carefully remove the poisonous parts of the pufferfish, like the liver and intestines, before serving it. It takes many years of training to do this safely.
A pufferfish is a slow swimmer, so it relies on puffing up to protect itself.
The pufferfish is a slow swimmer, so it relies on puffing up and poison to protect itself.
If a pufferfish is caught out of the water, it sometimes gulps air instead — but this is hard for it to release and can be dangerous for the fish.
When a pufferfish puffs up, the organs inside get pushed to the sides to make room for all the water filling its stomach.
A pufferfish has a very stretchy stomach that can fill with a lot of water.
To puff up, a pufferfish quickly gulps a lot of water into its stomach.
The pufferfish (butete) contains tetrodotoxin — a potent nerve poison in its skin and organs — that can kill predators; it gulps water to inflate its body making it hard to swallow.
The water of Pulangbato Falls comes from the slopes of Mount Talinis, a volcano, which is why the area has sulfur and hot springs.
An elevator uses a pulley and a counterweight so the motor needs less force to raise the cab because the counterweight pulls the other side down.
The groove around the pulley wheel holds the rope so it does not slip off.
The mechanical advantage of a compound pulley system equals the number of rope sections supporting the load — more sections means less force needed to lift.
A well with a pulley lets you pull the rope down on one side to lift the bucket of water on the other.
You can feel your pulse at your wrist or at your neck.
When you feel your pulse at your wrist, you feel each beat of your heart.
A pumpboat is a motorized outrigger boat that floats because it is lighter than water, and its engine pushes it forward to move.
A Punnett square is a grid used to predict the possible traits of offspring.
Inside the pupa, the insect's body is almost completely rebuilt before the adult form comes out.
Pure gold is too soft for jewelry, so 18-karat gold is an alloy mixed with copper or silver to make it harder and more durable.
Pure water is neutral (pH 7) because only a tiny amount of H+ and OH- forms in it and the two are present in equal amounts, so they cancel out.
Pure water with no dissolved minerals is actually a poor conductor of electricity.
When a purebred dominant parent is crossed with a purebred recessive one, all the offspring show the dominant trait.
Pus is made of dead white blood cells and germs that were killed during the fight against an infection.
The purple color of puto bumbong comes from pirurutong, a naturally dark-violet variety of rice whose grain skin carries the color on its own.
Puto is a rice cake made from rice batter that is steamed until it rises and softens, making the inside light and fluffy.
Puto is cooked by the steam of boiling water, so it cooks without being soaked in water or fried in oil.

A pyroclastic flow is an extremely fast and deadly mixture of hot gas, ash, and rock fragments that races down a volcanic slope at speeds up to 700 km/h and temperatures up to 700°C; it is one of the most dangerous volcanic hazards.
Pythagoras lived in ancient Greece about 2,500 years ago (around 500 BC).
The Pythagorean theorem states that in a right triangle, a² + b² = c², where c is the longest side (the hypotenuse).
A python waits quietly and hidden, then strikes suddenly to grab prey that comes close.
A python's teeth curve backward, so once it grabs prey the prey cannot easily pull free.
With each breath the prey takes, the python tightens its grip until the prey's blood flow and breathing stop.
A python is cold-blooded, so it basks in the sun to warm its body before moving or hunting.
A python's skin and body can stretch, so even a large animal can pass through after being swallowed.
A python does not chase prey at high speed; it moves slowly and instead waits hidden until prey comes within striking range.
While a python slowly swallows large prey over a long time, it does not choke because it can push a breathing tube out the side of its mouth to keep breathing.
A python does not crush the bones of its prey; it mainly cuts off blood flow and breathing so the prey dies quickly.
A python is not just harmful; it is an important part of nature because it helps keep the number of rats and other small animals in balance in an ecosystem.
As a python grows, it sheds its old skin and grows a new one.
A python flicks its tongue to catch scents in the air and track its prey.
A QR code is a pattern of black and white squares that stores information, and when you point a camera at it, the phone reads the pattern and takes you to a website or message.
An orbital is a region around an atom where electrons are most likely to be found, and it is more like a cloud than a circular path.
Quarantine separates people who may have been exposed to a disease to prevent further spread, while isolation is for people who are already confirmed sick.
In a typical quartz watch, the crystal vibrates 32,768 times every second.
Quartz rates 7 on the Mohs scale, hard enough to scratch glass.
Quartz has a hardness of 7 on the Mohs scale, so it can scratch glass.
Quartzite forms when sandstone is subjected to high heat and pressure, fusing quartz grains together; it is very hard and resists erosion much longer than most other rocks.
A queen honeybee can live for several years, while worker bees live only a few weeks.
When counting bubbles or drips, agree on a quiet count so two people are not adding extra events that only one of them heard.
A volcano with no eruption this year can still be active; the last hundred years show long rests between some of the biggest events.
Eduardo Quisumbing wrote the famous book "Medicinal Plants of the Philippines" in 1951.
Eduardo Quisumbing is called the "Father of Philippine Orchidology" for his study of orchids.
R0 (basic reproduction number) shows how many people one infected person typically infects; measles has an R0 of 12–18 while influenza has an R0 of about 1–2.
Republic Act 9147, the Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act, prohibits capturing, selling, or killing protected animals and plants in the Philippines.
A rabbit is pregnant for about 31 days, or roughly one month.
A rabbit uses its back teeth to grind grass, which also wears those teeth down.
A rabbit can live about 8 to 12 years.
Children are at higher risk of rabies because they often play near dogs.
In the Philippines, dogs are the main source of rabies in people.
Many of the people who die of rabies worldwide are children, so it is important to teach children to be careful around dogs.
One symptom of rabies in people is a strong fear of water because swallowing becomes difficult.
It can take weeks or months before rabies symptoms appear, so do not wait to get treatment.
In the Philippines, Animal Bite Treatment Centers provide free anti-rabies services, and a law requires dogs to be vaccinated.
Not only bites — scratches or an animal licking an open wound can also spread rabies.
An animal with rabies may become aggressive, act strangely, or drool a lot.
Louis Pasteur made the vaccine against rabies in 1885.
The rabies virus slowly travels from the bite to the brain along the body's nerves.
From the wound, the rabies virus travels along the nerves until it reaches the brain.
The Sun's heat reaches Earth by radiation — electromagnetic waves, mainly infrared, that need no medium and can cross the vacuum of space.
In radiation, heat travels as invisible waves, which is why the sun's warmth reaches us even though there is no air between us and the sun.
The warmth we feel from the sun or from a campfire reaches us by radiation. It can warm our skin even though we are not touching the source.
The three main types of radiation are alpha, beta, and gamma.
Guglielmo Marconi is credited with inventing the first radio, the wireless telegraph, in 1895.
Some telescopes use a large dish-shaped antenna to collect radio waves from space instead of light, letting us study objects the eye cannot see.
A radio wave is a transverse electromagnetic wave that can carry a station's signal through space without needing air as a medium.

In the late 1880s, Heinrich Hertz was the first to produce and prove that radio waves are real in his laboratory, years before they were used for communication. To honor him, the unit of frequency 'hertz' was named after him.
Not all radio waves are made by people — stars, galaxies, and even the Sun naturally give off radio waves. Astronomers use giant radio telescopes to 'listen' to them and learn about distant space.
Some radio waves bounce back to the ground off the ionosphere, a layer of the atmosphere full of charged particles. This is why an AM radio signal can reach very distant places, especially at night.
To put sound onto a radio wave, the wave is changed a little: in AM the strength (amplitude) is varied, while in FM the frequency is varied. This is why radios have AM and FM stations.
Radar sends out a radio wave and waits for it to bounce back off an object like an airplane or cloud. From how fast the wave returns, it can tell how far away and how fast the object is moving.

Each radio station uses its own frequency, so they do not overlap. When you turn the dial or press tune, you are simply choosing which frequency your radio catches — which is why you hear one station clearly.
Radio waves are the band used to send radio and television broadcasts.

A microwave is like a younger sibling of the radio wave: both are electromagnetic, but the microwave has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency. That is why microwaves are used for GPS, satellites, and ovens, while radio waves handle broadcasting and simple signals.
Guglielmo Marconi demonstrated his wireless radio around 1895, in the late 1890s.

In beta decay, a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton, and it shoots out a fast-moving electron called a 'beta particle.' Because there is now one more proton, the atom also becomes a new element.

In hospitals, radiation from decay is used to treat cancer. Strong gamma rays (for example from cobalt-60) can target and kill cancer cells. Doctors carefully measure it to hit the disease while protecting the healthy parts of the body.

Scientists use radioactive decay to find the age of old things. Carbon-14 in once-living things (bones, wood) slowly decays, so by measuring how little is left, they can tell how many thousands of years old a fossil or artifact is.

When an atom decays, it does not just vanish — it becomes a different atom called the 'daughter product.' Sometimes the new atom is still unstable, so it decays again and again until it finally becomes a stable atom.

One element can have different versions called 'isotopes' — same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Some isotopes are stable (do not decay), and others are unstable (radioactive). For example, carbon-12 is stable but carbon-14 decays.

Where does radioactivity come from? There is natural radiation all around us — in soil, in rocks, even in air and food. This is called 'background radiation' and it is very low, so it is safe for us. This means radioactivity is not only made by people.

It is a misconception that radioactivity is a contagious disease that spreads from person to person like a germ. In truth, it is energy and particles coming from inside atoms. A person can be exposed to radiation, but they do not become a 'germ' that spreads it.
It cannot be predicted exactly when one nucleus will decay, but a large group of identical atoms decays at a predictable rate, which lets scientists estimate the age of rocks and fossils.

You cannot predict exactly when one particular atom will decay — it happens spontaneously and seems 'random.' Nothing from outside triggers or pushes it; the nucleus changes by itself when it is ready. (But with very many atoms, the average rate can be studied.)

Why do some atoms decay? When the number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus is not balanced, the nucleus is 'unstable.' To become more stable, it releases energy or a particle — this is radioactive decay.

What is the difference between radioactive decay and an ordinary chemical reaction (like burning)? In a chemical reaction, only the electrons on the outside of atoms change, and the element stays the same. In radioactive decay, the nucleus itself changes, so the atom truly becomes a new element — and far more energy is released.
Some isotopes are radioactive, meaning their nucleus is unstable and breaks down on its own while giving off tiny particles or radiation.
Radioactivity was discovered in the year 1896.
Radium is a radioactive element that naturally glows in the dark.
The elements radium and polonium were discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898.
The chemical symbol for the element radium is Ra.
The Rafflesia bud is wrapped in brown scale-like covers called bracts, which protect the delicate petals inside while it grows.
After it blooms and fruits, the tiny Rafflesia seeds are carried by animals like rats or ants to other vines, where a new bud may grow someday.
A Rafflesia bud can take more than a year to develop before it finally opens.
The Rafflesia is called the "corpse flower" because it smells like rotting flesh to attract flies.
The Rafflesia smells like rotting meat; this foul smell attracts flies, which help carry its pollen to other flowers.
The Rafflesia has the largest individual flower in the whole world.
Before it blooms, a Rafflesia bud slowly grows for many months, looking like a brown cabbage. The wait is long, but the flower opens quite suddenly once it is ready.
Rafflesia smells like rotting meat. This is not a flaw; the stink attracts carrion flies, and those flies carry pollen from one flower to another so the plant can reproduce.
Because it has no green parts, the Rafflesia does not make its own food through photosynthesis.
Most plants are green because they make their own food from sunlight, but the Rafflesia is not green and does not make its own food — it depends fully on the vine it lives inside.

In some places, Rafflesia buds have been used in traditional remedies, for example by women after childbirth. But because the plant is now rare, picking it carelessly could push it toward disappearing.

Some plants like mistletoe are only part-parasites, because they still have green leaves that make some of their own food. Rafflesia is a full parasite, with nothing green, so it depends completely on its host.
Inside the Rafflesia flower is a plate-like disk with bumps or spikes, and it can be slightly warm. This warmth and shape help attract and guide the flies toward the pollen so they can carry it away.

Long ago, the ancestor of Rafflesia had leaves and made its own food. Because it came to rely on stealing food from a vine, it slowly lost the need for leaves and chlorophyll, which is why it looks so strange today.
The Rafflesia is a parasitic plant that takes water and nutrients from a host vine.
Compared to a sunflower that is only about the size of a plate, a Rafflesia flower can be even bigger than a car tire — and instead of smelling sweet, it actually stinks!
The reddish color and slight warmth the Rafflesia gives off help attract flies, because to a fly it looks and smells like a dead animal where it could lay its eggs.
Some soils, particularly those containing limestone, can neutralize mild acid rain and protect plants and groundwater from damage.
Rain falls when tiny water droplets in a cloud join together until they become heavy enough to fall to the ground.
Frontal rain occurs when cold and warm air masses meet; the cold air pushes the warm air upward, causing steady rainfall.
Rain is the earth material water falling from clouds, a non-living part of the environment that can fill a drum or a river.
Rain getting louder is not the Doppler pitch slide; Doppler is a high-to-low change tied to motion of the source or the listener.
The wind signal is mainly about wind speed, though heavy rain and floods may happen at the same time and need their own PAGASA warnings.
Orographic rain occurs when moist air is forced to rise over mountains, cool, and drop rain; the Sierra Madre range of Luzon provides this effect for eastern Luzon.
Rain that soaks down into the soil refills the water hidden underground.
The global average annual rainfall is about 990 mm; places near the equator, like the Philippines, typically receive more rain than higher-latitude locations.
Like other trees in the bean family, the rain tree helps enrich the soil around it.
Rainwater carries minerals down from the top layer into the subsoil.
A rainbow forms when sunlight refracts into a raindrop, reflects inside it, and refracts out again — splitting white light into its colours.
In a rainbow, each raindrop acts like a tiny prism that splits sunlight into colors.
A tiny raindrop can fall more slowly than a compact hailstone because air matters more for the drop's small weight and open shape.
Besides storm signals, PAGASA also issues color-coded rainfall warnings: yellow (be aware), orange (be ready), and red (evacuate), showing how heavy the rain is and the flood danger.
Many tall rainforest trees have wide buttress roots that prop them up in the thin soil.
A tropical rainforest canopy stays green nearly all year because it is warm and rainy throughout, so the leaves do not all fall at once.
Most of a rainforest's animals and plants live in the canopy because that is where sunlight, leaves, and fruit gather.
The emergent layer is the few very tall trees that rise above the canopy and meet strong wind and full sun.
The emergent layer is made of a few very tall trees that rise above the canopy, where they catch strong sunlight and wind; large eagles often perch and nest here.
An epiphyte is a plant that grows on the branches of other trees in the canopy to be closer to light, but it is not a parasite.
The forest floor is the darkest layer, so few plants can grow there.
The soil on the rainforest floor is thin and poor because plants quickly take up nutrients from the decaying leaves.
A tropical rainforest has four layers: the emergent top, the canopy, the understory, and the forest floor.
Each forest layer is like a different home, so different animals live at each level and do not compete for the same food.
Large rainforests are sometimes called the 'lungs of the Earth' because their many plants release oxygen and absorb carbon dioxide, helping keep the air clean and the climate balanced.
In a rainforest, dead leaves and animals rot very fast in the heat and moisture, and roots quickly soak the nutrients back up — so the rich soil stays thin and nutrients are recycled rapidly.
In Philippine rainforests, the tarsier lives in the understory while the Philippine eagle hunts from the canopy.
Many understory plants have broad leaves to catch the little light that slips through.
Rainwater is slightly acidic from dissolved carbon dioxide, so it slowly eats away limestone.
Rainwater is nearly clean because it comes from evaporated sea and river water that left salt and dirt behind, like natural distillation.
Inside the rambutan is a white, juicy flesh that surrounds a single seed.
A ramp lowers the force needed to raise a load, but you must push it over a longer distance.
The Ramsar Convention is an international agreement that protects important wetlands worldwide — some Philippine wetlands are listed as Ramsar sites because of their importance to migratory birds.
Some falcons can dive downward extremely fast through the air to suddenly grab their prey on the ground or in the sky.
Birds of prey like the Brahminy kite have very sharp eyesight to spot prey from far away and high up.
A longitudinal rarefaction is a spread-out region of the medium, not a missing crest; mixing those labels is a common mix-up of the two types.
A rat's front teeth keep growing all its life, so it gnaws on things to keep them worn down.
These big birds cannot fly because their breastbone is flat and lacks the strong muscles needed for wings.
Rattan is good for furniture because its stem is strong yet can be bent without breaking, so it is easy to shape into different forms.
Rattan grows faster than large timber trees, so with good management it can be harvested again and again as a renewable resource.
Rattan (uway or yantok) is a kind of palm that climbs up other trees in the forest, so it looks like a vine rather than an ordinary upright tree.
Rattan, or yantok, is a climbing palm that scrambles up other trees using sharp thorns, and its strong stems are used to make furniture and baskets.
Rattan stems are split into thin strips that workers weave by hand to make baskets, mats, and furniture.
Rattan is part of the forest ecosystem: its fruit and leaves feed some animals, and the tangled plants give shelter to small creatures.
The spotted eagle ray is a large ray with white spots that swims through the sea by flapping its broad, wing-like fins like a bird.
In a chemical reaction energy is not lost but only changes form, from the stored energy of bonds into heat or light, or the other way around.
Most chemical reactions go faster when it is hot, because the particles move and collide more quickly. That is why sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in cold.
Among the alkali metals, elements become more reactive going down the group, so potassium reacts more violently with water than sodium does.
Read the label every time you take a medicine, not just the first time.
Always read which city or province has the signal, because describing the weather for the wrong place is not following the PAGASA bulletin.
Read the full 'what we need to do' list aloud once before starting, so quiet group members hear the plan too.
If you use sunscreen, put it on again after swimming or heavy sweat, because wet skin can lose that protection from the Sun's light.
In this lesson the receiver is whoever hears the sound, such as you on the sidewalk, not only a microphone on a stand.
The receptacle is the enlarged tip of the flower stalk to which the sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils are attached.
Rechargeable batteries can be refilled because electricity from a charger reverses the chemical reaction inside.
Record numbers while you do the steps, not after you pack up, because memory mixes trials once the table is clean.
Scientists write down each trial as they go, because a result you only remember later is easy to mix up or round wrongly.
Write or record the exact words you are allowed to keep, so a later reader can tell a community story from your own summary.
You can record a passing horn on a phone, then compare the note before and after it passes to hear the drop more clearly.
Dissolved salt can be recovered by evaporating the water until only the salt crystals are left, like in salt beds.
Corals recover slowly because they grow slowly, so a reef can take many years to come back after severe bleaching.

Materials are easy to recycle if they can be melted and reshaped (like glass and metal) or mashed back into fibers (like paper); things made of many different materials mixed together are hard to recycle.
Before recycling, waste is sorted by type—paper, plastic, metal, and glass—so each kind can more easily be made into new things.
The 5Rs—Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover, and Refuse—are ways to cut down waste and protect the environment.
Steel is the most recycled material in the world; old steel from cars and buildings is melted down and reused, saving energy and reducing the need to mine iron ore.
Recycling aluminum saves up to 95% of the energy needed to produce new aluminum from bauxite ore, making it one of the most energy-efficient materials to recycle.
Materials are easier to recycle when they are clean, so it is good to rinse bottles and cans before putting them in the recycling bin.
Recycling means collecting and sorting old bottles, plastic, and paper so they can be made into new products, which reduces the waste that piles up in the environment.
Old glass, like bottles, is crushed and melted at very high heat, then shaped again into new bottles or jars.
Different types of plastic melt at different temperatures and do not blend well together. So plastics must be sorted by type before recycling, because even one wrong piece can ruin a whole batch.

The small shampoo or coffee sachets common in the Philippines are made of thin layers of material stuck together. These layers are very hard to separate, so the sachets are almost never recycled and usually end up as trash.

Styrofoam is mostly air and very thin plastic, which makes it extremely light and cheap. Because of this, almost no plant recycles it — it is not worth the cost for the tiny amount of plastic recovered.
One old plastic bottle can be melted and become part of a new bottle or even cloth fiber — so each bottle that is recycled is one bottle that doesn't have to be made from new plastic.
Glass can be melted and made into new bottles over and over without losing quality — so recycling glass is a big help in reducing waste and saving sand.
When we recycle old metal, there is less need to dig new rock out of mines — so recycling reduces the mining that damages land and mountains.

It's a mistake to think every plastic can be recycled — some thin bags and dirty plastics are hard or impossible to recycle, so it's better to use less and rinse containers before putting them in recycling.
In the Philippines, junk shops or "bote-dyaryo" buy old bottles, cans, and newspapers to send to recycling factories — so less waste ends up on streets and in rivers.
In the Philippines, a law tells people to separate trash into biodegradable and non-biodegradable so that materials that can still be used are easier to recycle.

The color in red cabbage comes from a natural pigment called anthocyanin. This is the substance that changes color when mixed with acids or bases, so it is the real reason behind the whole effect you see.
Some think any vegetable can be an indicator, but no. Green or white cabbage barely works because it lacks anthocyanin; the strong purple color of red cabbage is what is needed.

It is a misconception that you can drink red cabbage juice after mixing test substances into it. Once soap, cleaner, or other chemicals are added, it is no longer safe to drink even though it came from an edible vegetable.

An interesting example: the same kind of pigment is why some flowers like hydrangea change color depending on soil pH. Acidic soil gives blue flowers, basic soil gives pink—the same principle as red cabbage.
Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.
Human red blood cells have no nucleus, leaving them more room to carry oxygen.
Red blood cells live for about 120 days, so the body constantly replaces them with new ones.
Scientists measure how threatened a species is and place it in levels such as 'vulnerable', 'endangered', and 'critically endangered' on what is called the Red List.
Red light scatters much less, so it passes more straight through the air to reach us.
Even during red tide, fish are usually still safe to eat if they are fresh, washed well, and gutted — what is banned are mussels, oysters, and other filter-feeding shellfish.
One reason red tide happens is when fertilizer from farms and waste from cities flow into the sea, because they give extra nutrients that the plankton eat to multiply.
Reducing red tide can be helped by not dumping waste and sewage into rivers and the sea, because less nutrients from waste means less food for the plankton to multiply.
If someone eats red-tide shellfish and feels numbness in the lips, tongue, or hands, they should be taken to a hospital right away, because that is the first sign of paralytic shellfish poisoning.
The red tide toxin starts in tiny plankton, but when shellfish eat them and then a fish or person eats the shellfish, the toxin is passed and builds up higher along the food chain.
Red tide in the sea is different from the green scum seen in ponds and ditches: both are lots of tiny water plants, but most green pond scum is not toxic, while red tide can make a poison.
Because the light from almost all distant galaxies has longer wavelengths (it is redshifted), astronomers believe that the whole universe is expanding.
According to BFAR, fish, squid, and shrimp caught in red tide areas are usually still safe to eat if fresh, washed, and gutted, but shellfish are not.

Even when an oyster or mussel is full of poison, it stays alive and is not harmed. A shellfish's body is different from ours, it is not much affected by saxitoxin. But when a person eats it, our nerves are the ones affected. So a mussel can look fine yet still be dangerous to humans.

There is no direct medicine or antidote that kills the red tide poison. In the hospital, doctors only help the patient breathe and stay alive while the body slowly clears the toxin. This is why prevention matters so much: it is easier to avoid eating it than to treat the poisoning.

Shellfish like oysters, mussels, and clams are the most dangerous during red tide because they strain seawater to feed, so the poison collects inside them. Other sea creatures that do not filter water, like most fish, do not store much toxin in their flesh.

Many think red tide comes only from garbage or pollution. It is true that extra nutrients from runoff can help, but the poison itself is naturally made by plankton, even in clean seas, when the warmth and water conditions are right. So a red tide can happen even where the sea is not dirty.
Cooking does not destroy the red tide toxin, so affected shellfish are unsafe to eat even when fully cooked.

The red tide poison in the Philippines is made by a very tiny kind of plankton called Pyrodinium. It is too small to see with the eye; it is a little organism that drifts in the sea. When it multiplies too much, the poison it makes builds up in shellfish.

When food spoils, it is because bacteria multiply and it starts to smell bad. Red tide is different: the shellfish is still fresh and does not smell rotten, yet it already holds poison from plankton. So its freshness will not save you, the problem is the toxin, not rotting.
A reef grows upward as new coral builds on top of the skeletons of dead coral over many generations.
Reef fish use the coral as a home and a place to hide from danger.
Fish have a lateral line — a row of specialized cells along their side — that detects pressure waves in water, helping them avoid obstacles and follow a school.

Not all reef fish are awake at the same time. Some are active in the day and hide at night to sleep. When night comes, other fish that slept all day come out. They take turns, so there is always something moving on the reef.

The lionfish is a reef fish with long spines that carry venom. It does not use them to hunt but to defend itself from predators. Because of this, other fish leave it alone. People should not touch it either, since its sting is painful and venomous.
Many reef fish swim together in large schools because many bodies moving in unison confuse predators and make it hard to single out one fish to chase.

Many reef fish swim together in a big group called a school. This is not just for looks but for safety. When hundreds of fish move as one, a predator gets confused about which one to chase, making them harder to catch.

Not every brightly colored reef fish is colorful just to look pretty. In some, the vivid color is a warning that says 'I am bad to eat' because they are poisonous or have spines. Predators learn to avoid these colors, so the color works as a defense.
Coral needs clear water because mud and pollution block sunlight and can kill the coral.
Although surrounded by nutrient-poor (oligotrophic) water, coral reefs support extremely rich life because nutrients cycle efficiently among corals, zooxanthellae, and other organisms.
One example of a reef shark is the blacktip reef shark, known for the black tips on its fins. It is often seen in shallow water near the reef.
The blacktip reef shark and whitetip reef shark are two of the most commonly seen sharks on Philippine coral reefs — blacktips are more active by day while whitetips are more nocturnal.
A reef shark has tiny pores on its snout that can feel the weak electricity made by other animals' bodies. This lets it find fish hiding in the sand even when it cannot see them.
Many reef sharks live in the reefs of the Philippines, such as Tubbataha Reefs in Palawan. This area is protected so the fish and sharks there are not lost.

A coral reef hosts hundreds of types of species interactions in one place — including predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism — resulting in one of the most complex ecological webs in the living world.
When a straight wave hits a barrier in the tank, it bounces and travels back, a reflection you can see as a second set of lines.
A mirror reflects, or bounces back, the light that hits it, which is why you can see your image.
Reflected crests can meet incoming crests and make a busy crisscross near a wall, so look carefully before you name a single travel direction.
Sunlight bouncing from pavement or water can still reach you under a small visor, so standing in real shade is a stronger safety measure.
Reflection is light bouncing back off a surface such as a mirror.
A reflex arc is the fast, automatic path a signal takes from a sensor to the spinal cord and back to a muscle, which is why we pull away instantly before even thinking when we touch something hot.
In a reflex, the signal travels through the spinal cord instead of going to the brain first, which makes the action very fast.
When dust or a bug flies toward your eye, it shuts on its own right away. Blinking is a reflex that guards your eyes.
Sneezing is a reflex too. When something tickly or irritating like dust gets inside your nose, a sudden burst of air pushes it back out.
When there is a sudden loud noise like a firecracker, you flinch or freeze on your own. This startle reflex is your body's way of getting ready for possible danger.
When food or water touches the back of your throat, certain parts close on their own and push the food downward. Swallowing is a reflex, so you do not have to think about it.
When you trip, your arms shoot out automatically to catch yourself—this is a balance reflex.
You usually cannot stop a reflex because it happens without your choosing or controlling it.
When something reaches too far back in your throat, you automatically gag — this is the gag reflex. It protects you so that your airway does not get blocked or you do not choke.
When a doctor taps just below your knee with a little hammer, your leg kicks out on its own. Doctors do this to check that your nerves and spinal cord are working well.

A reflex has five parts: the receptor that senses, the sensory neuron carrying the signal in, the spinal cord that processes it, the motor neuron carrying the order out, and the muscle that acts. They connect like a relay.
When there is a sudden loud sound like a firecracker, you jump or jerk on your own. This is the startle reflex — your body is ready to respond at once to a possible danger.

When you step on something sharp, that foot lifts up on its own while your other leg stiffens to support you. The spinal cord sends different orders to each leg at the same time — all without you thinking.
Coughing is a reflex that pushes irritating things out of your airway.
A reflex is a very fast, automatic action, like pulling your hand away from something hot.
When you touch something hot, your hand jerks back even before you feel the pain.
When you suddenly slip, your body automatically reacts and throws out your arms to keep from falling, before you even think about it.
When a doctor taps just below the knee with a small mallet, the lower leg kicks out on its own—this is the knee-jerk reflex.
When the spot below your knee is gently tapped, your lower leg kicks out on its own—this is the knee-jerk reflex.
In a reflex, a sensory neuron carries the signal in and a motor neuron carries the command out to the muscle.
Most reflexes are inborn—we are born already able to do them and do not have to learn them.

Surprisingly, you sometimes shiver even with a fever when your body is hot. It does not mean you are really cold — the brain simply raised the 'target' temperature to fight germs, so you briefly feel cold.
When you shiver, your small muscles quickly tighten and relax over and over. This movement does no useful work — instead the energy it uses turns into heat that warms your body.

Shivering and goosebumps are different reflexes even though both happen when it is cold. Shivering is muscle movement that makes heat; goosebumps is the hair standing up to try to trap heat near the skin.
When you wear thick clothes or wrap in a blanket, your body does not need to shiver. The clothing keeps heat from escaping, so you stay warm without spending energy on shivering.

It is a misconception that the body warms because parts 'rub together' when shivering. In truth, the heat comes from the muscles themselves working as they tighten and relax, not from skin or bones rubbing.
A sneeze is a reflex, which means it happens automatically without you thinking about it. That is why it is hard to stop once it starts, like blinking your eyes.
For example, when you sweep or clean a dusty room, you breathe in tiny dust particles. They tickle the inside of your nose, and you often sneeze several times in a row.
Kids often ask why their eyes close when they sneeze. The eyes shut automatically as part of the same reflex; you cannot stop it, but it is not harmful either.
It is not good to hold in a sneeze by pinching your nose and shutting your mouth. The trapped force can push into your ears and hurt them, so it is better to let it out while covering it.
When someone has a cold or flu, the tiny droplets that come out in their sneeze carry the virus. That is why covering a sneeze helps keep other people from catching the sickness.

Before you sneeze, you take a deep breath to fill your lungs with air. Then your chest and belly muscles squeeze tight and suddenly blast the air out very fast to drive away whatever is irritating you.
Sneezing and coughing are sibling reflexes, but they come from different places. A sneeze clears irritants from the NOSE, while a cough clears the THROAT and the airways going to your lungs.
In many reflexes the spinal cord gives the command to move, so the signal does not have to travel to the brain first.
The gag reflex pushes food back out when it goes down the wrong way, so you do not choke.
Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one material into another, such as from air into water.
When you look at objects through thick glass or water, they appear shifted slightly to the side because refraction bends the light before it reaches your eye.
Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one material into another, such as from air into water.

There is a famous experiment where a coin is hidden behind the rim of a cup so you cannot see it. When you pour water into the cup, the coin suddenly appears because the light bends in the water and reaches your eye.
Light bends more when the material it enters is denser or more packed. For example, light bends more strongly in glass or diamond than in water, and more in water than in air.
Eyeglasses use refraction to help us see clearly. The lens bends the light before it enters the eye, so it focuses correctly and objects look sharp.

Refraction and reflection are different. In reflection, light bounces back off a surface like a mirror. In refraction, light passes through into another material and bends there, instead of bouncing back.
Not all light bends in water. If light enters the water's surface perfectly straight on or perpendicular, it passes through without bending. Light only bends when it enters at a slant or angle.
The bending of a straw or pencil shows up more when it is slanted in the water; when it points straight down, you can barely notice the refraction.
Each color of light bends by a different amount, so a prism — a triangular piece of glass — uses refraction to split white light into the seven rainbow colors.
Light slows down when it enters a denser material like water or glass — this change in speed is what causes it to bend.
Refraction and reflection are different: in refraction, light bends as it passes through something like water; in reflection, light bounces back like off a mirror.
Refrigerator walls are filled with foam insulation — preventing heat from outside from entering and keeping the interior cold without the compressor working too hard.
A refrigerator uses a liquid called refrigerant; when it evaporates it soaks up heat from inside, so the food stays cold.
Jacob Perkins built the first working refrigerator using vapor compression in 1834.
Cold from the refrigerator slows bacteria from growing, so food lasts longer.
It is better to eat slowly and chew your food well. This helps digestion and prevents stomachaches even when you eat regular meals.
We feel hungry when we wake up because no food came in for about eight or more hours while we slept. That is why breakfast matters, to refill the energy lost overnight.
A healthy Filipino regular meal example is rice, fish or chicken, vegetables like kangkong, and fruit. Different foods give your body different nutrients.
Regular nutritious meals are different from eating junk food. Junk food often lacks real nutrients, so you feel hungry again quickly even after eating it.
Besides regular meals, drinking enough water is also important. Water helps digest food and carry nutrients throughout your body.
In relative dating, in an undisturbed column of rock the oldest layers are at the bottom and the youngest are at the top (the law of superposition).
Cultures could rely on constellations because Earth's spin and orbit are steady, so the sky's direction and season cues repeat instead of shuffling at random.
A source is more reliable when another person could find it again, such as a named book, a museum label, or a recorded interview with a date.
The milkfish used in rellenong bangus is popularly known as the national fish of the Philippines, raised in fishponds and known for its many tiny bones.
Sometimes a remora will stick to boats or even to scuba divers when no big animal is around to ride.

Sharks aren't the only ride for a remora's disc. It also attaches to whales, sea turtles, manta rays, and sometimes even the hull of a boat or a diver's body! Almost any large, smooth surface works for the disc to grip.

You'll often see a remora stuck to the UNDERSIDE or belly of a shark, even upside down. Why doesn't it fall off? Because the disc's suction is stronger than the pull of gravity — as long as the seal holds, it stays gripped even inverted while the host swims fast.

Thanks to the disc, the remora stays right against its host's body — and sometimes it even helps! Some remoras eat tiny parasites off the shark's skin or mouth, so they act like cleaners in exchange for the free ride. It can become a give-and-take partnership.

A newborn remora doesn't have a full suction disc yet — it starts as an ordinary-looking fin. As the fish grows, the dorsal fin gradually shifts forward onto the head and becomes the complete disc. So very young remoras can't grip as firmly as adults.

How does a remora let go once stuck? It simply slides forward a little, and that motion lets water back under the disc, breaking the suction. It doesn't have to struggle — the remora controls exactly when to grip and when to release.

The remora's disc is oval and divided into two rows of thin plates called lamellae. Each lamella carries tiny tooth-like spinules that help it hold on — so up close it looks like a slatted suction pad.
The remora's disc has slat-like ridges that give a strong grip even on the host's smooth skin.

The remora's disc is one of the strongest suction grips in nature. It can keep the fish attached even when the shark swims very fast or a strong current pulls at it. That small disc can hold against a force many times the remora's own body weight.

How does a remora stick? It presses its flat disc against the shark's skin, then raises the ridges to push water out from inside — this lowers the pressure there (like a vacuum), so the higher-pressure water outside holds the remora firmly against the shark.

Both a remora's disc and an octopus's sucker create suction, but they work differently. The octopus sucker is soft and uses muscle to grip; the remora's disc is a stiff plate with movable ridges. Different animals, same solution for sticking.

The remora (Echeneidae) has a specialized suction disk on its head modified from the first dorsal fin — it uses this to attach to sharks, whales, and manta rays and feed on host food scraps and parasites.
A remora fish clings to a shark with a special sucking disc on its head; it benefits by riding the shark to get food scraps, while the shark is unaffected.
By riding on the shark, the remora saves energy because it does not have to swim far on its own.
The remora fish sticks to a shark's body to hitch a ride and eat leftover scraps, while the shark is not harmed.
Take off clothing or jewelry near a burn before the area swells.
Instead of wiping out all insects with pesticide, farmers use 'biological control': they bring in the natural enemy of a pest, like ladybugs that eat aphids. This uses the food web to help, not harm.

Many ask: can the ecosystem heal again? Sometimes yes, especially if caught early and the missing species is brought back or protected. But if it has been gone too long, it is hard to restore to how it was. Prevention is easier than repair.

Some 'indicator species' like frogs are the first to disappear when the environment has a problem. Scientists use them as a warning: when they vanish, it signals something is already wrong with the water or air, even before people can see it.

It is a misconception that nothing happens when one species is removed. Often the effect is slow: things may seem fine at first, then after some time the balance suddenly collapses. The damage is not always instantly visible.
If you remove a predator like a snake or owl, nothing eats the rats, so they multiply too much. Then the rats eat up the crops. So removing one animal can cause another to overpopulate.
A good example: sea otters eat sea urchins. When otters disappear, urchins multiply and eat all the kelp (giant seaweed that shelters fish). So just one animal protects a whole kelp forest.

In the Philippines, the tiny tarsier eats many insects, including crop pests. If tarsiers vanish from the forest, insects multiply and other plants and animals are affected. So protecting one animal saves many.
Solar and wind energy are not always available — battery storage systems store excess energy from sunny or windy periods to use at night or during calm weather, helping the grid stay stable.
Biogas is a renewable energy made by digesting livestock waste (such as pig or carabao dung) in a sealed tank — the methane gas produced can be used for cooking and lighting on Philippine farms.
A community solar project allows multiple families to benefit from solar power even without their own rooftop — they share the cost and earnings of a single shared solar installation.
The Philippines is one of the world's top producers of geothermal electricity — underground heat from the country's many volcanoes contributes a significant share of the national electricity supply.
After steam is used to drive turbines, geothermal plants inject the water back into the underground reservoir — this maintains pressure and ensures the resource is not quickly depleted.
Philippine hydroelectric plant output varies by season — during the rainy season, heavy rainfall raises water levels and increases output; during the dry season, less rainfall reduces hydro output.

The Agus River hydropower plants in Mindanao, which harness the power of Maria Cristina Falls, supply a large share of Mindanao's electricity — it is one of the country's most important hydroelectric systems.
The BacMan Geothermal Field, spanning Bacon, Albay and Manito, Sorsogon, is one of the Philippines' key geothermal fields, supplying renewable electricity from the volcanic heat of the Bicol region.
Rice hull — the outer shell removed from grain during milling — can be burned to produce heat and electricity in biomass plants in the Philippines' rice-farming areas.
The Philippine Department of Energy has set a target for renewable energy to make up at least 35% of the country's total electricity capacity — including solar, wind, geothermal, and hydro.
Electric tricycles (e-trikes) in the Philippines use an electric motor and battery instead of a gasoline engine — they produce no exhaust, reducing air pollution in cities and towns.
The Philippines imports much of the coal and oil used for electricity — developing renewable energy such as solar, wind, and geothermal helps reduce its dependence on imported fuel.

Geothermal plants in the Philippines provide jobs in rural communities — from geologists and engineers to maintenance workers and plant operators, the industry brings income to areas near geothermal fields.
Geothermal plants use steam from underground water heated by geothermal heat — they do not use lava directly. Wells are drilled where Earth's heat is close enough to the surface.
Magat Dam in Isabela is a multi-purpose dam — it generates hydroelectric power for Luzon, provides irrigation water for rice fields in the Cagayan Valley, and helps control flooding.
The Philippines has one of the highest solar irradiance levels in the world — because it lies near the equator, the sun shines at nearly ideal angles for solar panels for most of the year.
Under the Philippines' net metering program, homes with rooftop solar panels can sell excess electricity back to the grid — the meter runs backwards when selling, reducing the electricity bill.

The Philippines' WESM (Wholesale Electricity Spot Market) is a marketplace where electricity producers and distributors buy and sell power at real-time prices — prices change based on supply and demand.
The Philippines has large potential for wind energy — especially in Ilocos Norte, the northern tip of Luzon, and parts of Mindanao, where winds are strong and reliable.
In the Philippines (latitude 5°–21° N), solar panels should face south and be tilted at an angle equal to the local latitude to capture maximum sunlight throughout the year.

Laboratory solar cells have achieved over 40% efficiency using multi-junction cell designs — more than double the 15–22% efficiency of typical commercial panels. This research gives hope for cheaper and more effective solar energy in the future.
Most household solar panels convert about 15–22% of sunlight energy into electricity — the remaining energy becomes heat that is lost to the environment.
A tidal barrage is a large structure built across a bay or estuary — the height difference between high and low tide drives turbines and generators to produce predictable electricity.
A wind turbine has a 'cut-in speed' — the minimum wind speed (usually 3–4 metres per second) needed for it to start generating electricity. Below this speed the blades may spin but produce no power.
Renewable energy is cleaner because it does not release smoke or pollution while making electricity, unlike burning coal or oil.

Except for solar panels, most renewable energy makes electricity the same way: something spins a turbine that turns a generator. This spinning makes the electricity, whether driven by wind, water, or steam.

Renewable energy is energy from natural sources that do not run out and are quickly replenished, such as the sun, wind, and water. Unlike coal or oil, it does not get used up no matter how often we use it.
Renewable energy is energy that does not run out because it is naturally replaced, such as sunlight, wind, and water.
Unlike a power plant that must buy coal or oil every day, the sun and wind are free and keep arriving on their own, so solar and wind power buy no fuel once they are built.
Renewable energy does not run out because nature keeps replenishing it: the sun shines every day, the wind keeps blowing, and water keeps flowing.
Renewable energy never runs out, but it is not always available—there is no solar at night and no wind when the air is calm, so batteries or other storage are needed.
Sun, wind, and water are renewable because they do not run out, while coal and gas run out and dirty the air.
A surprising result is a reason to repeat the trial, not a reason to stop and tell a story that has only one measurement behind it.
Repeating the whole fair test on another day is a strong check, because it shows the result was not just one classroom afternoon.
Replication means doing the whole test again the same way, not just looking once and deciding the first look was enough.
A long quiet period does not mean a volcano is finished; the next unrest often begins with quakes and extra gas before any ash.
In fragmentation, an organism breaks into pieces and each piece can grow into a new complete organism, like some starfish that can regrow from a single arm.
Ferns and fungi reproduce through spores that are released into the air and grow into new organisms when they land in suitable conditions.
Asexual reproduction is faster and needs no partner, but sexual reproduction creates genetic variation that helps organisms adapt to changing environments.
A reptile is a vertebrate with dry skin covered in scales and is cold-blooded. Examples: snake, lizard, and turtle.
Because reptiles are cold-blooded, when the weather turns very cold their bodies slow down and they become sluggish; they eat little and hide until it warms up again.
Most reptiles, like snakes and crocodiles, lay their eggs on land or in sand.
When it gets too hot, reptiles move into the shade to cool their bodies down.
A life vest or life jacket helps a person float in water, so it should be worn when riding a boat.
Resistance is how much a material opposes the flow of electric current, and it is measured in units called ohms.
Resonance occurs when a driving force matches the natural frequency of a structure — the Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed in 1940 because wind set it oscillating at its own natural frequency.
Every object has a natural frequency at which it vibrates most easily — when struck by sound matching that frequency, the vibration grows dramatically, called resonance.
The hollow body of a guitar acts as a resonator — the vibrating string causes air inside the guitar body to vibrate, amplifying the sound.
The glucose that cells use for respiration comes from digesting carbohydrates in food like rice and bread — the small intestine absorbs glucose and sends it into the blood.
Respiration in our bodies is exothermic because it releases heat from food.
Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are reverse reactions — photosynthesis takes in CO2 and gives out O2, while cellular respiration takes in O2 and gives out CO2, creating a natural balance.
After a long time around loud sound, it is good to give your ears a quiet rest to help them recover.
Looking away from a bright screen to rest the eyes is a small protection from tiring light, even though it is not as dangerous as the Sun.
While a child has measles or chickenpox, they need rest, plenty of water, and family care until they get better.
If one object is compact and one is fluffy, they may not land together, and the honest explanation is air, not a failure of gravity.
When an alert level later drops, families may go home, but they keep watching because some volcanoes grow restless again within the same decade.
Some newer rockets can be reused because part of the rocket flies back and lands gently after launch.
In some reversible reactions, the forward and reverse reactions can happen at the same time at equal rates, so the amounts of substances stay balanced.
The coconut rhinoceros beetle is a pest in the Philippines because it bores into coconut trees and damages the plants.
A rhizome is a stem that grows sideways under the soil, so the plant slowly spreads outward.
When the ginger's leaves die back in the dry season, the rhizome stays alive in the soil and sprouts again when the rains come.
Rhyolite is the extrusive equivalent of granite; it is rich in silica and very viscous, which is why it can produce extremely powerful volcanic explosions.
Ribosomes are very tiny cell parts that make the proteins the body needs.
In Philippine rice fields, azolla, a tiny water fern, is used as a natural source of nitrogen for the rice.
Rice blast, caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, is the most damaging rice disease worldwide—it creates white lesions on leaves and panicles that reduce yield.
A rice cooker uses a thermostat — when water reaches 100°C and boils away, the thermostat switches from cook mode to warm mode so the rice does not burn.
In the Philippines, some foods are fortified with iron, such as iron-fortified rice, to help fight anemia.
A rice grain consists of the husk (ipa)—the outermost layer; bran—the next layer rich in nutrients; endosperm—the white starchy interior; and the germ—the seed embryo.
As the grains ripen, they fill out and the panicle turns golden, bending over from the weight.
The harvested grain with its husk is called palay; once the husk is removed it becomes bigas (milled rice); and once cooked it is kanin.
If rice is harvested too early many grains are unripe and empty, but if harvested too late the ripe grains fall off and are wasted on the ground.
Farmers traditionally use a small curved blade called a sickle (karit) to cut the rice stalks by hand, bundle by bundle.
In the Philippines rice can be harvested twice a year, once in the rainy season and once in the dry season where there is enough irrigation.
To remove the light husks and chaff from the heavier grains, the rice is tossed in the wind or in front of a fan so the light bits blow away.
A rice grain has an outer husk and a thin bran layer beneath it covering the white grain.
Before grains form, rice must first flower and the pollen must pass within its flowers; from the pollinated flower the grain of rice we eat develops.
When planting rice, farmers move the young seedlings from a seedbed into a flooded paddy so each plant has enough room to grow.
The Richter scale was created in 1935 by Charles F. Richter to measure the magnitude of earthquakes.
Engineers use magnitude data from past earthquakes to design buildings that can survive strong shaking. This is why there are building codes that match the expected earthquake strength in an area.
The Richter scale was created in 1935 by the American scientist Charles Richter, which is why it is named after him.
Each step up by one number on the Richter scale releases about 31 times more energy.
The magnitude scale is logarithmic, so a magnitude 6 quake shakes 10 times more than a magnitude 5.

A real Philippine example is the 1990 Luzon earthquake, which reached magnitude 7.7. It was so strong that it caused great damage in Baguio and other places, showing how powerful the shaking is at a high magnitude.

The news often says Richter scale, but most modern magnitudes reported today actually come from moment magnitude, not the original Richter. Richter has simply become the everyday name even when a different scale is used.
The Richter scale can show very small numbers, even zero or negative, for quakes so weak that only sensitive machines can detect them. That does not mean there was no earthquake.

At first, Charles Richter made his scale only for earthquakes close to California using one specific kind of seismograph. This is called local magnitude, and it was the very first version of magnitude.

For very large earthquakes, the old Richter scale seems to hit a ceiling and can no longer show the true strength correctly. This is why scientists created the newer moment magnitude scale for big quakes.
The Richter scale is a measurement that gives a single number to show how strong an earthquake is.
Magnitude is written as an ordinary decimal number (e.g. 7.2), while PHIVOLCS intensity is written in Roman numerals (e.g. Intensity VII).
When a continental plate begins to split, a deep valley called a rift valley forms, like the East African Rift — and over time it can fill with water and become a new ocean.
A right angle measures 90 degrees, like the corner of a square.
When ringworm grows on the scalp, the hair can fall out and leave a round bald patch.
In a ripple tank, the bright moving lines are crests, the high parts of the water wave, which you can watch as they travel across the tray.
When the rain is heavy and long, more water enters the river until it can no longer hold it and overflows. This is why areas near rivers sometimes flood.
The biya, or goby, is a small river fish whose belly fins are fused into a suction-cup shape, letting it cling to rocks even in fast-flowing water.
In an estuary, where a river meets the sea, fresh and salty water mix together, making it a special home for fish and mangroves.
The riparian zone is the strip of plants beside a river that acts as a natural filter, stopping soil and agricultural chemicals from entering the river and helping maintain water quality.
Over very many years, a river's flowing water slowly wears away the land and rock. This is how it can form valleys and deep channels.
A river begins at a source in high ground such as a mountain, and flows downhill to its mouth, where it empties into a lake or the sea.
Many small streams or creeks join together to form one big river. These smaller channels that flow into the river are called tributaries.
Both the flowing water and the stones in a riverbed are earth materials; the fish living in that river are not.
Over millions of years, a flowing river can carve deep canyons into rock, like rivers cutting through mountains.
Robert Hooke first used the word "cell" in 1665 when he saw tiny box-like spaces in a piece of cork under a microscope.
Cleavage is when a mineral breaks along smooth, flat surfaces in specific directions; fracture is an irregular break — for example, quartz breaks with a conchoidal (shell-like) fracture.
In the rock cycle, one kind of rock can slowly turn into another kind over very long periods of time.
In the rock cycle, rocks slowly change from one type to another through heat, pressure, weathering, and hardening, while the total amount of material stays the same.
The rock cycle has no real beginning or end, so rocks keep changing from one kind into another again and again.

A rock's hardness determines what it is best used for: hard rocks (such as granite and quartzite) are used for roads and high-traffic floors because they are durable; softer rocks (like limestone) are easier to cut and used for buildings and cement.
A rock is an earth material because it is a non-living solid from the ground, even when plants later grow beside it.

If there is a crack, fracture, or hardened lava that cuts across many layers, it means it is younger than the layers it cuts through. Why? Because the layers had to be there first before a crack or lava could pass and cut through them. This is called cross-cutting and it helps tell which came first.

A famous example of rock layers is the Grand Canyon in America. Over millions of years, the Colorado River slowly carved into the land and exposed many rock layers like the pages of a book. There you can clearly see the history of the Earth.

How do rock layers form? Water, rivers, and wind carry tiny bits of mud, sand, and rock. When the flow slows down, these bits sink to the bottom of a lake or sea. Over very many years they pile up on top of one another until they harden into rock.
In layered (sedimentary) rock, fossils in the deeper layers are usually older than those near the top, so scientists can read from them the order in which living things appeared on Earth.

You don't need to travel abroad to see rock layers. Right here in the Philippines, when the side of a mountain is cut to make a road, clear layers often appear, especially the white limestone in places like Bohol and Rizal.
If any rock sinks deep enough underground, it can melt back into magma and later become igneous rock again.
A rock is made of one or more minerals joined together, while a mineral is a single natural substance.
A rocket carries its own fuel, which it burns and ejects so there is mass to push out the back.
A rocket moves even in airless space because as it throws gas downward, the rocket gains equal momentum upward — keeping the total momentum the same.
A rocket rises because it blasts hot gas downward very fast, and by conservation of momentum the rocket itself is pushed upward.
A rocket flies because of Newton's Third Law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
A rocket lifts off because it pushes hot gas downward, and in reaction the gas pushes the rocket upward.
A rocket works even in the airless vacuum of space, because it pushes against its own gas, not the surrounding air.
As a rocket climbs, it drops off the parts that have run out of fuel so it becomes lighter and can reach higher into space.

On rocky shores, organisms live in distinct zones based on how high above the water they are — barnacles occupy the highest zone, followed by periwinkles, then mussels, and below that sea stars and anemones.

Rocky planets have only a thin layer of air (atmosphere) — thin on Earth, even thinner on Mars, and almost none on Mercury. Gas giants, on the other hand, are almost entirely a thick atmosphere of gas.
Rocky planets are denser (heavier for their size) than gas giants. In fact, Saturn is so light that if there were a big enough ocean, it would float! Rocky Earth would not float.

How does the parasite get back into the water? The blood fluke's eggs leave the body in the stool of an infected person. If that waste reaches a river or rice paddy, the eggs hatch and seek out a snail. This is why proper toilets matter so much.

Schistosomiasis is one of the so-called neglected tropical diseases, illnesses often overlooked because they strike poorer communities in warm climates. Because of this, health programs give free medicine to whole villages to bring the disease down.

Schistosomiasis is a disease caused by blood fluke parasites that pass through a specific freshwater snail (Oncomelania) as intermediate host; risk is high in Leyte and Mindanao where people wade or work in water.

How can schistosomiasis be avoided? Wear boots or footwear when entering rice fields or water, use a toilet instead of going outside, and avoid swimming in water suspected to be contaminated. These are small habits but they give big protection.

The blood fluke needs two homes to complete its life: first the snail, then a human. Inside the snail the parasite multiplies; inside the human it grows up and lays eggs. If either host is removed, the cycle breaks and the disease stops spreading.

How is schistosomiasis different from malaria? Both are carried by an animal, but malaria comes from a mosquito bite, while schistosomiasis comes from a parasite that passes through a snail and enters the skin. The carrier is different, so the way to avoid each is also different.

A scorpion's outer shell glows green when shone with ultraviolet (UV) light.
A scorpion is not an insect but an arachnid with eight legs, a relative of the spider.
Although a scorpion has several eyes, its vision is poor and it relies on sensing movement.
Scorpions often hunt at night and hide under rocks during the day.
Scorpions are usually active at night and hide during the day.
A common scorpion's sting hurts like a bee sting but is usually not deadly to people.
A scorpion has a sharp stinger at the tip of its curved tail that it uses to sting.
A scorpion has a raised tail tipped with a stinger that it uses to inject venom into prey or to defend itself.
Most scorpions have mild venom that is painful but rarely deadly to humans.
Scramble is made from crushed ice mixed with sweet milk; the ice melts in the warmth and turns to water, so the drink slowly gets thinner.
The picture on a screen is made of millions of tiny dots of light (pixels) too small for your eye to see one by one, so the picture looks smooth — but you can see the dots with a magnifying glass.
Looking down at a phone for a long time puts extra strain on the neck and upper spine.
A phone or TV screen is made of millions of tiny lights called pixels in red, green, and blue; together they form the picture you see.
An Archimedes screw uses a rotating helical blade inside a tube to carry water upward and is still used in some irrigation and water treatment systems.
A screw holds better than a nail because its threads grip inside the wood.
A screw makes it easier to hold two things together or lift things; it turns a twisting motion into a strong forward force.
A special screw called the Archimedes screw lifts water upward when it is turned.
A screw multiplies the force of our hand so it can fasten tightly into wood or metal.
The pitch of a screw is the distance it advances per full turn — a finer thread (smaller pitch) gives greater mechanical advantage but requires more turns to drive in the same distance.
A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a rod, so when you turn it, it digs in and holds tightly into wood or metal.
The thread of a screw is essentially an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder: each turn converts a small rotational effort into a large forward force.
When we turn a screw, the turning motion becomes a straight motion that pushes into the wood.
Ask separately about farming and about seafaring, because the same night sky can time planting inland and steer a boat along a coast.
At the coast, land heats faster than water, so warm air rises over the land and cooler air from the sea moves in as a sea breeze.
As the signal number rises, sea conditions are described as more dangerous, from rough for small boats up to impossible for almost all sea travel.
As it feeds and crawls, the sea cucumber stirs the sand so it can take in oxygen and stay healthy.

Sea cucumbers breathe by drawing water in through their rear end and expelling it — specialized respiratory trees inside their body extract oxygen from this water in a process called cloacal respiration.
As it feeds, the sea cucumber cleans the seabed, working like a janitor of the ocean floor.
When threatened, a sea cucumber curls up or stiffens its body, and some kinds release sticky threads to defend themselves.
When threatened, some sea cucumbers shoot out sticky inner parts to tangle or scare off an attacker.
The sea cucumber has tentacles around its mouth that it uses to scoop or grab food from the sand.
The sea cucumber helps recycle nutrients in the sea, keeping the water and sand healthy for other life.
Some sea cucumbers shoot out sticky threads to tangle and trap anything that tries to eat them.
As ice melts and warm water expands, the sea level slowly rises and creeps closer to coastlines.

It's a misconception that no mammal can live in saltwater. The sea otter can truly live in the sea because their kidneys are large and strong, filtering out the extra salt from their body. They also get water from the shellfish they eat, so they don't get thirsty even in the middle of the ocean.

You'll often see a sea otter combing and cleaning its fur—this isn't just for show. They must keep the fur clean and fluffy so it can trap air. If the fur gets dirty or oily, it can no longer hold air, and the otter can die from the cold.

When sea otters sleep, they often hold hands so they don't drift away from each other while asleep. This group of linked otters is called a 'raft'. Sometimes they also wrap themselves in long kelp (seaweed) so they're anchored and don't float away.

Sea otters are a big help against climate change. Because they let kelp grow more, and kelp soaks up carbon dioxide (the gas that warms the planet) from the water and air, more carbon gets stored away. So protecting sea otters is also a way to help our planet avoid getting hotter.
The sea otter is a keystone species because it eats the sea urchins that destroy kelp forests, keeping the underwater plants alive.

The sea otter is called a 'keystone species'—meaning that even though they aren't the most numerous animal in the sea, they have a huge effect on the whole system. Like the most important stone in an arch, if you remove the sea otter, the balance of the entire underwater community collapses.

Even though they're always in the water, sea otters are not fish—they're mammals, like us and dogs. They breathe air with lungs, so they need to come up to the surface to breathe. They also feed their babies milk. They can't breathe underwater like fish that have gills.

There are no sea otters in the Philippines! They only live in the cold parts of the North Pacific Ocean like Alaska, California, and Russia—our water is too warm for them. But we have our own important sea mammal: the dugong, which eats seagrass and also helps keep our seas healthy.
Because sea snakes are cold-blooded, they live only in the warm waters of the tropics and not in cold seas.
If you see a sea snake, do not touch or harm it because it is venomous; just let it swim away.
Even with strong venom, sea snakes rarely bite people because they are shy and usually avoid us.
The Philippines is home to many species of sea snakes because it lies in the Coral Triangle, where sea life is very rich.
A sea snake has a flattened, paddle-shaped tail that helps it swim.
A sea snake has a special gland in its mouth that removes extra salt from its body.
The yellow-bellied sea snake has a yellow belly and can float far out in the open ocean.
The sea spider has no lungs or gills, so it breathes by letting oxygen seep through tiny pores in the skin of its long legs.
Some sea stars eat clams and oysters by using their tube feet to force open the shell slightly, then the sea star everts its stomach outside its own body and digests the mollusk flesh directly.
A sea turtle lays about 100 or more eggs in one nest.
Sea turtles come up onto the beach to dig a nest in the sand and lay their eggs.
A turtle cannot exit its shell — the carapace is fused to the spine and ribs so the shell is actually part of the animal's skeleton, not simply a protective covering.
A sea turtle comes up onto the beach to bury her eggs in the sand.
Sea turtles mature slowly and typically do not breed until they are 25–35 years old — this long wait before reproduction makes it hard for their populations to recover quickly after decline.
