A sea turtle spends almost its whole life in the ocean, but the female returns to the beach to bury her eggs in the sand. She often comes back to the very beach where she was born.
Sea turtles have special glands near their eyes that remove excess salt from their bodies — the 'tears' that appear when they are on land are not from sadness but from salt excretion.
In sea turtles, nest temperature determines the sex of the eggs — warmer temperatures (above 29°C) produce more females while cooler temperatures produce more males.
Many marine reptiles like sea turtles are threatened by plastic trash and getting caught in fishing nets.
Sea urchins have a complex five-part jaw structure on their underside called 'Aristotle's lantern' — they use five teeth to scrape algae from rocks and coral.
Sea urchins play a key role in reef health by grazing algae; if sea urchins are removed from a reef, algae quickly overgrows the coral and can smother and kill it.
Sea walls and dikes are built to hold back the water from flooding coastal towns.
Seafloor spreading is confirmed by symmetrical magnetic stripes in the rock on both sides of the ridge, and by the fact that the sea floor is youngest near the ridge and older farther away.

In the middle of the oceans, long underwater mountain chains called mid-ocean ridges are where magma rises, cools, and forms new sea floor — a process called seafloor spreading that pushes plates away from each other.
When seagrass leaves die and break down into detritus, they become food for animals living on the seafloor.
Tiny algae grow on the surface of seagrass leaves, and small crawling animals graze on these algae.
Seagrass is a true flowering plant with roots, not a seaweed.
Seagrass produces flowers and seeds underwater, so it is a true flowering plant and not a seaweed.
Dugongs are not the only ones that eat seagrass; sea turtles eat it too.
Seagrass meadows trap mud from the water and keep the sea clear, which helps the coral reefs nearby.
Rabbitfish like danggit and samaral are fish that graze on seagrass and the algae growing in the meadow.
Growing seagrass and transplanting it to damaged bed areas is a coastal restoration method used to rebuild habitat for dugongs and sea turtles.
The roots of seagrass hold the sand on the seafloor so it is not easily washed away by the waves.
Shrimps and crabs hide among the seagrass leaves to escape from predators.
Sea snails crawl along seagrass leaves and eat the algae that sticks to them.
Besides changing color, a seahorse has small bumps and skin flaps that help it look like seaweed or coral so predators cannot spot it.
A seahorse uses its curly tail to grip onto seagrass and coral.
The seahorse is a camouflaged ambush predator — it waits quietly among seagrass or coral, then suddenly sucks in zooplankton and small crustaceans through its long snout in under a millisecond.
Seahorses usually live in shallow, warm seawater like the seas around the Philippines.

The seahorse has relatives called pipefish and sea dragons. They are alike because they all have long snouts and the father cares for the eggs, but a pipefish has a straight body instead of standing upright.
Bits of old shells in beach sand are non-living now, so they sit with sand as part of the earth materials of that shore.
Some animals in cold countries turn white in winter to match the snow and brown in summer; this change is triggered by the changing length of daylight, not by the temperature.
The Sun's light hits some parts of Earth more directly in some months, which is why seasons change and crops have planting times.
Seasons are not from distance: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January, yet the northern half has winter then — the tilt, not the distance, makes the seasons.
Seawater contains about 35 grams of salt per liter; it is too salty to drink because the body uses more water to excrete the excess salt than the seawater provides.
The sea is salty because rivers carry dissolved minerals and salts from rocks into it over a long time.
Many seaweeds grow very fast, so they can be harvested in just a few weeks.
Seaweed is soft and sways back and forth with the movement of the water.
Seaweed comes in three main groups by color: green, brown, and red.
The second most abundant metal in Earth's crust is iron.
For the same mass, doubling the force doubles the acceleration — force is directly proportional to the change in motion (F = ma).
For the same force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration — acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (a = F/m).
Jupiter has the second most moons, after Saturn.
Secondary consumers eat herbivores; for example, a frog eating grasshoppers is a secondary consumer.
Write the year of the book or interview, because sky lore can be recorded long after it was used, and that date is part of the evidence.
A secondary source is an account already written or recorded by someone else, such as an ethnography, not the sky itself and not your guess.
If the class votes that the Moon heats the day, a secondary science source can correct it: daytime heat comes from the Sun.
Sediment turns into solid sedimentary rock when the weight of upper layers presses it together (compaction) and minerals act like glue between the grains (cementation).
As flowing water slows, heavy pebbles settle first and lighter mud and sand travel farther—so the sediment ends up sorted by size.
In sedimentary rock, minerals glue the grains of sand together as they are pressed, turning them into solid rock.
Cross-bedding consists of angled layers inside a larger rock layer; these show that sediment was deposited by moving water or wind and can reveal the direction of ancient currents.
Limestone, sandstone, and shale are examples of sedimentary rock, and much Philippine limestone formed from old coral.
Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment such as sand and mud pile up, get pressed together, and harden.
Sedimentary rock forms when sand, mud, and small bits pile up, get buried, and cement together over long times, such as sandstone and limestone.
Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment such as sand and mud are pressed together and hardened over a long time.
If food poisoning is severe or comes with a high fever, a person should see a doctor.
A seesaw is a lever that balances when two children of equal weight sit the same distance from the middle support.
When we look at distant stars, we see their old light, so we are really looking into the past.
Seed banks store seeds of rare and important crop plants at low temperatures to preserve their genetic diversity; this is crucial to protect endangered plant species from extinction.
If you hang a string in sugary water, crystals collect on it and slowly grow larger over days.
When birds or animals eat fruit, they move the seeds far away in their droppings.
Some seeds have hooks or spines that cling to animal fur or human clothing; as the animal walks, it carries the seeds far from the parent plant.
When birds or animals eat fruit, they drop the seeds far away along with their droppings.
In the Philippines, fruit bats help spread fruit seeds as they fly around at night.
Some seeds like the amorseko (bur) have tiny hooks, so they cling to animal fur or your clothes and get carried elsewhere — this even inspired the invention of Velcro.
Seeds need to travel away from the parent plant so the new plants have enough space, light, and water, and do not crowd together in one spot.
A seed can stay resting for a long time, waiting until there is enough water and warmth to germinate.
Inside the seed is a tiny baby plant called the embryo, which will grow into the new plant.
Most seeds do not need sunlight to start sprouting because they are buried under the soil.
A seed has three main parts: the seed coat, the stored food, and the tiny baby plant inside.
Even with no light underground, a sprouting seedling knows which way is up because it uses gravity as a guide.
When an animal eats a fruit, the seeds inside come out in its droppings in a faraway place and can grow there.
As a pod dries, its walls tighten until they suddenly snap and fling the seeds out several meters.
If seeds just fell beside the parent plant, they would crowd together and fight for light, water, and soil. So seeds travel to get their own space far away.
Some seeds have tiny hooks or barbs that cling to animal fur or our clothes. Like the amorseko grass seed, an animal or person carries it far before it falls off and grows.
Some kids think a seed moves to a new spot on its own. That is not true—a seed cannot move by itself. Something always carries it: wind, water, animals, or people.
Some seeds have soft fluff like tiny parachutes. The fluff slows their fall so even a gentle breeze can push them far away.
Pollen and seeds are easy to mix up. Pollen travels between flowers to help make a seed. A seed travels later to start a new plant in a new place.
A great example of a wind seed is the dandelion. When you blow on its round white head, the seeds break apart and fly away like tiny parachutes.
In the Philippines, cogon grass spreads quickly because its tiny seeds have white hairs that the wind easily blows onto new open land.
These plants make very many seeds because most of them will land in poor spots. With so many seeds, there is a better chance that at least a few will grow.
Many plants release their seeds when the weather is very dry, because the wind is stronger and drier then, so the seeds can fly farther.
Some seeds have wing-like flaps that spin like a helicopter as they fall, so they drift slowly and the wind can carry them farther.
Being wind-carried is not always lucky. Many seeds land on rock, water, or places with no soil, so they cannot grow. That is why a plant makes so many seeds.
A heavier child can balance a lighter child by sitting closer to the fulcrum. The closer to the center you sit, the less your weight tips the lever.
A seesaw is a first-class lever — the fulcrum is in the middle, between the two riders.
One earthquake can send both types: a longitudinal P-wave example and a transverse S-wave example traveling through the same ground.

A 'seismic gap' is a segment of a fault that has not ruptured for a long time while adjacent segments have been active; these gaps may have accumulated stress and are more likely to rupture in the near future.

PHIVOLCS produces seismic hazard maps of the Philippines showing where earthquake risk is high; architects and engineers use these maps to ensure new buildings are strong enough for the earthquakes in their area.
Seismic waves are waves of energy that spread through and across the Earth during an earthquake, and the shaking we feel is caused by these waves.
A seismograph is an instrument that measures and records the shaking waves of the ground during an earthquake, so scientists can tell how strong it was.

A seismograph uses a heavy mass suspended from a spring; when an earthquake occurs, the ground moves but the mass stays relatively still due to its inertia, and this difference is recorded as a seismogram.
After a strong earthquake, seismographs keep recording aftershocks, the smaller tremors that follow; this helps scientists know whether the ground is settling down or not yet.

A seismograph is so sensitive that it can sense earthquakes even from the other side of the world; the earthquake waves travel through the inside of the Earth and reach the machines even from very far away.

It is a misconception that a seismograph can predict earthquakes; in truth it only records the shaking while or after it happens, and no machine yet can say exactly when the next earthquake will come.

A seismograph records two kinds of waves: the fast P-wave that arrives first, and the slower S-wave that follows; from the time gap between them, scientists can tell how far away the earthquake started.
A seismograph has three main parts: a base fixed to the ground, a hanging mass that holds a pen, and a rotating paper drum where the movement is recorded.

The ground moves up-and-down and side-to-side, so usually three seismographs work together: one for vertical motion and two for the different sideways directions, to capture the full movement of an earthquake.

The seismometer is the sensing part that feels the shaking, while the seismograph is the whole system that both senses and records it on paper or a computer; people often swap the two words, but that is the small difference.
The base of a seismograph must be fixed firmly to solid ground or rock so that it surely moves with the real shaking of the earth, and not from other causes like wind or a passing truck.
The instrument that records the ground shaking during an earthquake is called a seismograph.
By combining data from many seismometers in different places, scientists can find where an earthquake started and how strong it was.
Farmers and animal raisers choose plants or animals with desirable traits to be parents. In this way, useful traits — such as a bigger harvest or healthier cattle — are passed to the next generation.
In artificial selection, humans choose which animals or plants reproduce, instead of nature doing the selecting.
Self-medication is dangerous because you might take too much or too little of the medicine.
Inside the ear are three tiny curved tubes filled with fluid that sense when your head turns or moves.
A semiconductor like silicon is between a conductor and an insulator, and it is used in computer chips.
A semiconductor like silicon is in between a conductor and an insulator, and is used in computer chips.
There are two kinds of nerve cells in the flow of signals: sensory neurons that carry information from the senses to the brain, and motor neurons that carry commands from the brain to the muscles.

The separation method is chosen from the substances' properties: size, weight, whether magnetic, whether it dissolves, or different boiling points. No new substance forms — it is only a physical change.
In a series circuit the resistances of the parts add up, so the total resistance is higher and the current is smaller.
Records from the last hundred years show Philippine eruptions can send ash, lava, or fast hot flows, not only one kind of event.

A child's sex is determined by the chromosomes they inherit — females have two X chromosomes, males have an X and a Y. The father passes the chromosome that decides whether the child is male or female.
Because females chose the brightest males over many generations, the feathers became even more showy.
Sitting in shade or using an umbrella lowers the sunlight that hits your skin and eyes, a simple protection from too much light.
An opaque object makes the darkest shadow, while a translucent object makes a fainter one.
A shadow forms when an object blocks light, leaving a dark area behind it.
A hand-shadow on the wall forms because the hand blocks the light from reaching the wall behind it.
Shadow puppet theatre places puppet shapes between a light and a screen to make shadows — demonstrating that light travels in straight lines.
An object's shadow grows larger when it is moved closer to the light and smaller when moved away, because it blocks a different amount of the light.
Outdoors, the sun is the main light that makes our shadows.
A sundial uses the moving shadow cast by the sun to tell the time.
Translucent objects that let some light through, like thin paper, make a faint, weak shadow.
Our shadow changes length and direction through the day — it is long in the morning and afternoon when the Sun is low, and shortest at noon when the Sun is high.
Outdoor shadows point away from the Sun, a simple observation that the bright heat and light in the yard come from that one star.
When a suspension medicine is shaken it mixes for a while, but the particles settle again when it stops.
A light crumpled paper can fall faster than a flat heavy poster if the poster catches more air, so shape matters as well as weight.
Say the finding out loud in one or two sentences so the group agrees on what was learned before packing the materials away.
A fair investigation shares the raw numbers from all trials, not only the one trial that looks neatest on a poster.
In a covalent bond, the shared pair of electrons counts for both atoms, so each atom's outer shell seems full.
Naming a star group as an animal or a tool made the pattern easier to teach, so the next generation could still find direction and season.
Scientists group living things by the traits they share, such as having a backbone or wings, to make them easier to study.
Most baby sharks are born already having a full set of teeth, so they can hunt for food on their own right away.

Some shark species (such as whale sharks, thresher sharks, and oceanic whitetips) are listed on CITES Appendix II — meaning their international trade must be regulated; the Philippines supports these international protection measures.

According to the IUCN Red List, over one-third of all shark species are threatened with extinction — primarily due to overfishing (for fin soup and meat), accidental catch in fishing nets, and habitat loss.
Because sharks drop so many teeth and the teeth are hard, shark teeth are some of the most common fossils found.
Sharks help keep the ocean healthy because they often eat weak or sick fish.
Many kinds of sharks must keep swimming so water flows over their gills and they can breathe.
Sharks have excellent hearing for low-frequency sounds — splashing water or the struggling movements of a wounded animal can be heard by a shark from several kilometers away.

Shark skin is not smooth like fish — it is covered in tiny tooth-like scales called dermal denticles that create V-shaped grooves which reduce water drag and allow sharks to swim faster than a smooth surface would permit.
Long ago, people used dried shark skin as real sandpaper to scrub and smooth wood. It was called shagreen, and it worked well because the denticles are so rough.

Shark skin is very tough — even tougher than ordinary cowhide leather. Because of this, shark skin was once used to make strong leather for goods and for sword handles that would not slip even when wet.
Sharks have a very strong sense of smell, so they can sense blood in the water even from far away.
Some sharks lay eggs while other sharks give birth to live young.
A shark's teeth are not rooted deep in bone like ours; they are only loosely attached to the skin of the jaw, so they come off and get replaced easily.
When a shark's tooth falls out, a new tooth from behind quickly replaces it, so it never runs out.
Sharks have no swim bladder, so they must keep swimming or use their large oily liver to avoid sinking.
Meat-eating animals have sharp, pointed teeth to tear and cut flesh.
Transverse waves in solids are sometimes called shear waves, which is why S-waves sit on the transverse example list with rope waves.
A sheep is a farm animal raised for its thick coat of hair called wool.
Sheep live together in a group called a flock.
Sheep have thick, soft hair called wool.
In sheet erosion, rain removes a thin, even layer of topsoil across a wide area without being very noticeable.
When seashells are burned and ground up, they become white lime; this white powder is calcium carbonate and is used as a white pigment.
Most snail shells coil to the right, so a snail whose shell coils to the left is rare and special.
As they suck in and strain water, mussels and oysters help make the water cleaner.
A shellfish has no hands to pull in water, so it uses countless tiny hairs called cilia on its gills that keep beating to create a current of water flowing in.
When many shellfish live together in a bay, they filter the water all at once, making the surrounding sea clearer and cleaner.
Mussels and oysters draw water into their body, and their gills trap tiny bits of food as the water flows through them.
A single oyster can filter a very large amount of water in one day — many dozens of liters — so even though it is small, it helps clean the water a lot.
Inside a shellfish is a thin layer called the mantle that helps move the water through and also builds the hard shell using the calcium it collects.
When oysters grow in big clusters and clump together, they build a rocky home where other small fish, shrimp, and crabs can hide and live.
When the water is warm and rich in nutrients, plankton (the shellfish's food) multiplies — so there are seasons when filter feeders have much more food than at other times.
Clams, oysters, and mussels are mollusks, the same group as snails and squids with soft bodies.
During a red tide, clams and oysters must not be eaten because they can hold a poison.
During a red tide, mussels, oysters, and other shellfish should not be eaten because they may hold a toxin that is harmful to people.
Shield volcanoes usually erupt gently, with runny lava simply flowing out.
A shield volcano is low and broad because its runny lava flows far before it cools and hardens.

A shield volcano has wide gentle slopes because its basaltic lava is very fluid (low viscosity) and flows far before cooling; it does not erupt explosively like the stratovolcanoes of the Philippines.
The shiitake is a kind of mushroom that belongs to the fungi kingdom, not the plant kingdom, and grows on decaying wood.
Shiny, silvery surfaces reflect radiation instead of absorbing it, which is why some buildings use shiny roofs so they do not get too hot in the sun.
Heavy steel ships float because their wide, hollow shape pushes aside a lot of water. The upward push from that water is enough to hold the whole ship up.
Vehicle shock absorbers work with springs to absorb vibrations when wheels hit bumps — reducing the vibration felt by passengers.
While roots grow downward, the shoot grows upward against gravity so it can reach the light above the ground.
Many shorebirds have brown or sandy feathers that match the ground so they are hard to see.
Candaba Marsh in Pampanga is one place where many migratory birds gather during the rainy season.
The Philippines is part of the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, a long migration route birds follow from Siberia all the way to Australia.
Scientists put small leg bands or tags on the birds to learn where they came from and where they go.
Right beside the city, the Las Piñas–Parañaque Wetland Park shelters migratory shorebirds near Manila Bay.
Many shorebirds have long, thin bills to probe for food beneath the mud or sand.
Mangroves and muddy coasts are important feeding grounds for migratory shorebirds.
A short circuit happens when current finds a path with almost no resistance, so it suddenly becomes very large and can cause overheating or fire.
When you press a guitar string down on a fret, you make the vibrating part of the string shorter. The closer to the body you press, the shorter the string and the higher the note.
On a harp, you can see strings that get longer and longer. The short strings make high notes and the long ones make low notes. That's why a harp has its triangle shape.
Inside a piano, the keys that make high notes are connected to short strings, and the low notes to long strings. So even though you can't see them, the string-length rule is working inside.
Our voice works like a string too! Inside the throat are small parts that vibrate. When the body tightens and shortens them, the voice goes higher, which is how we sing high notes.
There are two ways to raise a string's pitch: make it shorter, or make it tighter. Tightening is what tuning does, while shortening is done while playing using a finger on a fret.
A ukulele is smaller and has shorter strings than a guitar. That's why it sounds higher and brighter compared to the deeper sound of a guitar.
Blue light has shorter waves than red light, so it gets scattered much more strongly in the air.
The female Dolania americana mayfly has only about five minutes as an adult before dying—the shortest of any insect.
The mayfly has one of the shortest lives—many kinds live as adults for only about one day.
Violet light has the shortest wavelength of the visible colors.
Mercury has the shortest year (only about 88 days) because it is the planet closest to the Sun.
A shout down a hallway is a longitudinal sound example; naming it helps you remember everyday compressional waves, not only lab springs.
A shrew does not sleep for long; it is active in short bursts both day and night so it can keep eating.
There are shrews found in the Philippines too, especially in fields and forests. They eat insects, worms, and small creatures, which helps keep nature balanced. They move fast to catch their food.

Because of its fast metabolism, a shrew can eat food almost equal to its own body weight in a single day. That is like a child eating their own weight in food every day. Most of this food is insects and worms.

Because a shrew burns energy so fast, it must eat almost every few hours. If it goes too long without food, it can actually starve to death. That is why a shrew is almost always searching for something to eat.
Shrews live very short lives, often only a year or less, partly because of their very fast metabolism.
A shrew has a pointed snout and eats insects, while a rat usually eats plants and seeds.
A shrew's tiny body loses heat quickly, so its heart beats fast to keep its body warm.
A shrimp is an arthropod, like insects and spiders, an animal group known for a hard outer shell and jointed legs.
Many shrimp live near the bottom of the water and hide in sand or plants to avoid enemies.
A shrimp is cold-blooded, so its body temperature depends on the temperature of the water it lives in.
When the water gets very cold, a shrimp slows down and may even stop eating, as if weak, because its body works more slowly.
A shrimp does not shiver from cold the way we do because it does not need to keep itself warm; instead, its body simply matches the water's temperature.
A shrimp grows faster and molts more often in warm water, so they are ready to harvest sooner during warmer weather.
Because a shrimp does not have to make its own heat, it saves energy and does not need to eat as much as a warm-blooded animal of the same size.
Water plants give shade that keeps the water beneath them cooler, so shrimp often shelter there when the sun is hot.
A shrimp uses the warmth of the water as a signal for when to breed — usually they lay more eggs when the season is warmer.
A shrimp is sensitive to sudden changes in water temperature; moving it abruptly from warm to cold water (or the reverse) can shock it and even kill it.
If you touch a live shrimp in the water, it feels cool — not warm like our bodies — because its warmth just matches the cool water.
In places where it gets very cold in winter, a shrimp nearly stops moving and hides, almost as if sleeping, until the water warms up again.
Farmed shrimp need clean water with enough oxygen; if the water becomes dirty or low in oxygen, the shrimp can get sick or die.
A shrimp has many small jointed legs; it uses some for walking and others for swimming.
In the Philippines, many people raise prawns in brackish-water ponds near the coast and mangroves to sell as food.
Shrimp and prawns are animals that live in water, such as the sea, rivers, and fishponds.
At the front of a shrimp's head is a pointed, saw-toothed spike called the rostrum, found between its eyes.
A shrimp's body has two main parts: a joined head-and-chest, and a curved segmented tail.
When threatened, a shrimp rapidly flips its tail (telson) downward, propelling itself backward at speed — one of the fastest escape reflexes in the animal kingdom, occurring in milliseconds.
If one of a shrimp's two antennae breaks off, it can slowly grow back each time the shrimp sheds its hard shell.
Because a shrimp's body has two main parts, the firm front carries the legs while the curved back flicks to make it swim.
A shrimp's two eyes can sense light and dark, so it knows to hide when it is bright and move around when it is dark to stay safe from hunters.
The shrimp's two body parts have names: the front combined head-and-chest, and the rear belly section where the tail is.
Each of the shrimp's two body parts has its own hard shell: a stiff cover over the front and overlapping plates along the bendable tail.
SI stands for the International System of Units, the worldwide system of measurement.
The kilogram (kg) is the SI base unit used to measure mass.
The second (s) is the SI base unit used to measure time.
The SI units are defined by the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) through the BIPM.
The Sierra Madre in eastern Luzon is the longest mountain range in the Philippines and acts as a shield against typhoons.

The Sierra Madre, the Philippines' longest mountain range, acts as a barrier that intercepts rain from the Pacific in a 'rain shadow' effect — the eastern side gets heavy rain from typhoons while Cagayan Valley to the west is drier; it also protects the Cagayan Valley from direct typhoon hits.
In a sieve, particles smaller than the holes pass through while larger ones stay on top.
Sieving separates pieces of different sizes using a sieve with holes — small pieces (like flour) pass through while bigger ones (like gravel) stay behind.
Weather under Signal 1 can already toss light outdoor objects, so bringing in chairs and tying light roofs is matching the described wind, not overreacting.
Signal 1 is already a warning, not 'no storm'; it describes weather that is starting to turn rough and may grow worse if the number rises.
Under Signal 1, expect cloudy to rainy weather and a steadily strengthening wind, not yet the most destructive typhoon winds.
Under Signal 2, walking against the wind becomes hard, and light materials may fly, which is the outdoor weather that number is warning about.
When Signal 2 is up, sea travel is more dangerous and some classes or work may stop, matching winds too strong for ordinary outdoor days.
Signal 3 weather can bring down some trees and power lines, so brownouts and blocked roads are part of the conditions that number describes.
Under Signal 3, people are expected to stay indoors away from windows, because flying debris and hard rain make outdoor weather unsafe.
When Signal 4 is in force, coastal flooding and very dangerous winds may occur, so official evacuation orders match those extreme weather conditions.
Signal 4 weather is a mix of very strong wind and often torrential rain, so going outside to 'check the sky' is not a safe reading of the signal.
Under Signal 5, the described weather is life-threatening outdoors, so people should already be in strong shelter, not traveling through the storm.
The same typhoon can put Signal 2 over one province and Signal 1 over another, because the weather is not equally strong everywhere.

Where do the heat and light of a reaction come from? Atoms hold energy stored in their bonds. When new, more stable bonds form, extra energy is released as heat or light — which is why these are signs that a reaction has happened.
Clues that a chemical change happened include a color change, bubbles or gas, heat or light, smoke, or a new smell.

Even on a farm, reaction signs are used to test things. When vinegar is poured on soil or rock and it bubbles, that is a sign that lime is present and reacting — so a farmer can tell whether the soil still needs treatment.

Why does the fizzing of baking soda and vinegar stop after a while? Because one of the substances has been used up. When a sign like bubbling stops, it usually means the reaction is finished — there is nothing left to keep it going.

Scientists use the signs of a reaction as tests. For example, when iodine is dropped on food with starch, it turns blue-black — the color change proves starch is present. In the same way, limewater turning cloudy is used to test whether a gas is carbon dioxide.

It is a misconception that anything giving off light must be hot. A glow stick and a firefly shine while staying cool — the reaction's energy goes almost entirely into light, not heat. So light, whether hot or cold, is still a sign of a chemical reaction.
A strong sign of a chemical reaction: you usually cannot undo it. Once paper has burned or an egg has cooked, you cannot turn it back to what it was, because it has formed a completely new substance.

Rust on an old jeepney or an iron fence is a visible sign of a chemical reaction: the iron reacts with oxygen and water in the air to form a new brownish substance. It happens faster in the Philippines because the air is humid and near the salty sea.

Not only heating up — a sudden cooling is also a sign of a chemical reaction. In an instant cold pack used on a swollen foot, a reaction inside absorbs heat from its surroundings, so the temperature drops without any ice.
The spiciest part of a chili is not the seeds but the white spongy part inside that holds the seeds, because that is where the most capsaicin is found.
Silicon is a semiconductor — not a pure conductor or insulator — and is the main material used to make computer chips, solar cells, and electronic devices.
Long green chili is green when unripe, but if you let it ripen on the plant, it slowly turns red. It tastes a bit sweeter and spicier when it is red.
In the Philippines, long green chili is often added to dishes like sinigang and tinola. It is not very spicy, so it gives just a mild kick and a nice aroma to the food.
Fresh long green chili is mostly water inside, which is why it is crunchy and juicy. When it dries out, it shrinks and wrinkles because the water leaves it.
Silk comes from the silkworm, a caterpillar that spins a thin fiber to build a cocoon, and that cocoon fiber is unwound and woven into silk cloth.
Silk is a natural fiber that comes from an animal, unlike cotton which comes from a plant.
In the Philippines, some farmers also raise silkworms and grow mulberry to make silk.
Silk-making was discovered long ago in the country of China. From there, silk spread to many different parts of the world.
Inside the cocoon, the silkworm changes into a moth. When it is ready, it breaks the cocoon to come out and fly away.
The silkworm eats the leaves of the mulberry plant. From these leaves the worm gets the nutrients it needs to make silk.
Silk is made of protein, the same kind of material found in our hair and nails. That is why it is a natural fiber and not plastic.
Silk comes from a tiny caterpillar called a silkworm. It looks like a small worm that eats leaves, and it is the one that makes the thin silk thread.
Silk is smooth and soft when you touch it, and it shines when light hits it. Because of this, it is a beautiful cloth to use for clothing.
Because spider silk is strong and biocompatible, scientists study it for medical uses such as dissolving sutures and tissue scaffolds for wound healing.
Silver is the best metal at conducting electricity, but copper is used more because it is cheaper.
The best metal conductor of electricity is silver, with the symbol Ag.
In both class acts the children stay in their places after the pulse passes, a similarity that shows energy moved but the people did not travel.
Gears, pulleys, and wheels do not create extra energy. They only reduce the force you need, but in trade you must pull more rope or make more turns.
Archimedes, an ancient Greek mathematician (around 250 BC), was the first to study and explain how the lever and other simple machines work.
A singer's voice resonates in head, chest, and throat cavities — these resonating spaces amplify certain frequencies and give the voice its distinctive quality.
Two atoms can share one pair of electrons (a single bond), two pairs (a double bond), or three pairs (a triple bond).
In a single replacement reaction, one element takes the place of another element in a compound, such as a more active metal replacing a less active one.
Many plastics like sachets and plastic bags are used only once before being thrown away.
When the roof of an underground cave grows weak and collapses, a large hole can suddenly open at the surface called a sinkhole.
A sinkhole forms when an underground cave in limestone grows too large and its roof collapses; sinkholes can appear suddenly and are a hazard in karst limestone areas such as Cebu and Bohol.
A sinkhole can open suddenly and become dangerous when buildings or roads sit above it.
A sinkhole can suddenly appear under a road or house with no warning, because the ground above has been quietly hollowing out for a long time before it finally collapses.
Siopao is soft and fluffy because the yeast in the dough makes tiny gas bubbles that puff it up before it is steamed.
Sirius is in the constellation Canis Major, which means the Great Dog.
Sirius is about 8.6 light-years away from Earth.
Sirius is about 8.6 light-years away from Earth.
The apparent magnitude of Sirius is about −1.46, which makes it the brightest star.
Sisig sizzles on a hot metal plate because metal heats up quickly and the liquid in the food suddenly turns to steam.
A nearsighted child may have trouble reading the board and prefers to sit at the front of the class.
When you sit, your weight presses down on the chair, and the chair pushes you back up with an equal force.
Even shallow but fast-moving floodwater can knock a person off their feet.
Size alone does not decide floating; a tiny stone sinks but a huge ship floats, because of density.
The muscles attached to bones move when we choose to, so they are called voluntary muscles.
Our skeleton has two main parts: the central axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton of the arms and legs.
Bones and muscles work together so that we can move.
The whole framework of the body's 206 bones is called the skeleton.
The spine is made of many small stacked bones called vertebrae.
When you feel embarrassed or hot, the tiny blood vessels in your cheeks widen so more blood flows close to the skin. That is why your face turns red.
When you are scared, the blood vessels in your skin narrow so blood is sent to muscles you might need to run or fight. That is why you look pale — little blood stays near the skin.
The skin has tiny blood vessels, which is why our face turns red when we are hot or shy.
When hot, blood vessels in the skin widen to release heat; when cold, they narrow to keep heat in.
There are tiny blood vessels under your skin. When you are hot, they widen to release heat from the blood, which is why your face may turn red. When you are cold, they narrow to keep heat inside.
A newborn baby's skin is not yet good at controlling temperature, so babies get cold easily. That is why we wrap them in blankets to help them stay warm and safe.
The skin has layers stacked together, and beneath it is a thin layer of fat. This fat works like a blanket that keeps heat from escaping too fast, so we do not get cold so easily.
People cool down by sweating all over the skin. A dog has almost no sweat glands, so it pants with its tongue out to release heat instead. Animals have different ways but the same goal.
Sweat itself has almost no smell. But when it stays on the skin for a while, tiny bacteria feed on it, and that is what causes the smell. This is why regular bathing helps.
The skin is the body's first barrier, blocking germs from getting inside us.

Goosebumps are part of an old body alarm that switches on when you are scared. In furry animals it raises the fur so they look bigger and frighten an enemy. Humans have little hair left, so only the bumps remain.

It is a mistake to think goosebumps by themselves mean you are sick. Usually they are just from cold or emotion. But if they come together with shivering and a hot, feverish feeling, then tell a parent so it can be checked.
Once you warm up or calm down, the tiny muscles relax, the hairs lie back down, and your skin becomes smooth again. That is why goosebumps only last a short while.

If you do not want goosebumps from the cold, the easiest fix is to put on a jacket, sweater, or thick clothes, or wrap in a blanket. By keeping your body warm, the skin no longer has to trap heat, so the bumps go away.
In parts of the skin that are rubbed a lot, like the palms or soles, it thickens and forms a callus. This is the skin's way of protecting itself from frequent pressure or rubbing.
The very outer skin is made of tightly packed dead cells. That is why it does not hurt when you touch it, and it works like armor that blocks water and dirt from getting in.

The tips of your fingers have tiny ridges in the skin that form a fingerprint. They help you grip things better. Every person's fingerprint is unique — even identical twins have different fingerprints.
In an adult, the skin can cover about two square meters and weigh several kilograms.
The skin is the largest organ of the body, and it protects us from germs and injury.
Skin is the body's largest organ — if you spread it out flat it would cover almost two square meters, because it wraps around the whole person.

In a hot tropical country like the Philippines, the sun is very strong, especially at noon. Too much exposure makes skin red and blistered — that is sunburn. An umbrella, a hat, or sunblock helps protect your skin.

Skin helps keep the body at the right temperature. When you are hot, blood vessels near the skin widen to release heat (which is why we flush red) and we sweat. When you are cold, those vessels narrow to keep heat inside.
Skin has three layers. The epidermis is the outer layer you see and touch; the dermis is the middle layer holding blood vessels and nerves; and a fatty bottom layer that gives warmth and cushioning.

Skin does not just feel plain touch. It has different tiny sensors (receptors) inside: some for light touch, some for heat, some for cold, some for pressure, and some for pain. That is how skin can tell different kinds of feelings apart.
The sense of touch helps protect us because we can feel sharp, hot, or dangerous things.
Under the skin is a layer of fat that acts like a soft cushion. It helps absorb bumps and knocks so our inner organs and bones are not hurt so easily.
Skin is the largest organ of the body because it wraps around our whole self from head to foot. Since it covers every side, the protection it gives to our insides is complete.
The skin releases sweat to cool the body when we are hot or tired.
When a fever starts to break, you often sweat a lot. This is the body's way of lowering the extra heat back toward normal — so sometimes it is a sign you are starting to feel better.
When it is hot, the skin sweats to cool down. When it is cold, we don't sweat — instead our hairs stand up (goosebumps) and we shiver to warm up. They are opposite ways the skin manages temperature.
The skin has millions of tiny sensors that feel touch, pressure, heat, cold, and pain. They send signals to the brain through nerves so we can feel.
The ability of an animal to drop a part of its own body, such as the tail, is called 'autotomy' by scientists.
A skink's broken-off tail keeps moving by itself because it has its own nerves and muscles that can twitch even when separated from the body.

How does the tail come off? It does not just fall. Special muscles in the tail suddenly tighten and squeeze while the skink twists, so the tail splits at the break point. It is on purpose, not an accident.

Notice this: the regrown tail is often shorter and a different color than the original. Sometimes the color is duller or the shape is blunter. That is how you can tell which skink lost its tail before.
A skink stores some fat for energy in its tail, so dropping it has a cost — that saved food is lost and must be replaced.
A skink is a kind of small lizard with a smooth, shiny body, short legs, and a long tail; it is often found in grass, under rocks, and near houses.
Two children holding a rope and sending a bump toward each other are making a transverse wave you can watch in the schoolyard.
Skipping rope is an exercise that speeds up the heartbeat and breathing, which strengthens the heart and lungs.
Star names and eclipse sayings were ways of teaching, so your investigation is about how knowledge was communicated, not only about listing pretty pictures.
A skydiver falling belly-down reaches a terminal velocity of about 200 kilometers per hour (120 mph).

Besides convection, two other forces help move plates: 'slab pull,' where the weight of a sinking plate drags the rest of it down, and 'ridge push,' where a plate is pushed away from the raised ridge.
Drinking coffee or soda with caffeine and eating a heavy meal before bed can delay sleepiness and disturb sleep. It is better to eat lightly at night.
When we do not get enough sleep, we feel tired and find it hard to think clearly.
Getting enough sleep helps children grow and makes their bodies strong.
While we sleep, our heartbeat and breathing slow down so the body can rest.
Getting enough sleep helps keep our mood steady; when we lack sleep, we get stressed or irritable more easily.
Enough sleep helps the body fight illness and stay healthy.
When we lack sleep, the body's reactions slow down and we make more mistakes or stumble. That is why enough sleep helps us stay alert and safe.
Enough sleep helps us feel calm and in a good mood. When we lack sleep, we get more irritable and grumpy and find it harder to control bad feelings.
Babies sleep much more than adults because they are growing quickly.
The longer we stay awake, the more sleepiness builds up in the body, so by night we strongly want to sleep. Sleep resets it back to zero.
Slime molds are protists that live as individual cells but come together to form a fruiting body for reproduction, a remarkable example of cooperation among microbes.
Pushing and pulling a slinky along its length is a classroom example of a longitudinal wave, because the coils move back and forth the same way the pulse travels.
Shaking a slinky sideways makes a transverse wave, because the coils move across the direction the pulse travels down the spring.
Because a sloth moves so slowly, algae grows on its fur and turns it greenish, helping it hide among the leaves.
Tiny moths live in a sloth's fur. They help algae grow there, and the algae in turn gives the sloth its hiding color, so they all help one another.
Many people think sloths are lazy, but that is not true. Their slowness is a way to survive on very little food, so it is a smart way of living, not laziness.
There are no wild sloths in the Philippines; they live in the rainforests of Central and South America. In the Philippines you can only see them in some zoos, not in our forests.
Both the sloth and the monkey live in trees, but they move differently. The monkey is fast and jumps around a lot, while the sloth moves slowly and quietly to save energy.
Food digests very slowly inside a sloth's stomach, sometimes taking weeks to fully break down the leaves. This slow digestion is why even a small amount of food is still enough for it.
A sloth spends almost its whole life hanging from tree branches in the rainforest.
A sloth has long, curved claws like hooks that let it grip tightly onto branches.
The name sloth means slow or lazy, because of the way it moves.
Digestion in a sloth's stomach is so slow that one meal can take several weeks to break down.
There are two main kinds of sloth: the two-toed sloth and the three-toed sloth.
Always slouching or hunching over a gadget for a long time can harm our posture.
Slouching or sitting hunched over all the time strains the back muscles and can cause back pain.
When the water evaporates slowly, the crystals that form grow bigger.
When a drumhead is loose or large, it vibrates slowly when struck, so the boom is low and deep. This is why big drums have a lower sound.
A person's voice comes from vocal cords vibrating in the throat. Longer, thicker vocal cords vibrate more slowly, which is why some people have lower, deeper voices.

Some vibrations are slow enough that you can see them move, like a long ruler hanging off a desk that you flick. But for vibrations that make a sound you can hear, they are still too fast to count by eye, even the 'slow' ones.
When something vibrates slowly, it makes a low-pitched sound.
The slower something vibrates, the lower the pitch of the sound it makes.
Some think a low sound travels to your ear more slowly. That's wrong! 'Slow' only describes the vibration that makes the sound. All sounds — high or low — travel through air at the same speed.
The sloth is the slowest mammal on land.
A slug and many snails have four (4) tentacles: two for seeing, two for feeling.
PHIVOLCS counts steam-driven explosions as eruptions too, so the pattern includes small events, not only famous giant blasts.
The small intestine has tiny finger-like projections called villi that absorb nutrients from digested food into the bloodstream.
Nets with very tiny holes catch even small young fish before they have a chance to breed.
A meteorite's outside gets hot while flying, but it is usually cold by the time it is found on the ground.
When only very few animals are left, they go extinct more easily because a single disease or disaster can strike all of them.
Some eruptions start with steam and a little ash, then grow stronger, so early PHIVOLCS reports matter even when the first event looks small.
The bee hummingbird is the smallest bird, measuring only about 5 centimeters long.
The smallest flowering plant in the world is Wolffia, which floats on water and is about the size of a grain of sand.
The bumblebee bat is the smallest mammal, weighing only about 2 grams.
By weight, the lightest mammal is the Etruscan shrew, only about 1.8 grams.
The smallest prime number is 2, and it is also the only even prime number.
Edward Jenner created the world's first vaccine, the vaccine against smallpox.
Smells come from tiny particles of a thing that float in the air.
You can often tell food has spoiled when it smells bad, turns slimy, or changes color.
When you smell or see tasty food, your stomach gets ready and may start to growl.
A smoke detector sounds an alarm when it senses tiny smoke particles in the air, warning people before a fire grows.
Breathing smoke is bad for the lungs because its tiny particles get into your breath and can cause coughing and lung illness.
When smoking fish, the smoke dries it and helps kill microbes so it lasts longer.
SMS in text messaging stands for "Short Message Service."
In nature, snails help out by eating dead and rotting leaves, which assists in cleaning up and returning nutrients to the soil.
As a snail scrapes, the front teeth of its radula wear down, but it keeps growing new teeth at the back to replace the old ones.

To reduce golden apple snails without using poisonous chemicals, many farmers let ducks loose in the rice field. The ducks eat the small snails and their eggs. This is a safe method because it does not harm the soil and water.

The golden apple snail lays many tiny eggs that are bright pink. It places the eggs on plant stems or objects above the water, not underwater. The bright pink color works like a warning to birds and animals not to eat them.
Snails and slugs are mollusks, a group of soft animals with no bones inside.
In the Philippines, some kinds of snails are cooked and eaten as food.
Snails lay small round eggs in moist soil.
A snail glides on a slimy mucus trail produced by its foot, which keeps it from getting hurt and helps it move smoothly.
Snails are most active at night and after rain when the surroundings are damp.
The muscle that pulls the snail is attached to the central column inside the coiled shell. This gives the body a firm anchor so it can pull in quickly.
A snail has a strong muscle attached inside its shell. When this muscle tightens, it works like a spring and pulls the snail's body back inside the shell.
Most snail shells coil to the right when you look at them from the tip. Only a rare few coil to the left. This right-handed coiling is called dextral and is normal for nearly all snail kinds.
When a snail dies, its empty shell is left behind. Over time it breaks down and the calcium returns to the soil. Some small animals even use calcium from old shells for their own bodies.
A snail never swaps its shell; the shell grows along with the animal by adding new material at the open edge.
A snail's shell has lines or ridges that follow its edge. These growth lines show how the shell got bigger little by little. In some snails, the lines hint at how long the shell has been growing.

In the Philippines, a well-known snail is the golden apple snail with a round, yellow-brown shell. It is a pest in rice fields because it eats young rice plants. Its bright pink eggs are often seen stuck on stems.
Why is a snail's shell coiled? As the snail grows, new shell is added at the open edge, so it winds around in a spiral. Each turn of the spiral is called a whorl.
A snail has a single coiled, spiral shell that protects its soft body.
The thick slime helps protect the snail so it is not hurt even when crawling over sharp things.
A snail moves very slowly and only creeps along the ground little by little.
Because a snake is cold-blooded, it moves more slowly when it is cold and more actively when the weather is warm.

A snake has no thermostat, so to control its body heat it keeps moving back and forth: out into the sun when it gets cold, into the shade when it gets too hot. By shuttling like this it keeps its body at just the right warmth.
A cobra's fangs sit at the front of its mouth and stay fixed, unlike the long folding fangs of some other snakes.
A venomous snake has sharp fangs that it uses to inject venom into its victim.
If a snake loses or breaks a fang, a new fang grows in to replace it.
Some snakes like the cobra have hollow fangs that inject venom into their prey.
A snake has hundreds of tiny backbones, which let it bend and curve its body very easily.
A snake uses its forked tongue to smell the air and find prey.
A snake's forked, split tongue picks up tiny scent particles from the air.
Snakes do not chew; they swallow their prey whole after the venom kills it.
The Philippine cobra, a snake found in the Philippines, uses its tongue to smell out rats and other prey even in the dark of night, when it cannot see them well.
A snake's tongue is moist or a bit sticky, so tiny scent particles in the air cling to it more easily. It is like a damp cloth that picks up dust better than a dry one.
Some snakes have venom that they inject into prey through sharp fangs; not all snakes are venomous, and many have no venom at all.
A snake is a reptile with no legs, so it moves by sliding its body along the ground.
You should cover your mouth and nose when you sneeze or cough so germs do not spread to others.
A layer of snow acts like a blanket on the ground: because it traps a lot of air, it blocks the extreme cold and keeps the soil beneath from freezing even deeper.

In the Philippines, many local soaps are made from coconut oil, which our country has in abundance. Coconut oil is reacted with lye (a base), and through the saponification reaction it becomes soap. So the country's rich coconut supply can be turned into homemade soap.

In some places the water carries hard minerals that make soap hard to lather and leave a white scum. Detergent is human-made so those minerals do not affect it, so it cleans laundry more powerfully even in hard water.

Oil and water normally do not mix — they separate like fat floating on broth. Soap breaks the oil into very tiny droplets and wraps each one, so it stays spread out in the water. This kind of oil-in-water mixture is called an emulsion, like milk.

People discovered soap a very long time ago. They noticed that when animal fat mixed with the ash of burnt wood (which holds natural lye) and water, it became a slippery, cleaning substance. From this simple fat-and-ash mixture came the first soap, thousands of years ago.

When there is enough soap in water, its molecules group together into tiny balls called micelles. They point their oil-loving ends inward and their water-loving ends outward, so a droplet of grease gets trapped inside the ball and is carried off by the water.

When oil spills into the sea, responders sometimes spray a special detergent called a dispersant. Like dish soap, it breaks the thick oil into very tiny droplets that ocean bacteria can break down more easily. But it must be used carefully because it can also harm some sea animals.

Shampoo is a kind of soap made for hair. Our scalp makes a natural oil that leaves hair greasy and dirty over time. Shampoo breaks up and wraps this oil so water can rinse it away, leaving the hair clean.
Many viruses have a coat made of fat, and soap tears this coat apart so the virus falls apart.
The virus has a thin oily coat, and soap breaks this coat apart, which destroys the virus.
Soap helps remove grease and dirt because it lets oil and water mix together.
Grease does not dissolve in water, but soap helps because it grabs both oil and water so the grease can be washed away.
Soap helps oil mix into water as tiny droplets, and this mixture is called an emulsion.
Glycerin (glycerol) is a byproduct of soapmaking that moisturizes skin by attracting water; most commercial soap has the glycerin removed and sold separately as a skin care ingredient.
In hard water rich in calcium and magnesium minerals, soap forms an insoluble soap scum on surfaces, while synthetic detergents work effectively in hard water without forming scum.
Soap and household cleaners are usually bases.
Soap can be made from animal fat or from plant oils like coconut or palm. Both are fats, so both can react with a base to become soap.
Soap breaks down in nature more easily than some strong detergents. That is why in some places people prefer soap or 'biodegradable' products to avoid polluting rivers and soil.
Traditional soap is made by cooking fat or oil together with a strong chemical called lye.
Soap is important for health because it helps remove germs from your hands. Soap wraps and washes away the oily layer that some viruses and bacteria cling to, which lowers the chance of getting sick.
In 'hard water' that has lots of minerals like calcium, soap forms a thick scum instead of lather. This is why soap sometimes seems not to bubble well in certain places.
Each soap molecule has two ends: one end loves water, and the other end loves oil or grease. Because of this, soap can connect water and oil together.
Even though soap is made from fat or oil, it is not food and should not be eaten. The fat changed during the reaction and became soap, which can harm your body if swallowed.
In chemistry, soap is a kind of 'salt' formed from a fatty acid and a base. It is not the salt you put on food, but a chemical product made in a similar way.
The reaction between fat and a base to make soap has a special name: saponification. The word comes from the Latin word 'sapo,' which means soap.
In hard water, soap reacts with minerals and forms a sticky white scum that is hard to rinse off.
Hard water needs more soap because the first part of the soap is wasted reacting with minerals before any lather can form.
Many soap molecules surround a drop of oil to form a tiny ball around it.
Inside this ball, the oil-loving tails point into the grease while the water-loving heads face the water.
Soft drinks are acidic because of carbonic acid, which can damage teeth.
When salt forms, sodium gives one electron to chlorine, so sodium becomes a positive ion and chlorine becomes a negative ion.
Use a toothbrush with soft bristles and brush gently so the gums are not hurt.
Soft water is water that has very few dissolved minerals, like rainwater.

Contour farming is planting across (not down) slopes to slow runoff and stop soil washing away; the Banaue Rice Terraces are a famous Philippine example of terracing that protects soil and allows farming on steep mountains.
Decomposers like bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil.
Carbon collects in the soil from decaying dead plants and animals.
The C horizon is the soil layer made of partially weathered rock that the upper layers came from; it is not yet fully soil but is in the process of breaking down.
Soil is an earth material made of tiny bits of rock, bits of dead plants, air, and water, covering much of the land we walk on.
Loam is best for crops because it holds just the right amount of water, air, and nutrients.
A healthy soil microbiome with diverse bacteria and fungi supports crop growth by releasing nutrients, suppressing pests, and strengthening plant roots.
When the same soil is farmed over and over without rest, its nutrients get used up and it becomes less fertile.

According to soil science, soil forms under the influence of five main factors (CLORPT): (1) Climate, (2) Living organisms, (3) Relief (topography), (4) Parent material (the rock below), and (5) Time; changing any one of these factors produces a different type of soil.
Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline soil is; most crops grow best in neutral soil (pH about 6-7); acidic soil can be corrected by adding lime.
Each plant needs the right soil pH, so farmers add lime when the soil is too acidic.
When soil is sieved, large stones and gravel get separated from the fine sand and dust.
A solar panel works best when it faces the sun directly so it can catch the most light.
A solar cooker uses a large concave mirror to focus sunlight onto a single point, creating enough heat to cook food — useful in areas without electricity.
You can cook using just the sun: shiny mirrors gather sunlight onto one spot so it gets very hot, letting you cook food with no electricity or fuel at all.
A solar dryer uses the Sun's heat to dry fruits, fish, or rice by evaporating the water inside them, which helps the food keep longer without spoiling.
A solar eclipse can only happen at new moon, because that is the only time the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun.
The Sun and Moon look almost the same size in the sky because the Sun is much bigger but much farther, so the Moon can cover it.
A total solar eclipse can only be seen along a narrow path of Earth where the Moon's dark shadow falls.
A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, blocking its light so the Moon's shadow falls on Earth. It can only happen at new moon.
A solar eclipse can only happen during a new moon, because only then is the Moon between the Sun and Earth.
A safe way to view a solar eclipse is a pinhole projector, where light passes through a tiny hole and shows the Sun's shape on paper.
A solar eclipse is rarer for one village, so stories often mark it as a special darkening of the Sun, not as an everyday calendar tick.
An inverter changes the panel's DC electricity into AC, the kind used by appliances at home.
A solar panel still works on a cloudy day because it uses light, not heat — but it makes less electricity when thick clouds block the sun.
Surprisingly, a solar panel works less well when it gets too hot; so it can actually make more electricity on a sunny but cool day than at a scorching hot noon.

A solar panel does not make electricity by getting hot — instead, when light hits the special material (silicon) inside it, tiny particles called electrons are knocked loose, and that flow is the electricity.
A solar panel on a house roof turns sunlight into electricity that can power the things inside the house.

Many spacecraft and satellites, including the International Space Station, use solar panels to obtain their electricity from sunlight; the ISS has solar arrays covering nearly one acre total and can generate up to 120 kilowatts of power.
A solar panel makes electricity directly from sunlight, without a spinning turbine.
A solar panel turning sunlight into electricity is a modern check that the Sun's energy is real and useful, not only a story.
Solar panels on a roof make electricity from sunlight, which lowers the electricity a home must buy.
Solar energy works well for the Philippines because it is tropical and has many sunny days all year. Solar panels help bring electricity to far islands and barangays.
Satellites and space stations use solar panels to get electricity in space.
Solder is an alloy that melts at a low temperature, so it is used to join wires in electronic devices.
Solder is a low-melting alloy, traditionally tin and lead, used by electricians to join wires and components on circuit boards.

There are strong pulls, or attractions, between the particles of a solid that hold them tightly side by side. Because of these strong pulls, the particles do not drift apart, so the fixed shape is kept.
In a solid, the particles are packed tightly and orderly, so it keeps a fixed shape.
Solids can carry both types, which is why earthquake P-waves and S-waves can both travel through rock, unlike air which does not carry S-waves.
There are two kinds of wasps: social wasps that live in a large colony like bees, and solitary wasps that live and hunt alone.
Solubility is the largest amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a certain temperature.
Philippine salt must be iodized by law. Iodine is a mineral dissolved in the salt needed by the thyroid gland to function properly. Iodine deficiency can cause goitre.
More of a solid (like sugar or salt) usually dissolves in hot water than in cold — so when a saturated hot solution is cooled, the extra dissolved solid can come back out as crystals.

When a lake's water warms (for example, due to climate change or an algal bloom), its dissolved oxygen decreases. Fish and other aquatic animals need dissolved oxygen — if it gets too low, fish may die.
For most solids, the higher the water temperature, the more can dissolve; drawn on a graph, the line rises as the water gets hotter.
In saltwater the salt is the solute (what dissolves) and the water is the solvent (what dissolves it).
A solution stays mixed and does not separate even if it is left standing for a long time.
A solution is homogeneous, meaning it is evenly mixed throughout and often clear.
In a solution the particles are so tiny that they fully dissolve and cannot be seen.
A saturated solution is one that cannot dissolve any more solute because it is already full.
In a solution, the solute is the substance that dissolves (like sugar), and the solvent is the substance that does the dissolving (usually water). Together they make the solution.
Not all solutions are liquids—air is a solution of gases and bronze is a solid solution (an alloy).
A few fish such as catfish can gulp air at the water's surface to survive when oxygen is low.
Sonar measures how deep the sea is by timing how long the echo takes to return from the bottom.
A sonar ping used to find the seafloor is a longitudinal sound wave sent through water, then heard as an echo coming back.
A sonic boom is the loud bang made when an aircraft flies faster than the speed of sound.
A sonic boom happens when an aircraft goes faster than the speed of sound (Mach 1, about 343 m/s in air).
The black stain under a pot or on a wall near a stove is soot — carbon that collected from the smoke of burning fuel.
Soot is fine black powder — mostly pure carbon — that forms when fuel does not burn completely because there is not enough oxygen.
A useful class sort is two baskets: living things such as leaves, and earth materials such as stones, dry sand, and a cup of water.
Bone conduction transmits sound vibrations through the skull bones directly to the cochlea — used in special headphones and helpful for some types of hearing loss.
We cannot see sound, but we can hear it because it is a vibration moving through the air.
A difference: you cannot send a lasting side-to-side sound wave through air the way you send a transverse wiggle along a rope.
There is no sound in outer space because there is no air or matter for it to travel through.
Sound is a form of energy that moves from an object to our ears.
Sound gets fainter with distance because its energy spreads out over a larger and larger area — the further away, the quieter the sound.
Sound travels faster through solids and water than through air because their tiny particles are packed closer together.
Sound travels fastest through solids like steel, reaching about 5,000 m/s.
Sound travels faster in water than in air — about four times faster — which is why whale calls can reach so far across the ocean.
Sound travels faster in solids and liquids than in air — in steel sound moves at about 5,100 m/s, compared to about 343 m/s in air.
Sound travels fastest through solids like steel or wood, because their particles are packed close together and pass the vibration along quickly.
Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases like air.
Sound travels fastest through solids (like steel), faster than through water or air.
Even when the source is moving, sound in air is still a longitudinal wave; Doppler changes the spacing, not the side-to-side idea.
Sound is a longitudinal wave — air particles alternately compress together and spread apart in the same direction the sound travels.
Sound cannot travel through empty space because there is no air or other medium to carry it.
We see lightning before we hear thunder because light (300,000 km/s) travels much faster than sound (343 m/s).
Moving does not remove the need for air: the sound still travels through a medium, while Doppler only changes the spacing of those waves.
Sound is made by objects that vibrate, or shake back and forth quickly.

Sound travels faster through solids and water than through air. This is because the tiny particles in a solid are packed closer together, so they pass the sound along faster. That is why you can sometimes hear a coming train through the rails before you hear it through the air.

Sound does not travel only through air. It can also travel through solid things like wood, a table, or a wall. If you tap one end of a long table, your friend at the other end can hear it because the sound moved through the wood.
Sound is a form of energy that travels through the air as waves.
Soundscape ecology studies the overall sound of an environment — changes in the sounds of a forest or reef indicate ecosystem health and biodiversity changes.
The source is the thing making the sound, such as a horn, a bell, or a loudspeaker on a moving truck.
When a sounding object moves toward you, its sound waves bunch up, so you hear a higher pitch than when it stands still.
As long as the source is slower than sound, waves still get ahead of it; they are just closer together in the forward direction.
In southern skies, other patterns such as the Southern Cross were used to find south, so direction-finding worked without a northern pole star.
The Southern Cross is the constellation called Crux.
In space where there is almost no friction, a spacecraft can keep moving for a very long time even after its engine is off.
A space probe is a robotic craft with no people aboard, so it is sent to faraway planets that would be too dangerous for astronauts.

NASA's Space Shuttle was the first reusable spacecraft; it consisted of an orbiter, two solid rocket boosters, and an external fuel tank. The programme ran from 1981 to 2011 and completed 135 missions.

GPS satellites must correct their clocks by about 38 microseconds per day to remain accurate; this is due to two relativity effects: gravity (general relativity) slows time at Earth's surface, while speed (special relativity) speeds up time for the fast-moving satellites — the corrections partially cancel but not entirely.
When a spacecraft returns to Earth, it plunges into the atmosphere so fast that friction with the air makes it extremely hot, so it needs a heat shield to keep from burning up.
A spacesuit supplies oxygen, the right pressure, and protection from extreme heat and cold so an astronaut can survive in space.
During a spacewalk, an astronaut goes outside the spacecraft wearing a special suit to repair or build things on the outside.
If a cup might spill, put a spare cup on the materials list so one accident does not stop the whole investigation.
A speaker cone pushing air in and out launches a longitudinal sound wave, a household example of compressions leaving the speaker.
When two groups of one species stay separated for a long time, they can change enough to become different species.
A species is made up of organisms that can mate with one another and produce offspring that can themselves reproduce.
Water needs a lot of energy to raise its temperature, so it heats up slowly and cools down slowly — one reason the sea keeps coastal weather milder.
Water has a very high specific heat capacity — it needs a large amount of energy to heat up or cool down — this is why oceans warm and cool more slowly than land.
Each element emits light at a unique set of frequencies when heated — this pattern acts like a fingerprint and can identify elements even in distant stars.
The full spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays.
Speed is how fast something moves, meaning how far it travels in a certain amount of time.
A similarity is that mechanical waves of either kind change speed when they enter a different medium, such as air versus water versus rock.
Speed is found by dividing the distance traveled by the time it takes.
Light travels at a speed of about 300,000 kilometers per second.
Light is the fastest thing in the universe — nothing can travel faster than it.
The speed of light is about 299,792 kilometers per second, or nearly 300,000 km/s.
The speed of light is about 300,000 kilometers per second (exactly 299,792 km/s).
Light travels at about 300,000 kilometers per second.
In meters per second, the speed of light is about 300 million meters per second (299,792,458 m/s).
Because of the speed of light, sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth.
The speed of light is represented by the letter "c" in physics, as in the formula E = mc².
A scale difference: light, a transverse electromagnetic wave, is far faster than sound, a longitudinal mechanical wave in air.
Light is much faster than sound — that is why we see lightning before we hear the thunder.
Sound travels through air at about 343 meters per second, which is why we hear thunder after we see lightning.
Mach 1 means moving at the speed of sound (about 343 m/s); faster than that is called supersonic.
Sound travels faster in warmer air; at 20°C it is about 343 m/s.
The speed of sound in air is about 343 meters per second (about 1,235 km/h).
Sound travels through water at about 1,500 meters per second (m/s), faster than through air.
Sound travels faster in water than in air, at about 1,480 meters per second.
Speed is measured in units like kilometers per hour (km/h) or meters per second (m/s); each unit is a distance per time.

Speed is how fast an object moves, but acceleration is how fast its speed is CHANGING. You can be fast yet have no acceleration if your speed stays constant; you only have acceleration when you are speeding up or slowing down.

An airplane has two kinds of speed: airspeed (speed relative to the surrounding air) and ground speed (speed relative to the ground below). With a tailwind, the ground speed is higher so the flight arrives sooner; flying into a headwind, it is slower. That is why a return trip can take longer than the outbound one.

Suppose you travel 240 kilometers from Manila to a far city in 4 hours. Your average speed is 240 divided by 4, or 60 km/h. This means it is as if you went steadily at 60 km/h — even though sometimes you were fast and sometimes stopped along the way.

On a distance-time graph, the steepness of the line shows the speed. A steeper line means a faster object; a flat line means it is stopped (no distance is added as time passes). So you can read off the speed even before doing any calculation.

Speed and frequency are easy to mix up, but they are different. Speed is how fast something moves from one place to another, while frequency is how many times a motion repeats per second — like how fast a guitar string vibrates. High frequency means a high-pitched sound, not fast travel.

A speedometer measures speed by sensing how fast the wheel is spinning. The faster the wheel turns, the higher the speed it shows — because the machine knows the wheel's size, it can work out how far you travel each moment.

The faster a car goes, the longer the distance it needs to fully stop after the brakes are pressed. It does not just double — when you double the speed, the stopping distance grows more than double. This is why speeding on the road is dangerous.

The same speed can be written in different units. For example, 36 km/h is exactly the same as 10 meters per second — they are the same speed, just measured with different units. Always check the units before comparing two speeds, or you might draw the wrong conclusion.

Speleothems are rock ornaments that form in caves from dissolved calcite in dripping water; they include stalactites (hanging from the ceiling), stalagmites (growing from the floor), flowstone (flat sheets), and helictites (twisted bizarre shapes).
A testis is a factory for sperm: inside it, tiny tubes make the sperm cells and then send them onward.
A baby sperm whale drinks milk from its mother even underwater, just like other mammals.
The sperm whale breathes through a hole on top of its head called a blowhole, so it must come up to the surface to breathe.
Besides finding food, sperm whales also use patterns of clicks to talk with their family.
The sperm whale is a large toothed whale that dives very deep to hunt squid. It is also found in the deep seas of the Philippines.
In the dark deep sea where there is no light, the sperm whale uses loud clicking sounds to find food — like a ship's sonar.
The sperm whale's click is one of the loudest sounds made by any animal on Earth — louder even than a jet plane.
Before it drops, a spider first sticks the end of its dragline to a surface so the line has a firm anchor.
Many kids think spider silk comes from the mouth, but it actually comes out from the tip of the belly, not the mouth.
Dragline silk is dry and not sticky, which is why the spider can walk on it—unlike the sticky web threads used to trap prey.
As it moves, a spider trails a silk line like a safety rope to catch itself if it falls.
Dragline silk is amazingly strong for how light it is, so it does not snap easily even though it is thin.
A dragline is often made of two thin threads laid side by side and joined, which makes it stronger.
To grow bigger, a spider must shed the old hard skin on the outside of its body.
A spider is not an insect but an arachnid, in the same group as scorpions.
Some spiders spin a round, wheel-shaped web called an orb web.
A young spider can regrow a lost leg each time it sheds its old skin while growing.
Spider silk is a runny liquid inside the spider, but it hardens into thread once it comes out into the air.
A spider walks on the non-sticky threads so it does not get stuck in its own web.
A spider does not stick to its own web because the radial threads it walks on are not sticky; only the spiral catching threads are covered with sticky droplets.
A spider makes a web from its own silk, which is surprisingly strong, to catch the insects it eats.
Some threads in the web are sticky, so a trapped insect sticks and cannot escape.
A spider uses its web as a trap to catch flying insects.
A spider has eight (8) legs, and it is not an insect but an arachnid.
