Injury to the spinal cord can block signals from the brain to muscles, causing loss of movement (paralysis) in parts of the body below the injury.
The spinal cord is protected by the back bones called vertebrae.
The spine is the line of small bones in the back that helps us stand up straight.
Between the spine's bones are soft discs that act like cushions so the bones do not rub together.
Nerves branch out from the spine, carrying messages between the brain and the rest of the body.
Spinosaurus reached about 15 meters long, longer than Tyrannosaurus rex.
Spinosaurus reached about 15 meters long, even longer than Tyrannosaurus rex.

Spiral arms of galaxies do not contain more stars than elsewhere; rather they are regions of denser interstellar gas and dust where the most new star formation occurs, producing bright blue stars that illuminate the arm's shape.
The spleen removes old and damaged red blood cells and recycles some of their parts.
A sponge is an animal that pulls water through its tiny pores and filters food from it.
Sponges reproduce by making tiny swimming larvae that float in the water before settling down to grow.
Sponges serve as a home and shelter for small fish, shrimp, and other sea animals.
A single sponge can filter a huge amount of water each day, far more than its own size.
Some old bath sponges were really made from the soft bodies of true sea sponges.
Many sponges have tiny hard parts called spicules that give the body its shape and support.
Ferns do not flower; they reproduce through spores—the brown spots (sori) visible on the underside of fern leaves contain millions of spores that can grow into new plants.
If you set a mushroom cap on paper for a few hours, it leaves a pretty colored pattern made of the millions of tiny spores that fall from underneath it.
A spore is different from a seed — it is dust-tiny, has no stored food inside, and comes from plants like ferns and mosses.
To keep the Visayan spotted deer from disappearing, there are programs that care for and breed it on Negros and Panay.
The spotted dove (batobato) is a dove-like bird with a black-and-white spotted patch on its neck, often seen in fields and yards, and it eats seeds and grains.
The spotted hyena has a very strong bite that can crush the bones of large animals.
If a small gland sits under a bladder and a pouch of two ovals hangs outside, the diagram is male.
If two oval organs sit beside a pear-shaped center, the picture is showing ovaries beside the uterus.
The spring constant (k) measures how stiff a spring is — a high k means more force is needed to stretch or compress it by the same distance.
Elastic deformation is reversible — the material returns to its original shape; plastic deformation is permanent — the material stays in its new shape even after the force is removed.
Many toys and click pens work using a spring that stores energy when squeezed and lets it out when released.
Hooke's law states that the force of a spring equals its spring constant multiplied by how much it is stretched or compressed.
The more a spring is stretched, the stronger the force it pushes back with.
A spring scale weighs things by measuring how far the spring stretches when an object hangs from it.
In the Northern Hemisphere, the March equinox marks the start of spring.
A stretched or compressed spring stores energy that can push an object when it is released.
A spring returns to its original shape after you release it once you have stretched or squeezed it.
The suspension springs of a vehicle support its weight and absorb the energy of road bumps so passengers feel a smoother ride.
A spring tide (the highest tides) happens at new moon and full moon, when the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up.
A pulse sent down a long spring lying on the floor, by pushing the end, is a longitudinal example you can see as a bunching of coils.
In a jack-in-the-box toy, the spring is held compressed inside the box; when the lid opens, the spring's stored energy pushes the figure up suddenly.
A spring scale measures weight by using Hooke's law: the spring stretches in proportion to the force (weight) applied to it, and a scale reads the stretch.
Sputnik 1 was launched on October 4, 1957.
When you squeeze a gas into a smaller space, its particles hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises. That is why a syringe feels harder to push when you cover the tip and press the plunger.
Squid and cuttlefish are carnivores that eat small fish, shrimp, and other little sea animals.
Squid and cuttlefish have fins along their body that help them glide and steer gently through the water.
The giant squid is one of the largest invertebrates and can grow several meters long in the deep sea.
Unlike most mollusks with external shells, the squid has a small internal shell called a gladius or 'pen' — transparent and plastic-like — that provides structural support to its body.
A squid has no outer shell; instead it has a thin, flexible internal support called a pen.
Squid and cuttlefish have three hearts: two pump blood through the gills and one pumps it to the rest of the body.
Many squirrels bury their nuts in the ground one at a time, hiding them until they need the food.
A stadium crowd wave is a transverse-style example: people stand and sit while the 'wave' travels sideways around the stands.
Staghorn coral (Acropora) is one of the fastest-growing corals, with branches resembling a deer's antlers; it is vital to reef building.
Stainless steel (steel that resists rust) was discovered by Harry Brearley.

Stainless steel is also used in buildings, bridges, and stair railings. Because it is not easily damaged by rain, wind, and weather, it lasts a very long time without needing much paint or repair. So it saves money in the long run even if it costs more at first.

Not all steel is stainless. To be stainless, the steel must contain enough chromium inside it, usually at least about 10 to 11 percent. Ordinary steel that lacks chromium rusts easily, while steel with enough chromium stays shiny. So the amount of chromium is what matters.
Stainless steel resists rust because it contains the metal chromium.

Stainless steel was discovered in the early 1900s in Sheffield, England by a scientist named Harry Brearley. While he was looking for steel that would not wear out inside gun barrels, he noticed that the batch mixed with chromium did not rust. Since then it has become a very important material worldwide.

Not all stainless steel is the same; there are different types or grades made for different purposes. Some grades are food-safe and used for cutlery, while other tougher grades are used in buildings or machines. The difference comes from what elements are mixed in.

Many rings, watches, and necklaces are made of stainless steel. Because it does not rust and is gentle on the skin, fewer people get itching or allergies from it compared with other cheap metals. That makes it good to wear daily even when damp with sweat.

The chromium in stainless steel reacts with oxygen in the air and forms an extremely thin, invisible film called chromium oxide. This film shields the steel underneath from rusting. You cannot see it, but it is why stainless steel stays shiny.

Even though stainless steel resists rust well, it is not completely impossible to rust. In salty places like near the sea, the salt in the air can slowly damage the protective film over time. So even stainless still needs proper care in harsh environments.

When stainless steel gets scratched, you might think the metal will start to rust there. But the chromium inside immediately reacts with oxygen again and builds a fresh protective film. It is like the metal heals itself, so it stays protected even with scratches.

In hospitals, surgical tools like scissors and scalpels are made of stainless steel. Because it does not rust and can be easily sterilized with hot steam, it stays clean and safe for patients. This matters so the tools do not spread infection.

As rainwater passes through air and soil, it picks up a little carbon dioxide and turns into a weak acid that can dissolve limestone — that is why the water dripping into a cave carries dissolved mineral.
Scientists use stalagmites like a book of the past — inside they have ring-like layers, and by reading these layers they can learn how wet or dry the climate was thousands of years ago.
Most stalactites are white because they are pure calcite, but if other minerals like rusting iron mix in, the formation can turn reddish, brown, or yellow.

Stalactites and stalagmites are not the only cave shapes — when mineral water flows down a wall instead of dripping, it can build smooth 'flowstone' or thin sheets of rock that look like hanging curtains.

Many kids ask: can they grow fast? In a natural cave it is very slow, but tiny 'stalactites' under a concrete bridge or building can grow much faster because cement dissolves easily — though these are weak and not true cave rock.
When a stalactite and a stalagmite meet, they form a stone column in the cave.
Stalactites do not form in every cave — they need limestone rock that water can easily dissolve, so you will not find them in caves made of hard, non-dissolving rock like granite.
Even though we say a stalactite 'grows,' it is not alive like a plant — it is just rock that gets bigger as thin mineral layers pile up from dripping water; it does not eat or breathe.
The water dripping in a cave comes from rain on the ground above that slowly seeps down through tiny cracks in the rock until it reaches the cave ceiling and begins to drip.
Stalactites in a cave grow incredibly slowly — often only about a centimeter every few hundred years — so the big ones have been built by dripping water for thousands of years.
Inside a cave, stalactites grow down from the ceiling and stalagmites grow up from the floor as mineral-filled water drips over many years.
A stalagmite is a stone mound that grows upward from the cave floor.
A person standing still beside a road can still hear the Doppler change, because the sounding vehicle is the moving source.
Standing waves form when reflected waves combine with incoming waves — nodes are points of no movement, and antinodes are points of maximum displacement.
The stapes, or stirrup bone, inside the ear is the smallest bone in the human body and helps transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear.
Betelgeuse is a famous red star in the constellation Orion — you can spot its reddish color in the night sky. Its red color is a sign that its surface is cooler than hot blue or white stars.

Astronomers sort stars into groups based on their color and temperature, from the hottest (blue) to the coolest (red). Our Sun falls in a middle group (yellowish-white). This lets them quickly tell a star's temperature just from its color.

In photos from large telescopes, the true colors of stars stand out — some reddish, some blue, some yellow, all together in one image. From this, scientists can tell at a glance which stars in the picture are hot and which are cool.
A star's color shows how hot it is: blue stars are the hottest and red stars are the coolest.

When we say a red star is 'cool,' it is not cold like ice! 'Cool' here is only compared to other stars — a red star's surface is still extremely hot, hot enough to glow. So they are only 'cool' in the world of stars.
What happens to a star at the end depends on its mass: small stars become cooling white dwarfs, while very massive stars explode and leave behind a neutron star or a black hole.
The birth and death of stars is still going on right now — as old stars die, new stars are being born inside clouds of gas and dust.
The nearest star to our Sun is Proxima Centauri at about 4.2 light-years away; even though it is the closest, a fast rocket using current technology would still take over 70,000 years to reach it.
When starch like cornstarch is heated in water, the granules swell and dissolve, thickening the liquid — this gelatinization process is used to thicken gravies and soups.
A starfish's mouth is in the center of the underside of its body, so it must press down onto its food in order to eat.
Even though it is called 'starfish' in English, a sea star is not really a fish because it has no backbone or fins like a fish; that is why it is also called a 'sea star'.
The keystone species idea was discovered when a scientist removed starfish from a shore, and mussels multiplied so much that other species disappeared.
Many starfish and sea urchins reproduce by releasing their eggs and sperm into the water, where they join together and grow into new baby animals.
Ancient cultures used constellations as a night compass because the same star patterns sit in the same directions night after night.
They also used constellations as a seasonal clock, because the pattern that rises just after sunset changes slowly through the year.
Stars come in many sizes; some are smaller than the Sun, and others are hundreds of times bigger.
Travelers long ago used familiar stars to keep direction at night, so those sky objects affected how people crossed land or water after dark.
After the Big Bang, gas slowly gathered because of gravity and formed the first stars and galaxies.
A star's color tells its temperature: blue stars are the hottest, while red stars are cooler.
Stars have a life cycle; they are born, shine for millions of years, and finally die.
Not every bright-looking star is huge. Sometimes a star looks bright just because it is close to us. Some truly giant, powerful stars look dim only because they are extremely far away.
A star shines because of nuclear fusion, where hydrogen atoms join together and release huge amounts of energy.
A star's color tells us how hot its surface is. Blue stars are the hottest, while red and orange stars are cooler. Our yellow Sun is somewhere in the middle.
Stars are not all the same size. Some small ones are called dwarfs, and some huge ones are called giants or supergiants that are much bigger than our Sun. They also differ in heat and brightness.
The main fuel of most stars is hydrogen, the simplest gas in the universe. In fusion, hydrogen is joined together to make helium, releasing huge amounts of energy that becomes the star's light.
Starlight travels for a very long time before reaching Earth. Some stars are so far that the light we see left them many years ago. In a way, we are looking into the past.

Stars seem to twinkle because their light passes through the thick moving air of our atmosphere. The shifting air bends the light, making it look like it shivers. The star itself is not really flickering.

Cepheid variable stars are stars that regularly change in brightness in a predictable pattern; the period of their brightness cycle is directly related to their true luminosity. Astronomers use this relationship as a 'standard candle' to measure distances across the universe.
The stars in a galaxy come in different colors — bluish stars are hotter, while red and orange stars are cooler.
Indigenous night watchers could see star groups drift westward overnight, a repeating motion they used as a clock long before wristwatches.
A simple investigation starts by writing a clear problem, such as which material dries faster, so you know what you are trying to find out.
Whether matter is a solid, liquid, or gas depends on how hot or cold it is.
Changes of state can be reversed—ice can melt back into water, and water can freeze again.
In solids, particles are packed close together and only vibrate; in liquids, they are close but move around; in gases, they are far apart and move quickly.
In everyday Philippine life we see all three states of matter: ice in halo-halo is a solid, tap water is a liquid, and steam from cooking is a gas.
The fourth state of matter is plasma, found in the sun and in lightning.
The three common states of matter are solid, liquid, and gas.

Why do plastic or balloons get static easily but metal doesn't? On plastic and rubber, the charge can't move around, so it stays put and builds up. On metal, charge flows away quickly, so it's hard to build static while you're holding it.

Is static attraction stronger up close or far away? It's stronger when the two objects are close, and it gets weak quickly as you move them apart. That's why you have to bring the charged object really close to pick up small bits of paper.

Have you noticed it's harder to make static here in the Philippines? Our air is often humid (a bit moist), and the water in the air carries charge away before it can build up. On dry days or in an air-conditioned room, you'll feel static more easily.

How does static charge leave an object? When it touches a large piece of metal or the ground, the extra charge flows out into the ground. This is called grounding. After that, it can no longer pull paper because the charge is gone.

Why does a charged object pull paper that has no charge? When the charged object comes close, the charges inside the paper shift a little: the opposite charge moves to the near side. So the neutral paper ends up being attracted, even though overall it has no charge.

Static has real-life uses! In car factories, the paint droplets are given a charge, and the object being painted is given the opposite charge. So the object pulls the paint in and it coats evenly, even on the back side.

What's the difference between static and flowing current? Static is charge that stays in one place and lets go suddenly, like a spark. Flowing current keeps moving steadily through wires to light a bulb or run a device. They are two forms of electricity.
Ball lightning is a rare phenomenon where a glowing ball appears during or after a thunderstorm — science has not yet fully explained what causes it.
Static charge stays longer on plastic or rubber because charge does not flow through them, but it escapes quickly through metal.
A comb rubbed on hair becomes charged, so it can pull and bend a thin stream of water toward it.
When you walk on a carpet or rug, you can pick up static charge. When you then touch a metal doorknob, the charge suddenly leaves as a tiny spark, so you feel a small electric 'shock'.
Static is easier to feel when the air is dry, because damp or humid air carries the built-up charge away quickly.
In the Philippines' dry season (March to May), static shocks from touching metal are more common because dry air does not easily carry away built-up charge.
Static electricity is stronger and more common when the air is dry, like on cold or low-humidity days. In damp or humid air, the charge leaks away more easily, so sparks are rarer.
Benjamin Franklin experimented that lightning is electricity using a kite in 1752.
Static charge comes from the movement of tiny particles called electrons. When two objects rub, one loses electrons (becomes positive) and the other gains electrons (becomes negative).

When a known positively charged object is brought near an electroscope already carrying positive charge, the leaves spread further — this method is used to determine whether an unknown charge is positive or negative.
Rubbing two materials together (friction) is the most common cause of static charge. As they rub, tiny charges move from one material to the other, so they end up with opposite charges.
At petrol stations, vehicles must be grounded before fueling because a small static spark can ignite gasoline vapor and cause a fire.

Try this: rub a balloon on your hair to give it static, then it sticks to the wall. But when you touch it with a wet hand or set it on metal, the sticking suddenly stops — the balloon grounded, the charge flowed out, and it became neutral again.

Did you know your own body can act as a path to the ground? People conduct electricity somewhat. If you are standing with no rubber in between, charge can flow from your hand, through your body, down to your feet and into the ground.

In the Philippines, where the air is often humid, static charge leaks away faster. Why? The thin layer of water in humid air acts as a path for charge to slowly drain to the ground. That is why static shocks happen more in dry climates than in damp ones.

It is a misconception that charge 'disappears' when something is grounded. In truth, charge is not destroyed — the electrons are just moved into the huge Earth where they spread out and are no longer noticeable. It only moved; it did not vanish.

Have you noticed some plugs have three pins? The third pin is the ground wire. If electricity leaks onto the metal body of an appliance, the ground wire carries it safely down to the ground, so you won't get shocked when you touch it.

Kids often ask: how do I avoid the stinging spark? One trick: before grabbing a doorknob, first touch metal or a wall slowly with one finger. The charge drains out gradually, so there is no big spark to feel.

In many homes, the electrical system is connected to a metal water pipe buried in the ground. Why? Because the long metal pipe is a good conductor down to the moist soil, so it serves as a safe path for any extra electricity.
When every strand of hair has the same charge, the strands push away from each other so the hair rises and spreads out.
By induction, an object can be charged without touching it — a nearby charged object causes charge separation inside the neutral object.
A lightning rod on top of a Philippine building has a sharp metal tip that attracts lightning and carries its current safely down a copper or steel wire into the ground.
Lightning reaches a temperature of about 30,000 Kelvin — about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun — which is why it is so brief yet blindingly bright.
In static electricity it is the light electrons that move, not the heavier protons that stay in the atom.
The photoelectric effect is light knocking electrons out of a metal — Einstein showed that light travels in energy packets called photons. This is the principle behind solar cells.
An electrostatic precipitator in factories uses static charge to attract tiny smoke and dust particles before they are released into the air, reducing air pollution.
Small static shocks from touching metal after walking on carpet are generally harmless — they are very different from the dangerous 220-volt household electricity used in the Philippines.

There are simple ways to avoid a surprising spark: put lotion on your skin so it is not too dry, use fabric softener in the wash, or touch metal first with a key so the charge jumps to the key instead of your finger. All of these help the charge leave gently.

When you rub a balloon on your hair, charge moves and builds up. Your hair stands on end and the balloon sticks to the wall because of it. If enough charge piles up, it can even come out as a tiny spark—this is how static gets started.

When clothes rub together, especially fabrics that charge up easily, static builds up. That is why clothes sometimes cling to your skin or to each other, and you hear a little 'tick' when you pull them apart—those are tiny sparks.
A spark happens when the built-up static charge suddenly jumps from one object to another, sometimes even crossing through the air. This quick movement of charge is called a discharge.

When two things rub together, tiny bits of charge called electrons move from one to the other. The extra charge piles up on one object until there is a lot, and when it gets near another object the charge suddenly jumps across—that jump is the spark.
A tiny spark happens when built-up charge suddenly jumps across the air to another object.

Lightning is like a giant static spark in the sky. In a cloud, charge builds up just like on your body, and when there is too much, it jumps between the cloud and the ground—that is lightning. Same idea, but lightning is millions of times bigger.

A static spark is different from the electricity that flows in a wire. Static builds up and jumps for just a moment, then stops. The electricity from a battery or socket flows steadily as long as there is a path. Both are 'electricity', but they behave differently.

There are two kinds of charge: positive and negative. If one object has too much negative and another has too little, they want to balance out. The spark happens when the extra charge jumps across to the side that is short, so both objects return to balance.

Inside a cumulonimbus cloud, ice particles collide — large particles move downward carrying negative charge while small crystals rise with positive charge, creating charge separation that leads to lightning.
Thunder is the sound made when lightning suddenly heats and expands the air around it.
Static charge stays in one place, while the current flowing in a wire keeps moving along.
The triboelectric series is a list of materials showing which becomes positively or negatively charged when rubbed together.
Static electricity is different from current electricity. In static, charge gathers and stays still on a surface; in current, charge flows steadily through a circuit, like the electricity in a light.
An object is in equilibrium when all the forces acting on it balance — the net force equals zero and the object does not accelerate.
The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France to the United States.
When there is lightning and thunder, it is safest to go inside a sturdy building or house.
Steam at 100°C causes worse burns than boiling water at 100°C — when steam condenses on skin it releases extra latent heat on top of the heat from its temperature.
The steam engine, improved by James Watt in the 1700s, uses the steam of boiling water to power machines, and it led to the rise of factories, trains, and ships.
Thomas Newcomen built the first useful steam engine in 1712, before Watt improved it.
A steam engine works by using steam from boiling water to push a piston.
James Watt, a Scottish engineer, greatly improved the steam engine in the 1760s-1770s to make it far more efficient.
James Watt patented his separate condenser for the steam engine in 1769.

Steam carries extra heat energy from being boiled. That's why a steam burn hurts more than boiling water — the steam releases that stored extra heat when it touches your skin. Be careful around steam!

Steam is water in its gas form. Water has three forms: ice (solid), liquid water, and steam (gas). They are all the same water — only the form changes depending on heat. Heat is what changes water from liquid into the gas we call steam.
Why does a kettle whistle? When the water boils, lots of steam wants to rush out the kettle's tiny hole all at once. The steam squeezing fast through the narrow opening makes the whistling sound.
Steam from a kettle is the earth material water as a gas; it is non-living, like the liquid water it came from.
George Stephenson, known as the "Father of Railways," built early steam locomotives.
Steam (water vapor) is the gas state of water.
Steel is an alloy made of iron and a small amount of carbon.

Plain iron rusts easily when it gets wet and exposed to air. That's why many steels have other ingredients added or are coated with paint or a layer to stop rust. Stainless steel is the best example—because of added chromium, it doesn't easily rust compared to plain iron.

How is steel made? First, iron is melted in a very hot furnace until it becomes like liquid. Then, the right amount of carbon and other ingredients are mixed in while it's still hot. When it cools down, it becomes a hard block of steel that can be shaped into many forms.

It's a wrong idea that just mixing any two things will instantly make something stronger. Not every mixture gets stronger—many mixtures actually become weaker. Steel is special because it's the RIGHT amount of carbon mixed with iron that gives the strength. It doesn't just happen with any random mixing.

You won't find 'steel' on the periodic table because it is not an element. Iron and carbon are separate elements on the periodic table, but steel is just a mix of them—a mixture, not a new element. That's why steel has no symbol of its own like Fe for iron.

One great property of steel is that it can be recycled. Old steel like broken cars or cans can be melted again and turned into new steel without losing its strength. That's why a lot of new steel today comes from old scrap metal—this is good for the environment.

The 'stainless steel' used in spoons, forks, and sinks is a type of steel with the metal chromium added. Chromium forms a thin protective layer on the surface that stops rust. That's why stainless steel doesn't rust even when it gets wet often.
Steel is iron mixed with a little carbon, which makes it stronger and harder to break than pure iron, so it is used in big buildings and bridges.

Many people think that the more carbon you add, the stronger steel becomes. That's not always true. When there is too much carbon, the steel does get harder but it also becomes brittle—it snaps easily like chalk instead of bending. That's why only the right amount of carbon is mixed in.

Many tools like knives, bolos, scissors, and hammers are made of steel. Because steel is hard and tough, it can stay sharp for a long time and doesn't easily wear down or bend. If only soft pure iron were used, it would quickly go dull and break with use.
A plant's stem bends and grows toward where the light comes from.
Leaves and flowers grow attached to the plant's stem.
Plant stems show negative gravitropism—they grow upward, against the direction of gravity—so the leaves can reach sunlight for photosynthesis.
As a plant gets older, its stem grows thicker and stronger.
Good steps say how long to wait, how many times to stir, and what to look for, so the doing part is not a guess.
Keep the written steps in the notebook while you work, because a plan that lives only in someone's head is easy to change by accident.
A stethoscope is used to listen to sounds inside the body, like the heartbeat and the breath in the lungs.
The eggs of some stick insects have a fatty part that ants like. The ants carry the eggs underground, eat the fatty part, and the eggs stay protected until they hatch.
In most stick insects, the female is bigger and longer than the male. The female needs a larger body to carry many eggs.
Many stick insects have no wings or only tiny wings, so they cannot fly.
Many stick insects can reproduce by parthenogenesis—females lay unfertilized eggs that hatch into female clones without any male involvement.
The stigma is the sticky top of the pistil that catches the pollen that lands on it.
If both the sound source and the listener stay still, the pitch does not slide up or down from motion.
A stinging plant's hair is like tiny glass; its tip breaks off and pricks the skin like a needle.
Nettle is a plant with tiny stinging hairs that cause a strong itch when touched.
The Philippines has native stingless bees (pukyutan) that also produce honey; they are smaller than regular bees and cannot sting.
A stingray eats clams, shrimp, and small fish on the sea floor.
A stingray's eyes are on top of its body while its mouth is underneath to eat from the sea floor.
The stingray has a sharp spine on its tail coated in protein venom; this is used for defense, not attack — most stings happen when a stingray lying under sand is accidentally stepped on.
A stirring rod is used in the lab to mix liquids, which speeds up how fast substances dissolve and blend together.
In the stomach, food is mixed with juices and acid that break it down into smaller pieces before it moves on to the intestines.
Stomach acid is so strong it can break down food, yet it does not digest the stomach itself because a thick layer of mucus protects the stomach's lining.
The stonefish hides like a rock on the seafloor and has sharp venom-filled spines along its back.
A flat palm held toward someone is a movement that often means stop, a message many people can read even in a noisy street.
Stop when the written steps end and then write the finding; adding extra unplanned tests can scramble what you can honestly claim.
An object that is at rest and not moving has no kinetic energy.
The faster a vehicle moves, the longer the distance it needs to come to a complete stop, because it has more momentum and motion energy to lose.
PAGASA raises five levels of storm signal, from Signal No. 1 up to Signal No. 5, based on how strong the wind is expected to be in an area.
In a narrow or funnel-shaped bay, storm surge water gets trapped and rises even higher.
In many strong typhoons, the storm surge is the deadliest hazard, killing more people than the wind itself.
A storm surge is a sudden rise of seawater pushed onto the coast by a typhoon's strong winds, and it can cause serious flooding.
Mangrove forests along the coast help weaken the force of a storm surge and protect communities.
The height of a storm surge is measured in meters, based on how far the water rises above the normal sea level.
The safest thing to do when a storm surge threatens is to evacuate to higher ground far from the sea.
PAGASA issues storm surge warnings to alert coastal communities before a typhoon arrives.
With a higher sea, storm surges from typhoons reach farther inland and cause worse flooding.
Generally, the stronger the typhoon's winds, the higher and more dangerous the storm surge it brings.
A storm surge is different from a tsunami: a storm surge is caused by a typhoon, while a tsunami is caused by an earthquake or movement under the sea.
PAGASA's storm surge warnings come in different levels depending on the expected height of the water, from low to most dangerous.
On top of the rising water, large wind-driven waves ride over the storm surge and add to the destruction.
Many people die in storm surges because they do not expect the water to rise so fast and so high.
In 2013, the storm surge from Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) in Tacloban reached more than five to six meters high and killed thousands of people.
PAGASA issues storm warning signals before and during a typhoon so people can know how strong the coming winds will be and when to take cover.
At STP (standard temperature and pressure), the temperature is 0 °C (273.15 K) and the pressure is 1 atmosphere.
A straight metal barrier in the tank is the wall you use to watch reflection; curve it and the bounced pattern changes shape too.
A kitchen strainer separates cooked or washed food from water by letting the water drain through its holes.
The stratosphere holds the ozone layer, which absorbs the Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays.
Scientists measure ozone using satellites in space and special balloons that rise into the stratosphere. This lets them watch whether the ozone hole is growing or healing each year.
Long ago, many spray cans and refrigerators used CFCs that destroyed ozone. Today, almost all products have switched to safer ingredients, so an ordinary spray no longer harms the ozone layer.
The air we breathe contains oxygen made of two atoms (O2). Ozone, on the other hand, is made of three oxygen atoms (O3). It is great at blocking UV up high, but it is toxic if we breathe it in.

It is a mistake to think the ozone hole causes global warming. They are two different problems: the ozone hole is about UV getting through, while global warming is caused by greenhouse gases trapping heat on Earth.
Unlike the layer below it, the stratosphere gets warmer as you go up. This is because ozone absorbs UV and turns it into heat. That makes the air there very stable, with little rain or storms.
Jet airplanes fly in the lower stratosphere because the air there is calmer and free of stormy weather.
Stratovolcanoes often erupt violently and explosively because their lava is thick and sticky.
Another name for a stratovolcano is a composite volcano, because it is built of mixed lava and ash.

Most active Philippine volcanoes (such as Mayon and Pinatubo) are stratovolcanoes (composite cones): they have steep sides and are built of alternating layers of lava and pyroclastic material; they can erupt very explosively because of their thick, viscous lava.
Many Philippine volcanoes are steep stratovolcanoes, so hot flows and rocks often race down the same valleys used in past eruptions.
When a straw is placed in a glass of water, it appears bent at the water-air boundary because light refracts as it passes from water into air.
A mineral's streak color is often different from its surface color, so streak is more reliable.
A streak plate is a piece of unglazed porcelain tile used to make a mineral's streak.
A smooth, pointed (streamlined) shape lowers air resistance because air slips around it easily. That is why airplanes, race cars, and birds have tapered fronts.
An acid's strength is different from its concentration: strength is how readily it releases H+, while concentration is how much acid is dissolved in the water.
On the other side of the same drawing, the circles are more spread out, which is why that listener hears a lower sound.
A stretched rubber band stores energy, and when released it uses that energy to launch itself or whatever is hooked on it forward.
The stretched rubber of a slingshot stores energy that sends the stone flying when released.
When you stretch or press a spring, you do work that is stored in it as energy.
When a string is tightened, it vibrates faster and the sound gets higher—this is how instruments are tuned.
When a string is pulled tighter, its note gets higher—this is why we tune a guitar.
A flashing strobe can freeze the pattern so you can measure crest spacing while the real water is still moving.
The faster the wind blows, the more electricity a turbine can make.
The strongest insect is the dung beetle (Onthophagus taurus), which can pull 1,141 times its own body weight.
Concrete is very strong in compression but weak in tension; steel is strong in both — this is why they are combined in reinforced concrete to use each material's strengths.
Diagonal bracing adds triangles inside a rectangular building frame — preventing the frame from racking (leaning sideways) under lateral forces like wind or earthquakes.
Earthquakes apply strong lateral (sideways) forces to buildings — structural engineers design stiff bracing and shear walls to resist these seismic forces.
A building's foundation transfers the total weight of the building safely into the ground — it must be wide and deep enough to distribute the load without the ground collapsing.
Suspension bridges can span the greatest distances of any bridge type — long cables carry the load to tall towers, enabling spans of hundreds or even thousands of metres.

The angle at which a plate subducts affects the position of the volcanic arc; a steeper subduction angle places the volcanic arc closer to the trench; different angles in different parts of the Philippine subduction system shift where volcanoes appear.
When one plate sinks beneath another, it melts and forms magma that rises to create volcanoes.
Around the Philippines, one plate slides beneath another in a process called subduction, forming deep ocean trenches.
Along the Ring of Fire, one plate sinks beneath another in a process called subduction, melting rock into magma that feeds volcanoes.
Camphor can turn directly from a solid into a gas without first becoming a liquid, a process called sublimation.
In freeze-drying, the frozen water in food sublimates out so the food stays dry and lasts longer.
In sublimation, a solid turns straight into a gas without first becoming a liquid. Examples are dry ice that seems to 'smoke', and mothballs that slowly shrink until they disappear.
In sublimation, some molecules at the surface of a solid gain enough energy to escape and become gas.
Even snow and ice can sublimate, so they can slowly disappear without melting into water.
Sublimation is when a solid changes straight into a gas without first becoming a liquid.
When normal ice melts it becomes water first, but dry ice turns directly into gas with no water left behind.
The Turtle, built by David Bushnell in 1775, is considered the first submarine used in war.
A pure substance is made of only one kind of particle, while a mixture contains two or more different substances physically combined.
At a substation, the high voltage is lowered before the electricity is distributed to homes in an area.
In subtractive colour mixing used in paints and printers, the primary colours are cyan, magenta, and yellow — each absorbs certain light wavelengths when mixed.
Sugar can also come from sugar beets, a root crop grown mostly in cooler countries.
After eating sweets, mouth bacteria produce acid for about 20 minutes; this is why rinsing with water soon after eating sugary foods helps reduce acid attack on enamel.
Sugarcane is a tall grass that stores sweet juice inside its stalk, and sugar is made from that juice.
When you stir sugar into water, it dissolves and seems to disappear, but it is still in the water.
Sugary drinks like soda and juice increase the risk of cavities because they provide sugar for mouth bacteria to produce acid that erodes tooth enamel.
Boiling does not create more sugar — the sugar was already in the juice. Only the water evaporates away, leaving the sugar more concentrated.
The chemical formula of table sugar (sucrose) is C12H22O11.
Lots of sugar in jam pulls water out of microbes, which helps the food last longer.
Salt needs much more heat to melt (801°C) than sugar, which already caramelizes at about 160°C.
Bagasse is the leftover cane stalk after juice extraction; it can be burned as biofuel to generate electricity, or used as raw material for making paper and cardboard.
In making sugar, the substance changes form: from liquid juice, to thick syrup, to solid sugar crystals — these are physical changes.
Negros Occidental is known as the sugar capital of the Philippines; a large portion of the country's sugarcane is grown there and the sugar industry is vital to the province's economy.
Sugarcane stores sucrose—a type of sugar—inside the internodes of its stem; this stored juice is the source of table sugar.
The sweet substance in sugarcane is a kind of sugar called sucrose — the same white sugar we use at home.
The sugpo, or tiger prawn, is one of the animals raised in Philippine fishponds to be sold as food.
Summer is hotter because that part of Earth is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight hits more directly and strongly and the daylight lasts longer.
The summer solstice is the day with the most hours of daylight in the year, around June 21 in the northern half of the world, when that half is tilted most toward the Sun.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old.
People still set daily schedules around sunrise and sunset, a social importance of the Sun you can confirm on a clock and a window.
Places near the equator like the Philippines are hotter because the Sun's rays strike them more directly, while regions near the poles get the same sunlight spread out at a slanted angle.
When its fuel runs low billions of years from now, the Sun will swell into a red giant, then shrink and cool into a faint 'white dwarf.'
You should never look straight at the sun because its light is so strong it can permanently damage the delicate retina.
The Sun is at the center of our Solar System, with the planets orbiting around it.
Nicolaus Copernicus proposed the Sun-centered (heliocentric) model, with the Sun at the center of the solar system.
The Sun's core is about 15 million degrees Celsius, hot enough for fusion.
The core of the Sun reaches about 15 million degrees Celsius.
The corona is the Sun's outermost atmosphere, seen as a glowing ring during a total eclipse — strangely, it is even hotter than the Sun's own surface, a puzzle scientists are still studying.
The Sun's diameter is about 1.39 million kilometers (1,390,000 km).
The Sun is huge — its diameter is about 109 times that of Earth.

The Sun does not rotate like a solid body; its equator rotates faster (about 25 days per rotation) than its poles (about 35 days). This differential rotation twists the Sun's magnetic field and helps produce sunspots.

Earth's distance from the Sun varies slightly because Earth's orbit is an ellipse, not a perfect circle; the closest point (perihelion) is about 147 million kilometres in January, and the farthest point (aphelion) is about 152 million kilometres in July.
The sun sends out not only visible light but also ultraviolet and infrared.
By day the leaves must stay open to catch sunlight, which the tree uses to make its food.
The Sun's light and heat make life on Earth possible, especially for plants and animals.
Tiny ocean plants use sunlight near the sea surface, so fish that eat them, and people who eat fish, still depend on the Sun.
In the Sun, hydrogen is fused together to make helium through fusion.

After about 5 billion more years, when the Sun's hydrogen fuel runs low, it will swell up huge and turn red — becoming what is called a red giant. But this is so far away that we have nothing to worry about now.
Our Sun and the other stars do not simply fly out of the Milky Way because the gravity of the whole galaxy keeps pulling them to stay inside it.
The Sun's heat reaches the Philippines through radiation, traveling across the empty space. This is the only way heat can move through the gap between the Sun and Earth.
The heliosphere is the vast bubble of solar wind created by the Sun; its boundary, the heliopause, is considered the edge of the solar system, and the Voyager 1 probe crossed it in 2012.
The Sun is highest in the sky at noon, which is why it feels hottest and shadows are shortest at that time.
The Sun is a star, the nearest one, which is why it can light and heat a whole planet; a science book will state that clearly.
Our Sun will live for about 10 billion years, and it is roughly halfway through its life now.
Sunlight evaporates water from seas and puddles, starting the water cycle that later brings rain to farms and forests.
Sunlight reaches Earth in only about eight minutes, but light from other stars takes years to arrive because they are much farther away.

Earth has an invisible magnetic shield (the magnetosphere), made by the iron deep inside it — it blocks most of the harmful particles from the Sun's solar wind from reaching us, keeping life on Earth's surface safe.

The sun is so far away that even its light takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. So when you look at the sun, you see light that left it about eight minutes ago. Light is the fastest thing there is, yet the sun is still that far.

Deep inside the giant Sun it is so hot and so packed that tiny bits of hydrogen join together (fusion) and become helium. This is where its enormous energy that gives light and heat comes from. The Sun must be huge for this to happen.
Our Sun is not at the center of the Milky Way — it sits in an ordinary part far from the center, so we are not the heart of the galaxy.

Even though the Sun looks like it is blazing, it is not burning like a candle flame — there is no oxygen in space to burn. Instead, its light and heat come from fusion of particles in its core, a completely different process.
Our Sun sits in a smaller arm called the Orion Arm, far from the crowded center of the Milky Way and toward the outer part of the galaxy.
A sun pillar is a vertical streak of light that appears above or below the sun when its light reflects off tiny flat ice crystals floating in the air.
The Sun is powered by nuclear fusion, in which hydrogen is fused into helium.
Almost all renewable energy secretly comes from the sun: its heat stirs up the wind for wind power and evaporates water that returns as rain to fill the dams.
The Sun spins like Earth, but because it is gas and not solid, it does not spin at one speed — its middle (equator) rotates faster than the parts near its poles.
Daytime is when our side of Earth faces the Sun, so the Sun times when people can work outdoors without lamps.

The number of sunspots and solar flares changes in a regular cycle of about 11 years — there are times of many sunspots and many bursts, and quiet times of almost none, because the Sun's magnetic force keeps changing.

A solar flare is a sudden, powerful burst of energy and light from the Sun's surface, usually near sunspots — it is one of the most powerful explosions in our Solar System, releasing its energy in just minutes.
The solar wind is not wind like the air on Earth — it is a constant stream of tiny particles that the Sun blows out in all directions into space, reaching all the way to Earth and beyond.
The Sun does not disappear at night—the Earth simply turns so our side faces away from it.
The number of sunspots on the Sun changes in a cycle of about 11 years; at solar maximum there are many sunspots and more frequent solar flares, while at solar minimum there are few sunspots.

A sunspot is a dark patch on the Sun's surface that is cooler than the area around it — it is not truly black, but because it is cooler it looks dark next to the hotter, brighter parts of the Sun. It is caused by strong magnetic forces.
The Sun's surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius hot.
The Sun's surface is blazing hot, about 5,500 degrees Celsius, and it is a giant ball of glowing gas made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
The Sun's surface has a temperature of about 5,500 degrees Celsius.
People plan outdoor work for daylight because the Sun makes the day bright enough to farm, travel, and play without lamps.
The Sun warms land and water, and that uneven heating helps make wind, so weather itself depends on sunlight reaching Earth.
When it runs out of fuel billions of years from now, the Sun will first swell into a red giant, then leave behind a small, hot core called a white dwarf.
The Sun is a type of star called a yellow dwarf.
The Sun is a yellow star with a medium temperature compared to other stars.
Our Sun is a medium yellow-white star, with a surface temperature of about 5,500 °C.
The sunbird builds a hanging pouch-shaped nest on a branch, like a tiny bag with a hole on the side.
Strong midday sunlight can make families move playtime to morning or late afternoon, so the Sun's light changes when children stay outside.
The correct design of a sundial changes depending on where you are on Earth. In the Philippines, near the equator, the right gnomon angle is different from countries far from the equator.
The gnomon is not straight up but tilted, pointing toward the north. This makes the shadow's motion match the Sun's real path, so the time it shows is more accurate.
Sundials were one of the earliest ways to measure time, used by ancient people thousands of years ago. Long before battery clocks, people relied on sundials.
Sunglasses can protect eyes from bright glare on a sunny road, a light protection that still is not enough for looking at the Sun.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
Weather reports mention sunshine or cloud because clouds block some sunlight, changing how warm a day feels for people and crops.
Sunlight reaching Earth is a transverse electromagnetic wave example that traveled through space, where there is almost no air.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
Most of what we see outdoors in the day is sunlight bouncing off things, so vision in the yard still depends on the Sun.
The sun is the main source of the energy that plants use to live and grow.
The Sun's white light is actually made of all the colors of the rainbow mixed together.
Almost all the energy in an ecosystem comes from the sun, because plants use its light to make the food that powers every animal.
The Sun's light takes longer (8 minutes) than the Moon's (1.3 seconds) because the Sun is much farther from Earth.
Sunrise is when many market and farm jobs start, because that first light from the Sun tells people the work day has begun.
Sunscreen protects the skin from the sun's harmful rays that can cause burns and damage.
The sky is blue during the day because air scatters blue light the most; but at sunset the light passes through much more air, which removes the blue and leaves the reds and oranges.
The sky turns red at sunset because the light travels through much thicker air before reaching us.
Sunsets look red or orange because most of the blue light has scattered away, leaving the red light.
Sunset tells many outdoor workers it is time to go home, because after the Sun drops, seeing the path and the fields becomes harder.

Wool and trapped air are poor conductors of heat, making them good insulators — used in clothing and roof insulation to keep buildings warm or cool inside.
Cold water in the ocean is denser than warm water so it sinks to the bottom. This drives ocean currents that circulate heat and nutrients from the deep.
When two objects at different temperatures touch, heat flows from hotter to cooler until their temperatures equalize — this is called thermal equilibrium.
Bridges have special expansion joints, like interlocking teeth, so they don't crack as the steel grows and shrinks with heat and cold.
Lines are cut into concrete sidewalks to give them room to expand so they don't crack in the heat.
Metal dental fillings expand and contract slightly when you eat hot or cold food. Dentists take this into account when choosing the right material for fillings.
Repeated expansion and contraction of metal in electrical sockets can loosen connections over time. That is why electricians periodically inspect and tighten sockets.
Without room to expand, railway tracks can buckle or bend on very hot days.

When air inside a hot air balloon is heated, its volume increases according to Charles's Law. The expansion lowers the average density of the balloon and the lighter balloon rises to greater altitude.
A balloon or tire left in the heat puffs up because the air inside expands.
Most things get bigger when heated and smaller when cooled.

Power lines sag and droop more in hot weather because the metal gets longer in the heat.
Small gaps are left between railway tracks so the steel has room to expand when it gets hot.
The bigger the rise in temperature, the more a thing expands.
Many devices like flatirons have a thermostat that uses bending metal to switch the heat on and off automatically.
Solids, liquids, and gases all expand when heated, but gases expand the most and solids the least.
Unlike most substances, water expands when it freezes — its volume increases. That is why ice is less dense than liquid water and floats on top.
When seawater warms, it expands and takes up more space, raising the sea level even without extra water.
Builders add gaps in concrete roads and pipes because repeated heating and cooling can crack them.
In cold parts of the world, cold and salty seawater becomes heavy and sinks to the deep ocean, driving a slow global flow that carries heat through the world's seas.
The normal human body temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius.
Temperature is measured in degrees, such as degrees Celsius (°C), degrees Fahrenheit (°F), and kelvin (K).
The body maintains temperature near 37°C by sweating when hot — evaporation of sweat cools the body — and shivering when cold — muscle vibrations generate heat.
A thermos works so well because it blocks all three ways heat moves: conduction, convection, and radiation.
A thermos keeps a drink hot because its walls block heat from escaping into the cooler air outside.
The inside of a thermos is shiny like a mirror to reflect heat that travels as radiation back where it came from.
The thermosphere is extremely hot because it absorbs strong energy from the Sun, but the air there is very thin.
Some trees have thick bark that shields their living tissue even during a forest fire.

A car or jeepney moves forward because of the third law. The spinning tire pushes the road backward (action), and the road pushes the tire forward (reaction). Without enough friction — like on mud or ice — the tire just spins but the vehicle does not move ahead.
Even though the action and reaction forces are equal in size, the lighter object speeds up more than the heavier object.

Many think that because action and reaction are equal and opposite, they should cancel and nothing moves. This is wrong! They do not cancel because they ACT ON DIFFERENT OBJECTS — the action is on one object, the reaction on the other. Forces only cancel when they act on the SAME object.

A rocket flies because of the third law: it burns fuel and shoots hot gas DOWNWARD very forcefully (action), which pushes the rocket UPWARD (reaction). It does not need to push against air or ground — that is why it works even in space where there is no air.

When you swim, your hands and feet push the water BACKWARD (action), and the water pushes you FORWARD (reaction). That is how you move ahead in the water. A boat's paddle works the same way — it pushes water backward so the boat moves forward.
Action and reaction always happen between TWO different objects — an object cannot push itself. There is always an A pushing on B, and B pushing back on A. So there are always two participants.

Besides the three Rs, there is a partner called composting. Biodegradable things like vegetable peels and leftover food can be piled up and left to rot to become fertilizer that enriches soil. This is why it is sometimes called the fourth R: 'Rot.'

Making a product from recycled materials usually needs much less energy than making it from brand-new raw materials. For example, it takes far less electricity to melt an old can than to dig up and refine new metal from the ground.

The three Rs help animals. When we make less trash, less plastic ends up in the sea and on land. Many animals like turtles and fish get harmed when they mistake plastic for food. So cutting down on waste helps protect them.

Glass (bottles) and metal (cans) can be recycled over and over with almost no drop in quality. They can be melted and made into new bottles or cans many times. This is different from plastic, whose quality goes down each time it is recycled, so it cannot be recycled endlessly.

The recycling symbol is three arrows forming a triangle that loops around. The three arrows stand for the three Rs, and the loop shows how materials are reused and remade again and again. When something has this symbol, it can usually be recycled.
'Reduce' means using less so that we make less trash in the first place. For example, if you bring your own cup, you don't need to buy a plastic cup. Less stuff used means less garbage.

Some people add a fourth R even before the three: 'Refuse.' It means saying no right away to things you don't need, like a plastic straw or plastic spoon when you already brought your own. If you refuse it, it never becomes trash.
The three Rs also save money. When you reuse a thing or buy less, you don't have to spend on new ones. For example, using a refillable water bottle is cheaper than always buying bottled water.

Recycling means melting or shredding materials to make a new product. Upcycling means making something new and even nicer from old things WITHOUT melting them, like turning old denim into a bag. Upcycling is a creative kind of Reuse.

In the old 'take-use-throw' habit, a thing is used only once and becomes trash right away. With the three Rs, we try to reuse and remake materials so they keep cycling instead of becoming trash immediately. This is cheaper and better for nature.

We have three types of cones in the retina — one sensitive to red, one to green, one to blue — which together allow us to see all colours.
Eggplants come in different shapes and sizes — some are long and thin, others are short and round. Most are purple, but some are white or green.

The roots of eggplant, tomato, and okra are under the soil. They hold the plant so it does not fall over, and they drink up water and nutrients from the ground.
You can save seeds from a ripe tomato or eggplant, dry them, and plant them again to grow new plants. This is a way to make more vegetables for free.
A young tomato is green, but when it ripens it turns red. The red color is a sign that it is sweet and ready to eat.

When lightning is close, thunder sounds like a sharp crack; but when it is far, the sound from different parts of the long bolt arrives at different times, so it becomes a long rumble.
The sound of thunder travels through air at about 343 meters per second (about 1,235 km/h).

Mercury is not perfectly tidally locked like the Moon to Earth; instead it has a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance — it rotates three times for every two orbits around the Sun. This is caused by the Sun's strong tidal forces combined with its somewhat elliptical orbit.
The Moon's gravitational pull on Earth's oceans causes tidal friction that is slowly slowing Earth's rotation; over billions of years, days have been getting a few milliseconds longer each century.
A big advantage of tidal energy is that the rise and fall of the sea can be predicted years in advance, so we know exactly when the power will come — unlike wind, which is unpredictable.
A tsunami is not a tidal wave — it starts from a large underwater disturbance like an earthquake or landslide, not from tidal forces caused by the Moon.
Between the two high tides, the water drops in other parts of Earth — this is low tide, when the sea pulls back and more shore is exposed.
Most coastal places experience 2 high tides and 2 low tides each day.

Most coastlines have two high tides and two low tides each day.

A tsunami is not a single wave but a series of waves that arrive one after another. Sometimes the second or third wave is the biggest, so it is dangerous to return to the shore too soon.

It is not only a tsunami's height that causes harm. Because it is a huge mass of moving water, it carries a powerful push, like a strong flood surging onto land, so it can knock down houses and trees.
When the seafloor suddenly rises or drops during a quake, it pushes a huge amount of water above it. That sudden push gives the water the energy to become a tsunami.

A tsunami and a storm surge are different even though both flood the land from the sea. A storm surge comes from a typhoon's strong winds, while a tsunami comes from sudden movement of the seafloor like an earthquake.
Even though a tsunami is low in deep water, its energy is not lost—it is just hidden through the whole depth and shows up when it reaches the shallow coast.
In the deep ocean a tsunami travels extremely fast—as fast as a jet plane—yet it stays low, so you would barely notice it from a ship.
A tsunami is not one wave but a series of low, long waves that come one after another, so it is dangerous to return to shore while more are still passing.
When there is a tsunami warning, boats already in deep water can be safer, because the wave is still low there compared to the shallow coast where it grows tall.
A tsunami starts when the seafloor suddenly moves because of an earthquake, pushing the whole water above it and forming a broad but low wave.

A tsunami is not just a wave—it surges powerfully onto land, bringing floods that destroy houses and trees.

Many animals like dogs, cats, and horses can swivel their ears to point toward a sound. We humans can't move our ears, so instead we turn our whole head to face where the sound is coming from.

Besides hearing, the inside of each ear has a part that helps with balance. This is why you can stand upright without toppling over. When you spin around fast and feel dizzy, it's because this part of the ear gets briefly confused.

Bats also use two ears, but in an amazing way. They make sounds and listen for the echoes bouncing back to find insects or obstacles. Because they have two ears, they can pinpoint exactly which direction the returning echo came from.

In a noisy place like a fiesta with many people talking, you can still choose to focus on just one voice. Two ears help with this because they locate where your chosen sound comes from, so your brain can tune out the other surrounding noise.

Your brain has a clever trick: for low sounds like a rumble, it relies more on the tiny time gap between the ears. For high sounds like a whistle, it relies more on the loudness difference. It blends both clues to locate sound well.

It's a myth that people with bigger ears always hear better. Good hearing and direction-finding depend on healthy inner parts and the brain, not just the size of the outer flap. Whether large or small, two ears still work well together.

There's a reason the two ears sit on opposite sides of the head instead of side by side. Their separation gives enough gap for differences in timing and loudness to appear. If they were right next to each other, both would hear almost the same thing and the brain would struggle.

AB and O are opposites: AB has BOTH A and B antigens but no antibodies, making it the universal recipient. O has no antigens but has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, making it the universal donor. They are mirror images!

Average speed is the total distance traveled divided by the total time of a trip, even if you went fast sometimes and slow other times. Instant speed is your speed at one exact moment, like what a speedometer shows. So your average might be 60 km/h while you hit 80 km/h at one instant.

The cheetah is the fastest land animal, reaching almost 100 kilometers per hour in a short sprint. It uses this speed to chase its prey. But it cannot keep this speed for long—only a few seconds before it gets tired.

Constant speed means an object's speed stays the same at every moment—not speeding up or slowing down. For example, when a plane is cruising, it flies at an almost steady speed. At constant speed, equal distances are covered in equal amounts of time.

Speed is how far something travels in a certain amount of time. You calculate it by dividing the distance traveled by the time taken. So if you walk 6 kilometers in 2 hours, your speed is 3 kilometers per hour.

GPS apps on a phone know your speed by tracking how far you moved over a short time. They check your location from satellites every few seconds, find the difference, and divide by the time. That is how Waze or a speedometer app works even if the vehicle has no speedometer.

Imagine a jeepney traveling 12 kilometers from the market to school in half an hour. Its speed is 24 kilometers per hour. But because of Manila traffic, it is often much slower than the speed it could reach on an open road.

When a vehicle moves faster, it needs a longer distance to stop. This is not just about the brakes—there is also time that passes before the driver reacts, called reaction time. That is why slow speeds near schools matter for safety.

Speed depends on what you compare it to. If you walk inside a moving bus, you are slow compared to the other passengers, but very fast compared to a person standing on the road. There is no single 'true speed'—it changes depending on your reference point.

Speed only tells you how fast something is going, but velocity also tells you the direction. For example, '5 m/s' is speed, but '5 m/s heading north' is velocity. So they are different even though people often mix them up.

Some people think COVID-19 mainly spreads through food. But in truth, it spreads far more through the air from a sick person's coughs and sneezes, not through the food itself. Clean air, distance, and washing hands before eating matter more.

Not every mosquito carries dengue. The main carrier is the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which is small and black with white stripes on its body and legs. It usually bites during the daytime, morning and late afternoon, unlike ordinary mosquitoes that bite at night.

Symptoms do not show up right after a mosquito bite. Usually, fever and other symptoms appear about 4 to 10 days after you are bitten. So sometimes a person has already forgotten the bite by the time they get sick, because there is a gap of several days.
Dengue is a disease caused by a virus that spreads through the bite of the Aedes mosquito, a common problem in the Philippines.

There are simple ways for you to avoid dengue. Wear long sleeves and pants especially in the morning and afternoon, use mosquito repellent, and sleep under a mosquito net. It also helps to put screens on windows and remove standing water around you. In this way, you lower the chance of being bitten by a mosquito.

In the Philippines, dengue cases rise during the rainy season, usually from around June to the end of the year. Because of the rain, more water collects in containers, tires, and corners where the mosquito breeds. So there are more mosquitoes and a higher risk of dengue during this time.

It is important to know that a second dengue infection, especially with a different type of the virus, can sometimes be more serious than the first. This is because the body's defenses can get confused when a different type attacks. So even if you have recovered from dengue before, you still need to be careful and avoid being bitten again.
