A virus cannot multiply on its own; it must get inside a living cell to make copies of itself.
Scientists debate whether viruses are alive because they cannot make their own energy or reproduce without a host cell — they depend entirely on other living cells.
Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) was the first virus ever discovered; in the 1890s, scientists found that the tobacco disease agent was too small to be caught by filters that stopped bacteria.
Polio is caused by poliovirus, which can cause permanent paralysis; the oral polio vaccine (OPV) has helped reduce polio cases worldwide dramatically.
Rabies is caused by a virus you can get from the bite of an infected animal, which is why vaccinating dogs is important.

Unlike the flu, rabies almost never passes from one person to another. You can safely care for or hug a person with rabies — you will not catch it just by being near. The danger comes from animal bites.

Rabies is easy to confuse with tetanus because both can come from wounds. But rabies is caused by a virus from animal saliva, while tetanus is caused by a bacterium often found on dirty or rusty objects. Each one needs a different vaccine.
The first rabies symptoms can look just like the flu — fever, headache, and tiredness. But often there is an odd tingling or itching at the bite site. This is a warning that the virus is moving up.

Rabies has two forms in people. In the 'furious' form, the patient is restless, agitated, and afraid of water. In the 'paralytic' form, the muscles slowly grow weak and paralyzed. Both forms are deadly.

A bite near the head, face, or neck is more dangerous because these are close to the brain. The virus has a shorter path along the nerves, so the disease can appear faster than from a bite on the foot.
The rabies virus travels from the bite wound to the brain along nerves — once it reaches the brain, the disease is almost always fatal if untreated beforehand.

Some people who are often around animals — like veterinarians or forest workers — get the rabies vaccine before they are ever bitten. This gives them a head start of protection in case they are exposed.

The rabies virus is extremely tiny — it cannot be seen with the eyes and needs a powerful microscope to spot. Under such a view, its shape looks like a bullet. This tiny thing is what causes the frightening disease.
A virus replicates in five steps: (1) attachment to the host cell, (2) entry into the cell, (3) synthesis of viral components, (4) assembly of new viruses, and (5) release to infect other cells.
A typical virus is 20–300 nanometers in size, too small to be seen with a light microscope; only an electron microscope can make viruses visible.
Smallpox is the only human disease to have been completely eradicated worldwide, in 1980, thanks to a global WHO vaccination campaign.
Many viruses spread through tiny droplets of fluid released when a sick person coughs or sneezes.
The Visayan spotted deer (Rusa alfredi) is a critically endangered deer found only on Panay and Negros islands in the Philippines.
The Visayan warty pig (Sus cebifrons) is critically endangered and endemic to the Philippine islands of Negros, Panay, and Cebu.
The Visayan warty pig is critically endangered due to widespread forest loss in the Visayas and overhunting.
Different subspecies of the Visayan warty pig live on different islands — those on Cebu, Negros, and Panay differ slightly from one another.
The female Visayan warty pig typically gives birth to four to six piglets at a time.
During the breeding season, the male grows a long, tall mane of stiff hair on its head.
The Visayan warty pig has a pale stripe that crosses over the top of its snout.
The higher a liquid's viscosity, the slower its flow speed.
You can compare viscosity by tilting a glass and watching which liquid runs down faster.
The different colors we see come from differences in the wavelength of light: red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest.
Visible light is a transverse electromagnetic wave, which is why it is grouped with radio and microwaves, not with sound.
Visible light is the only band of the electromagnetic spectrum that the human eye can see.
Visible light is only a very narrow band of the whole electromagnetic spectrum—it is the only range of wavelengths the human eye can see, from violet to red.
Visible light detectable by the human eye has wavelengths from about 400 nanometres (violet) to 700 nanometres (red) — a small slice of the electromagnetic spectrum.
A lack of vitamin A can cause trouble seeing in the dark, so it is important to eat sweet potato and squash.
Vitamin A, found in carrots, squash, and malunggay, helps with clear eyesight and fighting off sickness.
The B vitamins help the body turn food into energy.
Green leafy vegetables like malunggay and kangkong are rich in B vitamins and iron.
The scientific name of Vitamin C is ascorbic acid.
Fruits like oranges, calamansi, and guava are rich in Vitamin C.
Vitamin C, found in calamansi and other fruits, helps the body fight illness and heal wounds.
Vitamin C helps the body fight illness and heal wounds, and we get it from oranges and other fruits.

Why do some people need more time in the sun? Darker skin has more melanin (the coloring pigment), which acts like built-in sunscreen — so it needs a bit longer in the sun to make the same amount of vitamin D.
Vitamin D doesn't come only from the sun — it's in food too! Oily fish like tuna and salmon, egg yolk, and some milk with added vitamins (fortified) are good sources of it.

There's something unusual about vitamin D: most vitamins must come from food, but vitamin D can be made by your own body using sunlight. Because of this, it behaves more like a hormone — a messenger inside the body — than an ordinary vitamin.
Vitamin D is made by the skin when it gets sunlight, and it helps make bones strong.
Vitamin D is made by our skin when it is hit by sunlight.

Does sunscreen block vitamin D? Partly, because it reduces the UV reaching your skin. But that's not a reason to skip sunscreen — a little morning sun is enough, and protecting skin from too much sun still matters.
Vitamin E helps protect the body's cells and keeps the skin healthy.
Not all vitamins come from fruits and vegetables — some, like vitamin B12, are mostly found in meat, fish, eggs, and milk. That is why a balanced diet from both plants and animals matters.
Many vitamins are first made by plants as they grow in sunlight. When we eat fruits and vegetables, those vitamins are passed on to us.
Bananas like saba and lakatan are cheap Filipino fruits that contain vitamin C, vitamin B6, and potassium. They make a good nutritious snack instead of candy or chips.
Vitamin D is different from most vitamins because it does not only come from food — our own skin makes it when we get sunlight. That is why a little time in the morning sun is important.
No single food has all the vitamins, so we need to eat a variety of vegetables, fruits, and other foods.
Vitamin K, found in leafy greens like kangkong and malunggay, helps the blood clot when we get cut, so the bleeding stops.
Even athletes who take vitamins still need to eat plenty of carbohydrates before they play. Vitamins help their bodies work properly, but the energy to run and jump comes from food.
The B vitamins help the body release the energy stored in food. But no matter how many B vitamins you take, you get no energy if there is no food to burn.
Many vitamins work as partners to enzymes. Enzymes speed up reactions, including the ones that release energy from food. So vitamins help with energy, but they are not the energy itself.
Vitamins act like helpers inside the body that assist chemical reactions; they are not the fuel that gets burned for energy. The energy comes from carbohydrates, fats, and protein.
Iron is a mineral, not a vitamin, but like vitamins it is not energy either. Iron helps carry oxygen in the blood so the body can make energy, but iron itself is not energy.

Protein is like bricks used to build and repair the body, and it can also be turned into energy. Vitamins, on the other hand, are neither bricks nor energy; they are just helpers that keep everything working.
When the vocal cords are looser, they vibrate more slowly so the sound that comes out is lower.
When the vocal cords are tightened and stretched, they vibrate faster and the sound becomes higher in pitch.
Inside the larynx are two vocal cords that vibrate when air passes through, and this vibration makes sound.
We make our voice when air from the lungs passes through two thin flaps in the throat called vocal cords, which vibrate and produce sound.

When a large volcano (such as Pinatubo in 1991) erupts a huge amount of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, the SO2 converts to sulfate aerosols that reflect sunlight; this effect can lower global temperature by about 0.5°C for 1-2 years.
Volcanic ash is an earth material: tiny bits of rock from a volcano, non-living even when it covers plants after an eruption.
Volcanic ash is not soft like burnt paper but tiny sharp pieces of rock that can harm the lungs.
A dyke is a vertical sheet of igneous rock cutting through other rocks, while a sill is a horizontal sheet; both form when magma forces its way into cracks in existing rock.
The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) measures eruption size from 0 (no explosions) to 8 (supervolcano); each step up the scale means 10 times more material was erupted.
Sulfur dioxide (SO2) is a main gas released by active volcanoes; it is harmful to lungs and can create 'vog' (volcanic smog) that causes breathing difficulties in areas near the volcano.
Some mountains are volcanoes built up from lava and ash that piled up after eruptions, like Mayon Volcano.

The three main volcanic rock types differ in silica content and colour: basalt (low silica, dark, fluid lava — not explosive), andesite (moderate silica, grey — typical of Philippine volcanoes), and rhyolite (high silica, light-coloured — very explosive eruptions).
After a volcano erupts, its ash enriches the soil, so plants slowly grow back and animals return to live on the slope.

Andosol is a type of soil that forms from volcanic ash; it is very rich in mineral nutrients like potassium and phosphorus, which is why areas near Philippine volcanoes (such as around Mayon) are known for very fertile farmland.
Soil near volcanoes like Mayon is often rich farmland because volcanic ash is full of minerals.
An active volcano releases gases like sulfur that smell like rotten eggs. When this gas suddenly increases, it is a sign that the magma inside may be heating up.
People use the heat beneath active volcanoes to make electricity. This is called geothermal energy, and the Philippines has plants that get power from this underground heat.
Beneath an active volcano sits a magma chamber, a pool of hot melted rock. As magma and gas build up, pressure rises until it bursts out as lava.
Active volcanoes are not all the same shape. Some are steep cones like Mayon, some are wide with gentle slopes, and some have a large sunken bowl called a caldera, like Taal.
At Alert Level 3, the volcano's unrest is high and magma may be getting close to the surface. It means an eruption could happen within days or weeks if the signs continue.
Alert Level 4 means a hazardous eruption is likely within hours or days. People in the danger zone are ordered to evacuate because it is no longer safe to stay there.
PHIVOLCS uses alert levels from 0 to 5 to show how dangerous a volcano is. The higher the number, the nearer or stronger the expected eruption.

What story can old ash tell? When a volcano erupts, it leaves a layer of ash on the ground. After many years, that layer becomes part of the rock. Scientists study these layers to learn how often and how strongly a volcano erupted long ago, even when no one was there to see it.

What other harm does ash cause besides health? It gets into car and airplane engines and damages them, so flights are sometimes canceled. It also dirties drinking water and clogs drains. That is why you should cover water containers and avoid driving when ash is thick.

Did you know there is lightning inside ash clouds? As millions of ash pieces bump and rub against each other in the air, they build up static electricity, like rubbing a balloon on your hair. When it is strong enough, it flashes as lightning — called volcanic lightning.

How do we know where ash will fall? Scientists at PHIVOLCS watch the volcanoes of the Philippines. They check how strong the eruption is and the wind direction to predict which towns will get ashfall, then they issue warnings so people can prepare.

A real Philippine example: in 1991 Mount Pinatubo erupted and thick ash buried parts of Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga. A typhoon also arrived, so the ash got wet and heavy, and many roofs collapsed. It was one of the largest eruptions in the whole world in the 20th century.

What makes ash different from other rock a volcano throws out? Pieces smaller than 2 millimeters — smaller than a grain of sand — are called ash. Bigger pieces are called lapilli, and the biggest are volcanic bombs. So ash is the smallest kind.
A crater is the bowl-shaped opening at the top of a volcano where lava, ash, and gas come out when it erupts.
Volcanoes like Taal release ash and gases such as sulfur dioxide, so PHIVOLCS watches the air whenever they erupt.
Beneath a volcano is magma — melted rock so hot that it is liquid. From deep inside the Earth, the magma slowly rises because it is lighter than the solid rock around it.
Mayon Volcano in Albay is famous for its nearly perfect cone shape. It is one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines and is closely watched by PHIVOLCS because it erupts often.

In 1991, Mount Pinatubo in Luzon erupted in one of the largest eruptions of the past century. It released so much ash and gas that it slightly cooled the temperature of the whole world for a few years.
A pyroclastic flow is an extremely hot cloud of gas, ash, and rock that rushes down a volcano's slope very fast. It is one of the deadliest volcanic hazards because a person cannot outrun it.
The kind of eruption depends on the lava. If the lava is runny and flows easily, it pours out gently. If the lava is thick and sticky, gas gets trapped until it bursts out violently and dangerously.
The vent is the opening in a volcano through which magma flows from inside up to the surface.
The Philippines has much gold because it sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where hot underground water carries minerals.
The unit 'volt', which measures voltage, is named after Alessandro Volta.
The volt, the unit of voltage, is named after Alessandro Volta, the Italian scientist who built the first battery.
Alessandro Volta of Italy invented the first true battery.
The unit of voltage is the volt, named after Alessandro Volta.
To measure the volume of an oddly shaped object, we put it in water and see how much the water rises.
Some muscles we can control, like in the arm, while others work on their own, like the heart.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the farthest human-made object ever; it has passed beyond our solar system's heliosphere and continues travelling away at about 17 kilometres per second.
Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to leave our solar system and enter interstellar space—the space between the stars.
Voyager 1 is now so far away that its radio signal, even at the speed of light, takes more than 20 hours to reach Earth.
The first space probe to leave the Solar System into interstellar space was Voyager 1.
Voyager 1 was launched in 1977.
Voyager 2 flew past four (4) planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
According to VSEPR theory, the electron pairs around an atom push apart as far as possible, which gives a molecule its three-dimensional shape.
Raw rubber is heated with sulfur to make it stronger and less sticky or soft — this is called vulcanization.
There are different levels of risk: 'vulnerable' is starting to be at risk, 'endangered' is more serious, and 'critically endangered' is closest to extinction.
A vulture has a strong, hooked beak to tear through the tough skin and meat of a carcass.
Vultures rise on warm air and circle high in the sky to spot dead animals below.
Wait thirty minutes after the last thunder before going outside because lightning can still strike.
The waling-waling usually blooms once a year, often during the warmer dry months.
Walking needs friction to grip, which is why it is hard to move forward on slippery ice where there is almost no friction.
When you walk, your foot pushes the ground backward, and the ground pushes you forward.
A wallaby is like a small kangaroo and also carries its joey in a pouch.
There is a small air space inside the egg that helps the chick start to breathe before it hatches.
Because they make their own heat, warm-blooded animals can stay active even at night or in cold weather.
A thick jacket acts like insulation that traps your body heat so you do not feel cold.
Some currents are warm and come from the tropics, while others are cold and come from the polar regions.
Warm food smells and tastes stronger than cold food. The heat sends more particles into the air to reach the nose, so the flavor seems richer.
In the sun, hot metal feels much hotter than hot wood even at the same temperature.
A typhoon grows stronger over warm seas because the rising vapor from the warm water gives it energy.
Warming up and stretching before exercise helps keep muscles from getting hurt.
Birds and mammals are warm-blooded, while fish, amphibians, and reptiles are cold-blooded.
Soap cleans grease faster in warm water because the grease softens and breaks apart more easily.
Warm water is less dense than cold water, so warm water tends to rise above colder water.
Measurements show that the past few decades are among the warmest ever recorded in Earth's history.
Besides higher temperatures, the evidence for global warming includes melting glaciers and polar ice and the gradual rise of sea level around the world.
When water is already full and will not dissolve any more sugar, heating it lets even more sugar dissolve.
If a toy makes a painful bang near the ear, stop using it close to anyone's head and tell an adult, a protection for the whole group.
Some animals that are poisonous or taste bad have bright colors like red, yellow, or black — a warning that tells predators not to eat them.
When you get a cut, wash it with clean water to remove dirt.

Many kids ask: do you still need to wash a banana if you are going to peel it anyway? Yes, it is still good to, because microbes on the peel can transfer to your hands or to the flesh while you peel it.
For leafy vegetables like pechay or lettuce, you should separate each leaf and rinse them one by one, because dirt or sand often hides between them. Washing them all at once is not enough.

It is a misconception that fruit should be washed with soap. Soap and dishwashing liquid are not safe to eat and can soak into the skin, especially in pores. For most fruit, clean running water is enough.

In the Philippines, fruits and vegetables pass through many hands at the palengke before reaching home. Many people touch them, so always wash the mango, banana, or tomato you bought before eating or cooking.
Small fruits that grow in clusters like grapes and strawberries are washed gently in a strainer under running water. They are delicate, so you should not scrub them hard or they will get crushed.

Some fruits like apples are coated with a thin layer of wax to look shiny and not dry out quickly. It is safe to eat, but if you want to remove it, scrub the fruit in warm water with clean hands or a brush.
Washing hands with soap removes germs and stops illness from spreading to others.
It is important to keep nails clean and short because dirt and germs can hide under them.
If you touch a stinging plant, rinse the skin with water and do not rub it, so the itch does not get worse.
Washing soda (sodium carbonate, Na2CO3) is a base used in laundry to soften hard water by removing calcium and magnesium ions, improving the effectiveness of soap and detergent.
Wasps are most likely to sting when you get near their nest, so it is best to stay away and not disturb it.
A wasp lays eggs inside the cells of the nest, and each egg hatches into a larva that grows into an adult wasp.
They feed their young differently: wasp larvae are fed chewed-up insects or meat, while bee larvae are fed pollen and nectar.
When a wasp stings, it pushes its sharp stinger into your skin, and a small venom sac inside its body squeezes and pumps the venom in. It works like a tiny, very fast injection.
Even though it hurts, scientists study wasp venom because some of its chemicals may be able to kill germs or harmful cells. They hope it could one day become part of new medicines.
A wasp stings using the stinger at its rear, while most ants bite using their jaws and sometimes add a little venom. Both can hurt, but they use different body parts to do it.
The stung spot swells and turns red because your body rushes blood and defenders to that area to fight the venom. That is why the skin around the sting feels warm, looks red, and puffs up.
Not all wasps are bad — many of them eat pests and caterpillars that damage crops, so they help farmers.
Wasting is a kind of malnutrition where a child is too thin for their height because of fast weight loss.
The body keeps the right amount of water: when it is low we feel thirsty, and extra water leaves the body as urine.
About 60% of the human body is water; water is needed for all body processes including digestion, transporting nutrients, and regulating temperature.
On the Kelvin scale, water boils at about 373 Kelvin (373 K), equal to 100°C.
Water boils at 100°C (Celsius) at normal sea-level pressure.
At normal pressure, water boils at 100 degrees Celsius (100°C).
On the Kelvin scale, water boils at 373.15 Kelvin (373.15 K).
On a high mountain, water boils below 100°C because the air pressure there is lower.
Resting in shade with drinking water is a safety measure against heat from the Sun's light, not only against sunburn on the skin.
Clean water is transparent, but muddy water becomes translucent or even opaque.
Acid rain forms when pollutants (sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides) from vehicles and factories mix with cloud moisture to produce acidic rain.
The water cycle acts like a natural way of cleaning water, because when water evaporates the dirt and salt are left behind, and clean rain falls.
The water cycle is the never-ending movement of water from the ground up to the sky and back down again.
The dew point is the temperature at which water vapor in the air begins to condense, forming dew or clouds.
About 97% of Earth's water is salty; only 3% is freshwater, and most of that is locked in glaciers and polar ice.
When seawater evaporates, the salt is left behind, so the rain that falls is fresh water.
No new water is ever made — the water cycle keeps reusing the same water, so the water you drink today may once have been drunk by a dinosaur.
The rain shadow effect in the Philippines causes the leeward side of mountains to receive much less rainfall than the windward side.
Plants and trees also add water to the cycle — they release vapor from their leaves (transpiration), which is why the air around a forest is moist.
We can measure a rock's volume by seeing how much the water rises when we drop it in.
You can measure the volume of an irregular object by sinking it in water and measuring how much the water level rises.
Water is unusual because it expands when it freezes, so ice is less dense and floats on water.
Water is unusual: when it freezes it expands instead of contracting, which is why ice floats.
A simple filter of sand, charcoal, and coconut shell removes mud and tiny bits of dirt from water by trapping the particles as the water passes through.

Charcoal (activated carbon) in a filter helps remove bad smells and tastes from water. Charcoal is full of tiny holes that soak up the chemicals causing odors, so the water becomes clearer and nicer to drink.
At home, you can use a clean cloth as a simple first filter for water. It catches large dirt like mud and leaves, but it still cannot remove germs, so the water is not yet safe to drink.

It's a mistake to think a normal water filter removes the salt from seawater. Salt is fully dissolved in water, so it is too small and passes right through the filter's holes. A different special process is needed to remove salt and make seawater drinkable.
The sand layer in a water filter catches the small bits of dirt that slipped past the bigger stones. Between the grains of sand are tiny gaps where fine dirt gets trapped as the water passes through.

Filtering and boiling water do different jobs. A filter removes visible dirt and some smells, but boiling is what kills the germs. So the two are often combined: filter first, then boil, to make the water safer to drink.
Water freezes (turns to ice) at 0 degrees Celsius (0°C).
Water freezes at 0 °C (zero degrees Celsius).
On the Kelvin scale, water freezes at about 273 Kelvin (273 K), equal to 0°C.
Because water molecules cling tightly together, water climbs up a plant's thin tubes like a connected chain — letting water reach the topmost leaves all the way from the roots.

Cohesion and surface tension are linked: inside the water each molecule is pulled on all sides, but at the surface nothing pulls upward, so the clinging there is stronger — and that creates the skin-like surface tension.
Because of its charged ends, water is excellent at dissolving many things like salt and sugar — that is why it is called the 'universal solvent' and can carry nutrients through the body.
When water hyacinth grows too much, it covers and clogs up the rivers.
The water hyacinth has thick, shiny, rounded leaves that are green in color.
Instead of just throwing away the water hyacinth they harvest, people turn it into baskets, bags, and other handicrafts. It can also be made into compost for plants.
One molecule of water (H2O) has two (2) hydrogen atoms.
Water (H2O) is made of two elements: hydrogen and oxygen.
Water in a river, a puddle, or rain is an earth material: it is non-living, yet it shapes the land and is part of the environment.
A water lily is a water plant whose wide, flat leaves (lily pads) float on the surface of a pond. Its roots are below, anchored in the mud at the bottom.
The flowers of some water lilies open during the day and close at night, as if following the time of day.
A water lily leaf floats because it has tiny air-filled spaces inside that make it light. The top of the leaf is smooth and waxy so water rolls off and it does not get soaked and sink.
A water lily has a long stalk that reaches from the mud at the bottom of the pond up to the leaf on the surface. Its roots are buried in the mud to hold it in place and to take in nutrients.
Water is called H₂O because each of its molecules is made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom stuck together.
A water molecule (H₂O) has two covalent bonds, because the oxygen shares electrons with each of its two hydrogen atoms.
A water molecule (H₂O) has a bent shape and is polar, so the oxygen side is slightly negative and the hydrogen side is slightly positive.
Water pollution has three main types: chemical (from factories and pesticides), biological (from bacteria and viruses), and thermal (hot water discharged by factories that depletes dissolved oxygen).
An artesian well flows without pumping because the underground water is under pressure. When the aquifer is tapped, the pressure pushes the water upward.
Water pressure increases as you go deeper. For every 10 metres of ocean, pressure increases by one atmosphere. That is why scuba divers must be careful about descending and ascending quickly.
Hydraulic systems use liquid pressure to transfer force from one place to another. A vehicle's hydraulic brakes use brake fluid pressure to slow and stop the vehicle.
To make dirty water safe to drink, it is first filtered to remove solid dirt, then boiled to kill germs. Filtering does not remove dissolved poisons.

Water has surface tension — the water molecules at the surface are pulled more strongly by their neighbours below than by the air above. This gives water a 'skin' that can support light objects like a needle.
The water table is the top level below which the ground is fully filled with water.
Water is often called the 'universal solvent' because more substances dissolve in it than in any other liquid. That is why salt, sugar, and many things dissolve in water.

Cloud seeding is a technology where particles (like silver iodide) are released into clouds to provide condensation nuclei. This encourages rain formation from water vapour in the cloud. It is used during drought periods.
The amount of water vapour in air varies from 0% (hot desert) to about 4% (hot, humid places like the Philippines). Warmer air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
On Philippine meadows and grasslands, morning dew is common. Air cools at night and water vapour condenses on grass blades and other surfaces that cool faster than the surrounding air.
The gas form of water is called water vapor.
True water vapor is invisible; the white mist we see above boiling water is tiny droplets that have already condensed.
Water vapor in air goes up and down with weather: humid days have more of this invisible gas in the mixture, dry days have less.
Water with dissolved salt or minerals can conduct electricity, so touching electricity with wet hands is dangerous.
A waterfall slowly creeps backward over time because the falling water keeps wearing away and breaking the rock at its base.
Watermelon is a large fruit, green outside and red inside, that is mostly water, which is why it is so refreshing to eat in the hot season.
Trees in a watershed help hold the soil and let rainwater soak in slowly, so when forests are cleared, floods and erosion happen more easily.
A watershed is an area of land where all the rainwater flows down into the same river, lake, or reservoir, so it must be protected as a source of our drinking water.
The unit of power is the watt (W), named after James Watt.
The unit of power called the 'watt' (for example, a 60-watt bulb) is named after James Watt.
The unit of power is the watt, named after James Watt.
Amplitude is the height of a wave from its resting middle line, and a larger amplitude means the wave carries more energy.
The highest part of a wave is called the crest, and the lowest part is called the trough.
Electromagnetic waves such as light and radio are waves of changing electric and magnetic fields that can travel even through empty space without needing a medium.
When an object absorbs the energy of a light wave, it can warm up — that is why a rock or sand that the sun shines on for a long time feels hot.
More wave energy is captured when a wider area catches it each second — this is why solar panels or wave-catchers are made large to gather more energy.
The energy a wave carries is linked to its amplitude, so a louder sound has a larger amplitude than a soft sound of the same pitch.
Like any form of energy, the energy of a wave can be changed into other forms, such as light that is absorbed by an object and becomes heat.
The energy of ocean waves is strongest near the surface and slowly fades downward, so even when there are strong waves on top, the water stays calm deep below.
A strong earthquake under the sea can give the water enormous energy, creating a tsunami — a wave with so much energy that it can reach and damage the coast.
It is often mistaken that high pitch means loud, but loudness comes from the energy or amplitude of the wave, while pitch comes from frequency — these two are different.
Many think a wave carries the matter itself, but really only energy moves through — that is why a floating object on the sea just bobs up and down in place instead of riding away with the wave.
Some think waves are made by the moon, but ordinary sea waves are made by wind — the moon pulls the water in the tides, which is a different thing from wave energy.
The Philippines is an archipelago surrounded by sea with a very long coastline, so it has strong potential to use the energy of waves as a clean source of electricity.
When you shake one end of a long rope, a wave runs to the other end — the energy from your hand travels along the rope, even though the rope itself does not move to the far end.
As it waves, two forms of energy keep swapping: when the water is at the crest there is more stored potential energy, and as it drops this becomes the kinetic energy of motion.
Wave energy is different from tidal energy: wave energy comes from the waves that wind makes on the sea's surface, and the up-and-down bobbing of each wave is turned into electricity.
For light, a wave carries more energy when its frequency is higher — that is why high-frequency ultraviolet is stronger than visible light and can burn skin.

Your cellphone uses radio waves of specific frequencies to send and receive calls and texts. Companies like Globe and Smart in the Philippines use different frequencies so that signals do not interfere with each other.
For light, frequency determines the color we see. Red light has a low frequency, while blue and violet light have high frequency. That is why a rainbow is a range of different light frequencies.
To find the frequency, count how many complete waves pass a point in one second. For example, if five waves pass a rock at the sea in one second, the frequency is 5 Hz.

When an earthquake happens in the Philippines, it produces seismic waves of different frequencies that travel through the ground. Low-frequency waves can shake tall buildings, so scientists at PHIVOLCS study earthquake frequencies to help design safe buildings.
Frequency is how many waves pass a point in one second, and it is measured in hertz.
Frequency is measured in a unit called hertz (Hz). One hertz means one complete wave passes by each second. So 10 Hz means ten waves pass in one second.

The human ear can only hear sounds with frequencies from about 20 Hz up to around 20,000 Hz. Sounds lower or higher than this we cannot hear, but some animals like dogs can hear much higher frequencies.

Each radio station in the Philippines has its own frequency. For example, 'FM 101.1' means it broadcasts at a frequency of 101.1 megahertz. So when you change stations, you are changing which frequency your radio picks up.
The frequency of a wave depends on how fast its source vibrates. When a guitar string vibrates quickly, the frequency is high. When it vibrates slowly, the frequency is low.
For the same type of wave, a higher frequency has a shorter wavelength, and a lower frequency has a longer wavelength.
When a wave hits the boundary between two different materials, part of it bounces back, and this reflection is what causes an echo of sound.
Geologists use seismic waves from earthquakes and their reflection at the boundaries between layers to discover the structure deep inside the Earth.
Sound is a pressure wave that needs a medium such as air, water, or a solid, so it cannot travel through a complete vacuum.
A wave can travel at different speeds in different materials; for example, sound travels faster in water and metal than in air.

People use the speed of sound to measure distance with an echo. If you know how long the sound took to bounce back and how fast it moves, you can find the distance. This is the principle behind sonar on ships.
Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength — the formula is v = f × λ. For sound in air, if frequency is higher the wavelength is shorter so their product stays the same speed.
The speed of a wave equals its wavelength multiplied by its frequency (speed = wavelength × frequency).
The speed of sound in still air stays about the same; motion of the source changes wavelength and frequency, not that air speed.

Light is much, much faster than sound. That is why during a storm you see the lightning flash first before you hear the thunder, even though they happen at the same time. Light is the fastest thing in the universe.

Why does far-off thunder rumble while nearby thunder cracks sharply? Because sound is slow, the sound from different parts of the lightning bolt arrives at different times when it is far. This stretches it into a long rumble.
In the deep part of the ocean, a tsunami races as fast as a jet plane. The deeper the water, the faster the wave travels. As it reaches the shallow shore it slows down but grows much taller.

In outer space, where there is no air, sound has no speed because there is no medium for the wave to travel through. That is why space is silent sound cannot spread there. Only light can cross empty space.
Wave speed is different from the speed a particle moves. The wave itself passes by quickly, but each particle only wobbles up and down in one spot. Do not confuse the two they are different.
When two waves of the same type meet, they can add together or cancel each other depending on how their crests and troughs line up, but after crossing they continue on unchanged.
A tsunami has a very long wavelength and travels extremely fast in the deep ocean, but it slows down and suddenly grows tall when it reaches shallow water near the coast.
Wavelength in the tank is the distance from one crest to the next, which you can measure with a ruler on the white screen or tray.
In front of a moving sound source the wavelength is shorter, so the frequency is higher for a listener standing there.
A practical difference is how you measure wavelength in a photo: peak to peak on water, or crowded-band to crowded-band on a slinky.
If you leave a small gap in a barrier, the waves that pass through spread into the quiet water beyond, a bending called diffraction.
As waves tumble the grains together, they rub each other smooth and round.
Many of the elements in our bodies, like carbon and oxygen, were first made inside stars long ago — so it is said that we are made of stardust.
The air you breathe out carries water vapor. That is why breathing on a cold mirror makes a thin film of fog on it.
When you breathe in, your body takes oxygen from the air, and when you breathe out, it releases carbon dioxide that it no longer needs.
We do not use all the oxygen we breathe in, so the air we breathe out still has some oxygen.
We do not use up all the oxygen we breathe in; exhaled air still contains oxygen, which is why rescue breathing can work.

Why do you see yourself in a mirror but not on paper? On a smooth mirror, light bounces all together so a clear image forms. On rough paper, light scatters in many directions, so no clear image forms.
Household acids like vinegar are weak and safe, but strong acids like the one in batteries are dangerous.
Wearing slippers or shoes helps avoid hookworm that enters through the feet.
An air mass is a large body of air with similar temperature and humidity throughout; the type of air mass that arrives in the Philippines determines the weather.
Air quality in Metro Manila and other Philippine cities is affected by vehicle numbers, industry, and wind movement; the habagat wind can disperse pollution but can also carry dust and smoke.
Weather balloons, like those from PAGASA, rise into the stratosphere to measure temperature and air high above.
Not just the current pressure but its trend matters: a rising barometer indicates improving weather; a falling barometer indicates worsening weather.
Beaufort 12 or hurricane-force wind has speeds over 117 km/h; waves become extremely large and the sea fills with spray and whitewater making visibility very difficult.

The International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the Philippines develops rice varieties that withstand drought and flooding; these new varieties sustain food security in the face of climate change.
The Philippines' warm humid climate provides ideal conditions for one of the world's richest biodiversities; the country is classified as one of the world's 'mega-biodiversity' nations.
On tall Philippine mountains like Mt. Apo and Mt. Pulag, climate changes with altitude: hot at the base, cooler in the middle, and very cold at the summit with grassland and mossy forest.
Cloud droplets are extremely small (about 0.01 mm) and so light they float in the air; a single raindrop is thousands of times larger than a cloud droplet.
The Philippine government has conducted cloud seeding during strong El Nino events to try to induce rain in water-scarce areas that supply Metro Manila.
Cloud seeding is only effective when there are already clouds with sufficient moisture; it cannot create rain from a clear cloudless sky.
Dew consists of water droplets that form on leaves and grass on cool mornings; it collected overnight when leaves cooled and water vapour condensed on their surfaces.
Dew that collects on crop leaves during cool nights provides small amounts of water to plants; during the dry season, dew can be a supplementary water source.
Lakes, rivers, and rice paddies release large amounts of water vapour into the atmosphere through evaporation; the sun's heat drives this evaporation.
Baguio City holds one of the Philippines' highest rainfall records; in 1911, 1,168 mm of rain fell in 24 hours, one of the highest 24-hour totals in world history.
A weather forecast is a prediction of what the weather will be — whether it will rain, be hot, or be windy — so we can prepare ahead of time.
Meteorologists use data from satellites, radar, weather stations, and powerful computers to make weather forecasts; computer models process millions of data points.
About 90% of the extra heat from climate change is absorbed by the oceans; this slows atmospheric warming but also warms the seas and causes coral bleaching.
PAGASA's Doppler radar shows wind speed and direction inside storms and maps rainfall intensity; this is essential for early typhoon warnings.
A radiosonde is a small instrument attached to a weather balloon; it measures temperature, pressure, humidity, and wind at high altitudes and transmits data to weather stations.
A tipping-bucket rain gauge is an automated instrument that records rainfall continuously; when a small bucket fills with a set amount of rain, it tips and sends a signal to a computer.

The Philippines has different government agencies monitoring natural hazards: PAGASA for weather and typhoons, PHIVOLCS for earthquakes and volcanoes, MGB for landslides, and NDRRMC for disaster response coordination.
The Asian monsoon provides water for agriculture supporting more than half the world's population; monsoon failure can trigger a major food crisis across Asia.
Pacific Ocean currents, including the warm Kuroshio Current, influence the sea surface temperature around the Philippines and affect rainfall patterns.
Metro Manila and Palawan fall under Type I climate (clear dry and wet seasons); Bicol and Eastern Visayas are Type II (no clear dry season); Cagayan Valley is Type III or IV.
Heavy rain on steep slopes removes fertile topsoil through erosion; this is why maintaining tree and grass cover on Philippine mountains is very important.
Geostationary satellites like Japan's Himawari are positioned above a fixed point on Earth; they provide continuous images of clouds and typhoons over the Philippines and Asia every ten minutes.
Large storms are watched from space using a weather satellite.
Weather satellites watch typhoons from space, so PAGASA can warn Filipinos before a storm arrives.

How do measurements become a forecast? A weather station sends its readings to a computer. The computer compares today's numbers with past weather patterns, so it can predict what will likely happen—like whether it will rain or be sunny.

Many weather stations around the world take readings at the same time. Why? So the measurements can be compared fairly and evenly. If they read at different times, the weather picture gets muddled and a correct map is hard to make.

A weather station is a place with instruments that measure the weather all at once, like temperature, rain, and wind. From these measurements, scientists can make a forecast of what the weather will be tomorrow.

Why do we need many weather stations? Because weather differs from place to place—it could be raining in Baguio but sunny in Manila. With many stations in different places, the picture of the country's weather is more complete and accurate.
Sundogs (parhelia) are bright spots that can appear on either side of the sun; they form when sunlight refracts through horizontally aligned ice crystals in cirrus clouds.
A synoptic chart is a weather map showing isobars (lines of equal pressure), positions of low and high pressure systems, and locations of storms and fronts.
A maximum-minimum thermometer is a special thermometer that records the highest and lowest temperatures of the day; it is used alongside digital thermometers at weather stations.

A tropical cyclone passes through different stages: tropical disturbance, tropical depression, tropical storm, and typhoon; it can dissipate at any stage when ocean conditions change or it crosses land.
During emergencies like typhoons, Filipinos can call 911 for emergency assistance, or the Red Cross and NDRRMC hotline for rescue and relief operations.
Rapid intensification occurs when a typhoon suddenly strengthens by 55 km/h or more within 24 hours; this makes forecasting harder and leaves people less time to prepare.
The urban heat island effect causes higher temperatures inside cities than in surrounding rural areas; concrete and asphalt absorb heat and retain it longer than soil or vegetation.
Weather instruments measure the weather day by day, but when their readings are combined over many years they reveal a place's climate.
The old saying 'red sky at night, sailor's delight' has a scientific basis: a red sky at sunset indicates dry air coming from the west, suggesting good weather ahead.
Rocks at the surface are slowly broken down by weathering and carried away by water and wind (erosion), becoming the sediment that forms new sedimentary rock.
In some big rocks, thin outer layers slowly peel off like an onion's skin because of repeated heating and cooling. This is called exfoliation.
There are two kinds of weathering: physical, which just breaks rock without changing what it is made of, and chemical, which changes the very material of the rock.
Weathering is the slow breaking of rock into sand by water, wind, and time.
Weathering is also why old stone statues, churches, and buildings fade and wear down after many years of rain and wind.
In the Philippines, hardened lava and volcanic ash slowly weather into very fertile soil, which is why crops grow well near volcanoes.
There are two kinds of weathering: physical, which only breaks rock apart without changing its substance, and chemical, which changes the minerals inside the rock.
Weathering and erosion are different: weathering breaks rock into pieces, while erosion carries those pieces away.
To pull distant leaves closer, weaver ants link their bodies into living chains to form a bridge.
Worker weaver ants hold their larvae and use the silk the larvae make as glue to bind leaves together.
Many weaver ants pull a leaf together because it is too heavy for a single ant to bend.
The entrance to a weaverbird nest often faces downward, sometimes with a long tube, to make it hard for snakes and other predators to get in.
A weaverbird knows how to weave by instinct, but it gets better with practice, so older birds build neater nests.
Unlike the simple cup nests of many birds, a weaverbird's nest is intricately woven, making it one of the best nest builders of all.
Weaverbirds are birds that weave their nests from long strips of grass and leaves, much like a person weaving cloth.
A banig sleeping mat is woven from dried plant leaves such as pandan or tikog, so it is a natural material that comes from plants.
When you push a wedge forward, it changes that force to push outward on both sides.
Inserting the edge of a coin under a paint can lid uses the wedge principle to pry the lid off.
A sewing needle is a very thin wedge whose sharp pointed tip passes through fabric easily by concentrating the force.
A wedge is like two inclined planes joined back-to-back, which makes its edge sharp.
A wedge is like two inclined planes joined back-to-back, such as the blade of an axe.
There are 52 weeks in one year.
Alfred Wegener was the scientist who proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined and slowly drifted apart.
On a planet with stronger gravity like Jupiter, you would weigh more than you do on Earth.
Weight is the force of gravity on an object, equal to mass times the acceleration of gravity (W = mg), so it is measured in newtons like any other force.
Weight equals mass multiplied by gravity: Weight = mass × g (W = m × g), measured in newtons.
Weight is a measure of how strongly gravity pulls on an object.
Weight is the pull of gravity on an object; a bigger mass has bigger weight, but that does not by itself make it land first in free fall.
Weight equals mass multiplied by gravity: Weight = mass × gravity (W = m × g).
Gravity on the Moon is much weaker than on Earth—only about one-sixth—so astronauts feel much lighter and can jump much higher there.
Astronauts feel weightless in orbit because they and their spacecraft are constantly falling (free fall) as they circle Earth.
A pump or bucket is used to bring water up from the well to the surface.
A well sweep is a lever: a weight on one end helps lift the bucket up from a deep well.
The West Valley Fault can produce a magnitude 7.2 earthquake known as 'The Big One' in Metro Manila.
The West Valley Fault is an active fault that runs near Metro Manila, so families there should be ready for a possible strong earthquake.
Wet sand at low tide is still an earth material; adding water does not turn the sand into a living thing.
In the Philippines, rice can be harvested twice a year—the wet season crop from July to November and the dry season crop from January to May where there is irrigation.

Some people think it rains nonstop all day in the wet season — but that is not true. Even in the wet season, there are days when the sun comes out or the rain stops. Wet season just means rain is more frequent and heavier than in other times of the year.

Who tells us when the wet season has started? In the Philippines, PAGASA is the agency that watches the weather. They measure how much rain falls and whether the habagat is blowing. When the rain becomes steady, they announce in the news that the wet season has begun.
Some egrets and herons travel to the Philippines from far countries during winter.
When we protect wetlands, herons and the Philippine duck have a safe place to live.
Because wetland soil is so full of water, very little oxygen reaches down to the roots.
A wetland acts like a sponge that soaks up and stores water, which helps reduce flooding.
Wetlands act like natural sponges that soak up and hold extra water during heavy rain, so they reduce flooding in nearby areas.
The wettest place on Earth is Mawsynram, India, which gets about 11,872 mm of rain each year.
A whale has a blowhole on top of its head that works like its nose.
A whale can hold its breath and dive deep for many minutes before coming back up to breathe air.
The whale shark is a fish, NOT a whale, even though it is very big. It breathes with gills and is not a mammal, unlike a true whale.
Some whales travel thousands of kilometers each year between cold waters where they feed and warm waters where they give birth, following the same route year after year.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the world, and it is often seen in Donsol and Oslob in the Philippines.
The whale shark is the world's largest fish but eats only tiny plankton and krill by filtering enormous volumes of water through its mouth.
Whale sharks use cross-flow filtration while sieving plankton — water passes across gill rakers at an angle rather than straight through, preventing particles from clogging the filter.
Even though it is called a whale shark, the butanding is actually a fish (a shark), not a whale.
The whale shark is the world's largest fish — bigger than any biting shark — but it is a gentle animal that feeds only on plankton and small fish and poses no danger to people.
Like other fish, the whale shark breathes using its gills, unlike a whale that surfaces to breathe air.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the world, but it eats only tiny plankton by filtering water — it is not dangerous to people. It is often seen in Donsol and Oslob in the Philippines.
The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is the largest fish species in the world.
Even though it is called a whale shark, it is a shark and a fish, not a whale.
Whale sharks aggregate in Donsol, Sorsogon from November to June each year — attracted by abundant plankton and fish spawn in the area, they allow controlled tourist interaction.
The blue whale, the largest animal on Earth, makes very low sounds that people can barely hear. This is quite different from the higher melody of the humpback whale.
Scientists do not yet fully understand every 'message' in a whale's song. But they believe it can say things like 'I am here' or 'I am a good mate,' as a way of communicating.
Scientists place special underwater microphones in the sea to listen to whale songs. This helps them learn how many whales there are and where they live, without disturbing them.
A whale does not use its mouth to sing. It moves air around inside its body, near its throat, to make sounds, almost like whistling or humming.
Humpback whales sing most often while they travel to warm waters to have their babies. The singing seems to be part of finding a mate during this time.
Some people think whales sing just for fun like people do. But their songs are really a way of communicating, with a purpose, not just music for entertainment.
Noise from big ships can get in the way of whale songs. Sometimes the whales cannot hear each other well, so it is important to reduce ocean noise to help them.
A humpback's song is long and melodic, but dolphins use fast clicks to find food. They are used differently: one is mainly for communication, the other for hunting.
Whale song traveling through ocean water is a longitudinal wave example, because sound in water is still a back-and-forth compression wave.
Sound travels farther in water than in air, so whales can hear each other even far apart.
Although they live in the sea, whales came from ancestor mammals that once walked on land; scientists saw this in fossils that show a gradual change from four legs to flippers.
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish scientist (from Scotland).
A landform is a natural shape on Earth's surface, such as a mountain, hill, plain, or valley.
A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers.
Leeuwenhoek called the microbes he saw "animalcules," meaning "little animals."
The wheel was first made in ancient Mesopotamia.
Inside many wheels, there are tiny steel balls called ball bearings between the wheel and the axle. They roll instead of rub, so the wheel spins more smoothly and for longer.
On a cart, an axle bar joins the two wheels on opposite sides. Because of this, both wheels turn together and the load is carried more steadily. They don't move separately from each other.
Inside a clock, the hands are attached to different axles that turn around the same center. Wheels and axles spin the hands at different speeds—so the second hand is fast and the hour hand is slow.
A doorknob is a wheel and axle: the wide knob is the wheel and the thin shaft inside is the axle that opens the latch.
When you turn the large wheel, the small axle turns with greater force, so it helps lift or move heavy things.
Gears are toothed wheels mounted on axles that lock together to pass on the turning, like in a bicycle.
Before the wheel was invented, people used rolling logs to move heavy objects.
A wheel and axle does not reduce the total work, but it makes work easier by changing the size or direction of the force.
Oil or grease is put on an axle to reduce friction, so the wheel turns more smoothly and quietly.
A wheel and axle speeds movement and reduces friction, so heavy things are easier to move.
The wide handle of a screwdriver acts like a wheel and the thin tip acts like an axle, making it easier to turn a screw.
A large steering wheel gives mechanical advantage: a small force on the wide rim becomes a large turning force on the narrow axle.
A wheelbarrow is a compound machine that combines a lever and a wheel and axle.
A wheelbarrow is a second-class lever — the load is in the middle, between the wheel (fulcrum) and your hands.
Use a normal or quiet voice near someone's ear instead of shouting, because a shout right beside the head is a harmful sound you can choose not to make.
A whistle can carry a message farther than a speaking voice, so a teacher may use one long blast to mean 'line up' on a noisy field.
White blood cells are the body's soldiers that hunt down and kill germs.
The white light from the sun is actually made of many colors mixed together.
White objects reflect more light, while black objects absorb light and so get warmer.
The word "dinosaur" was coined by the English scientist Richard Owen.
James Christy discovered Charon, the largest moon of Pluto.
Galileo Galilei discovered the four large moons of Jupiter.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic that kills bacteria.
Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto.
Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan, the largest moon of Saturn.
William Herschel discovered the planet Uranus.
Robert Hooke was the first to use the word "cell" in 1665, based on the tiny boxlike spaces he saw in cork.
Whooping cough (pertussis) is a dangerous respiratory disease caused by Bordetella pertussis bacteria, especially dangerous for infants; the DTP vaccine protects against it.
Animals clean themselves, like a cat licking its fur. This removes dirt and tiny pests that could carry disease, so they stay clean and healthy.
Some animals sleep in the day and stay awake at night, like bats and owls. Night is cooler and quieter, so they can find food more easily and avoid the daytime heat.
Some animals like snakes and insects shed their skin or outer shell. As they grow, the old covering gets too tight, so they must shed it to make room for a bigger, new one.
A ball bounces because when it hits the ground it squashes, storing energy. Then it springs back to its shape and pushes itself up off the ground.
Sea water is warmer near the equator and colder toward the poles, so different fish and sea life live in each belt — warm-water corals in the tropics, cold-water animals near the poles.
Bread is stretchy and chewy because of gluten — a protein in flour that forms a stretchy network when kneaded, and it traps the yeast's gas so the dough can rise.
Bread goes hard and stale not only because it dries out but because the starch inside changes shape and loses its softness, even inside a bag.
A bruise changes color as it heals — it starts red or purple, then turns blue, green, and yellow, because the body slowly breaks down and cleans up the trapped blood under the skin.
There are bacteria in our mouth that feed on sweet bits left on the teeth and make an acid that damages them. Brushing teeth every day removes them so teeth don't get cavities or decay.
We cannot see ultraviolet and infrared because our eyes are only sensitive to a narrow range of light.
Your recorded voice sounds odd because in real life you hear yourself partly through the bones of your skull, not only through the air the way others hear you.
A chemical change is hard to reverse because the new substance has different properties from the original.
When you boil water and it gets lower, the mass is not lost — it became steam that moved into the air.
There is fluid inside our ears that helps with balance; when we spin fast, that fluid keeps moving even after we stop — so it feels like the room is still spinning and we get dizzy.
When a species goes extinct, it is permanent and cannot be brought back. Other animals and plants can also be affected because they are connected in the ecosystem.
A feather falls slower than a stone because air resistance pushes harder on its light, wide shape. Without air, like on the moon, they would fall together because gravity pulls on both the same.
When we stay in water a long time, the skin on our fingers wrinkles — scientists think this is controlled by the nervous system and may help us grip wet things more firmly.
After a long time in water, your fingertips wrinkle — your nervous system actually does this to help you grip wet things better, not because the skin soaks up water.
You float more easily in the sea than in a swimming pool because salt water is denser than fresh water. Because of that, the sea pushes up on your body more strongly.
Hair turns gray or white with age because its cells stop making melanin — the pigment that gives it color — so the new hair grows in without color.
Honey almost never spoils because it has so much sugar and so little water that bacteria cannot survive inside it.
Metal feels colder than wood even at the same temperature, because it quickly pulls heat away from your hand — it is not actually colder, it just carries heat away fast.
Constellations were not only pretty pictures; they were tools for asking 'which way is north' and 'is it the planting season yet'.
By letting others raise its eggs, a brood parasite saves energy and can lay many eggs.
The Philippines has no four seasons because it lies near the equator, where the Sun's rays are nearly direct all year — so it stays warm and we have no winter.
Wet things dry faster in the sun than in the shade because the sun adds extra heat — and water particles escape as vapor more quickly when it is warmer.

A pure substance has the same properties no matter which sample you take — every part has the same taste, color, and density. In a mixture the parts can differ, so a sample from one spot may not match a sample from another.
Solar, wind, and hydro do not warm the planet because they burn nothing, so no carbon dioxide is released — unlike coal and oil, which give off this gas when burned.

When a rubber ball hits the floor, it squishes and stores energy as it is pressed. Then it quickly springs back to shape and gives that energy back as a bounce upward. That is why a rubber ball bounces while a clay ball does not.
Electricity does not pass easily through rubber—this makes it an insulator. Because of this, rubber wraps electrical wires and is used in electricians' gloves to keep them from getting shocked.

It is a misconception that rubber melts quickly like ice or plastic when hot. In truth, most vulcanized rubber does not melt—instead, with too much heat it burns or breaks down. Heat only softens it, it does not turn it into liquid.
Old rubber gets cracks and turns stiff. Oxygen in the air and sunlight slowly break down the molecule links over time. That is why an old rubber band snaps much more easily than a fresh one.

The rubber slippers worn by many Filipinos are a great example. Rubber is soft so it cushions the foot, and it grips wet floors so you do not slip. That is why rubber is chosen instead of a hard material.
Rubber stretches and snaps back because its long, coiled molecules uncoil when you pull them and recoil when you let go. That is why a rubber band springs back.

Not all rubber comes from a tree. Most rubber today is synthetic, made in factories from petroleum (oil). It is made this way because it can be produced in large amounts and is tougher for some uses than natural tree rubber.

Both rubber and a metal spring snap back to shape when released—both are elastic. But a spring bounces back because of its coiled shape, while rubber bounces back because of the molecule chains inside it.

Plain rubber gets sticky when hot and brittle when cold. When it is heated together with sulfur, links form between the chains. This process, called vulcanization, makes the tough, springy rubber used in tires.
Jams and salted foods keep for a long time because very high salt or sugar draws water out of bacteria, so they cannot multiply.
A satellite does not fall to Earth because it moves so fast sideways that, as gravity pulls it down, it keeps missing the curve of the Earth—so it circles around instead of crashing.
When a wound is healing, it often itches because the skin is building new cells and the nerves under the scab get stirred — but it is better not to scratch it so it does not reopen.
Even though each ice crystal is clear, snow looks white because the many crystals scatter and bounce back all the colors of light to our eyes.
Sourdough bread is sour because the dough holds not just yeast but also helpful bacteria that make acid as the flour ferments.
Soy sauce is made by fermenting soybeans for a long time with mold and bacteria, which give it its dark color and savory flavor.
Two ears let the brain compare when a sound reaches each side. That is how we can tell which direction a sound came from.
Venus is the hottest planet — even hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the sun — because its thick carbon-dioxide air traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect.
Vinegar is sour because it contains acetic acid, which bacteria make when they change alcohol — that is why vinegar comes from a fermented juice.
We blink several times a minute without thinking about it, to spread tears and protect the eye from drying out.
Coughing and sneezing are reflexes that suddenly blast out air to clear germs, dust, or mucus from the nose and throat. That is why you should cover your mouth so illness doesn't spread.
We eat because food gives us the energy to move, think, and grow — it is like fuel for our body.
We feel hungry because when the stomach is empty, it releases a chemical that tells the brain it is time to eat — so the tummy rumbles and we start thinking about food.
Vitamins are nutrients the body needs in tiny amounts to stay healthy — vitamin C from fruit, vitamin D from sunlight, and vitamin A for clear eyesight.
We pass gas because as the helpful bacteria in our intestines break down some foods, they make gas; when that gas builds up, the body lets it out — it is normal and healthy.
We shiver when it is cold because our muscles quickly tighten and relax over and over; this rapid movement makes heat that warms the body.
We sneeze to push dust, pollen, or other irritants out of our nose.
In a motorcycle crash, the head and brain keep moving forward because of inertia, so a helmet helps reduce injury.
When we yawn, our cheeks and face gently squeeze the tiny glands that make tears, so sometimes our eyes water or a tear rolls out.
Milk turns into yogurt because helpful bacteria eat the sugar in milk and make an acid, which makes the milk sour and thick.
A wider gap lets waves go through with less spreading than a tiny gap, a change of pattern you can test with two barrier openings.
The 'width' of a wave in the tank is the spacing of the moving bands, which is the wavelength you were asked to observe.
Wi-Fi, radio, and phones all use the same kind of invisible waves (radio waves), but they do not get mixed up because each one is tuned to its own frequency, like different stations on a radio.
A Wi-Fi signal is a transverse electromagnetic wave example, even though we notice it only when a phone or laptop receives it.
The wild banana of the forest is full of small, hard seeds, so it is hard to eat — unlike the market banana that has almost no seeds.
Alugbati is a climbing vine that crawls up fences or trees. Some kinds have red or purple stems. Its soft leaves and shoots are cooked as a vegetable.
Besides pako, Filipinos gather and eat many other wild greens such as edible shoots and leaves.

When you cook saluyot, the broth becomes slimy and slippery. This is because of a natural gel (mucilage) inside the leaves — the same substance that makes okra thick. It is not dirt; it is really part of the plant.

Wild greens wilt quickly after being picked because they lose water. So it is best to cook them right away while still fresh, or stand the stems in water to last longer. They are not like vegetables that can sit in the fridge for many days.
Wild yeasts naturally live in the air and on the skins of fruit like grapes, so their juice can sour and ferment on its own.
In wildlife rescue, injured or captured animals are first nursed back to health and then released into their natural habitat to live freely again.
In wind instruments like the flute, it is the column of air inside the tube that vibrates to make sound.
The cup anemometer was invented by John Thomas Romney Robinson in 1846; before this, scientists had tried to measure wind using various methods since as early as 1450.
Wind-driven waves gradually erode sand and rock from Philippine shorelines; coastal erosion is worsening because of climate change and stronger typhoons.
The wind does work when it pushes a boat's sail and makes it move.
Wind is the main force that drives surface ocean currents like the Kuroshio Current.
Wind blowing across the sea surface is the main force that pushes the currents near the top of the water.
Unlike coal or oil, a wind turbine does not need to burn anything to make electricity.
Wind energy is energy from moving air. The wind spins the large blades of a wind turbine, and that spinning is turned into electricity.
A wind turbine has large blades that the wind spins; that spinning drives a generator to make electricity—like the turbines at Bangui, Ilocos Norte.
Wind blows sand and piles it up in one place to form hills called sand dunes, like the ones in Paoay, Ilocos Norte.

In some deserts, the ground looks like a floor of tightly packed pebbles. This happens when wind has blown away all the sand and dust, leaving only the heavier stones lying side by side like pavement. It is called desert pavement.

A famous example of severe wind erosion is the "Dust Bowl" in the United States long ago. Farmers plowed up huge areas of land, then a long drought came. With nothing holding the dry soil, the wind blew it away in giant clouds of dust.

People can speed up wind erosion. When trees are cut down, animals overgraze, or land is left bare and dry, nothing holds the soil, so wind carries it off more easily. This is one cause of land becoming damaged.

Why is wind erosion faster on dry soil than wet? When soil is wet, the water acts like glue holding the particles together, so wind cannot lift them easily. But once it dries, the particles separate and are easy to carry off. That is why wind erosion is stronger when there is no rain.
As sand grains hop along in the wind, they strike rocks over and over. Like sandpaper, they slowly scrape the rock until it is carved or smoothed. This is why some desert rocks have strange shapes.

A rock smoothed by wind and sand is called a ventifact. When wind keeps hitting it from one direction, that side of the rock becomes smooth with a flat face. It is a clue of wind erosion that scientists can see.

Why does dust disappear first, not the big rocks? Because dust is lighter and smaller, the wind can lift it easily. Big rocks are too heavy, so they are left behind. That is why what remains after wind erosion is mostly heavy stones.
In Bangui, Ilocos Norte, there is a famous row of large wind turbines by the sea that make electricity from the wind. It is one of the first big wind farms in the Philippines.
Many turbines built together form a wind farm, and together they make a large amount of electricity.
Wind is moving air, and much of that motion starts because the Sun heats some places more than others, an idea a weather book can confirm.
Global atmospheric circulation is shaped by three main cells: the Hadley cell (near the equator), the Ferrel cell (middle latitudes), and the polar cell (polar regions).
Wind blows from places of high air pressure toward places of low air pressure; the bigger the pressure difference, the stronger the wind.
Wind can carry sound toward you or away, but that is moving the air; Doppler from a horn is the source itself moving through the air.
Wind power is a renewable energy source because it does not run out as long as the wind keeps blowing.
Wind turbines make electricity without giving off smoke or polluting gases.
One challenge of solar and wind energy is that they are not always available — there is no sun at night and the wind is sometimes still. So batteries are needed to store extra energy for other times.
Wind strength can be described using the Beaufort scale, which runs from 0 to 12.

Tornadoes and typhoons are both powerful storms but differ: a tornado is smaller (a few hundred metres), shorter-lived (minutes), and has faster winds; a typhoon is much larger (hundreds of kilometres) and lasts days.
A turbine's tower is tall because the wind is stronger and steadier higher up.
Trade winds are steady winds that blow from 30° north and south toward the equator; they were historically used by sailing ships to cross the ocean.
Inside a wind turbine, the spinning blades are connected to a generator that makes electricity. The stronger the wind, the faster the blades spin and the more electricity is made.
At the Bangui Wind Farm in Ilocos Norte, wind spins large blades connected to a generator to make electricity.
A wind turbine uses the power of the wind to spin its large blades and make electricity, like in Bangui, Ilocos Norte.
Wind direction is important information for weather forecasting; wind from the southwest (habagat) brings rain while wind from the northeast (amihan) brings dry weather.
Moving a game indoors for the brightest hours is a safety measure, because walls and roofs block much of the Sun's direct light.
Air is real matter made of molecules, so it can push on and hold up a heavy plane.
Tilting the front of the wing slightly upward (the angle of attack) deflects more air downward and increases lift, up to a limit.
Drag is the force of air resistance that opposes the plane's motion and slows it down.
If you tilt your hand out of a moving car window, the air pushes it upward — this is the same way lift works on a wing.
A larger wing area produces more lift, which is why heavy or slow planes have wide wings.
You can see lift in a paper airplane: its wings hold it up in the air as it flies forward.
If the wing's angle gets too steep, the air no longer flows smoothly over it and lift suddenly drops, which is called a stall.

An adult usually has 4 wisdom teeth.
The very last teeth to come in are the wisdom teeth, which appear in the late teens or early adulthood — they got that name because they arrive at an age when a person is supposedly wiser.
Wisdom teeth are extra back molars that many people no longer need today.
Without the Sun's heat, Earth would be far too cold for liquid oceans and for the living things that need liquid water.
Wolves howl to communicate with their pack — to call the others or tell them where they are. A howl can be heard from very far away.
When wolves were brought back to Yellowstone, the number of deer dropped, the trees grew back, and other animals and birds returned too.
Ash is lighter than the unburned wood because much of the mass left as smoke and gas — it is not lost, it just moved into the air.
Wood is mainly composed of cellulose and lignin; cellulose gives strength to the tree's cell walls, while lignin binds those cells together into a rigid structure.
Wood floats on water because it is lighter than the same amount of water.
Smoke from burning wood can harm the lungs, so cooking areas need good ventilation.
Woodpeckers do not peck only for food; they also drum quickly on wood to send signals to other birds.
Woodpeckers also drill holes in trees to make nests for themselves and their chicks.
A woodpecker pecks in a straight line without twisting, which reduces harmful force on its head.
Work equals force multiplied by distance: Work = Force × Distance (W = F × d).
In science, 'work' has a specific meaning: work equals force multiplied by distance moved in the direction of the force, measured in joules.
In physics, work is done only when a force moves an object through a distance.
The amount of work equals the force used multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force, so the work is greater when the force is stronger or the distance is longer.
When you carry an object while walking on level ground, you do no work on it because the upward force holding it is perpendicular to your direction of motion.
Worker ants dig and build the nest. They make tunnels in the soil or inside wood so the whole colony has a safe home.
Even though worker ants are female, they usually cannot lay eggs. Only the queen lays eggs in the colony. The workers' job is to help and care for others, not to have babies.
In the farms of the Philippines, worker ants help the soil. As they dig their tunnels, air mixes into the soil, so the farmer's plants can grow more easily.
A worker ant lives a shorter life than the queen. Many workers live only a few months, while the queen can live for several years because all new ants come from her.

A wormhole (or Einstein-Rosen bridge) is a hypothetical spacetime structure connecting two distant points in space; it is predicted by general relativity but has never been observed or confirmed, and scientists do not know if one could be stable enough to travel through.
When you get a wound, your blood clots to stop the bleeding.
People do not all heal at the same speed. In people with diabetes or in older people, wounds heal more slowly because blood flow is weaker, so they must take extra care of a wound.
In the Philippines, boiled guava leaves have long been used as a wash for wounds. Studies show they contain compounds that help slow germs, which helps keep a wound clean.
A fresh wound often turns red, feels warm, and swells a little. This is the inflammation stage — the body rushes blood and white blood cells to the wound to fight germs and begin healing.
Humans can heal wounds and grow new skin, but cannot regrow a whole lost part like a finger. Some animals, like lizards, can regrow a tail that breaks off.
Deep, dirty wounds, like stepping on a rusty nail, can let in bacteria that cause tetanus. In the Philippines, an anti-tetanus vaccine is important for this kind of wound.
Healthy food like vegetables and fruit helps the body heal wounds faster.
To close the wound, new skin cells multiply until they cover the gap.
While the scab sits on top, new skin grows underneath it.
A scab is dried blood that forms a cover to protect the wound.
When a wound is deep, it can leave a scar because the new tissue that fills it is not exactly like the original skin.
A small wound heals faster than a large, deep one.

X-rays are an invisible light that passes through flesh, so doctors can see our bones.
X-rays are another transverse electromagnetic example; they travel as changing electric and magnetic fields, not as air compressions.
X-rays were discovered by the German physicist Wilhelm Roentgen.
Roentgen called the rays "X" because their nature was unknown to him at the time.
They were called X-rays because at first Roentgen did not know what the rays were, so he used the letter 'X' to mean unknown.
Doctors use an x-ray to see where and how a bone is broken.
X-rays pass through skin and flesh to take pictures of the bones inside the body.
X-rays were discovered in the year 1895.
X-rays were discovered in 1895 by Wilhelm Roentgen.

Xylem is a type of tissue in plants that carries water and minerals from the roots upward to the leaves.
Yakan weaving from Basilan makes brightly colored cloth by interlacing threads back and forth on a loom.
When the ears feel blocked on a plane or mountain, yawning, swallowing, or chewing opens the Eustachian tube to equalize the pressure and clear them.
Yeast is a single-celled fungus that reproduces by budding, where a small new cell grows out from the side of the parent.
The yeast used to make bread is a fungus made of just a single cell.
When there is air (oxygen), yeast multiplies fast but makes little gas. When there is no air, it makes much more carbon-dioxide gas — which is why dough is covered while it rises.
In a cold place like the fridge, the yeast does not die but it slows down a lot and barely rises. That is why dough is left in a warm spot so it rises quickly.
Yeast is a living thing — a tiny kind of fungus (like mushrooms) made of just one cell. Because it is alive, it needs to eat and grow, unlike a powder.
If dough is left too long, the yeast uses up its food and makes too much gas, so the dough can collapse or fall. That is why rising has a right amount of time — not too much.
A little salt is fine, but too much salt slows or kills yeast because it pulls water out of the yeast's cell. That is why bread recipes use only the right amount of salt.
In the Philippines, natural yeast is also used to make traditional drinks like tuba from coconut sap. The yeast eats the sugar in the sap and turns it into a fermented drink.
Dough needs time to rise, so a baker lets it rest for an hour or more until it nearly doubles in size before baking.
Scientists use yeast to convert sugars from maize or sugarcane into ethanol biofuel, a renewable alternative to gasoline for vehicles.
Yeast belongs to the group of fungi, together with mushrooms and mold, so it is neither a plant nor an animal but its own kind of living thing.
Yellow fever is spread by Aedes mosquitoes and is common in Africa and South America, but it is not found in the Philippines.
The yeti crab has hairy arms, and on those hairs it grows bacteria that it then eats.
Yogurt is made using two types of bacteria working together: Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus; they work symbiotically to produce the flavor and texture of yogurt.
The milk must be kept warm so the bacteria can multiply quickly and turn it into yogurt within a few hours.
Earth materials do not eat, grow, or have babies the way living things do, which is a simple test for a stone versus a seedling.

Zero (0) is a number that means "nothing" or no amount, and it is important for writing large numbers.

Zinc is a mineral essential for body growth, immune function, and wound healing; it is found in animal foods such as oysters, meat, and fish.
